items.title: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
items.summary: Alan Milburn's review will call for sweeping reforms to the education, work and welfare systems.

scraped.title: 'Complete reset' needed to get young people into work, says Milburn review
scraped.description: Alan Milburn's review will call for sweeping reforms to the education, work and welfare systems.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
scraped.body_text:
Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn.

Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade.

His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults.

But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state".

Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis.

The review says that, in 2024/25, for every £1 spent helping young people into work or education, £25 was spent on youth benefits.

By 2036, it says the aim should be for that ratio to be £2 on benefits for every £1 on work support.

In order to make change of this scale over the next decade, the review will call for:

A new target of 90% of children to be school-ready with basic life skills by five years old (this figure is now 68% in England, with a current government target of reaching 75% by 2028)

More emphasis on work skills in the school curriculum

Instant access to mental health support without diagnosis

A doubling of the number of young apprentices

Incentives for employers, such as lowering the National Insurance rate for young workers

At the heart of the changes recommended by Milburn would be a legal entitlement to support, provided through a new "Youth Opportunity Service" in England.

The service would put a young person in touch with a named adviser to help to secure them an apprenticeship, college place, supported employment or a job within four months.

To pay for these reforms, young adults would no longer be eligible for the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work, or Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which helps with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability.

The review's key welfare measures, some of which have already been announced , suggest replacing these benefits for under-25s with a new Youth Allowance at the current base rate of Universal Credit for young people, and a new Additional Cost Allowance to replace Pip.

The minority of young people who are unable to ever work would be supported through a new Severe and Complex Needs Insurance.

Kat, 21, from Devon, currently gets Universal Credit with the health top-up, so is potentially at risk of receiving a much lower level of benefits under the proposed new system.

She has fluctuating physical and mental health problems, including occasional seizures caused by functional neurological disorder, which recently left her needing crutches.

Kat says her health issues limit her ability to find work

Kat says she "really wants to work", but says she has to rely on welfare support as she has been unable to find a job where she can be employed in a "safe way" because of her health.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, says many young people are desperate for opportunity, but that many get knocked back repeatedly.

Josh, 19, has spent three years looking for work while on Universal Credit with the support of youth employment charity Spear.

Although they help him with applications to prospective employers, Josh says "none of them are getting back, and if they do they say you've not got the spot".

Grace Coates, who manages Spear St Helens, says she wants to see "more openness to employing people with limited experience".

Josh has been looking for work for three years

Milburn's review will suggest gradually lowering the rate of National Insurance which employers pay for young adult employees to make hiring and keeping them more attractive.

The existing Youth Jobs Grant, where employers receive £3,000 for hiring a young person who has been looking for work for six months, would be retained under the recommendations.

So would the existing Jobs Guarantee, in which the government underwrites the cost of a paid six-month job.

The government has recently announced that young adults will be eligible for the guarantee after 12 months of being on Universal Credit and looking for work, rather than the current 18 months.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said reforms will have a greater chance of success if support for young people is balanced with incentives for businesses to hire them.

It said that while cutting benefit entitlements would reduce the cash young people receive immediately, it might take longer for an increase in employment to make up for that for some young adults.

Responding to the Milburn review proposals, the Conservatives' Whately said: "Where Milburn gets it right, we'll back him," but added that the review "fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won't make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now".

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said cutting national insurance for young workers would "only partly undo the damage of Labour's job tax".

She said her party's plans would "shut off the Neets pipeline at source, with 100 hours of real work experience before 18 and a careers coach for every young person".

Reform UK's shadow education secretary Suella Braverman said the 10-year wait to see changes from Milburn's proposals "would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap".

"Reform UK would act now to axe Labour's jobs tax, double the number of apprenticeships and end university scam courses that laden students with debt," she said.

For the Greens, deputy leader Mothin Ali said Milburn's proposals announced so far were "extremely concerning", adding: "There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work."

items.title: Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond
items.summary: The 40-year old is best known for his role in films including Twilight, The Batman and The Odyssey.

scraped.title: James Bond: Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as 007
scraped.description: The 40-year old is best known for his role in films including Twilight, The Batman and The Odyssey.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Watch: As new Bond, Pattinson takes on one of film's most high-profile roles

Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.

The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply grateful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.

This video can not be played

'Big shoes to fill': Robert Pattinson asked about playing Bond in 2010

Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke.

Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain Scytale. The film is released next month.

In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.

"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

Robert Pattinson has starred in Twilight, Tenet, The Batman and The Odyssey

Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said the "legacy of James Bond is in great hands with Robert Pattinson".

"His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times."

At 40, Pattinson is one of the older actors who was thought to have auditioned for the role of Bond.

Reports last week suggested Pattinson's deal committed him to playing 007 for three films, , external rather than the four that had reportedly been discussed with some of the other actors, but that has not been officially confirmed.

Pattinson shot to fame in Harry Potter and went on to star in Twilight opposite Kristen Stewart (pictured in 2011)

Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire,

He went on to play vampire Edward Cullen in Twilight, the hugely popular film series based on Stephenie Meyer's best-selling novels.

Pattinson starred opposite Kristen Stewart in five Twilight films in total, which collectively made more than $3bn (£2.2bn) at the box office worldwide.

He has gone on to star in other major films such as 2022's The Batman and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, released earlier this year.

But he is also respected within the industry for how many roles he has taken in smaller movies - often independent, experimental or arthouse films.

His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, The Rover, Bel Ami, Primetime, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.

Pattinson follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond in the official film series – Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.

Daniel Craig was a popular 007 and appeared in five James Bond films

Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.

In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".

The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.

Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.

Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.

The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

items.title: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
items.summary: The gender care review author says the bill’s wording risks "serious unintended consequences" for parents and therapists.

scraped.title: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
scraped.description: The gender care review author says the bill’s wording risks "serious unintended consequences" for parents and therapists.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
scraped.body_text:
Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"

The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices -having previously welcomed it.

Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.

She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.

A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".

Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.

This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.

There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.

When the government introduced its draft legislation , external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it , external .

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".

She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.

But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".

Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."

But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.

"If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering.

"But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.

She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.

Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.

When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.

She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."

The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.

"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.

"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."

The committee hearings continue.

scraped.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
scraped.description: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/jennifer-rankin
scraped.h1: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
scraped.body_text:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania , it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe .

Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government , which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union , with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

scraped.description: An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.
scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/guardian-sport
scraped.h1: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
scraped.body_text:
Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree

Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria

An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.

Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison .

scraped.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
scraped.description: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human
scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/rachel-savage
scraped.h1: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
scraped.body_text:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.

During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick , a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement . “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”

It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

scraped.title: California sues OpenAI over hacking risks

scraped.h1: California sues OpenAI over hacking risks
scraped.body_text:
By

Huo Jingnan

California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday Nov. 16, 2026. In the complaint, California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. California Department of Justice/Screenshot by NPR hide caption

California sued OpenAI Monday, alleging that the frontier AI company failed to protect the public from its systems' advanced cyber capabilities. The lawsuit stems from OpenAI's agents' attack on open-source software platform Hugging Face over the summer but also touches on a wide range of other related incidents tied to the company's agents acting without authorization.

"Just because the technology is new or rapidly evolving doesn't mean the people behind it are above the law," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards." The lawsuit cited potential concerns about cyberattacks "on power grids, emergency infrastructure, hospital systems, and financial institutions."

In the complaint , California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. The state said the company admitted to the attorney general's office that "it lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing."

That number is higher than what OpenAI has so far disclosed publicly and more than what outside researchers have independently discovered, but OpenAI has otherwise provided little information, California said. The state also accused OpenAI of poor security practices, stonewalling the state's investigation into the company and discouraging employees from speaking up about safety.

In a statement to NPR, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab" and that the company has "engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."

After the most notorious of cyber incidents involving OpenAI's agents – the attack on Hugging Face over the summer – the company admitted that it did not monitor its agents in ways its own researchers deemed important. Since then, outside researchers as well as OpenAI itself have found more incidents in which AI agents have interacted with websites and communicated with each other on the internet in ways that OpenAI did not intend. The lawsuit mentions these events as well as other incidents that OpenAI started disclosing voluntarily to the public.

Other AI companies have also had to wrestle with their systems behaving in unexpected and undesirable ways. Anthropic and Meta have both said they found that their AI systems have hacked into places they shouldn't have. Major AI companies have since signed onto an agreement organized by the White House to develop AI responsibly, but the agreement is nonbinding.

Drawing from reports including from OpenAI's own disclosures, California alleges that the top AI company has engaged in unfair competition and created a public nuisance. It asked the court to stop the company from further engaging in such activities and order it to pay monetary damages.

scraped.title: U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout
scraped.description: The new rule closes a loophole that existed that allowed Chinese companies to still access advanced AI chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
scraped.h1: U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout
scraped.body_text:
By

Katie McQue

Data center company Megaspeed International's office in Singapore on Nov. 10, 2026. The company is suspected of selling remote access to U.S. AI chips to Chinese companies. A new Commerce Department rule would restrict that access. Taryn Ng/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.

The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.

Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.

The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.

The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security

However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.

"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.

The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.

Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.

Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.

"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.

Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.

The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."

Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.

The New York Times reported that Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.

"We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.

scraped.description: Countries are meeting in Geneva to negotiate rules on weapons that can select and kill targets without human intervention. But with the U.S., Russia and Israel resisting legally binding controls, campaigners fear the window to act is closing.
scraped.h1: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
scraped.body_text:
By

Imogen Foulkes

An armed robot developed by Turkish defense companies is demonstrated at a facility in Duzce, Turkey, on April 29. Omer Urer/Anadolu via Getty Images hide caption

GENEVA — Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as 'killer robots' are underway at the United Nations in Geneva.

Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late.

Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously.

In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, with Ukrainian civilians reporting being 'hunted' by drones as they shop or go to school. But these are still controlled remotely by humans.

Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill – and responsibility for that choice – must stay in human hands. Ahead of this week's meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be 'crossing a moral red line'.

The Red Cross is especially worried that existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons. War is often chaotic and confusing, and the situation can change rapidly. Under the Conventions, soldiers who are wounded or in the process of surrendering can no longer be targeted.

Georgia Haines, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, worries that autonomous weapons will not be able to distinguish between a soldier who is still fighting, one who is wounded and one who wants to surrender.

'The risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, they are not able to understand in the same way that a human is the contextual signals. And so the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target.'

Meanwhile, human rights groups warn that the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use. The more it is adopted by the military, the greater the danger of proliferation and its use by terrorist groups or law enforcement agencies in repressive regimes. In theory , a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or even everyone speaking a certain language.

Many of the countries now meeting in Geneva take such concerns very seriously. At least 50, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree on binding rules governing autonomous weapons.

But among states that are already developing and using semi-autonomous weapons, there is pushback. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules, with Washington proposing a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead.

The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties. It did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines, for example, although it did, over time, stop deploying them and reduce its stockpiles.

Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown. Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, and just this weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society, warned against "quoting laws to men with swords."

The problem for states meeting in Geneva is that U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus. This was achieved in 1995, when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers, but other agreements have proved elusive. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay finally took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention.

This week, there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period to come up with rules that individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding. For diplomats supporting such a solution, it is a way to ensure at least some progress. For campaigners, it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road.

scraped.title: Boston Globe compares Dianna Russini to Bob Woodward amid Vrabel-sourcing scandal
scraped.description: Dianna Russini's return to media after the Mike Vrabel photo controversy draws a Bob Woodward comparison from The Boston Globe. Neither she nor Vrabel has acknowledged a relationship.
scraped.author: Bobby Burack
scraped.h1: Boston Globe compares Dianna Russini to Bob Woodward amid Vrabel-sourcing scandal
scraped.body_text:
Craig Carton holds nothing back as he reacts to former NFL insider Dianna Russini making her controversial sports media return with BetUS following her resignation from The Athletic over her scandal with New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel.

The Boston Globe argues that NFL reporter Dianna Russini might be best described as the modern-day Bob Woodward.

Last week, Russini returned to media after a seven-month hiatus following various outlets obtaining photos of her in a pool, at a bar, at a casino, and renting a private boat (while pregnant) with New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel .

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Russini resigned from The Athletic in April amid an internal investigation into her failure to disclose her relationship with a source and subject, whether romantic or not. She now hosts a weekly podcast for offshore gambling company BetUS.

DIANNA RUSSINI'S CRINGE PODCAST DEBUT RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT THE VIABILITY OF HER COMEBACK

Despite the unusual circumstances, the Globe's Joan Vennochi drew parallels between Russini and Woodward, who also got too close to a source.

Split showing Patriots coach Mike Vrabel and NFL reporter Dianna Russini. (Getty Images)

"There’s no compromising photo of Woodward in a hot tub with Richard Darman, the powerful official in two long-ago presidential administrations, as there was of Russini and New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel while she was reporting on the NFL," Vennochi wrote .

"But in a piece in The New Yorker titled 'The Danger of Getting Too Close to a Source,' which is drawn from his new book, 'Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir,' Woodward describes an intimate relationship with Darman that, figuratively speaking, put him in similar hot water.

In the article referenced, Woodward acknowledges that he "should have realized the danger" of his relationship with Darman but also that "the information flow and the time with Darman was so valuable."

Dianna Russini attends the 2026 Fanatics Super Bowl Party at Pier 48 in San Francisco, California, on Feb. 7, 2026. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)

The Globe article did, however, distinguish the two reporters in one way:

"[O]nce sex is involved, or speculated about, as it was with Russini and Vrabel (although neither has acknowledged it), such a relationship is automatically wrong for the journalist.

"But take the sex out of it — which no one ever can — and, as all journalists know, the same ethics questions arise. At what point does closeness not only cloud objectivity but also hamper the ability to tell the full truth if that truth hurts your source?," wrote Vennochi.

BOBBY BURACK: DIANNA RUSSINI WANTS SYMPATHY WITHOUT ACCOUNTABILITY IN MIKE VRABEL SCANDAL

Despite the bizarre comparison, the Globe misses the point: Woodward acknowledged the error in his judgment. Russini hasn't.

Russini looks worse today than she did when the first photo of her and Vrabel alone at an adults-only resort in Arizona leaked. She has taken no accountability. Instead, she has blamed the media and unnamed "lies" for her circumstances.

Dianna Russini attends the "A Lifetime Of Sundays" screening at The Paley Center for Media in New York City on Sept. 18, 2019. (Astrid Stawiarz/WireImage)

Last week, ahead of her return, Russini cast herself as a heroine for other women.

"I really hope that I can be someone other women see: you can pick yourself up, get back in there and not be afraid," Russini told People.

At the very least, Russini should do what Woodward and countless other journalists have done: admit she crossed boundaries with a source and vow to do better.

Instead, she maintains her innocence as if the rest of us are that gullible. Her arrogance continues to be her downfall.

ESPN's Dianna Russini was photographed for 201 Magazine at Northern Valley Regional High School in Old Tappan, N.J., on Aug. 24, 2020. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

If anything, Russini has positioned herself as the poster child for how not to handle getting too close to a source. She is hardly the sympathetic figure she depicts herself as.

The comparison to Woodward only makes her refusal to take accountability look worse.

Bobby Burack is a writer for OutKick.

items.title: NFL promoting that Raiders coaches and players spoke to Francisco Mendoza in Spanish is a virtue signal stunt

scraped.title: NFL promoting that Raiders coaches and players spoke to Francisco Mendoza in Spanish is a virtue signal stunt
scraped.description: Fernando Mendoza's mic'd-up Spanish moments with other players and coaches looks like virtue signaling when NFL put it on its social media
scraped.author: Armando Salguero
scraped.h1: NFL promoting that Raiders coaches and players spoke to Francisco Mendoza in Spanish is a virtue signal stunt
scraped.body_text:
Fernando Mendoza has officially gone #1 overall to the Las Vegas Raiders. Deserved? Absolutely, but the dorky Mendoza heading to the gritty toughness of the Raiders has "bad fit" written all over it

I considered writing this column in Spanish because I've covered the NFL for 36 years and, apparently, now that Fernando Mendoza is a starting quarterback, America's most popular professional sports league wants everyone to know it embraces Spanish.

What a time to be alive!

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

I was born in Cuba and embrace Spanish, too. It's my first language.

But I've been doing my job in English seemingly forever because I live in the United States and English is the language here. And an NFL locker room has had about as much to do with communicating in Spanish as it does in Swahili.

But since Mendoza is of Cuban descent (yeah, we're everywhere) and his parents are of Cuban descent, and his grandparents came from Cuba, someone at the NFL decided this an opportunity for some sort of outreach to Hispanics.

So when the Las Vegas Raiders had players and coaches speak some Spanish to Mendoza on Sunday during their game, the NFL saw this as a chance to pump itself as a global brand.

Did I mention Mendoza happened to be mic'd up to pick up teammate Aidan O'Connell tell him to "respira," which means breathe in Spanish? What a coincidence.

Quarterback Fernando Mendoza, selected as the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft by the Las Vegas Raiders, poses with Raiders general manager John Spytek and head coach Klint Kubiak at a news conference in Henderson, Nev., on April 24, 2026. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

FERNANDO MENDOZA EMBRACES 'ONCE-IN-A-LIFETIME' CHANCE AS RAIDERS' QB1, CREDITS KIRK COUSINS' MENTORSHIP

The mic caught one Las Vegas coach throwing a random Spanish word here and there at Mendoza on the sideline.

And the league took those moments and did a look-at-us post on X to show that it's got some Spanish going on.

There is a phrase for this in my country: Virtue signaling.

THREE NFL TEAMS ROASTED FOR CELEBRATING INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' DAY ON COLUMBUS DAY, WHICH NO TEAM EVEN MENTIONED

Quarterback Fernando Mendoza, selected as the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft by the Las Vegas Raiders, attends a news conference at the Raiders Headquarters in Henderson, Nev., on April 24, 2026. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

It's not only unwelcome but opens up the NFL for mockery because it is not organic. It feels forced.

Why?

Firstly, Mendoza is American. Yes, his cultural origins cannot be denied. But he was born in this country and understandably speaks English much more fluently than he does Spanish – like many Hispanics his age living in the United States.

Secondly, is the NFL doing this for its quarterbacks of German descent? Or Italian? Or any other ethnicity?

Thirdly, the folks trying to somehow talk to Mendoza on the sideline in his non-native tongue weren't really speaking Spanish. They weren't stringing cogent sentences together. They were merely throwing out a Spanish word here and there.

It seemed forced.

Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores looks on during the fourth quarter of a game against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on Jan. 4, 2026. (Matt Blewett/Imagn Images)

At one point, a Raiders assistant coach told Mendoza, "Tu eres chingon."

The phrase is used by Mexicans and translates to 'You are awesome."

I think that's true because, although I speak Spanish fluently, I had to go look it up because I am not Mexican. And neither is Mendoza. And Spanish spoken in some countries, such as Mexico, is different from Spanish spoken in other countries, such as Cuba.

Breaking! People of Puerto Rican, Honduran, Mexican, Dominican or Venezuelan descent playing or coaching in the NFL don't all speak the same kind of Spanish. Some, like Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores , aren't comfortable speaking Spanish at all.

So those players and coaches might look at someone telling them "Tu eres chingon" just like someone from Iowa or West Virginia might.

People in Texas speak differently than those in New York. Americans go to England and understand that our shared language is not identical.

So it is with Spanish.

That's why this gimmick post by the NFL actually shows how little the league actually understands Hispanics.

Tom Flores, a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2021, poses with his bust during the induction ceremony at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium in Canton, Ohio, on Aug. 8, 2021. (Ron Schwane-Pool/Getty Images)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Look, it may seem nice that the NFL tried to give Mendoza's ancestry a tip of the cap. But anyone doing their homework would know that the first Raiders quarterback with Hispanic roots was Tom Flores , who also happened to coach the team to two Super Bowl victories.

He never had any of his coaches or players speak to Jim Plunkett in Spanish even though, you know, Plunkett was also of Hispanic descent.

Then again, virtue signaling wasn't a thing in the NFL back then.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

scraped.body_text:
BREAKING: United Airlines says it is experiencing a ‘widespread system outage’

For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

United Airlines on Monday afternoon said it was dealing with a “widespread system outage,” which comes on the heels of a nationwide FAA ground stop.

In a statement Monday, United said it was “working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible.”

The airline said it was troubleshooting a technology issue that was affecting departing flights. “There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” the carrier said in a statement.

The issue did not appear to be related to technical issues that prompted the ground stop that halted air travel across the United States for more than four hours Friday evening.

Other airlines did not appear to be affected by Monday’s United issue.

It’s the latest system relied on by millions of Americans to falter. Earlier Monday, JPMorganChase said a technical issue was causing some banking transactions to be delayed for both its own customers and others.

Late Friday, the FAA was forced to issue a nationwide ground stop after a fiber upgrade crashed a critical communication system. By Monday, air travel in the U.S. was largely returning to normal after a chaotic weekend for travelers, crews and airlines.

And last week, Microsoft Outlook went down due to what the tech giant said was a “bug” and overwhelmed servers.

While there is no evidence that any of the issues are related, they seem to be fulfilling concerns about America’s overreliance on aging infrastructure. They’re also occurring against a backdrop of warnings about AI risks and cyberattacks, stoking fears that wider problems may be afoot.

Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

scraped.description: A nationwide ground stop left Tara Harding and her employees stranded. Striking out on planes and trains, she opted to just buy an automobile.
scraped.h1: Women stranded by FAA ground stop buy a Bronco for a 27-hour road trip home
scraped.body_text:
BREAKING: United Airlines says it is experiencing a ‘widespread system outage’

For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota.

She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco.

Travelers across the U.S. were left scrambling Friday when the Federal Aviation Administration announced that it was grounding all flights as it saw inconsistencies in radar data and communications. Officials said that 20,000 flights were affected in the hourslong ground stop, with 12,000 “unable to recover” after the order lifted. Thousands more flights were either delayed or canceled the next day as airlines scrambled to recover service.

Harding, a nurse practitioner who owns a clinic, was ready to get home Friday after being in town for a training with two of her employees. Her group had been at the airport for about 30 minutes when the ground stop occurred.

All three women started out trying to find options through Delta Air Lines, but flights were delayed and rebooked until they gave up the idea of getting in the air altogether, Harding said.

“In the midst of all of that, though, we’re like, ‘We should probably look at trying to get a rental car,’” Harding said. “So we were trying to look, all three of us at one time, trying to get a rental car. There was zero available rental cars within a four-hour radius.”

Greyhound? Sold out.

Amtrak? No luck.

Uber? No rides to Bismarck.

Overwhelmed and out of ideas, Harding called her husband to ask what she should do. He relayed to her an idea from his mom.

“She said, ‘Why don’t you guys go buy a car?’” Harding recalled.

At that point, the women had been trying unsuccessfully to rebook their flights or find alternatives for more than an hour.

So they started texting with a sales agent at a Ford dealership who promised to stay open while they waited 30 minutes for an Uber out of the Charlotte Douglas International Airport. They arrived at 7:45 p.m. and left with a new Bronco less than two hours later.

Harding said the process gave her an adrenaline rush.

“When we were leaving the airport, I was three-way calling with my husband, the car dealer and my employees, and we were looking at each other like, ‘Is this really happening right now?’” she said.

Harding said she knows it sounds “insane,” but she did what she had to do, relying on a problem-solving instinct she tied to being both an entrepreneur and a nurse.

“If it was just me, it would have probably been different,” she said. “But I had two employees that needed to get home to their children, and we had patients on Monday morning.”

Even picking a Ford Bronco was a rushed decision, she said. Harding and her husband were discussing getting a vehicle with a good resale value, but her husband suggested getting a “fun” car just in case they couldn’t sell it once she got home.

“And being a Ford girl, I was like, ‘Broncos look kind of cute and fun,’” she said.

Driving the Bronco off the lot, the women drove 27 hours nonstop to Bismarck, making the most of the trip together. They had a rotation on who would sleep and who would drive.

“We took turns napping, stopped at gas stations and drive-thrus for food,” she said.

Despite the hefty price tag, Harding said she has no regrets about her decision. The women bonded over the journey, and in the end, they have a great story to tell, she added.

As for the Bronco, Harding said it’ll be with her for the long haul.

“I slept 12 hours when I got home, and when I woke up, my husband had drove it three times, and he said he wants to keep it,” Harding said. “So, we’re keeping it.”

Tom Costello is an NBC News correspondent based in Washington, D.C.

scraped.h1: United Airlines says it's experiencing a "widespread system outage" days after nationwide ground stop
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 16, 2026 / 5:36 PM EST / CBS/AP

United Airlines confirmed it was experiencing a "widespread system outage" Monday afternoon, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop .

"We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights," the airline said in a statement. "There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights."

A memo from the union representing United Airlines pilots indicated the issue was with the airline's weight and balance calculation system, noting: "The Company cannot provide outbound flights with final weights."

A United spokesperson said there's no indication the outage is related to a cybersecurity issue.

A recording posted on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.

The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown. Earlier in the day, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered every U.S. flight grounded because a new router that was installed malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system. And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email services. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

This is a developing story. It will be updated.

Kathryn Krupnik and Kris Van Cleave contributed to this report.

scraped.title: Major U.S. banks report widespread service outages
scraped.description: Customers at Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and other major financial institutions are reporting difficulty accessing their accounts.
scraped.h1: Major U.S. banks report widespread service outages
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 16, 2026 / 5:27 PM EST / CBS News

Customers at Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, U.S. Bank and other major financial institutions reported service outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com .

Other banks seeing a spike in customer complaints about difficulty accessing their accounts include Capital One, Truist and Wells Fargo, while users also reported problems with the digital payments app Zelle, according to the outage tracker.

Chase Bank's services are experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday.

"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."

Chase also said in a social media post that a software bug in its systems affected other institutions "when we were party to a transaction involving other banks." The issue is not systemic, the bank added.

Some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later."

Bank customers started reporting problems accessing online services on Monday morning. By the afternoon, reports of outages had surged, according to Downdetector.com. As of 2 p.m. ET, nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase, the most of any bank.

Chase customers reported issues accessing their online accounts, including viewing balances and performing transactions such as bank transfers and wire transfers, according to Downdetector.

Bank of America clients reported problems with ATMs as well as online and mobile banking services, according to the site.

U.S. Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app. They also had problems transferring funds, while Wells Fargo customers reported difficulty signing in to their accounts, as well as with getting account balances and conducting transactions.

A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS News that he tried to deposit a check at a Dallas branch early Monday, but the transaction could not be completed. A bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" without providing additional details, he added, expressing frustration at the lack of clarity about the situation.

A spokesperson for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted by the cyber outage. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the company said in a statement to CBS News.

A Capital One spokesperson said it hasn't been affected by the outage and continues to operate normally.

Zelle told CBS News that its service was "operating as it should," but that some users could be experiencing issues related to problems at their financial institutions, which could be delaying Zelle payments.

"Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," a Zelle spokesperson said. "Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."

Zelle's network operator, Early Warning Services, is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.

The banking outages occurred after Microsoft restored services on Saturday following a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, which disrupted users, companies and government operations worldwide. Microsoft said a technical issue caused the outage and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.

The glitches also came only days after overloaded routers forced the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, stranding travelers and causing thousands of canceled flights.

Cybersecurity experts said the root causes for the bank service disruptions, Microsoft outage and FAA system failure, while different on their face, also point to a common problem.

"Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week," Mike Chapple, an IT, analytics and operations expert at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement to CBS News. "When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day."

He noted that in each case, a technical issue quickly rippled through interconnected systems, causing massive disruptions nationwide.

"We don't yet know much about today's banking system outage, but it appears to stem from a technical issue at Chase that affected other banks through their shared payment networks," Chapple added.

When big companies like JPMorgan Chase experience technical disruptions, their impact often reverberates industrywide, added Karen Panetta, dean of graduate engineering at Tufts University.

"The larger companies have global reach that affords their customers flexibility and seamless integration with other businesses," she told CBS News. "Unfortunately, when one of these backbone providers has disruptions, the downstream effects are magnified. The multiple entities that rely on those services are also affected."

Kayne McGladrey, a security expert and senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said bank customers might have better luck going to their local branch in person, noting that financial services often still work on-site when online banking resources go down.

"Try ATMs, cards, phone banking and branches, which often keep working when the app doesn't," she said in a statement to CBS News.

She also advised people to keep records of any attempted or failed transactions.

"Screenshot failed transactions and error messages, since you may need them for reconciliation or fee waivers. Once service is back, ask the bank to reverse any fees the outage caused," McGladrey said.

She also urged consumers to ignore unsolicited emails about the bank outages, which she warned might be phishing scams. Instead, people should rely on their bank's official communication channels for information, McGladrey said.

Edited by Alain Sherter and Aimee Picchi

items.title: Ex-staffers claim lack of enforcement, "chaos" under Lutnick
items.summary: Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they allege are failures to act on evidence of computer chip smuggling.

scraped.title: Inside Lutnick's Commerce Department, lack of action on alleged AI chip smuggling came with a side of "chaos," ex-employees say
scraped.description: Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they allege are failures to act on evidence of computer chip smuggling.
scraped.h1: Inside Lutnick's Commerce Department, lack of action on alleged AI chip smuggling came with a side of "chaos," ex-employees say
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 16, 2026 / 5:21 PM EST / CBS News

Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they allege are failures to act on evidence of highly sensitive computer chip smuggling.

A key national security responsibility of the department is investigating and enforcing bans on the export to China and other U.S. adversaries of advanced computer chips used in artificial intelligence and sophisticated weapons.

"There was an inexplicable refusal to use the tools at their disposal for national security over the last year," one former Commerce official told CBS News.

Scrutiny of Lutnick's tenure has heightened in recent days with Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO after admitting an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believed to be a Chinese spy. China has denied the accusation of spying, calling it "an attempt to smear China."

As the scandal has unfolded, senior officials and members of Congress have questioned how Nvidia was permitted to sell chips to companies with deep ties to China, and whether the Commerce Department policed those exports effectively.

The answer, according to some of Lutnick's former staff, was not at all.

Four ex-Commerce officials spoke with CBS News, asking to remain anonymous, fearing professional reprisals for discussing their recent experience in government.

"We weren't able to add entities to the Entity List. That was just a complete stop," one former Commerce employee said, referring to the federal list of firms that the U.S. government has banned from buying the most advanced chips due to the belief they would route them to China or other adversaries.

Another former Commerce official said a whole year passed with no companies added to the list, noting that this was the first time that had happened in 18 years. The Federal Register shows the last time entities were added was Oct. 9, 2025, and the last yearlong gap in additions was in 2008.

The first former staffer said the agency's own enforcement officers found suspicious activity at Southeast Asian sites where Nvidia chips had been delivered, but that Commerce directors allegedly took no action.

Placement on the list triggers more stringent license requirements and creates a higher threshold to prevent sensitive products from getting where they shouldn't, the ex-official said.

Instead, "nothing happened," the ex-official said.

The Biden administration issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023, and in January 2025 issued an interim final rule to block China and other adversaries from obtaining the most advanced AI chips, both directly and through third-party countries.

In May 2025, President Trump's Commerce Department rolled back the rule, arguing it "would have stifled American innovation." Instead, the department said it would strengthen export controls for AI chips by issuing guidance to the industry and public.

There are growing signs that bans on exporting advanced U.S. computer chips have been circumvented in large quantities, according to published reports.

An April 2026 study by AI research nonprofit Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million cutting-edge AI chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025, comprising "roughly a quarter of the comput[ing power] China acquired through legal channels or domestic production."

Tech news site The Information reported that at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips allegedly ended up with Chinese companies since 2023 just through companies linked to Alice Huang , the suspected Chinese agent accused of an affair with Nvidia's ousted CEO. The report cited sources close to her for the estimate.

And a former researcher at OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, published a paper last week claiming to have found digital forensic evidence that top Chinese AI models were trained using Nvidia chips banned in China.

One former Commerce staffer described the department under Lutnick as "very chaotic, very frantic," with staff sometimes learning of major policy changes via media reports, including a pivot to allow the sale of Nvidia's H20 and H200 chips to China — the company's second-most advanced tier of GPUs.

"We found out about that in The New York Times," the ex-Commerce official said. "It was pretty clear that the decision was made between Trump and Jensen Huang."

The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment. CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment.

On Monday the department imposed a new rule requiring licenses for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand, aimed at closing a loophole through which chips were exported to China via an intermediary. But the Commerce Department suggested that its own involvement was limited, describing the rule as "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council—to address remote access to advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers."

The department lost two of its most senior and experienced experts shortly after Lutnick took office.

One was Matthew Borman, who served as principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration. Borman had been with the department for over 30 years.

Another veteran official, Eileen Albanese, was let go from her longtime role as director of the Office of National Security Controls. Reuters first reported their departures in February 2025, the same month Lutnick started running the department.

"They kicked off the administration by essentially firing the two most respected people," said one former employee.

A profile on the website of law firm Akin Gump, where Albanese now works, says she played a "key role in the development of U.S. export control policy and regulations for advanced artificial intelligence chips and semiconductor manufacturing tools."

"Matt and Eileen were treasures of the U.S. government," one former Commerce staffer said.

Albanese did not respond to a request for comment. Borman declined to comment.

Former officials said subsequent changes under Lutnick helped prompt an "exodus" of up to 50 skilled staff members over the past 18 months.

Over time, those who departed were among the most experienced officials who dealt with key areas including chips and export control enforcement, the ex-staffers said.

"It was an exodus of the finest engineers and scientists, the key experts on AI, on Russia, on diversion, our key expert on chips. Decades of institutional memory and skill went out," an ex-employee said.

Key roles remain vacant in Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, the department in charge of export controls, according to a registry of current senior federal employees. The principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration, the same role for export enforcement and the chief of staff roles are all currently unfilled, the records say.

Some staff described a bottleneck at the Bureau of Industry and Security, accusing its chief — Jeffrey Kessler, a top deputy to Lutnick — of "micromanaging" and blocking enforcement against companies suspected of smuggling chips.

"He made everything go through him. Literally every possible decision, the most minor things. It's impossible for one person to manage that level of things," one former employee under Lutnick told CBS News.

"He didn't want to make any decisions on his own. He would want you to make a memo and he would say, 'Package it up with options for me to bring to a decision maker,' which always cracked me up. Because it's like, who are you? A concerned citizen?"

"The career workforce felt frustrated and stymied," said one former staffer from the previous administration, who is close to many who remained in the department. "They felt like they were unable to do their jobs because [Kessler and Lutnick] were standing in their way."

The former staff members told CBS News that the critical view of Lutnick and his deputy was widely shared in the department.

Cabinet members have even voiced criticism, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen t telling CNBC last week that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement supported by Treasury, the State Department and others in the administration.

"Commerce has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told the channel.

"I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above" a certain sophistication, Bessent said.

items.summary: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.

scraped.title: Trump Asia trip live updates: There could be logistical hurdles with a Trump-Kim Jong Un meeting
scraped.description: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Trump Asia trip live updates: There could be logistical hurdles with a Trump-Kim Jong Un meeting
scraped.body_text:
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.

President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

See the most recent developments below.

President Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in reviving diplomacy with North Korea, but beyond the apparent lack of developed plans, there are logistical barriers that could make an impromptu meeting between the leaders on the sidelines of APEC unlikely.

Kim Jong Un has traveled internationally by plane before, but the last publicly documented time he did so was all the way back in 2018 -- when he borrowed a Boeing 747-400 from China to meet President Trump in Singapore.

Since then, he has traveled either by car for a couple short, cross-border trips or via notoriously slow armored trains. North Korea’s rail fleet travels at an average speed of around 35 mph -- topping out at 50 mph on China’s more advanced tracks.

While it is technically possible to travel by armored train from Pyongyang to Shenzhen, a one-way journey is projected to take as long as 60 hours.

Kim made a quick and quiet visit to China last month, taking a car over a newly opened bridge connecting the countries, according to Chinese state media. He did not meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the short trip.

South Korea's top diplomat previously said he believed there was little chance of Kim attending the APEC summit. North Korea is not a member of APEC, and Kim has never attended an APEC meeting.

-ABC News' Shannon Kingston

President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.

"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.

Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.

Read more about what to expect from Trump's trip.
