scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions
scraped.body_text:
JPMorgan Chase said customers still have access to their accounts and funds.

JPMorgan Chase said Monday it is working to resolve a technical issue that was impacting services, including transactions to other banks.

The bank said in a statement it has "experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems -- there is no evidence this is cyber-related."

"It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," the statement continued. "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue."

JPMorgan Chase said customers still have access to their accounts and funds.

"We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today," it said.

Amid the reports, U.S. Bank said that its systems are "not directly impacted" but that clients may experience transaction delays while trying to send or receive Zelle payments with another bank.

Zelle said in a statement that the digital payments network is not down and is "operating as it should," but that "an issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers."

More than 2,400 financial institutions use Zelle.

All financial systems operated by the Federal Reserve are currently operating normally, according to its website. That includes ACH transfers processed by the Federal Reserve between different banks.

Editor's note: A previous version of this story included an outdated statement from Wells Fargo.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

items.title: Germany thrash Netherlands to book quarterfinal spot
items.summary: Jurgen Klopp's side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2.

scraped.title: Germany thrash Netherlands to book quarterfinal spot
scraped.description: Jurgen Klopp’s side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2.
scraped.author: Alexander Hoad
scraped.h1: Germany thrash Netherlands to book quarterfinal spot
scraped.body_text:
Jurgen Klopp’s side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure the top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2.

Save

Share

An impressive Germany swept aside off-colour Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin to pip the Dutch to first place in UEFA Nations League Group A2.

Germany needed a win to stand a chance of reaching the quarterfinals, starting the night in third place behind Greece, who had won 1-0 in Germany in September, by virtue of their head-to-head record.

Jurgen Klopp’s side produced a fine attacking display to inflict the heaviest defeat on the Dutch in 67 years, as Xavi Hernandez’s side looked very ragged as they shipped four goals in 17 second-half minutes.

Greece’s win over Serbia left the top three sides level on 11 points, but Germany took the top spot on head-to-head while the Dutch finished second, qualifying for the last eight on goal difference thanks largely to their 7-0 win over Greece on Friday.

After a quiet opening 20 minutes, Kai Havertz headed straight at keeper Bart Verbruggen from a Joshua Kimmich free-kick, while Donyell Malen headed a Cody Gakpo cross from the left of the area over the bar from close range soon after.

Berlin-born Derry Scherhant fired a half-volley against the outside of the Dutch post on 32 minutes after collecting a cross from the right byline, but it turned out to be a range-finder as Scherhant scored his first international goal from a similar position on 44 minutes. After cutting in from the left of the area and working space, he flashed an unstoppable shot past Verbruggen and into the far top corner.

Scherhant almost grabbed his second a minute after the interval as he jinked and bundled his way through on goal on the left of the area only to lash a left-footed effort over the bar with only Verbruggen to beat.

Denzel Dumfries headed over the bar at the other end after running onto a bouncing cross at the back post after ghosting past Scherhant on 48 minutes. Meanwhile, the lively Brajan Gruda came close to a spectacular second at the other end after some neat control and cutting in from the right before flashing a shot past the upright from the edge of the Dutch box.

Soon after, Gakpo tested ter Stegen with a low strike from outside the box, but Germany made him pay as Florian Wirtz doubled the lead with a stunning strike into the top corner from the edge of the D with his left foot on the hour.

Nico Schlotterbeck glanced home a header from Gruda’s curling free-kick from the left within five minutes to make it 3-0, and the fourth arrived soon after as Gruda was allowed to glide into the area on the right and get to the byline before dinking the ball back into the middle for the unmarked Wirtz to lash home his second goal with a volley off the underside of the bar.

Gruda nearly added a goal to his two assists as his rising shot was stopped by Verbruggen after another silky run, but the 22-year-old eventually marked his second cap with his second international goal on 77 minutes when he fired home the rebound after Scherhant’s shot came back off the inside of the post.

It led to Verbruggen calling an impromptu huddle outside his area as the visitors sought to end their misery, and they saw the game out without further alarm.

Germany will be seeded in Friday’s draw for the last eight, which will be contested over two legs in March.

items.title: California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards
items.summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was 'entirely predictable' result of emphasis on rapid growth.

scraped.title: California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards
scraped.description: Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was ‘entirely predictable’ result of emphasis on rapid growth.
scraped.author: Brian Osgood
scraped.h1: California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards
scraped.body_text:
Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was ‘entirely predictable’ result of emphasis on rapid growth.

Save

Share

California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards.

The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet.

It proceeded to launch a days-long cyberattack on the AI hosting platform Hugging Face .

In the California complaint, Bonta argues that the incident indicates that OpenAI pursues growth over guardrails, leading to potentially dangerous errors.

“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit is the first brought by a state in response to the July incident. It alleges that OpenAI violated California’s consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance through its actions.

The complaint, filed in a state court in San Francisco, calls for civil penalties against OpenAI and an injunction to bar it from engaging in actions that constitute “unfair competition”.

“The simple truth is that the attack was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s decision to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” the complaint reads.

The Hugging Face incident became a catalyst for anxieties in the US about the explosive growth of the AI industry and the relatively light oversight it receives from the government.

President Donald Trump’s administration has largely opposed blanket regulations on the AI industry, warning that such rules could stifle the industry’s growth.

In December 2025, for instance, Trump issued an executive order attempting to limit the ability of individual states to pass laws that might govern AI development.

“United States AI companies must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulation. But excessive State regulation thwarts this imperative,” the order reads.

“My Administration must act with the Congress to ensure that there is a minimally burdensome national standard — not 50 discordant State ones.”

Polls, however, show that a majority of Americans want to see greater oversight of AI development and are wary that the technology could fuel economic and social disruptions.

The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, for instance, found in October that 64 percent of US adults believe AI is developing too rapidly. Roughly 81 percent said the technology should be kept under human control, rather than be left to operate independently.

Several high-profile resignations in the AI sector — notably that of Jacob Coxon in September — have also spurred concerns about the lack of oversight.

“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon, formerly a researcher at the AI firm Anthropic, wrote in a social media post about his departure.

“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.”

In Monday’s lawsuit, California officials accuse companies like OpenAI of failing to “adequately secure and monitor” their AI tests. It also alleged that the company had obstructed state investigators when they attempted to look into incidents like the Hugging Face hacking.

“OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said.

OpenAI has responded to July’s incident by stating that it would reinforce its safety measures and acknowledging the need for greater transparency.

In September, it also published a framework for “tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment” to better inform lawmakers and the public.

items.title: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
items.summary: Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

scraped.title: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
scraped.description: Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.
scraped.h1: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
scraped.body_text:
Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was appointed the federation's president in 2023 after being elected with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. The criticisms were led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round of 16 game against Belgium despite being shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

items.title: EU sanctions Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, Russia's richest woman
items.summary: Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, has been the target of Ukrainian attacks for its role in supplying the Russian military. The EU has now frozen its owner's assets and banned her from travel to the bloc.

scraped.title: EU sanctions Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim as well as enablers of Moscow's shadow fleet
scraped.description: Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, has been the target of Ukrainian attacks for its role in supplying the Russian military. The EU has now frozen its owner's assets and banned her from travel to the bloc.
scraped.h1: EU sanctions Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, Russia's richest woman
scraped.body_text:
Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, has been the target of Ukrainian attacks for its role in supplying the Russian military. The EU has now frozen its owner's assets and banned her from travel to the bloc.

The European Union added Russia 's wealthiest woman, online retailer Wildberries' CEO and owner Tatyana Kim, to its Russian sanctions list on Monday.

Kim's EU assets will be frozen as a result and she is barred from making financial transactions in or traveling to the bloc.

Wildberries is Russia's largest e-commerce retailer.

Kim, born in Grozny, Chechnya , to ethnic Korean parents, has an estimated net worth of $8.1 billion (€7.4 billion).

The sanctions were part of a larger regime targeting some 50 banks and oil export enablers and nearly 100 business leaders, propagandists and a major pro-Russian hacking group.

EU authorities say they targeted ​Kim due to the fact that Wildberries is "one of the largest taxpayers" in Russia and "operates as a supply network ​for the Russian military by facilitating the sale of military and ​dual-use ‌goods."

An EU statement went on to say that "Kim is supporting, materially or financially, and benefiting from Russia's military and industrial complex."

In its defense against invading Russian forces, Ukraine expanded its military target list this summer to include Wildberries warehouses inside Russia , saying the company's product list — which includes night-vision goggles, ammunition pouches and helmets alongside ‌regular clothing, cosmetics and electronics — is supporting Russia's illegal war.

Kim defended her company at the time, saying its offerings were no different than other online retailers like Amazon in the US and Alibaba in China.

The Kremlin, too, denied that the company and its warehouses were involved in the war effort.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a statement, Wildberries said Brussels' sanctions would have no impact on the company since it has no assets in the bloc nor does it conduct business there.

Other entities on Monday's sanctions list include firms in China, Oman, the Seychelles and the United Arab Emirates linked to the sale of oil from Russia's so-called shadow fleet of illicit tankers.

The sale of that oil also fuels Russia's invasion, which the EU is seeking to hamper through sanctions as well as direct financial and military assistance for Kyiv.

Brussels has imposed more than 20 sanctions packages in response to Russia's February 24, 2022, invasion of Ukraine , targeting thousands of individuals and companies to pressure President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the assault.

The 27-nation bloc intends to introduce another sweeping sanctions package by year's end.

items.title: Pakistan: Former leader Khan pleads for medical care
items.summary: Imran Khan appealed to judges to be treated "before it's too late." His wife was also included in the request.

scraped.title: Pakistan: Former leader Khan pleads for medical care
scraped.description: Imran Khan appealed to judges to be treated "before it's too late." His wife was also included in the request.
scraped.h1: Pakistan: Former leader Khan pleads for medical care
scraped.body_text:
Imran Khan appealed to judges to be treated "before it's too late." His wife was also included in the request.

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed to the country's Supreme Court in a bid to receive urgent medical attention for himself and his wife.

According to an open letter conveyed to the court through Khan's lawyer, the former leader's doctors had warned him of a risk for brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest and that his blood pressure had risen sharply.

He also said his wife Bushra Bibi required further eye operation, and that she is at risk of losing her eyesight should she not be granted the surgery.

The letter was released to the public by Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar.

"Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” the letter reads, asking the judges to give him "justice" before it was too late.

"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," Khan wrote.

An earlier court order ordered Khan's transfer to a hospital in Pakistani capital Islamabad, with Khan alleging that the authorities had not implemented it.

However, cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said Khan was receiving medical care , while also receiving food and books of his liking.

According to Chaudhry, the former leader has been taken to medical examinations at a hospital in Islamabad eight times, with his health and blood pressure being found to be in order.

Despite being in prison since 2023 for corruption offenses, Khan is still considered a popular figure in Pakistan, with his party demanding his release. His wife is alo serving jail time for graft offenses.

Khan argues the charges against him are politically motivated, which the government denies.

The government, led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif , also denied Khan was in solitary confinement. More than 900 visits to Khan have been registered since he started his jail time in 2023, according to the authorities.

In a previous case, Khan's attorney told the court that his client had lost about 85% of his right eye's vision. However, his sister later said his situation was improving.

scraped.description: A Mexican journalist was found dead on Saturday on the outskirts of Acapulco, a popular resort city in the southern Guerrero state, marking the latest in a string of alleged attacks targeting reporters in the country.
scraped.h1: Journalists call for justice after reporter found dead in Mexican coastal city of Acapulco
scraped.body_text:
Mexican journalist Eduardo Flores Salado was found dead over the weekend in Mexico's coastal city of Acapulco, intensifying concerns about reporters as the country remains among the world's deadliest for media workers.

His body was found Saturday night in the Canuto Nogueda neighbourhood, according to local authorities, in the outskirts of Acapulco, a popular resort city in southern Guerrero state.

On Sunday, the Guerrero state prosecutor's office said that the case was being investigated as an "aggravated homicide." It did not announce any arrests or provide a cause of death or motive.

Dozens of Flores's colleagues in Guerrero held a demonstration outside of the state attorney general's office on Monday, calling on Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and local authorities to undergo a comprehensive investigation and implement stricter measures to keep journalists and their families safe.

"There is a lot of fear, of course. You have to be courageous to do journalism, to be a journalist in Guerrero," Cristian Zamora, a journalist and director at the Digital Agency, who had been friends with Flores since 2015 and was in attendance at the Monday demonstration.

"Every day, we go out and we don't know if we're going to return. Every day, we say something and we don't know who we're going to bother. We don't have that freedom."

Eduardo Flores was a well-known journalist in Acapulco. (Eduardo Flores/Facebook)

Over nearly two decades, Flores covered missing persons cases, security and social issues, working as a reporter for multiple local outlets.

Most recently, Flores worked with digital news outlet Enfoque Informativo and was well known in Acapulco for his activism within the 2SLGBTQ+ community. He also co-founded tabloid news outlet La Prensa Rosa, which translates to the Pink Press.

Mexico is consistently named one of the most dangerous and deadliest countries in the world for journalists, with Reporters Without Borders ranking the country as the second-most dangerous place for reporters last year, after Gaza.

Zamora described Flores as a "great friend, supportive, attentive and polite."

"He was murdered," he told CBC News. "All of us, his fellow journalists, it caused us indignation, anger at what is happening in the country."

Local 2SLGBTQ+ activist Alberto Serna Mogollon said Flores — whom he and other friends called by the common nicknames "Lalo" or "Lalito" — was a vocal member and supporter of the movement.

"That is why we are here: stand in solidarity, asking for justice from the competent authorities," he told CBC News.

A number of international human rights organizations — including London-based advocacy group Article 19 and Amnesty International — have documented that attacks, threats and murders of journalists frequently go unpunished in Mexico.

In a post on X on Sunday, Article 19 said it condemned the alleged murder of Flores, calling on the Guerrero state prosecutor's office to "conduct a prompt, thorough, and impartial investigation ... that considers their journalistic work as a possible motive for the murder and keeps other lines of investigation open."

Article 19 has documented 181 such cases since 2000 in the Latin American country, many of these concentrated in states with a strong presence of organized crime groups.

It also called on the Protection Mechanism for Human Rights Defenders and Journalists, a state-run program meant to help protect journalists and human rights defenders, to assess the risks facing reporters' families and colleagues and to ensure their protection.

The program declined the Associated Press' request for an interview and did not provide comment for this story.

Last Wednesday, the AP reported on "exposed shortcomings" in the 2012 program meant to safeguard to more than 2,000 individuals, including approximately 500 journalists.

Under the mechanism's framework, each case first undergoes a risk assessment by a governing board, which creates a security plan. It can then provide tailored physical and emergency measures, such as panic buttons, bodyguards, armoured vehicles and temporary relocation. The mechanism ultimately works alongside federal and state authorities to implement and monitor these protections over time.

Eight journalists were killed while enrolled in the program between 2017 and 2022, according to a joint investigation by Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists.

Propuesta Cívica, a Mexican civil society organization that provides legal support to journalists and their families, estimates that 98 per cent of journalist homicides remain unpunished.

"The deeper structural problem is that the mechanism has been given a responsibility that belongs to the state as a whole," Vanessa Carrillo, Propuesta Cívica's co-director, told the Associated Press last week.

Cameras, a video recorder, a microphone and placards are placed together on the ground during a protest in July 2023, by journalists to demand justice for the murder of a regional correspondent who was found slain two days prior in, Guadalajara, Mexico. (Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty Images)

The Inter-American Commission for Human Rights has emphasized that the state must prevent attacks and reduce risks, not simply investigate them.

According to Propuesta Cívica, Mexico's federal Protection Mechanism is hampered by bureaucratic delays, insufficient staffing and a reactive approach. Protection measures are often inadequate, risk assessments delayed and safeguards withdrawn despite ongoing threats.

In 2025, President Sheinbaum said the program could receive additional funding if needed, but Reporters Without Borders said the government has made little progress in fulfilling its press freedom commitments, including a promised review of the program.

Violence against journalists in Mexico goes unpunished and ignored

Flores's death follows that of Roxana Guzman, who directed a Veracruz crime news ​outlet, Pulso Informativo del Sureste.

A video she recorded of masked men breaking down her front door before her abduction on June 2 was widely shared on social media. Her remains were found a month later. Authorities said eight people had been arrested over Guzman's kidnapping and killing, including four municipal police officers from a small town 300 kilometres south.

Flores's employer Enfoque Informativo condemned his death and demanded a thorough and transparent investigation.

"This attack not only takes the life of a colleague, friend, and valuable human being; it constitutes a direct attack on freedom of expression," it said in a statement on Sunday.

"They will not silence us. We will continue to report with the same determination and professional ethics that characterized the work of Eduardo Flores Salado."

Senior Writer

Sara Jabakhanji is a Toronto-based senior writer assigned to cover news developments in the Middle East. She has worked in CBC bureaus in Ottawa, London and Toronto. You can reach her at sara.jabakhanji@cbc.ca.

items.title: U.S. Supreme Court set to hear 3 major Trump agenda immigration cases
items.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court made at least two significant rulings to shape immigration policy last year. In the coming months, there will at least three more opinions that could be impactful, as U.S. President Donald Trump's administration seeks to reinterpret a number of laws concerning asylum, deportations and the detention of unauthorized persons in the U.S.

scraped.title: Here are the 3 major immigration cases U.S. Supreme Court will hear in coming months | CBC News
scraped.description: The U.S. Supreme Court made at least two significant rulings to shape immigration policy last year. In the coming months, there will at least three more opinions that could be impactful, as U.S. President Donald Trump's administration seeks to reinterpret a number of laws concerning asylum, deportations and the detention of unauthorized persons in the U.S.
scraped.h1: U.S. Supreme Court set to hear 3 major Trump agenda immigration cases
scraped.body_text:
The U.S. Supreme Court late last week agreed to take on a case central to the Trump administration's immigration agenda concerning the conditions under which migrants can request asylum.

While the announcement ended up being buried in a Friday afternoon news cycle that saw the unforeseen ground stop of U.S. air travel, it means that the top court will now hear at least three major immigration-related cases in its session that runs through June 2027.

The Trump administration's "retinterpretation of certain detention and deportation policies" has led to a "particularly high number of immigration disputes" compared to previous sessions," according to SCOTUSblog, which tracks the work of the top court. The blog, in an October post , also highlighted a handful of other cases that, while narrower in scope in terms of their ramifications, could also be described as immigration-related.

The top court in the 2025-2026 session rejected a Trump administration bid to end birthright citizenship going forward, but it made an impactful ruling that has paved the way for the federal government to deport large numbers of Haitian Americans and other residents who have been in the U.S. for years after fleeing natural disasters or turmoil in their home countries.

Overall, these new cases could lead to Supreme Court rulings that further reshape the American immigration and asylum system, or at least provide clarity in response to actions, some very controversial, that have been undertaken by President Donald Trump's second administration.

Here is a look at the three major cases, so far, of the 2026-2027 docket:

Generally speaking, U.S. laws have recognized through the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and other legislation the rights of migrants to make an asylum claim when arriving at a border entry point, or even if they are caught trying to cross into the country between entry points. In most years, denials have been greater than asylum claims being granted, though the percentage has fluctuated.

In his final year in office, former president Joe Biden sought to stem the tide of surging arrivals at the southern border and encourage appointment-based claims with what was described as an executive order meant to be temporary, which limited asylum eligibility based on the daily number of encounters at the border.

How Trump turned ICE into a mass deportation machine

On the very first day of his second presidential term in 2025, Trump signed an executive order deemed necessary due to an "invasion" at the southern border.

Trump's order has essentially amounted to a blanket asylum ban for migrants caught crossing between border points. The prohibition has also applied to migrants who arrive at official border crossings and lack certain medical or criminal history information, a requirement that advocates say is often impossible to meet for people fleeing violence.

It was blocked first by a federal judge and then in April by the U.S. Court of Appeals in D.C. The panel ruled 2-1 that the INA doesn't "a llow the president to remove [migrants] under summary removal procedures of his own making."

In a partial dissent, Judge Justin Walker wrote that the administration can broadly deny asylum applications, but that the INA and other laws forbid sending people back to countries where they would be persecuted.

On immigration, Trump administration has chalked up many more wins than setbacks

Trump names Miller, an architect of U.S. deportation agenda, as new chief of staff

Whether that has been practised in the asylum claims the government does consider is arguable. Denial rates in some cases have climbed to over 90 per cent , according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University. Denial rates that high have not been seen for decades , if ever.

Democratic House Rep. Rob Menendez of New Jersey, posting Friday after it was learned the Supreme Court would take on the case, said " fixing our broken immigration system means upholding our values as a nation of immigrants" while "protecting the right to seek asylum."

The Supreme Court justices will gather to hear oral arguments on Dec. 9 regarding a controversial plank of the Trump administration's deportation policies, also related to executive orders the president signed on his first day back in the Oval Office in 2025.

The U.S. traditionally has followed a principle of non-refoulement. That is, not returning persons to countries where it could be reasonably expected they'd face persecution or torture due to race, religion, sexuality, political views or other factors.

People deported from the U.S., all nationals of third countries, under an agreement to accept such deportees, arrive at the Juan Santamaria International Airport, near Alajuela, Costa Rica, on April 11. (Mayela Lopez/Reuters)

Flowing through the Trump executive orders, however, the administration has sought workarounds through third-country deportations. According to a website run by two human rights organizations , the Trump administration has spent more than $95 million US to deport over 28,000 people to 31 different countries and has struck agreements to potentially send people to four additional countries.

In many cases, people are being sent to countries to which they have no connection. In addition, some of the countries that have struck agreements with the U.S. have had questionable track records in terms of upholding human rights and freedoms.

U.S. Supreme Court says Trump can continue deportations to 3rd countries — for now

Liberia to begin accepting up to 1,200 deportees from the U.S.

"These migrants are being transferred to countries or territories with which they have no ties, which can be a traumatizing and isolating experience that compounds harms already suffered which triggered their fleeing to the U.S. in the first place," the UN's Human Rights Council said in a statement earlier this year condemning the practice.

The administration has said that it has struck deals with foreign governments where the safety of the deportees has been assured. But the New York Times reported last week after an extensive investigation that it had it identified 110 persons who were deported to a third country but then put on a plane back to their home country of origin, even after U.S. courts had established they had reasonable fears in leaving those countries to seek asylum.

Under past administrations, most non-citizens without a criminal record who were arrested away from border points had an opportunity to request a bond hearing. In many cases, that allowed them to work and remain free while their cases, which would ultimately determine if they would be deported, wound their through immigration court.

The Trump administration has ended that practice, citing an interpretation of existing 1996 legislation. After conflicting rulings in federal courts across the U.S., the Supreme Court will take up the issue after the American Civil Liberties Union filed a lawsuit on behalf of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha.

Canadian dentist detained by ICE in Minnesota released after federal court ruling

Winnipeg-born man deported back to Canada after 9 months in ICE detention

The Brazilian man entered the U.S. without authorization two decades ago and, according to his lawyers, has never been charged or convicted of a crime. Nevertheless, after federal immigration agents detained him on his way to work in September 2025, an immigration judge subsequently denied him a bond hearing.

According to the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA , the number of detention beds for people arrested within the U.S. has more than quadrupled in the past two years, meaning the stakes for this case are considerable.

As with the asylum case just announced Friday, no date has been set yet for oral arguments.

With files from the Associated Press and Reuters

items.title: Russia says Ukrainian aerial attack involved more than 1,300 drones
items.summary: Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in what would be the highest number of interceptions during an aerial attack since Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbour nearly five years ago.

scraped.title: Russia says Ukrainian aerial attack involved more than 1,300 drones | CBC News
scraped.description: Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in what would be the highest number of interceptions during an aerial attack since Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbour nearly five years ago.
scraped.h1: Russia says Ukrainian aerial attack involved more than 1,300 drones
scraped.body_text:
Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in what would be the highest number of interceptions during an aerial attack since Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbour nearly five years ago.

Ukraine has scaled up its long-range aerial assaults on Russia, as well as the illegally annexed Crimea Peninsula and the Black and the Azov seas, with more than 1,000 drones used in some daily attacks in recent months.

Russia, meanwhile, has battered Ukrainian civilian areas with relentless strikes that seek to choke the economy and break public morale, especially through strikes on the power grid.

U.S.-mediated talks have had no impact on the fighting. U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, say they expect to broker further discussions between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv following meetings last week, but no date has been announced.

The war has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of Ukrainian civilians, Western analysts and officials say.

Trump said he plans to discuss the war during a highly anticipated meeting this week in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

European Union countries accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the conflict. The bloc announced sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions and targeted several businesspeople with links to the energy sector.

Ukraine targeted the huge Kerch Bridge, a key span for moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea that is also a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov insisted the attack caused "insignificant damage," and bridge authorities said vehicular traffic resumed Monday evening.

Six people were wounded in an attack on Russia's southern Krasnodar region, according to local authorities. The town is home to the Ilsky oil refinery, a frequent target of Ukrainian drone attacks.

Firefighters work at the site of a cardboard factory hit by a Russian jet drone attack Monday, in Odesa, Ukraine. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)

In the Rostov region near the border with Ukraine, three people in the city of Azov were wounded by drones, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said.

Around 600 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. Most were downed far from the Russian capital, while 191 were shot down as they approached it, he said.

Ukraine's long-range strikes have repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, which are an economic mainstay for Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday night that Ukrainian attacks have disabled over 55 per cent of Russia's oil refining capacity.

Russian officials didn't comment on that claim, and independent verification wasn't possible. But Putin made a rare acknowledgment of the strikes' economic impact on Oct. 1, saying they had cost Russia about one per cent of its gross domestic product.

Ukrainian officials are also keen to make Russians feel the war at home, while mid-range strikes are disrupting Russia's front-line supply routes and hampering Moscow's efforts to get momentum on the battlefield, analysts say.

U.S. envoys talk to Zelenskyy in Dublin, after prior sitdown with Putin in Moscow

Russia-Ukraine talks mediated by U.S. end with news of 'good momentum,' large-scale prisoner swap

Kyiv says newly imposed speed limits on the U.S.-made Starshield system, SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, have weakened Ukraine's air defences. Ukrainian forces say they are adapting by launching pre-emptive attacks on Russian weapons production plants and launch sites for drones and missiles.

Kyiv also wants to show its supporters that it is still in the fight, as Moscow tries to depict its victory in Ukraine as inevitable.

There was no clear picture of the extent of damage caused by Ukrainian strikes in Russia. Moscow-based authorities and local officials rarely provide details.

Ukrainians are bracing for what could be the hardest winter since the war began, as Russia repeatedly batters the power grid and denies civilians heat, light and running water.

Russian strikes on power lines and substations in the southern Zaporizhzhia and central Dnipropetrovsk regions left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Monday.

Zelenskyy says the Russian strategy is to bombard specific areas for days, flattening energy infrastructure.

Since the start of September, the central Dnipro region has endured 131 strikes, while the Kyiv region around the capital has witnessed 125, he said.

Russian attacks violate Trump's 'energy ceasefire', says Zelenskyy

An attack Monday in Dnipro killed one person and injured three, local officials said, while one person was killed and four were wounded by a strike in the northeastern Kharkiv region.

Over the past week, Russia has launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles against Ukraine, Zelenskyy said.

They are "brutal strikes that are difficult to counter," he said on social media.

Four people were killed and three more injured in Russian shelling of towns and villages in the Donetsk region over the past day, said Vadym Filashkin, head of the Donetsk Regional Military Administration.

scraped.description: Treasurer Jim Chalmers confirms a "substantial" package of savings in the mid-year budget update, which will be delivered in December.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/tom-crowley/103219804
scraped.h1: Chalmers says mid-year budget update will include 'enough' spending cuts
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic: Federal Government

Jim Chalmers will deliver the mid-year budget update in December. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )

Jim Chalmers says the mid-year budget update will include a "substantial" package of cuts.

The treasurer also said the government was working on plans to cut government regulation.

The mid-year budget update will be delivered in December.

A "substantial" package of cuts to government spending will be revealed in next month's mid-year budget update, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed.

The cuts have been foreshadowed for several weeks, but without any sense of their magnitude. In a speech to an ASIC forum this morning, Mr Chalmers said the mid-year update would have cuts as its main focus.

"It will cut enough, but not too much. It will strike some fine balances," he said.

The government has sustained criticism over the elevated level of government spending, which the opposition and some economists have said is worsening inflation and driving interest rates higher.

Mr Chalmers has consistently rejected that characterisation, but today said the cuts were motivated by economic conditions.

"We take seriously and embrace our responsibilities in the fight against inflation," he said.

No details of individual cuts have been confirmed, but Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said earlier this month the public service would be one target of "belt tightening", and there have been calls to consider means testing for subsidies for electric vehicles and home batteries.

Mr Chalmers also announced he would write to businesses and investors to gather ideas for regulations that could be cut to simplify compliance for businesses.

He last wrote to government regulators on this matter last year, and told the ASIC forum the process had led to 400 ideas for how red tape could be cut, 140 of which had already been enacted and 200 of which were underway.

As the government pursues savings "across the board" ahead of the mid-year budget update, an ABC analysis shows only a handful of ministers have managed net savings so far this year.

"These regulatory reforms span everything from telecommunications to energy to tax, and lots in between ... cumulatively, these changes will make a real difference," he said.

The Business Council of Australia has been campaigning for a 25 per cent cut to the cost of complying with government regulation, which it said cost business billions each year.

The federal opposition has taken up the 25 per cent target. While avoiding a specific target of its own, the government has promised streamlining in several areas.

The ABC understands one such area to be featured in the mid-year budget will be the construction code, which has been subject to consultation with the industry.

The government opposed the Liberals' proposal to slash the building code from about 2,000 pages to fewer than 100, but has promised to find other ways to streamline it.

Another focus revealed by Mr Chalmers was on reducing tax compliance costs.

He said he would consult on a "pre-filling" option for sole traders paying tax and scrapping complex assessments of fringe benefits below $300.

He said these two measures could save businesses $52 million per year.

The treasurer is also seeking to pass two key tax bills through the parliament late this month, one to establish a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts and the other to give innovative start-up businesses the option to opt out of the new inflation-linked capital gains tax discount.

Both measures have been highly contentious with business and are opposed by the Coalition, but their passage will depend on the votes of the Greens, who support the government's tax agenda in principle but have raised some concerns.

On trusts, the Greens have focused on what they say are loopholes to exempt charitable giving from the new tax, including money to private schools and sporting clubs.

On the capital gains carve-out for start-ups, which business groups say does not go far enough, the Greens yesterday said they were open to considering an alternative model proposed by independent MP Allegra Spender.

Ms Spender's model would impose a flat 40 per cent discount on all "active assets", using an existing tax law definition to cover assets that are used, or may be used, for business purposes.

Ms Spender has cited analysis from the independent Parliamentary Budget Office suggesting these changes would make little difference to the amount of revenue raised.

She also said this would be a fairer and simpler model, avoiding the need to define what an "innovative'" business is.

Mr Chalmers said he had written to Ms Spender with Treasury analysis on her proposal, which suggested it was "unlikely to lead to a more productive economy" and would be complex and raise integrity issues.

"We had a longish discussion about it ... there are important reasons why I don't think the model that she's put forward is the right model," he said.

scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/josh-brine/102478468
scraped.h1: EVs are making their mark in motorsport but not everyone is convinced
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Josh Brine

ABC South East SA

Topic: Electric Vehicles

Tony Wallis has started racing in a Tesla Model 3. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine )

Electric cars have hit the track at the Legends of the Lake Hillclimb in Mount Gambier for the first time in the event's 21-year history.

While they performed well in the race that takes place in a volcanic crater, fans are not sold on the quiet achievers.

EV racers say they expect the number of drivers going electric to grow in the future.

As electric vehicles become increasingly popular for commuters, they are also starting to pop up in the world of motorsport.

After years racing petrol-powered internal combustion cars, Adelaide Hills resident Tony Wallis made the decision to purchase a Tesla Model 3 Performance to use both day-to-day and on the track about a year ago.

For Mr Wallis, the amount of power and acceleration outmatched everything in its price bracket.

"I was looking to upgrade to something a little bit newer, and I was looking at Audis and you had to spend $60,000 at a minimum," he said.

Tony Wallis set a time in the top 10 of all competitors at the Legend of the Lakes Hillclimb. ( ABC News )

The switch has brought plenty of success, with Mr Wallis topping the time sheets at regional time trials, and he said he had seen more people getting on board.

In Mount Gambier, in SA's south-east, racers have powered their way up out of a dormant volcanic crater for more than 20 years at the Legends of the Lakes Hillclimb.

This year, Mr Wallis's Tesla and Mike Paul Jonker's Kia EV4 GT were the first electric cars to take part.

Mount Gambier's Valley Lake plays host to the event. ( ABC South East SA: Bec Whetham )

Clerk of the course Peter Lock said while he was not personally a fan of EVs, they were likely a key part of the future of motorsport.

"But if it's about the speed and the capability, then that's what's going to impress you."

Peter Lock says EVs are likely to grow in popularity. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine )

On that front, the Tesla proved its worth, finishing with the seventh fastest time overall: 53.53 seconds.

"It's like you're being shot out of a cannon, but they are a heavy beast," Mr Wallis said.

The lack of noise from the EVs has divided spectators. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine )

While the cost-to-performance offering was what first drew Mr Wallis to his EV, he said the costs to run it on track had also been cheaper.

With solar panels at home, and running the car pretty close to stock, he was spending much less to keep the car going around the track.

"When I charge at the supercharger at lunchtime just to give it a top-up, it normally costs me $11-12 to do that," he said.

"But it's not as easy as in an [internal combustion engine vehicle] car. I can just get a jerry can and fill that up."

Subarus remained a crowd favourite and the fastest up the hill, despite the EVs. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine )

Legends of the Lakes spectators were split on the new additions.

"It's pretty different compared to all the other cars, so it's always good to see different things," Adelaide's Reece Garrick said.

"There's nothing that says I must look at this … we're old-school," Diane Holland said, while watching her husband Mike take part.

Classic Holdens still outnumbered EVs. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine )

But Mr Wallis said he expected more people to move to electric vehicles, particularly if they were winning events across the country.

Topic: Extreme Weather Events

Homes have been torn apart at South West Rocks, following what was a possibly tornado. ( Supplied: NSW SES )

The Bureau of Meteorology has confirmed a "possible tornado" tore through a town on the NSW Mid North Coast yesterday.

The SES said several homes were damaged, with roofs destroyed on three.

The SES is continuing to clean up the mess and tarp down homes.

Homes have been severely damaged after a "possible tornado" tore through a New South Wales coastal town yesterday afternoon.

The severe storm cell tore through South West Rocks on the Mid North Coast at 4:45pm, leaving three homes without a roof.

A Bureau of Metereology (BOM) spokesperson said thunderstorms were forecast in the area.

"This information combined with available pictures and videos indicates it is possible that a tornado occurred," the BOM said in a statement.

The State Emergency Service (SES) Mid North Coast deputy zone commander, Anthony Day, said the service received more than 30 calls for help in "short succession" in the holiday town.

Mr Day said SES volunteers would be working to clean up the mess and secure more homes with tarps today.

"We'll re-attend those jobs and make sure those tarps are secure for temporary repairs until the owners can get the builders in to fix those roofs," he said

The SES will be helping to cover homes in tarps after several roofs were blown off. ( Supplied: NSW SES )

The bureau said it was still assessing radar imagery and reports.

"Many severe thunderstorms carry with them a slight chance of tornado development," the BOM spokesperson said.

"Predicting tornadoes is difficult and specific warnings are only issued if signs consistent with tornadoes occurring are visible on radar or direct observations are received."

A broader clean-up is also underway across large parts of north-east NSW after widespread thunderstorms on Monday afternoon and overnight.

The BOM recorded 43 millimetres of rain in 30 minutes at Grafton at 4pm.

Hail up to 6 centimetres was recorded at Lawrence and 2–4cm hail fell north of Kyogle.

SES North Eastern superintendent Kristine McDonald said thunderstorms affected areas from Coffs Harbour up to the Queensland border, with 46 calls for assistance.

"We had trees down, roof damage, skylight damage, we had water entering properties," she said.

"There was a bit of flash flooding reported yesterday in Evans Head and we also, just locally, the areas that fill up quickly with that fast dump of rain, we had a variance of jobs across the zone."

See All by Charles Pulliam-Moore

Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking . Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.

Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.

Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.

The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.

As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.

As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.

Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.

Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge , the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.

What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.

All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

See All by Emma Roth

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Emma Roth

California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit on Monday , Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters .

The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.

After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website , a German wiki site , and the software package manager RubyGems . OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”

OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge . “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.”

The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday.

Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast , Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month , saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.”

AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles . Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”

Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying:

“The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”

Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

scraped.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
scraped.description: A hidden bug, shifting traffic, and reduced capacity led to cascading failures.
scraped.h1: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
scraped.body_text:
A hidden bug, shifting traffic, and reduced capacity led to cascading failures.

A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company’s history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft’s report lists the incident’s final status as “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents.”

Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.

The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft’s incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company’s status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report , and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft’s service-health updates .

Microsoft attributes the outage to three factors. A change deployed to Microsoft’s cloud gateway starting in July created a bug where, under certain conditions, CPU and memory resources could become exhausted and unresponsive. Microsoft contends that the defect was never discovered in pre-release testing because the hardware used was less powerful than some systems already deployed in production, where higher CPU core counts on newer machines apparently contributed to the lockout.

The second factor was server load. Microsoft said that “Traffic shifts during standard network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug.” The company keeps two independent gateway systems in place to access Microsoft 365 for resilience. If one system encounters trouble and users can’t get through the front door, the other is opened to keep traffic flowing. According to the report, about 15 hours prior to the outage, traffic from Teams was shifted from the alternate gateway to the primary, where Exchange Online access is maintained. The switchover was a standard fail-safe, but it left the gateway handling more traffic, with a different mix of requests than before. As requests continued to pile up, affected servers exhausted their capacity and refused new connection requests.

The traffic shift exposed a third factor: infrastructure capacity. An existing fault meant that Microsoft’s gateway server fleet was operating at 14 percent below optimal conditions. That missing headroom could have normally absorbed the demand, but when combined with the changed traffic patterns and underlying defect, it left the gateways with lock contention as requests kept piling up.

As US business operations began hitting their daily peaks, the gateway servers began to freeze. Backup systems that shifted requests away from unresponsive servers did their job, but were met with the same lockouts on the supposedly healthy backup gateways. This created a snowball effect, leaving more than 80 percent of Microsoft’s affected gateway servers frozen in the sweep. Mechanisms in place to isolate affected systems by region seem to have failed. Microsoft’s current report doesn’t address why these isolation systems may have failed.

Recovery took longer than normal because the fix required a targeted system update from Microsoft engineers. Attempts to restart the gateway servers were ineffective; when the servers came back online, large request queues were still waiting for access, immediately triggering the same resource exhaustion that contributed to the outage in the first place. Microsoft says that services like Teams, OneDrive, and other Office applications could be routed away from the affected infrastructure, but scaling limitations stopped Exchange Online from making a similar move.

Since the bug from July was still undiscovered, system rollbacks were equally ineffective. Simply returning to a previous state where things were “working” couldn’t happen, because the ghost was already in the machine. Servers were patched and returned to service gradually, and Microsoft says it has added additional capacity and traffic-distribution guardrails to try to avoid anything similar happening again. Microsoft also extended delivery timeouts on affected emails to stop delayed messages from bouncing back as undeliverable.

Microsoft expects to publish its full final incident report on November 20. This final report may provide additional clarification on why the regional isolation systems failed and what corrective actions will be taken to ensure this type of outage can be avoided in the future. All of Microsoft’s cloud services appeared online and operational as of Monday morning.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

scraped.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
scraped.description: Study attempts to tally hyperscalers’ energy use and emissions.
scraped.h1: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
scraped.body_text:
Study attempts to tally hyperscalers’ energy use and emissions.

One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.

A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward.

The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.

That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent.

Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

A recent Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated the total electricity use of all data centers of any kind in the US (minus crypto mining) at 76 terawatt-hours in 2018. In 2024, that number was up to 192 terawatt-hours. That means the hyperscale data centers identified by this study account for something like one-third to one-half of all data center energy use.

The researchers also wanted to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions associated with generating all that electricity. It’s fairly straightforward to get a reasonable number here—calculate the mix of generation in each data center’s region of the grid, and apply that CO 2 per watt-hour rate to a data center’s electricity use.

This yields 21 to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 for the year. That’s around 0.5 percent of total US fossil fuel CO 2 emissions.

These data centers aren’t located in areas of especially clean energy—their energy mix was only slightly cleaner than the US average. About 54 percent of the electricity was generated by fossil fuel power plants (dominantly natural gas), with 25 percent from renewables, and 21 percent from nuclear.

This doesn’t include any “behind-the-meter” generation on-site, though. The xAI data center in Tennessee notably ran a fleet of natural gas turbines during this study’s time period, for example. Cleanview, which describes itself as a market intelligence company, has tracked a boom in on-site generation since early 2025, including 116 current or planned data centers. While this may not affect this study’s numbers much, it is becoming increasingly significant over time.

This matters because the types of generators being used are much less efficient than utility power plants, emitting 60 to 80 percent more greenhouse gases to produce the same amount of electricity. (Conversely, if a data center built solar generation instead, it could reduce the carbon footprint of its energy.)

Although this study can’t pinpoint the energy use of AI data centers alone, repeating this analysis in subsequent years could reveal the growth related to the AI buildout—at least as long as that buildout lasts.

Nature Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7 ( About DOIs ).

scraped.title: Shareholders sue Intel, its CEO, and CFO after stock drops 28.6 percent in one day
scraped.description: The PC sales slump "more than offset” AI boom gains, shareholders say.
scraped.h1: Shareholders sue Intel, its CEO, and CFO after stock drops 28.6 percent in one day
scraped.body_text:
The PC sales slump “more than offset” AI boom gains, shareholders say.

Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel’s stock on October 30.

The lawsuit ( PDF ), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants.

The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period.

In the complaint, the shareholders argue that Intel misled them by failing to disclose: the full impact that the PC market sales slump would have on Intel’s third quarter and beyond; the impact of increasing PC component prices on PC sales for Intel’s OEM and distribution partners; that Intel was dealing with substrate supply constraints that would limit its ability to meet data center CPU demand; and “that any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset” by the PC sales slump.

“[S]tatements regarding Intel’s business, operations, financial results, and ability to capitalize on the boom for AI-related infrastructure spending were materially false and misleading when made, and such statements did not accurately reflect Intel’s then-present business and prospects,” the law firm representing the plaintiffs, Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd LLP, said in a statement on Friday.

On October 29, Intel announced what the complaint calls “disastrous” fiscal Q3 earnings. During the quarter, revenue for Intel’s Client Computing and Physical AI Group (CCPG) business declined 5 percent year over year.

At the time, Tan pointed to an “unprecedented memory crunch” and manufacturing supply shortages hurting the PC market.

The next day, Intel’s shares fell 28.6 percent in “the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years,” the complaint notes.

Intel hasn’t publicly commented on the lawsuit.
