scraped.title: These Companies Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds for Executive Bonuses
scraped.description: Stanley Black & Decker is getting at least $298 million in tariff refunds. The parent firm of TJ Maxx received $331 million. Both companies, and others, are using the money for corporate bonuses instead of repaying shoppers.
scraped.author: Robert Faturechi and Nick McMillan
scraped.h1: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Sign up for ProPublica's Big Story newsletter and get our latest stories delivered straight to your inbox.

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.

The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.

Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:

Its own leaders.

The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.

Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.

Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.

Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.

But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.

“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.”

The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.

Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries.

“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.”

Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.

That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.

The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year.

The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president , asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.”

Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event.

Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.

“The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference . “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.”

“I got a feeling the American people won’t see” the refund money.

In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs.

Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx , have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. The companies are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them.

A series of lawsuits are attempting to force companies that sell directly to consumers to share some of their refunds. Dozens of firms have been sued, including big-box stores Walmart and Target and apparel companies such as Nike and Lululemon. Apparel and leather costs were some of the hardest hit by Trump’s tariffs. Legal analysts have cast doubt on whether these lawsuits will succeed, though some trade experts have speculated that businesses that used the tariffs as cover to raise prices more than they needed to might settle to avoid embarrassing disclosures.

One of the companies facing a lawsuit is Stanley Black & Decker, the toolmaker that ProPublica found was using some of its refund on bonuses. The named plaintiff is a Wisconsin resident who bought a handheld blower, an impact wrench, a hedge trimmer and other tools from the company last year, but the lawsuit seeks to represent thousands of other customers as well.

“Unless restrained by this Court,” the complaint reads, the company “stands to recover the same tariff payments twice — once from consumers through tariff-inflated prices and again from the federal government through tariff refunds.”

On multiple occasions, the company has acknowledged publicly that it was raising prices because of the tariffs.

The month before the November 2024 election, as Trump was campaigning on dramatic new tariffs, the toolmaker’s then-CEO, Donald Allan Jr., told shareholders that Stanley Black & Decker was preparing for the possibility. “Obviously, coming out of the gate, there would be price increases associated with tariffs that we put into the market,” he said during an earnings call . Then, a few months after Trump unveiled his tariffs, Allan said his team was “remaining focused on executing our robust plan designed to mitigate tariffs” that he said included “targeted pricing actions to improve our gross margin.” Later that year, his successor as chief executive, Chris Nelson, described more price hikes : “We are implementing a second price increase during the fourth quarter to maintain our innovation and brand investments, given the pressures resulting from tariff-related cost increases.”

In its more recent disclosures, the company has been vague about how much of its refund was going to executives, simply saying that some of that gain “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation.” “Incentive compensation” is a term the toolmaker uses to describe bonuses.

The company has not responded to the allegations in the lawsuit brought by the Wisconsin resident and did not answer ProPublica’s questions about who is getting paid the bonuses, how much they’re worth and whether customers should be reimbursed.

Securities experts who reviewed the disclosures for ProPublica said it appeared the windfall boosted the company’s profits, which factor into formulas that help determine bonus pay for executives and other employees.

“It wasn’t the executive that triggered that extra profit, so why should their compensation go up?” Germain, the corporate law professor said. “This is one of many examples where these formulas don’t do what they should do.”

The company’s leaders, securities experts said, could have given money back to consumers or lowered prices. Retail giant Burlington Stores, formerly known as Burlington Coat Factory, appears to have done just that.

CEO Michael O’Sullivan recently said the company got $55 million in tariff refunds and “rather than taking a one-time boost to earnings” the company plans “to deliver even sharper values to our shoppers,”

“Over the last few years, the rising cost of living has made life difficult for many customers,” O’Sullivan said, adding that the coming discounts meant investors should expect the “direct impact of tariff refunds to be neutral.”

A company spokesperson confirmed to ProPublica that none of its tariff refund will be going to bonuses.

Not so for other companies.

Acushnet, the Massachusetts golf equipment company that includes the brand Titleist, disclosed an “incentive compensation expense of approximately $12.0 million” out of its refund. Acushnet declined to respond to questions from ProPublica.

TJX, the Massachusetts parent company of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, said it got back $331 million, but as a result, it “accrued incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible Associates globally.”

The company declined to answer questions from ProPublica about how far down the chain of command the bonuses would go and how much of them would be reserved for top managers. “Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” a spokesperson said. The company also declined to say whether it would lower prices or pay back customers with the rest of its refund, saying only that “the remaining amount will be used to support our future growth.”

ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such information.

Nick Guest, an accounting professor at Cornell University who has studied executive compensation, said the argument for granting leaders bonuses based on the tariff refunds could go both ways.

“If they were penalized for something out of their control,” he said, referring to earnings hits caused by Trump’s tariffs last year, rewarding them now “seems reasonable.”

“But you could say the same thing about customers. If they were penalized, then is it reasonable that they’re not getting rewarded now?” Guest asked. The companies, he said, are “not obligated to give refunds or reduce prices, but doing so could certainly build goodwill with customers.”

ProPublica searched through securities filings and earnings calls of publicly traded companies, using key phrases to isolate companies that mentioned refunds for the Trump administration tariffs that were struck down by the Supreme Court. We then used an open-weight AI model to make a first pass at classifying how refunds were being used, including if they were going toward bonuses or to refunds for customers. For the companies we highlighted in our reporting, ProPublica reporters reviewed disclosure filings and other records by hand, looking at context both within documents and across other records to make sure the results of our analysis were accurate.

Pratheek Rebala contributed data reporting.

I am a Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter at ProPublica.

Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses.

scraped.title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
scraped.description: With so much money dedicated to debt and pensions, city officials get to decide how to spend just one-third of the annual budget. As a result, residents’ health and safety needs aren’t being met.
scraped.author: Heather Cherone, Jared Rutecki, and Vernal Coleman
scraped.h1: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Sign up for ProPublica's Big Story newsletter and get our latest stories delivered straight to your inbox.

Co-published with WTTW News

Sign up for Dispatches , a ProPublica newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week. WTTW News is Chicago’s PBS station. Sign up for the Daily Chicagoan , a newsletter that explores the backstory of the city’s biggest issues.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top.

Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children.

Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds.

No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt.

New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show.

According to all four of the major Wall Street credit-rating agencies, New York’s and Los Angeles’ fiscal health make them much better choices for investors. Chicago’s history of questionable borrowing and budgeting — it chose to either ignore or short its pension payments for years — has undermined its credibility.

Its credit rating now sits just two or three levels above junk status, making the cost of borrowing even more onerous. And the city’s chief financial officer, tasked with managing city debt and relationships with credit agencies, resigned last week in stunning fashion , saying she no longer could continue in the role because it would compromise her “integrity and professional obligations.” She had come from Fitch Ratings, a credit agency, and had been on the job for only three months.

The city is an outlier among other large cities, where most pensions are at least 75% funded.

Options for a financial rescue are limited or unpalatable. Pension obligations, locked in by law and political realities, remain untouchable. There is little public or political appetite to raise property taxes or cut city jobs, particularly among the ranks of police, the city’s largest workforce. A windfall from the city’s still-under-construction casino grows more unlikely than ever.

The office of Mayor Brandon Johnson, who is finishing up his first term in office, blames “reckless financing methods” from past administrations for the city’s financial bind.

“Savings and efficiencies alone cannot solve the city’s persistent structural gap,” the city’s Office of Budget and Management wrote to WTTW and ProPublica in response to questions for this story. In searching for revenue streams, Johnson has sought to impose new taxes on the city’s biggest corporations — an effort that has met stiff resistance.

Tackling the pension crisis, the city since 2023 has paid an additional $1 billion into its four pension funds above what is required by state law, records show, an infusion that the city touts as a stabilizing force.

But, like his predecessors, Johnson continues to rely on borrowing. Since taking office in 2023, Johnson has added $1.9 billion to the city’s debt obligations, according to city data.

That borrowing has “advanced desperately needed investment in economic development and affordable housing in historically underserved communities on the South and West sides,” according to Johnson’s spokesperson.

It also has been used to keep the city functioning. In 2026, for example, Chicago borrowed $166 million to pay firefighters what they were owed for working without a contract — and annual raises — for four years. Officials acknowledged they failed to set enough cash aside annually to cover those widely anticipated costs. The city borrowed an additional $267 million to cover the soaring cost of lawsuits alleging Chicago police officers committed a wide range of misconduct.

In some cases, the Johnson administration has negotiated agreements with its lenders that allow the city to pay only interest for several years, backloading its debt burden.

With so much of the city budget dedicated to debt and pensions — and more cordoned off by federal and state laws that mandate spending for specific purposes, such as transportation — Chicago officials get to decide how to spend just one-third of its annual budget, records show.

The result for residents: Restaurant inspections are lagging. Complaints about crumbling sidewalks and injuries from those hazards pile up, without timely repairs. The city’s Public Health Department doesn’t have enough caseworkers to handle the intensive intervention needed for children suffering from lead poisoning.

The budget pressures are unrelenting. In August, Johnson announced another borrowing plan to fix a budget shortfall that emerged midyear. He blamed the City Council for overestimating the impact of new revenue streams while his council foes accused him of continuing a pattern of questionable borrowing habits.

Amid the finger-pointing, Johnson acknowledged the bind facing his administration and the city as a whole. “We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch,” he said.

“We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch.”

Watching the annual struggles of city officials to climb out of its money pit leaves many residents feeling more than a little uneasy about what comes next.

“It is the feeling that people get when they max out their credit card and they’re barely paying the minimum,” said Alderperson Andre Vasquez, who represents the 40th Ward and speaks often of growing up in a family that struggled to pay the rent every month. “You’re behind on your utilities. So you get mail every month, letting you know you’re behind.

“And at some point, you’re not even gonna open the envelope anymore, because the feeling of dread, even trying to see it, is a challenging one. That’s how people in Chicago feel.”

When Johnson ran for mayor in 2023, he repeatedly emphasized his commitment to invest in the city’s neighborhoods in order to build a healthier city. Central to his message was a pledge to reopen six mental health clinics closed by former Mayor Rahm Emanuel when he faced his own budget pressures in 2011.

Those closures fueled a terrible cycle, Johnson has said. Chicagoans in desperate need of counseling and medication instead found themselves in crisis, forced to call 911 for help or struggle alone.

But during Johnson’s time in office, the city has reopened just two clinics. The city’s lack of capacity has forced nonprofit organizations to pick up the slack, despite their own funding woes and staffing challenges.

Johnson, who has touted his record of investing in “historically underserved communities,” is promising to open another clinic in 2027. But fulfilling that promise hinges on the outcome of a court fight over whether Chicago can levy taxes on social media companies like Facebook and YouTube.

“The need is big and growing,” said Mark Ishaug, CEO of Thresholds, a nonprofit group that specializes in community care. “We don’t have enough money, and what we do have is being threatened.”

Hemmed in by the city’s budget, Johnson has worked to expand mental health services outside the traditional clinic setting by offering counseling at libraries across the city several times a week and launching a “street psychiatry” program focused on unhoused Chicagoans.

Chicago’s wide range of public health needs often have solutions that require money the city lacks.

In recent years, for example, the Public Health Department’s food safety programs have been “not in substantial compliance,” according to a 2025 state audit. The department has had to prioritize restaurants and other eateries that are considered high risk while lower-risk establishments are inspected less frequently. But even that effort falls short. State law requires three inspections a year for high-priority eateries, yet that happens at only 15% of those, records show.

Inspections also were at the center of a 2023 City Council proposal to prevent lead poisoning, especially among the city’s vulnerable children living in aging or neglected housing. More than 600,000 houses and apartments, the majority of the city’s homes, were built before 1978, when lead paint was banned by the federal government. Lead paint poses a hazard in 99% of homes built before 1978, officials have said.

One solution suggested by an alderperson would’ve mandated that the city inspect every Chicago home or apartment every five years for lead paint and other health hazards. But the proposal would have required the Public Health Department to hire 600 new inspectors, more than doubling its total workforce — and its budget. Ultimately, not a single hearing was held on the idea.

This March, the issue came up again, when the City Council created a working group to develop a plan to proactively inspect all Chicago homes offered for rent. The first step would be a study and recommendations within six months. But that deadline passed without any public progress, despite several community meetings.

The department’s current efforts to address child lead poisoning underscore the impact of budget pressures.

The department receives more than 1,000 notifications each year about children with lead poisoning. Each report kicks off a complicated remediation process, involving multiple city departments, designed to identify and remove the lead source from the child’s home. Health department nurses work with the families to monitor their children’s health and assess whether the city’s abatement efforts are working.

Public health records provide a snapshot of workloads for caseworkers during the first quarter of the year, with several handling more than 200 cases at a time. “Concerns remain for case managers with persistently high caseloads,” wrote a supervising nurse in an April email to department leaders.

A department spokesperson said it reaches out to all families in these situations, “providing at minimum direct outreach and educational materials.” More than 96% of families that are contacted get a home visit from department staff. The spokesperson did not say what percentage of families the city is able to reach.

In the coming months, Public Health will have to do even more with its limited budget. The state of Illinois has lowered the threshold for elevated levels of lead in the blood, which will lead to increases in positive tests.

Coupled with the city’s efforts to expand blood tests for children in areas on the South and West sides, even more families are expected to enter the queue for case management.

Felicia Nalls-Bradley just wanted to get to work. It was her first week on the job.

But she tripped over an uneven sidewalk on the South Side in 2022. As she fell, she struck a fence and suffered injuries to her head, neck, shoulders, hands and back that required surgery and almost a week in the hospital. Records describe the path as “unreasonably hazardous,” with a 2-inch difference in elevation between two portions of the walkway.

She sued the city for negligence and settled for $400,000 last year. It was one of more than 350 sidewalk-related cases the city has settled since 2010, records show. The city has paid at least $16.1 million to resolve such claims during that period.

Records and deposition testimony from those cases describe a largely reactive maintenance system that relies heavily on residents to report problems.

A city engineer testified in a sidewalk-injury deposition in 2024 that Chicago does not routinely inspect its sidewalks. He also said that employees investigating a complaint are not expected to identify other hazards nearby.

In separate testimony in 2017, another engineer said the city responded to about 13,000 sidewalk maintenance requests annually but had only a handful of crews rotating across Chicago to make repairs.

The engineer’s testimony in another case contrasted his professional desires with the limitations of his resources. “In a perfect world I would like to do that, yes,” he said about inspecting every sidewalk complaint.

He then added a caveat: “This is the real world.”

Injuries — and lawsuits — are not the only consequence of poor sidewalk maintenance. Iliana Haven, who uses a power wheelchair and scooter because of a neuromuscular condition, said they regularly encounter obstacles as they struggle to get around.

A thwarted trip to the Puerto Rican People’s Day Parade exemplified their problems as they encountered broken and uneven sidewalks on their scooter. After being unable to find a passable route, Haven called family for help.

It took about 30 minutes for relatives to find Haven. Family members returned home to get a motorized wheelchair, which could more easily carry Haven to the event. But it had nearly concluded by the time everybody got through the entrance gate. Haven appreciated the help and took it with good humor, but the ordeal highlighted a lesson.

“It is a rule of mine to never leave anywhere by myself if I can help it,” Haven said.

They also understand the frustration of others challenged by sidewalks. The lack of access impacts businesses in the end, they said.

“There’s a huge number of disabled people in the city of Chicago. We would love to go and spend our money,” Haven said. “We can only do that if we can leave our house.”

After declaring that he would run again for mayor in next year’s election, Johnson gathered the media in early October to tout what his administration called a success story, a concrete example of his commitment to building up neglected areas of the city.

Under bright skies, he cut the ribbon on seven new two-flats in North Lawndale, a West Side neighborhood that has seen its population dwindle and its crime rate remain stubbornly high. The only way to reverse those entrenched trends, he said, is to create safe, affordable new homes that will allow Chicagoans to “put down roots and build wealth.”

The homes were built on city-owned vacant land; they also were built on more city debt. The Johnson administration used $5.4 million from the $1.25 billion Johnson borrowed in 2025 to fund housing and economic development projects across the city.

The debate over that borrowing crystalized Chicago’s current governing dilemma: Should it reduce its dependence on debt or address crucial needs for Chicagoans? And is it possible to do both?

Some alderpersons warned the city could not afford to borrow another $1.25 billion and questioned the wisdom of a payment schedule that avoids paying any principal until 2028. If that debt is not retired until 2055, as scheduled, taxpayers will have paid more than $98.9 million in interest costs alone, records show.

That borrowing is at the heart of Johnson’s attempt to expand the city’s economic capacity and invest in neighborhoods that have long been ignored by City Hall. His administration defends the borrowing by saying there is a plan to pay it back with a new approach that doesn’t affect taxpayers. Nearly four dozen tax-increment financing districts are set to expire by 2039, allowing more than $2 billion to flow back to the city, Chicago Public Schools and other taxing districts in coming years, records show.

Some alderpersons remain skeptical of Johnson’s budget strategy, and his overall financial stewardship was dealt a significant setback when Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch resigned Friday. She described a deep rift with the administration over how to portray the city’s finances.

“The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about the City’s finances are relied upon by investors, rating agencies, City Council, and taxpayers, and they must be complete and accurate,” she wrote to Johnson. “I am not able to fulfill those obligations under the conditions in which I have been asked to serve.”

The city responded by criticizing her job performance, saying she had been “largely absent” as Johnson’s team worked on its 2027 budget.

In the aftermath, alderpersons are seeking an audit of city finances. A majority already have been sparring with Johnson over borrowing.

They moved in September to make it harder to take on new debt by requiring the votes of at least 30 alderpersons, not just a simple majority from the panel of 50. Johnson blasted that change, saying it would stop investment flowing to neighborhoods like North Lawndale, and vetoed it.

Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said Johnson faces hard choices as he tries to implement his agenda.

“I give the mayor credit for having aspirations to make housing more affordable and to expand behavioral and mental health care,” Marlowe said. “These are all noble goals. But the city can’t afford it.”

Less than two weeks later, Johnson was back at City Hall, giving his 2027 budget address and outlining his plans to fill yet another large gap. Among his solutions again was a corporate tax, which once again was deemed dead-on-arrival by key alderpersons. But the City Council may have no choice but to go along with Johnson’s plan for more borrowing.

He proposed borrowing $481 million in 2027 to cover the cost of resolving lawsuits alleging that police misconduct led to wrongful convictions and deadly pursuits. If approved by the council, it would mark the second straight year that the city has borrowed to cover its bills, a move that financial experts consider a sign of worsening financial distress.

Marlowe said the city has no choice but to borrow to cover those costs, calling it the “least bad option” available to the city.

But Joseph Ferguson, who heads the Civic Federation, a nonpartisan budget watchdog group, was unimpressed by Johnson’s presentation. He’s seen a pattern over decades in which city officials plan to make it through the next election cycle or the next budget fight without looking toward lasting solutions.

Johnson’s plan, Ferguson said, shifts costs onto future taxpayers and only manages to “dig the city deeper into a financial hole.”

I’m a Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter based in Chicago who writes about, among other things, law enforcement and veterans’ issues.

If you have a story to tell, I have an ear for you — especially if you can shed light on how policies enacted in Washington are harming people in the Chicago area. If you know of or are the victim of an injustice, I want to hear from you.

scraped.title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
scraped.description: Chicago’s leaders have repeatedly tried to fix the budget deficit by prioritizing political expediency over long-term solutions, putting the city in financial peril.
scraped.author: Heather Cherone
scraped.h1: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Sign up for ProPublica's Big Story newsletter and get our latest stories delivered straight to your inbox.

Co-published with WTTW News

Sign up for Dispatches , a ProPublica newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week. WTTW News is Chicago’s PBS station. Sign up for the Daily Chicagoan , a newsletter that explores the backstory of the city’s biggest issues.

Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess.

The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble.

The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund.

Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole.

In 2000, the city’s pensions were 85% funded, which meant the funds could easily pay benefits to employees as they retired, records show. But a series of decisions in both Chicago and the Illinois capital of Springfield unraveled that strong position, leading to the current mountain of $36.4 billion in pension debt.

First, the twin blows of the “dot-com” bubble bursting in 2000 and the Great Recession in 2007 wiped out nearly $16 billion from those funds.

Around the same time came a self-inflicted blow. In 2005, the state legislature, at the request of then Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, passed legislation allowing the city to contribute less every year than what was actually needed to pay retirees.

As a result, in 2006 and 2007, Daley was able to stop making annual contributions to four pension funds for police officers, firefighters, laborers and municipal employees. He received near-unanimous support from the Chicago City Council. Daley, who was mayor from 1989 through 2011, declined to comment for this story.

Daley’s “pension holiday” meant the city could balance its budget without a politically perilous property tax hike. But that maneuver laid the foundation of the current pension crisis facing the city.

In 2010, having seen the financial fallout from the pension legislation, state legislators passed a law that banned city officials from taking another pension holiday by setting a firm schedule for the city to pay back its skipped payments — no excuses allowed.

Two of Chicago’s pension funds must be funded at a 90% level by 2055, with the other two hitting that mark by 2058, according to state law. This requirement caused a spike in the city’s annual payments.

Trying to ease Chicago’s snowballing pension burdens, lawmakers passed a new measure reducing the retirement benefits offered to state employees who began work on or after January 1, 2011.

But that revised law touched off a new set of problems. The well-intentioned effort to reduce costs actually reduced pension benefits too drastically. Under federal law, public sector pension funds must pay workers no less than what they would have earned if they paid into Social Security.

In 2021 and 2025, lawmakers agreed to change the law and ensure that first responders — police and firefighters — in Illinois are paid at least the minimum required by law.

Fixing those funds will cost Chicago an additional $11 billion to get to the 90% funded level required by state law over the next three decades, according to city projections. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the legislation over the objections of city officials.

Facing big deficits in 2008 in the wake of the Great Recession, Daley and the City Council found what they thought was a creative solution to the city’s financial woes.

They would lease the city’s parking meters to a conglomerate of investment funds for 75 years in return for $1.5 billion up front. That massive influx of cash meant no one had to make any hard decisions to fill the city’s budget gap and avoid a politically unpopular property tax increase.

But the deal ended up a loser both politically and financially.

The new owners of the meters immediately jacked up the cost to park, infuriating residents. In a matter of months, members of the City Council began regretting their votes, and Daley announced he would not run for reelection.

By 2025, the city’s meters generated $2.2 billion in revenue for the investors, with another 58 years still left on the lease.

The city considered buying the parking meters back this year, but Mayor Brandon Johnson told reporters “the final purchase price was far too high.” The city would have had to borrow billions to finance the $3.2 billion purchase.

Elected officials across the political spectrum agree that the city would have been much better off raising property taxes instead of leasing the parking meters in 2008.

But even as the gap between the city’s revenues and its expenses continues to widen, property tax hikes remain the third rail of Chicago politics.

Chicagoans’ property taxes last jumped in 2021, when former Mayor Lori Lightfoot raised them by $93.9 million and passed a budget that automatically hiked property taxes to keep pace with inflation.

Johnson campaigned against those automatic property tax increases, forcing Lightfoot to drop a proposal to hike taxes by $42.7 million in 2023, just months before she lost her bid for reelection.

The automatic property tax hike was eliminated, even though it could have prevented the city’s credit rating from being downgraded repeatedly and significantly reduced the annual budget gaps.

In a postscript to the parking meter debacle, Chicago Parking Meters LLC sold the meters contract earlier this year to an investment firm, triggering a one-time payment to the city of $75 million. The City Council and Johnson then battled over how best to use that money for pension costs, creating a temporary hole in the 2027 city budget.

The 2014 police murder of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald changed nearly every aspect of City Hall politics around policing. Despite decades of scandals, misconduct and brutality, the Police Department had managed to fend off reform. But that ended with McDonald’s death, even as city leaders continued to fear a backlash from residents concerned about crime rates and a politically powerful police union.

After a massive outcry greeted footage of McDonald getting shot 16 times while he walked away from officers, the federal government launched a probe that in 2017 found ample evidence that the department ​​routinely violated the constitutional rights of Black and Latino Chicagoans.

In 2019, the Chicago Police Department agreed — under the oversight of a federal judge — to change the way officers are trained, supervised and disciplined. In taking so long to address a pernicious problem, a succession of city leaders set up Chicago for a huge financial hit.

The true scope of police misconduct and what it will cost the city is only now becoming clear.

From 2019 to 2025, as the city scrambled to fill budget holes, it agreed to pay nearly $730 million to resolve lawsuits alleging officers committed a wide range of misconduct, according to a WTTW News analysis of city records. The most expensive cases involve wrongful convictions that sent Chicagoans now declared innocent to prison for decades, as well as botched raids and police pursuits that violated CPD policy and led to injuries, according to that analysis.

In 2026 alone, Chicago has spent more than $277 million to resolve lawsuits alleging police misconduct, records show. That includes nearly $100 million to resolve 90 lawsuits filed by people who allege they were wrongfully implicated based on evidence gathered by former Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was convicted in 2013 of taking bribes. He has denied wrongdoing.

Johnson has urged the City Council to borrow an additional $481 million to cover the costs of resolving more lawsuits, with $260.8 million earmarked for 17 people wrongfully convicted based on evidence developed by former Chicago police Detective Reynaldo Guevara. A judge determined Guevara told “bald-faced lies” while under oath in 2017, a fact that will be presented to any jury asked to determine whether the city should be held accountable for claims of misconduct. He has repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right not to incriminate himself when pressed to testify in civil cases.

Another 25 lawsuits naming Guevara remain pending.

Guevara is now one of the most notorious members of the Chicago Police Department, costing taxpayers more than any other officer, including former Cmdr. Jon Burge, who tortured and beat more than 100 Black men from the 1970s to the 1990s, city officials have acknowledged.

Records show that Guevara, who retired from CPD in 2005 and lives in Texas, collects an annual payout of $91,000 from the city’s depleted police pension fund.

Finance ministers from countries around the world meet at COP31 to discuss the costs of energy and climate change. UN Climate Change/Kiara WorthThe 2026 United Nations climate talks are all about real-world impact. That’s evident as I listen to government officials and others from around the world at the COP31 climate su...

scraped.title: How the US elections and Iran war are influencing the UN’s COP31 climate talks – and discussions around fossil fuels
scraped.description: I have followed the talks for years as a policy expert and former climate envoy for Germany, and I’m seeing growing concern about the rising costs and harm from fossil fuels.
scraped.author: Jennifer Morgan
scraped.h1: How the US elections and Iran war are influencing the UN’s COP31 climate talks – and discussions around fossil fuels
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

The 2026 United Nations climate talks are all about real-world impact. That’s evident as I listen to government officials and others from around the world at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

World leaders are seeing their countries suffer from intensifying storms and heat fueled by climate change and from one of the worst global energy crises in history. A U.N. report found that global warming will overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), the level countries agreed a decade ago to try to avoid because of the growing risk of dangerous climate change.

The Middle East conflict has intensified oil and gas price and supply volatility , pushing economies to the brink as energy and food prices spike and energy security falters.

Countries that rely on imported fossil fuels for their energy sources have borne the brunt of the energy crisis. Those doubling down on renewable energy are weathering the crisis better.

In Pakistan, for example, the rapid expansion of solar power over the past six years helped the country avoid more than US$12 billion in fossil fuel imports before the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran began in February 2026. One forecast suggests solar could save the country more than $6 billion more by the end of the year. Spain, which relies less on natural gas and more on solar energy for electricity than most European countries, kept electricity prices lower and avoided the worst of the gas-driven spikes seen in more exposed systems such as Italy’s.

In formal negotiations and in meetings around the U.N.’s broader Global Climate Action Agenda , countries are working on ways to accelerate the use of clean energy and to provide poorer countries with the resources to adapt to climate change and expand clean energy.

I have been following international climate negotiations for years as a former special climate envoy for Germany and senior fellow at the Fletcher School at Tufts University. In 2026, after two years of the Trump administration’s pressure to get countries to abandon efforts to slow climate change , I’m seeing rising concern among leaders about the costs of fossil fuels on economies and people’s lives.

A step in transitioning away from fossil fuels is shifting to electrification powered by clean energy. The co-presidents of COP31, from Turkey and Australia, have proposed a global target of 35% of all energy use coming from electricity by 2035 – including for transportation and industry – and they are working to persuade other countries to sign on.

Hitting that 35% mark could save fossil-fuel-importing countries $400 billion a year , according to the International Energy Agency. In consumer terms, $100 spent on electricity powers a car up to three times farther than $100 of gasoline, based on global averages. Reaching the goal could slash energy emissions across transportation, buildings and industry by up to 55% by 2035 .

However, the source of electrification matters. Forecasts from the International Renewable Energy Agency show that at least 78% of the electricity powering the world must come from renewable energy sources to keep global warming under the 1.5 C limit. Electrification delivers for both the climate and energy security if it runs on clean power instead of energy from oil, gas and coal.

Getting the world to that point will require addressing some key barriers: the cost of infrastructure needed to deliver clean energy and the need for policies to encourage the changes.

Beyond the formal negotiations, countries are discussing multiple initiatives to provide technical support to one another , as countries develop power grids that can manage the variability of solar and wind power, and financial help to countries that need it.

The high financial and environmental costs of fossil fuels have been reshaping global politics. Voters came out in big numbers over the past few months to elect leaders who support clean, affordable energy solutions.

The world saw this notably with the reelection of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the biggest Democratic congressional victory in the United States in over three decades.

Lula, in his first international trip after winning his fourth term, called on the COP31 presidents to carry forward Brazil’s work as host of COP30 on a transition away from fossil fuels . He announced that Brazil will host a future conference on the fossil fuel transition, following the first in Colombia in April 2026 and a second planned in 2027 in the island nation of Tuvalu.

Brazil has clearly emerged as a climate superpower in Antalya. With its greatest one-year reduction in deforestation and its leadership in producing three plans, known as road maps, to help the world transition away from fossil fuels, end deforestation and provide the $1.3 trillion in financing needed for developing countries, Brazil has demonstrated it understands the urgency of the climate crisis.

We will see whether the co-presidents of COP31 will answer the calls from Lula and U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres to support these road maps becoming formal guidance for all countries.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and a delegation of 18 members of the U.S. House of Representatives also came to COP31 to signal the presence of American leadership on future climate policy. President Donald Trump has pulled the U.S. out of the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Paris Agreement and dozens of other international organizations and treaties . The U.S. did not send a formal delegation to the climate talks.

As former U.S. climate envoy John Kerry said in Antalya , “Americans did vote for clean, affordable energy, and they also voted for clean governance.”

The international community will be watching to see whether the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress can help safeguard U.S. climate science after the Trump administration’s extensive funding cuts , and whether it will restore critical funding to international efforts dealing with climate change.

At COP31, the shift in the real-world politics of energy has dominated several events and the formal negotiations. But the countries that are likely to lose from such a transition are also working diligently to slow this transition . On the opening day, a coalition of oil-producing countries led by Saudi Arabia announced it opposed any mention of Brazil’s road map away from fossil fuels in the official COP31 agreement.

For COP31 to be a success, the diplomatic process must demonstrate that it can catch up to the real economy and meet this moment of energy and climate crisis. I believe the summit’s final agreement should accelerate the electrification of infrastructure around the world and, at the same time, drive the transition away from fossil fuels in order to protect global security, economic stability and everyday citizens.

Senior Fellow, Center for International Environment and Resource Policy and Climate Policy Lab, Tufts University

items.summary: Some Puritans hoped they could convert Native Americans peacefully. As history shows, the reality was rarely so simple. The 'Eliot' Bible, published in 1663, was the result of collaboration between a Puritan minister and a Montauk interpreter. Wikimedia CommonsIn 1663, colonial printers in New England produced a translation of the Bible into Wampanoag, an Algonquian language spoken in southern New England. Also known as Wôpanâak or Massachusett, it was one of several Native American languages...

scraped.title: New England’s first Bible, published in an Indigenous language, had one aim: Converting Native Americans
scraped.description: Some Puritans hoped they could convert Native Americans peacefully. As history shows, the reality was rarely so simple.
scraped.author: Peter C. Mancall
scraped.h1: New England’s first Bible, published in an Indigenous language, had one aim: Converting Native Americans
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

In 1663, colonial printers in New England produced a translation of the Bible into Wampanoag, an Algonquian language spoken in southern New England . Also known as Wôpanâak or Massachusett , it was one of several Native American languages in the region.

Printing the book would be an important story on its own. But it is even more remarkable because it was the first Bible that English colonists published in North America.

As a historian of early America , I believe this Bible sheds important light on relations between New England’s Native peoples and English immigrants, who saw themselves as crucial players in the spread of Protestant Christianity. Consumed with the idea that their culture was superior, many English Protestants believed they could conquer North America without much bloodshed : that Indigenous peoples would voluntarily abandon their cultures and embrace the faith of the newcomers.

The historical record is more complex. My 2026 book, “Contested Continent,” details the struggle to control North America in the generations after Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic Ocean. There were many moments, including the fabled first Thanksgiving of 1621 , when Indigenous peoples and colonists coexisted. But there was brutal violence as well , such as English colonists’ efforts to destroy the Pequot of southern New England in 1637.

In the aftermath of early warfare, some Puritan clerics looked for new ways to convert Native Americans – and decided religious texts were the answer.

During the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther argued that the only infallible source of religious understanding was the Bible , a doctrine known as “sola scriptura.” Protestants believed the laity needed to become literate, in order to read Scripture for themselves.

The Puritans embraced this teaching, and in 1638, the Rev. Joseph Glover paid to transport a printing press to Cambridge , Massachusetts. Two years later, that press published the Bay Psalm Book , a collection of songs for worship – the first book printed in English North America.

In the years that followed, printers offered many religious tracts , often based on sermons. They believed that print would bring Protestant Christianity to a widening audience and provide guidance for existing believers.

A Puritan minister named John Eliot sailed from England to Boston in 1631 and soon took a leading role in the church at Roxbury, just south of the city. Eliot was so devoted to books that he purportedly brought 23 barrels of them with him from England.

By the 1640s, he began trying to spread his faith among Native residents of the region. To do so, he needed to be able to communicate with those he hoped to convert, and he understood that books could advance his cause.

Other colonists also hoped that print could foster good relations with the Native residents of New England. The most famous was Roger Williams, founder of Rhode Island. “ A Key into the Language of America ,” a book he published in London in 1643, provided phrases in Narragsansett , another Algonquian language. Such efforts were crucial to Europeans eager to trade with Native peoples – and to those, like Williams, who wanted to spread their culture without violence .

Eliot was intent on translating the Bible. He did not know Wampanoag, but he met an interpreter who impressed him: Cockenoe, a Montauk man from Long Island who had been taken captive during the Anglo-Pequot War in 1637. He became crucial to the Cambridge-educated cleric’s cause.

Eliot was unstinting in his praise of Cockenoe , whom he called a “pregnant witted young man.” He pronounced words clearly, which was crucial for Eliot: Like almost all Native languages in North America at the time, Wanpanoak did not have a writing system, so Eliot needed to transcribe what he heard.

Cockenoe’s instruction enabled Eliot to produce religious works in Wampanoag, including the Ten Commandments and the Lord’s Prayer. In 1663, printers Samuel Green and Marmaduke Johnson published “ Mamusse Wunneetupanatamwe Up-Biblum God ,” Eliot and Cockenoe’s full translation of the Bible.

Their Bible included some lines in English so that a literate person could recite the Native words out loud to others, even if they did not know the meaning. Green ordered enough paper to produce 1,000 copies of the book, although it is difficult to know how many existed.

Cockenoe was not the only Indigenous resident who worked on the Bible. Wawaus , a Nipmuc man from what is now central Massachusetts , helped set type for the book. Also known as James Printer, he was studying at Harvard’s Indian College , which had been established in 1655 to spread Christianity among Native peoples.

Eliot’s efforts to convert Indigenous peoples extended beyond translation , giving him the sobriquet “apostle to the Indians.”

He also worked with a missionary society to establish new towns where Algonquian-speaking peoples would abandon their traditional practices and live like colonists. Residents were to halt seasonal migrations, which had been crucial to their economies, and instead live year-round in houses. They were to dress like colonists, follow colonial laws and embrace Protestant religious practices .

Meanwhile, the growth of the colonial population was putting added pressure on Indigenous peoples who lived nearby. By the mid-1670s, any remaining goodwill between many Indigenous peoples and English colonists faded in a contest over limited resources , which was particularly difficult for Native Americans not living in the missionary communities.

In 1675, tensions erupted into what was called Metacom’s or King Philip’s War , named after the Wampanoag leader who led a widespread rebellion against colonists. The two-year conflict spread across southern New England and reached the shores of Casco Bay in present-day Maine. According to historian Jill Lepore , it was the deadliest war in American history , in proportion to the population.

Among the victims were the Native converts in the towns Eliot helped to establish, including Natick , a community west of Boston. Colonial authorities rounded them up, transported them to an island in Boston harbor and sold many into slavery . Even those who escaped the ravages of war found themselves struggling to maintain their shrinking lands .

Eliot believed that literacy was crucial for spreading his faith. In Cockenoe he found a talented partner. But mastering literacy could be a double-edged sword.

In 1676, in the midst of Metacom’s War, soldiers came across a note in English in the smoldering ruins of Medfield, a colonial town destroyed by Native Americans. Possibly written by Wawaus, the brief message warned that Indigenous residents would fight for years to maintain their lands .

Some colonizers, including Eliot, hoped to avoid using guns and bloodshed to advance their faith. But their goal was still destruction: to eliminate Algonquian cultures. As Wawaus’ note and Algonquian-speaking peoples’ presence in New England today reveal, those efforts failed.

Distinguished Professor and Professor of the Humanities, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences

items.title: US loses measles elimination status – an epidemiologist explains what it will take to regain it
items.summary: Americans forgot how serious measles can be – and misinformation on the dangers of vaccines proliferated. Outbreaks caused by falling vaccination rates led to the loss of a public health achievement attained in 2000. wildpixel/iStock via Getty ImagesThe United States has lost its measles elimination status – an international designation reflecting an absence of local measles transmission for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held since 2000. A commission of the Pan American Hea...

scraped.title: US loses measles elimination status – an epidemiologist explains what it will take to regain it
scraped.description: Americans forgot how serious measles can be – and misinformation on the dangers of vaccines proliferated.
scraped.author: Katrine L. Wallace
scraped.h1: US loses measles elimination status – an epidemiologist explains what it will take to regain it
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

The United States has lost its measles elimination status – an international designation reflecting an absence of local measles transmission for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held since 2000 . A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a formal announcement expected Nov. 17 .

Canada lost its measles elimination status in 2025 , as did the United Kingdom and other countries in Europe and central Asia in early 2026.

These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and still circulates in much of the world . What keeps the disease in check is herd immunity – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s at least 95% . But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine .

I’m an epidemiologist who studies misinformation in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage that kept measles from spreading.

A measles vaccine has existed in the U.S. since 1963 . The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about 97% effective . A federal program created in 1993 made it free for eligible children . After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases dropped more than 99% , and by 2000 measles was declared eliminated .

But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that maintaining elimination status would require sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread.

So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does.

Before the vaccine , measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases .

About 1 in 20 children who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called immune amnesia , leaving children open to infections they had already beaten.

In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis , which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a child in Los Angeles died of it .

As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 5,412 cases for 2026 – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, 1 in 6 have been hospitalized .

Six deaths appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which now relies on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in Pennsylvania , one in New York and two in Wisconsin .

Pennsylvania’s outbreak alone has produced 1,542 cases and 305 hospitalizations, by the state’s Nov. 13 count. Major outbreaks have also hit South Carolina, Utah and Arizona since the West Texas outbreak of early 2025, which was the start of the national surge of measles outbreaks. Utah’s outbreak , which began in June 2025, has gone well past the 12-month mark. That outbreak alone breaches the WHO’s definition of measles elimination and could have triggered the loss of elimination status .

When no one remembers the disease, the vaccine becomes the only thing left to fear. Misinformation feeds on that imbalance.

Parents who had never seen measles had nothing vivid to weigh against claims of vaccine risk, so even discredited risks felt plausible. A 1998 paper fraudulently linking MMR to autism was retracted in 2010 , and its author lost his medical license . But the damage was already done, and this myth persists to this day , even though studies that included millions of children have found no link .

During the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine misinformation proliferated in echo chambers on social media. It is no surprise that the percentage of kindergartners who have received their MMR shots has fallen every year since the 2019-20 school year.

In a 2025 KFF poll, parents who believed any false measles claim were more than twice as likely to have skipped or delayed vaccines . Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the anti-vaccine movement has also used the banner of medical freedom to gain a larger, more mainstream audience .

Now these arguments have found an audience in federal policy.

On Aug. 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an order calling for MMR to be split into three single-disease shots , which are not sold in the United States . There is no published evidence that separating MMR offers any benefit, and more doctor visits mean more chances for missed doses .

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested in August that Pennsylvania’s first two measles-associated deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” State officials had investigated both. While questioning the vaccine and measles deaths, he has promoted vitamin A and nutrition as measles cures. The CDC classifies vitamin A as a supportive treatment , not a cure or vaccine substitute.

Vaccination rates for the MMR vaccine among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in 2019-20 to 92.4% in 2025-26 . Exemptions from any required vaccine rose to a record 4.2% .

Of this year’s cases, 96% were unvaccinated or of unknown status. The 92.4% kindergarten vaccination rate leaves about 280,000 kindergartners without documented MMR. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with 75.2% among Idaho kindergartners , while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates.

Adult immunity also has gaps : Adults are 41% of this year’s cases, and 15% of them were hospitalized. Many who were vaccinated before 1989, when a second MMR dose was added, got only one.

Regaining elimination status means the U.S experiencing at least 12 months without continuous transmission . That will require the same factors that led to the U.S. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates.

But it will also require federal health leadership that is focused on bringing those things about.

The Department of Health and Human Services blames current vaccination gaps on missed pediatrician appointments during the COVID-19 pandemic. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said that the agency would not make any changes in measles response efforts in light of losing elimination status.

Additionally, orders like August’s about the MMR vaccine, and revisions to long-standing vaccine recommendations , are weakening vaccination efforts .

Also, on top of a chronically underfunded public health infrastructure , many career public health scientists lost their jobs in 2025. The surveillance capacity that made elimination possible has been substantially weakened .

So what does this mean for Americans? The loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. does not change the fact that the vaccine is safe and effective – and it is now more important than ever.

Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago

scraped.title: Democrats Signal US Return to Global Climate Talks - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: A congressional delegation at the United Nations COP31 climate conference says it hopes to rebuild the country’s credibility.
scraped.author: By Bob Berwyn
scraped.h1: Democrats Signal US Return to Global Climate Talks
scraped.body_text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections , a delegation of Democratic U.S. House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for U.S. climate and energy policy.

“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said.

President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the U.N. talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In , a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes and universities.

Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.

Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the U.S. from the U.N.’s climate framework, the extent of U.S. participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, U.S. congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.

“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News.

The U.S. would still be excluded from the formal government-to-government negotiations, but a congressional delegation representing the majority party, potentially capable of advancing climate and energy legislation, could make a difference, Huffman said.

“We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners … and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” said Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).

The new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the U.S. has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, said U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).

Casten said some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts.

“We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).

“I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she said. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the U.S. can rejoin that agreement, she added.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari said.

“But we will come back,” she said, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are … supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.”

Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena.

“We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” said Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation . “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.”

Singh said the U.S. has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power.

“As the world’s largest historical emitter, the U.S. carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he said. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.”

Singh said until the U.S. pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.”

Brandon Wu , with ActionAid USA , said the new Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress.

“What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping new climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added.

While meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman said he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible U.S. return to the climate talks.

“The fact is the U.S. has become kind of an unreliable partner and we’ve lost our credibility,” he said. “So we’ve tried to bring humility to this moment. We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.”

Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.

That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.

Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.

Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?

Please take a moment to make a tax-deductible donation. Every one of them makes a difference.

Thank you,

David Sassoon Founder and Publisher

Vernon Loeb Executive Editor

Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.
