scraped.title: Wildfire Lawsuits Against Utilities Fuel a Debate Over Who Should Pay - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Mounting legal actions against utility companies now have Western states—including California—mulling protections for electricity providers to curb the fallout.
scraped.author: By Gloria Dickie
scraped.h1: Wildfire Lawsuits Against Utilities Fuel a Debate Over Who Should Pay
scraped.body_text:
Trial by Fire: Second in a series about the impacts of wildfire litigation.

A week before Christmas 2025, 100-mile-per-hour wind gusts punished the foothills of Boulder, Colorado. An unusually dry summer and fall had parched trees and tall grasses. Snowfall across the county was roughly half the long-term average, and record-warm temperatures left none on the ground in the city below the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains. When the National Weather Service warned of exceptionally high wildfire danger, Xcel Energy cut power to more than 50,000 customers.

The utility’s caution came from experience. Under similar conditions almost exactly four years earlier, the Marshall Fire had burned more than 1,000 homes to the ground within hours, totaling over $2 billion in property losses. Investigators with the Boulder County Sheriff’s Office later concluded that an unmoored Xcel Energy power line was partially to blame for the blaze. Homeowners, businesses and insurers sued Xcel, which denied any fault, wrongdoing or negligence, but nevertheless settled for $640 million one day before a major civil trial was set to begin in September 2025.

In the aftermath of the fire, Xcel Energy implemented “Public Safety Power Shutoffs” on days when weather conditions are especially conducive to wildfires. Utilities in California have been doing the same since 2019, after their power lines ignited a series of catastrophic wildfires that brought billions of dollars in legal claims against the companies.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Xcel calls such proactive shutoffs a risk reduction measure. But the strategy—which has been used in Boulder County four times since 2024—left some residents furious. Many business owners lost revenue as the shutoff fell during the busiest shopping season of the year. City council members voted to send a letter to Xcel noting that “many residents feel the increasing instances of power outages when we have high winds … as being a consequence of prioritizing litigation avoidance ahead of protecting our community.”

“We understand that losing power for any amount of time is impactful and frustrating, but the safety of our customers, crews and the communities we serve remains a top priority,” an Xcel Energy spokesperson said.

Such criticism highlights the difficult situation utilities now find themselves in. Either cut power and enrage customers, or keep electricity flowing and risk igniting a devastating wildfire that could leave them exposed to multibillion-dollar lawsuits.

U.S. utility companies have faced more than $18 billion in wildfire liabilities over the past decade. As governments and communities struggle to respond to the staggering losses caused by the wildfire crisis burning the West, lawsuits against the utilities that ignite the blazes have emerged as the de facto recovery strategy. But the steep increase in wildfires’ destructiveness is the result of a combination of factors: a climate warmed by the burning of fossil fuels; decades of fire suppression and forestry policies that have increased the amount of flammable fuel in forests; and rapid development into fire-prone landscapes.

With another historic fire season gripping the West, and lawsuits already filed against electricity providers, states—from Oregon to Montana—are facing a reckoning over how much utilities can be expected to bear the costs of ever-worsening wildfires. Even California, the ground zero of sky-high wildfire litigation against utilities, appears to be coming to terms with the idea of offering some protections to utilities. Such reforms have become a key aspect of Governor Gavin Newsom’s political mission as he nears the end of his term in office, working to get a deal with legislators.

Attorneys behind cases against utilities argue high-dollar lawsuits force companies to operate more safely and deliver much-needed payouts to victims. But with those costs often passed onto customers through higher electricity rates, state governments are now considering how best to intervene. Policy experts observe that placing full blame on the entity responsible for sparking a wildfire may create a disincentive for homeowners and communities to carry out wildfire mitigation measures that could reduce destruction. And the approach raises questions of fairness in the judicial system—even for multibillion-dollar corporations.

Relying on lawsuits to cope with worsening wildfires has worked, in part, because ignition is everything in the U.S. legal context.

But the spark that ignites a wildfire has little to do with how much damage it ultimately does.

The actual number of U.S. wildfire ignitions has not dramatically increased over the past half-century. Around 50,000 to 70,000 wildfires burn across the country every year. The difference is that many more of these fires are growing into huge conflagrations—U.S. annual burned area is up roughly 60 percent since 1990.

Many of today’s catastrophic fires have been made more intense and more likely by climate change. Warmer temperatures, reduced humidity and greater aridity have bred increasingly favorable conditions for wildfires across the American West. In California alone, the average summer burned area is now five times larger than it was in the latter half of the 20th century. And nine of the largest wildfires in state history occurred in the last 10 years.

“We’ve been burning fossil fuels as a global society, and that’s really what’s driving it,” said Park Williams, a hydroclimatologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “Greenhouse gas molecules are not zapping the ground, starting fires on their own. But what they are doing is loading the dice for a fire to grow large quickly.”

Holding fossil fuel majors accountable has so far proved difficult. No groups or local governments have successfully won a final judgment against an oil company for climate impacts in a U.S. court. The U.S. Supreme Court is hearing a case that could knock out more than two dozen active claims, and Congress is considering legislation to shield the industry from such lawsuits altogether.

With fossil fuel companies so far avoiding accountability for helping to make landscapes more flammable, utility companies are bearing the brunt of claims over worsening wildfires.

Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, said wildfires should theoretically have proportional culpability. This would allow for different actors to be held liable for the extent to which they contributed to the damages from a fire.

“It’s scientifically inappropriate to pin [a wildfire] on just one thing,” he said. “It is not just a question of who ignited the spark or how we got to the point where that spark could create a catastrophe in the first place. It’s a question of both things.”

Teasing out the significance of each contributing factor, however, is a challenge. When determining culpability, “You can ask the question of had a utility-ignited fire begun in the same place, in the same setting, 100 years ago, were there other factors at play that would have resulted in a different outcome?” Swain said.

Scientists have found that the likelihood of years with extreme fire weather in the world’s forested regions is now far greater than in the late 19th century.

And some researchers specialize in parsing out the role climate change plays in making extreme weather events worse or more likely, a field known as attribution science. One such study by the World Weather Attribution group found that climate change had made the 2025 Los Angeles fires, which caused billions of dollars in property losses, 35 percent more likely. But models can vary widely, Swain cautioned. And while scientists have high confidence in being able to attribute worsening heat waves to climate change, wildfires present a more complex mix of factors including temperature, wind, soil moisture and land use. This makes such studies difficult to use as evidence in the courtroom.

Federal fire suppression policies have also left their mark on America’s woodlands. Historically, many western forests—ponderosa pine, mixed conifer and oak woodlands—burned at regular intervals, often every five to 30 years. But for much of the past century, U.S. land managers suppressed almost all naturally occurring wildfires.

Without frequent, low-intensity groundfires, forests have grown thick with woody fuels. Those heavy fuel loads are prone to burn far more intensely than wildfires did in the past.

Some of California’s costliest wildfires have struck communities along the Sierra Nevada’s forested foothills. Here, scientists estimate that some forests now contain three to 10 times as many trees as they did around the beginning of the 20th century. A 2022 report from the California Natural Resources Agency noted that between 10 and 30 million acres in the state would benefit from some form of fuel reduction treatment.

Policies requiring full suppression of wildfires have “gradually started changing, but it’s one of these issues that has strong cumulative effects,” said Chris Field, a climate scientist at Stanford University.

Moreover, the value of property at risk from wildfires has soared. In the past 35 years, millions of Americans have moved into the zone known as the “wildland-urban interface,” building homes in fire-prone forests, grasslands and mountainsides. By some estimates, approximately one-third of the U.S. population now lives in this flammable space.

Still, many homeowners have not hardened their homes against wildfire by building with non-combustible materials and creating defensible space around the property. A 2025 report commissioned by the Natural Resources Defense Council found that it would cost between $16 billion and $20 billion to moderately harden all homes in California’s high-risk wildfire zones. The 2024-25 state budget provided just $50 million for home-hardening programs.

“We’re seeing tensions between the way that the law assigns responsibility for fires and the way that we might think about the causes of fire in a more modern fire science context.”

Climate change, fuel suppression policies and riskier building practices should ultimately complicate the legal argument for putting the blame for the destructiveness of wildfires entirely on one thing, experts say. But so far, that’s not what has happened in courtrooms.

“We’re seeing tensions between the way that the law assigns responsibility for fires and the way that we might think about the causes of fire in a more modern fire science context,” said Eric Macomber, a wildfire legal fellow at Stanford University.

“You certainly need ignition for a fire. That’s one of the crucial elements. But in California, at least, we’ve acted to just assign complete liability to the party that sparks the fire. … It seems a little bit wrong to put the entire responsibility on the individual or the entity that sparks it.”

To date, much of the compensation awarded in wildfire cases has gone to cover direct losses, such as destroyed property, providing a critical stop-gap for those who were underinsured or unable to obtain home insurance in the first place. Hundreds of thousands of homeowners in the West are no longer able to renew their policies as insurers retreat from areas they consider too vulnerable to wildfire.

“There is a real conversation to be had about how you allocate risk between utilities and insurance,” Macomber said. “You can move the ball to the different sides of the seesaw, but it’s so big that it’s just going to unsettle whatever industry ends up bearing most of it.”

California’s Pacific Gas and Electric filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection following destructive 2017-2018 fires in Northern California that left the company facing legal claims in excess of $30 billion over its aging and allegedly inadequately maintained equipment that had sparked the blazes. It ultimately reached a $13.5 billion settlement with victims and undertook a significant financial restructuring. Some of that money went to victims of the Camp Fire, which ravaged the town of Paradise and racked up an estimated $16.5 billion in economic losses, according to reinsurance giant Munich Re.

Victims were also able to claim compensation for non-economic losses—the trauma and emotional suffering inflicted as the flames took lives, destroyed neighborhoods and shattered memories.

In a 2023 ruling against PacifiCorp, a large utility that provides electricity to about 2.1 million customers in six Western states, a jury awarded 17 plaintiffs $67.5 million in pain and suffering for the 2020 Labor Day fires in Oregon that killed 11 people and displaced tens of thousands. The verdict was reversed by an Oregon appeals court in April 2026 over improper instructions to the jury. The Oregon Supreme Court is now reviewing that decision, and survivors of the fires have filed a motion to disqualify the appeals court judge, who had previously represented PacifiCorp in private practice.

Utility companies have dealt with the onslaught of lawsuits in part by raising energy rates for customers to cover legal claims and pay for wildfire mitigation efforts, including infrastructure upgrades. In California, wildfire costs have been the single largest driver of investor-owned utility rate increases over the past five years, with experts estimat ing that wildfire-related costs accounted for 14 percent to 19 percent of the average California residential electricity bill in 2024, up from 7 percent to 12 percent between 2019 and 2023.

A report from the California Public Utilities Commission, published on Nov. 1, found that from 2020 through 2026, Pacific Gas and Electric, Southern California Edison, and San Diego Gas and Electric ratepayers alone paid more than $35 billion in wildfire-related costs, with mitigation work making up the lion’s share of charges.

“What has happened in California has reduced wildfire risk from utilities,” Macomber said. “But it’s also generated a lot of other costs that ultimately get passed onto utility customers in a way that can be a lot more aggressive than simply funding fire mitigation work through something like taxation.” Tax systems would spread the costs more broadly and cheaply across a population, as opposed to higher rates borne by a smaller group of utility customers.

Investor-owned utilities are generally more vulnerable to wildfire liabilities than municipal utilities that operate largely in cities. Private utilities have extensive infrastructure located in remote areas to deliver electricity to rural customers. Thousands of miles of power lines are overgrown with vegetation that utility crews often struggle to clear, and are susceptible to high winds that can blow live wires and sparks into the dry fuels.

All of this makes it easy for power lines to start fires—and difficult for firefighters to quickly reach a blaze. Although investigators fail to find the ignition source for between a third and half of all wildfires in the Western U.S., fires caused by power generation, transmission or distribution are a growing source of ignitions, according to a 2025 study in the journal Earth’s Future.

To avoid the risk altogether, some utilities have turned to power shutoffs.

In Colorado, Xcel Energy said it has invested $1.5 billion since 2020 as part of a wildfire mitigation plan that includes replacing older wires susceptible to wind damage, installing protected insulated wires in some areas and burying select portions of distribution lines in the highest wildfire risk areas.

But even once fully implemented, power shutoffs—which began following the Marshall Fire—will remain part of Xcel’s strategy to prevent disasters during extreme fire weather, the company says. That has become a mainstay strategy of California utilities, too.

An analysis by Inside Climate News of California Public Utilities Commission data found that that state has had a total of 128 public safety power shut-offs involving more than 4.5 million customers between January 2018 and the end of October 2026. (If a customer was cut off on more than one occasion, they are counted once for each event.) Since October 2021, when the commission started providing data on the areas covered by each shut-off, they have mostly coincided with the National Weather Service issuing a “red flag” warning of high wildfire risk, corresponding to strong winds, low humidity and dry fuels.

While some shutoffs have occurred outside of red flag conditions, these have typically affected a small number of customers, suggesting utilities are reluctant to pull the plug on thousands of people without clear signs of danger. For 93 percent of the customers that had their power cut, a red flag fire warning overlapping with the affected area was issued within three days of the shutoff.

Utilities can face liabilities if they continue to provide power under hazardous conditions. PacifiCorp was initially found liable for the 2020 Labor Day Fires by a jury for failing to shut off power during severe fire weather warnings. And, in the aftermath of the Eaton Fire that devastated the suburb of Altadena in January 2025, killing 19 people and destroying more than 9,000 buildings, Los Angeles County sued Southern California Edison , alleging that the utility failed to de-energize power lines and other equipment in the face of a red flag warning.

In an unfortunate irony, public safety power shutoffs present their own unique climate health risks. Recent health research shows that widespread and long-lasting power outages during hot days have disproportionately large effects on death rates.

A 2026 study in the journal Science Advances found that 42 percent of burned area from 2001 to 2024 in the West occurred during and immediately following heat waves—when many Americans need electricity for air-conditioners and fans to combat stifling temperatures.

Some states are beginning to recognize the limitations of utility companies in assuming such a large burden for catastrophic wildfires. Wyoming , Idaho and Montana all passed legislation in 2025 creating liability protections for utilities that ignite wildfires, provided the company deemed responsible for the blaze followed a government-approved wildfire mitigation plan.

Utah has had a similar law on the books since 2020, and in 2024 further protected power companies by allowing large utilities to proactively charge their customers additional fees to build a fund for future fire liabilities as a supplement to existing insurance.

Critics have contended that this provides a disintentive for utilities to operate more safely. Legislators argue the measures will help to stabilize utilities and prevent bankruptcies .

Berkshire Hathaway, which owns Western utilities through its subsidiary PacificCorp and was long run by billionaire Warren Buffett, has been accused of pushing such “shield laws” to limit payouts. At a 2024 shareholders meeting, Buffett threatened to sell off some of the company’s electric utilities if more Western states did not set limits on wildfire liabilities.

PacifiCorp told Inside Climate News it has spent $2.2 billion since 2020 to resolve more than 4,500 “reasonable” wildfire claims—approximately 90 percent of all wildfire claims made against the company. PacifiCorp today is valued at around $70 billion.

“The risk of wildfire makes operating a utility more expensive for customers by restricting access to crucial investments and contributing to higher costs,” PacificCorp spokesperson Simon Gutierrez told Inside Climate News. “With that in mind, wildfire-related issues must be solved holistically, with governments, businesses and key stakeholders working together to design and implement constructive, enduring solutions as we have seen implemented in several states.”

Though red states have led the charge in introducing utility protections, blue states are beginning to follow in their footsteps. Last year, Hawaiʻi approved a yet-to-be-determined liability cap for utilities facing claims over catastrophic wildfires. Similar legislation was under consideration in Oregon , though it did not proceed. California—the state with the most insured wildfire losses over the past decade—is also starting to reckon with how much money wildfire victims can potentially claw back from utility companies.

In 2019, the state set up a $21 billion wildfire fund to help cover wildfire claims tied to utility equipment, acknowledging that investor-owned utilities themselves were now struggling to get insurance to cover their operations. The fund is supported both by utilities’ shareholders, via a capital injection, and ratepayers through a surcharge on their bill. If a utility is found to have acted imprudently, it must reimburse the fund for the amount paid out. So far, the fund has issued more than $1 billion to PG&E for the 2021 Dixie Fire and 2019 Kincade Fire.

California lawmakers recently approved an additional $18 billion fund over concerns that damages from the 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles County could otherwise consume much of the existing fund.

The state has also considered further measures to aid utilities. In April, following directions from Governor Gavin Newsom, the agency that administers the original wildfire fund released a report exploring how the state could fairly allocate the costs of wildfires and stabilize the energy utility sector.

The report considers eliminating a rule, known as inverse condemnation, that holds California’s utility companies liable for wildfires sparked by their equipment, even if they did not act negligently, and considers other liability reforms, such as capping payouts for non-economic damages like emotional pain and suffering, and eliminating punitive damages for alleged utility-sparked wildfires.

Behind the scenes, Gov. Gavin Newsom had proposed to legislators a plan to reduce the costs for electrical utilities that included curbing reimbursements to insurance companies for massive payouts to homeowners when power lines spark a fire, and limiting how much local governments can recoup for incinerated infrastructure, according to reporting by CalMatters .

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

But legislators came back with a narrower proposal that did not provide any new protections for utilities. Ultimately, the bill failed to receive a second vote, effectively killing the legislation and leaving no clear pathway to resolve who should pay when utilities ignite wildfires.

Altadena resident Joy Chen is the founder of the Every Fire Survivor’s Network, a nonprofit representing the more than 10,000 survivors of the Eaton and Palisades fires. She strongly objected to any move that would reduce utilities liabilities for wildfires.

“[Newsom’s] original proposal was breathtaking. It would have crippled the ability of survivors to recover from future wildfires,” she said.

“We have a basic principle we teach our children: ‘You break it. You fix it.’ Not, ‘You break it, you cause catastrophic harm, kill people, destroy the lives of tens of thousands of people. And you walk away scot-free with record profits, record shareholder dividends and record executive pay.’”

Plaintiff attorneys who have worked on some of the state’s largest wildfire lawsuits also denounced any move by the state to cap utility liability.

“People that have lost their homes, lost their businesses, lost loved ones, need to be compensated,” said Gerald Singleton, a managing partner with Singleton Schreiber law firm in San Diego who also serves as chair of the American Association for Justice’s Wildfires Litigation Group .

In the long-term, costly lawsuits, he said, play an important safety role in pushing utilities to invest in infrastructure upgrades and act more responsibly. For example, after PG&E filed for bankruptcy as a result of the $13.5 billion settlement, “they brought in a completely new team and fundamentally revamped their corporate culture,” Singleton said. “Now it’s not a panacea. They’ve started fires since then. But they’ve gotten a lot better.”

To address affordability issues, he added, states should municipalize utilities, transferring control to a state or local government.

“Without the mass tort attorney bar holding the utilities accountable, they will continue to burn down California,” said Richard Bridgford, a California trial attorney who has represented thousands of victims in suits against Southern California Edison and PG&E. “They make a fatal decision every time there are high winds between profits and the public safety.”

Like Singleton, he advocated for governments to have more control over utilities, especially decisions on power shutoffs. “This is highly dangerous equipment, and when there are high winds, that’s not a decision that a for-profit entity should be allowed to make,” Bridgford said.

Utility profits, Bridgford argued, have contributed to cash bonuses for executives despite soaring wildfire claims. In 2024, Southern California Edison infrastructure ignited 135 fires , up from 86 in 2023, according to the company’s regulatory filings with the California Public Utilities Commission. Still, cash bonuses went up for four of Edison’s top five executives that year.

David Eisenhauer, a spokesperson for Southern California Edison, noted that 82 percent of those 135 ignitions were smaller than 0.25 acres in size, and the company is required to report any ignition that travels larger than one linear meter from a spark.

Since 2020, “safety appropriately plays a role in how our executives are compensated,” Eisenhauer said. California’s Office of Energy Infrastructure Safety reviews and approves executive compensation programs every year, which includes safety metrics and performance.

This March, Edison announced that a half-dozen senior executives would lose an estimated $2 million in bonuses as a result of the 2025 Eaton Fire.

In the wake of the most expensive fires in California history, Southern California Edison is beginning to test the waters of proportional culpability in the courts.

After Los Angeles County sued Edison over the Eaton Fire, alleging the utility’s equipment had caused the blaze, Edison filed cross claims against the county and several other public and private entities, arguing that they contributed to the fire’s devastating spread. To many observers, it seems like an inflection point.

Edison does not accept that its infrastructure started the fire, but lawyers for the company argue that even if that was the case, Los Angeles County failed to clear the brush that contributed to the intensity of the blaze. Among other alleged shortcomings, company lawyers have also asserted the county failed to ensure a sufficient water supply to fight the fire.

The case is now part of sprawling mass-tort litigation that is heading for a jury trial .

LA County did not respond to a request for comment.

“That fire would not have traveled as far, gotten as hot, and been as damaging if it weren’t for the actions and inactions of others,” said Douglas Dixon, a founding partner of law firm Hueston Hennigan, who is representing Southern California Edison in the lawsuit. “When it comes to the wrongful death lawsuits that have been asserted, we think that there are folks who do share some of the responsibility for the tragic deaths of these people.”

Dixon has represented roughly a dozen utilities or other defendants accused of igniting wildfires across the Western U.S. since 2018. He told Inside Climate News he has often highlighted contributing climate factors in his defense arguments.

For example, the role of climate change was a key focus in the lawsuits against PacifiCorp for sparking Oregon’s 2020 Labor Day fires. Those fires were “clearly enabled by record-setting atmospheric aridity across much of the West,” one study in the journal Global Change Biology found.

“The environmental angle was something we made front and center in the trial because we felt it was an important part,” Dixon said. “Then you combine that with urban sprawl. People are now living in areas that are more susceptible to wildfires and that absolutely has an impact on the extent of destruction.”

PacifiCorp was still found liable in the ruling. It’s since been reversed by the Oregon Court of Appeals and is awaiting review by the Oregon Supreme Court.

Juries, Dixon said, have largely ignored contributing climate factors and focused on ignition alone when delivering their verdicts.

“I think what happens is that you have a jury who sees people who have gone through a terrible ordeal. It’s a very heart-wrenching story. And they happen to see that there’s a corporation, a utility, that’s blamed for starting the fire,” Dixon said. “The cynic in me says, it’s just easier for them to say, ‘OK, they must have some money, and we think that they should help pay to make these people whole.’”

In the case of Colorado’s 2021 Marshall Fire, for example, investigators determined two separate ignition points—one from Xcel Energy, and another from embers from a burn of refuse on private property owned by the Twelve Tribes, a religious group. Yet no civil lawsuits were brought against Twelve Tribes—only Xcel. (Investigators found that Twelve Tribes had extinguished its fire “responsibly.”)

“Utilities make an easy target. They’re viewed as deep pockets,” Dixon said.

Some may feel uncomfortable arguing that utility companies found to spark a wildfire should not be entirely liable financially—especially when the victims suing them have lost everything. But experts see worrying implications for how the nation builds resilience to wildfire and responds to climate change when utilities alone are on the hook for a much larger crisis fueled by the oil and gas industry and the governments that refuse to kick their fossil fuel habit.

“I’m not necessarily defending any of these people or entities,” said Swain, the scientist. “But the broader problem is that if we focus on these entities as the singular culprit, then we’re really going to miss the more important question: How do we make it so these disasters become less likely and less terrible over time?”

Inside Climate News data journalist Peter Aldhous contributed reporting.

scraped.title: Carbon dioxide is a climate problem. It might also be a laundry solution.
scraped.description: A technology born in aerospace uses liquid CO2 to wash clothes without water or a dryer. The challenge is making it work in a home appliance.
scraped.author: Naoki Nitta
scraped.h1: Carbon dioxide is a climate problem. It might also be a laundry solution.
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain.

Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer.

Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons .

Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on.

In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat.

Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps, and compressors.

Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one third of what’s inside a full scuba tank . As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’s chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing.

For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry.

The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said.

As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint.

Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance?

LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work.

LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to sugars, salts, and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS , raising questions about environmental trade-offs.

Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.”

Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously.

The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag . CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium.

Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings, and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration, and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said.

Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend.

The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question.

Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance.

Andrew Joseph

Andrew covers the biopharma industry, scientific research, and public health across the continent. You can reach Andrew confidentially on Signal at drewqjoseph.71.

The Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved a new breast cancer drug from Roche, teeing up the launch of a medicine that the Swiss company has said could become its top-selling product ever.

The approval of Wilserdly, also known as giredestrant, was one of the most important regulatory decisions Roche had been awaiting. It also gives the company another foothold in breast cancer treatments, a field in which it has a storied history with the drug Herceptin through its subsidiary Genentech, though in recent years it’s fallen behind rival pharma companies in oncology.

Advertisement

The approval is specifically for patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that has picked up a mutation in the ESR1 gene, a sign that the tumor is developing resistance to standard treatments. The evERA trial showed that the drug, an oral treatment known as a selective estrogen receptor degrader, or SERD, extended the time period before patients’ tumors progressed.

By Margaret Manto

Nov. 16, 2026

Washington Correspondent

Margaret Manto

Margaret is a Washington correspondent covering the Food and Drug Administration and other federal health agencies. Reach her on Signal at margaretmanto.61.

WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration is proposing a new classification for a product that’s existed in a legal gray area for years, a win for proponents of dietary supplements, including members of the MAHA movement.

The proposed rule would classify N-acetyl-L-cysteine, known as NAC and already widely sold over the counter, as the agency’s first “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition” — in essence, not not a supplement.

Advertisement

The need for the legal backbending stems from the fact that the FDA previously approved NAC as a drug, and FDA regulations prohibit the agency from including approved drugs in the dietary supplement category. scraped.title: The small African lab sounding the alarm on AI bioweapons
scraped.description: After researchers in Accra stripped the guardrails off a drug-discovery AI, it designed 1,020 toxic proteins—sparking urgent calls for DNA synthesis screening and global biosecurity regulation.
scraped.h1: The small African lab sounding the alarm on AI bioweapons
scraped.body_text:
Innovation

MinoHealth researchers in Ghana jailbroke their own LLM as a test. What emerged were thousands of toxin recipes—and an urgent push for regulation.

Out of curiosity, researchers at a small artificial intelligence lab in Accra, Ghana, removed the guardrails on their drug discovery AI model in 2024. They asked it to design toxins instead.

The model produced designs for 1,020 proteins and 5,000 small molecules. The researchers never made any of them in a lab, but software that predicts how poisonous a substance is scored all of them as likely toxic. Some of them resembled ricin, a deadly poison. The study was uploaded to the preprint server arXiv in May 2025.

“We were all shocked,” Darlington Akogo, founder of MinoHealth AI Labs, told Rest of World.

For Akogo, the results also raised a new question: If someone took designs like these to a company that makes DNA to order, would anyone stop them?

Across Africa, the need to regulate DNA synthesis providers is now echoing through the highest levels of government, Brenda Obuya, a senior official at Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, told Rest of World.

Akogo has traveled the world warning that AI poses an existential bioweapons threat. He discussed it on the sidelines of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund Spring Meetings held in Washington, D.C., last year. He discussed the broader risk over dinner with Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates in 2023, whom he described as “on the fence” at the time. This year, Gates has issued numerous public warnings. “A.I. has crossed the threshold that its ability to empower a bioterrorist to kill hundreds of millions, that exists today,” he said on The Ezra Klein Show in September. The study has been discussed within Interpol, showing just how far it has reached.

“I think the fact that the Ghanaian AI lab examined this and highlighted the potential for misuse shows that African institutions are contributing to … potentially to the governance [of AI],” Adam Abdullahi, a fellow at the International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science, told Rest of World .

LLMs have become even more capable since the study came out and the barrier for entry has lowered, Ayantola Alayande, a researcher at the Global Center on AI Governance, told Rest of World. “It wouldn’t be a surprise now to see even … [lay] users generate this sort of output via chatbots.”

Dual use

Scholars have long warned about AI’s bioweapons threat, but it is only recently that AI systems have truly outperformed Ph.D.-level biologists .

In 2022, scientists at a U.S. drug company ran a similar experiment as the MinoHealth team. They built a generative machine learning software that produced designs for possible chemical weapons.

What is different with the MinoHealth Lab study, Akogo said, is the kind of AI involved. His team used a general purpose LLM trained for biology and drug discovery.

Researchers have since gotten a number of LLMs to drop their inbuilt safeguards in a process called “jailbreaking”, and generated bioweapons advice and other kinds of hazardous content. This includes Kimi, by the Chinese company Moonshot AI; Grok; Claude; and ChatGPT, said Peter Garraghan, founder of AI security company Mindgard . All it takes is persistence and creativity with language to learn how to phrase requests to the model, he told Rest of World .

“You don’t need to be a technical expert to do jailbreaking,” he said . It took his team one day to break Kimi .

SpaceXAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Moonshot did not respond to a request for comment.

The latest AI models have stronger safeguards , particularly when it comes to biological misuse requests, but even these are not foolproof, according to the AI Security Institute, a U.K. government research organization.

The danger became more real this September when Anthropic reported five cases where people tried to use its AI models in ways that could support biological weapons development. Bioweapons are now the top AI misuse risk , according to Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, the U.K.’s intelligence agency. “The misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight – is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” he said.

All-in-one health AI model

When Akogo founded MinoHealth Labs in 2016, he wasn’t worried about bioweapons. Rather, he wanted to make care available to all by solving Ghana’s health worker shortage using AI.

That goal took Akogo to the edge of AI development in 2022, when his team began work on an LLM named Moremi AI. A year later, they received $149,533 from the Gates Foundation to build a foundation model that can analyze medical images for radiologists. The model would eventually process both text and images, answer medical questions, help interpret scans, and draft reports. It would also help design drugs.

The ambition is similar in scope to top Silicon Valley labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, Leo Anthony Celi, a principal research scientist at the MIT Laboratory of Computational Physiology, told Rest of World. In October 2025, Anthropic launched Claude for Life Sciences , and this April, Open AI launched GPT-Rosalind . Both are AI tools developed to accelerate biology research and drug discovery. Investment in AI powered drug discovery reached $8.4 billion in 2025, more than double the $4.1 billion invested in 2023, according to a 2026 McKinsey report .

MinoHealth has a fraction of these resources and a 20-member team working in a modest bungalow in Accra that is the anti-thesis of Silicon Valley’s futuristic campuses .

In the early days, Akogo had sleepless nights. He worried his competitors were better funded, and had more talent. But he has since decided there is room for multiple companies working on specific use cases.

“I have a small team of extremely capable people so if that means we’re punching above our weight, I guess … it’s just more exciting,” he said.

When his team tested their model, Moremi Bio, in 2024 to see if it could be made to ignore safeguards, it took them only a few days, Akogo recalled. Few people back then knew that biology LLMs’ could have a dual purpose, so he decided to publish his findings. “To the best of our knowledge, [looking at published studies], this was the first time anyone was showing that LLMs specifically could design biological weapons,” he said.

AI models shouldn’t be able to design potential bioweapons, Abdullahi said. “The whole idea of putting guardrails is that it should never really kind of get to that stage, so to speak.”

Synthesis

Bad actors could potentially send the bioweapon designs to DNA synthesis labs to make the molecules. Although some labs screen orders for potentially toxic sequences, this process could be hacked by a malicious actor using AI, Akogo said.

In June, the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind joined a call for U.S. lawmakers to make such checks mandatory .

Governments across Africa recognize that open-source frontier models have lowered the technical barrier to generate toxins, said Obuya from Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy. Cloud laboratories and AI models have created a need for regulation, she said. Intelligence agencies are setting up specialized desks to track threats at the “intersection of cyber defense and biology,” she said.

As AI design tools develop, screening must keep pace, Sandra Roy, program manager at the International Gene Synthesis Consortium, a voluntary group of nucleic acid providers, told Rest of World . They support legislation that would mandate screening across the nucleic acid supply chain, she said.

“We are also working with model developers to strengthen our ability to detect AI-designed sequences that may be engineered to evade screening, and we will keep updating our tools as the threat evolves,” she said.

AI for healthcare

Moremi Bio is currently good at a few things. For instance, it has proposed hundreds of drug candidates for diseases such as cancer, tuberculosis, and dengue. The team is now working as part of a European Union-funded consortium to develop monoclonal antibodies and diagnostics for mpox and malaria. The company is predominantly funded through sales of its AI system, Akogo said.

The promise of AI in healthcare and biology aside, Akogo continues to raise the alarm over AI risks, especially bioweapons. He believes the United Nations should set up a dedicated working group to study the risks of AI. He also suggested tighter controls over synthesis. His goal isn’t to scare people, but rather, to balance AI optimism with caution.

“I think there’s several things we can do that could limit and minimize those dangers,” he said.

Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

The founder’s stunning departure removes Beijing’s biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling, and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next.

scraped.description: Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless.
scraped.h1: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
scraped.body_text:
Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here .

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

scraped.h1: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
scraped.body_text:
Sponsored

While we’re used to predictable technology, AI challenges that assumption. Therefore, the goal must be bounded, observable, and controllable AI.

Provided by UL Solutions

In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.

Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

scraped.h1: The Download: testing tech promises and searching for cognitive immortality
scraped.body_text:
Plus: Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

How do you measure progress towards the future? In the Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , our series “ Are we there yet? ” examines how far six potentially transformative technologies have come after years of promises.

We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten. Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise. Nuclear-powered spaceships Exercise in a pill Interspecies communication Solid-state batteries Cleaning up PFAS Eliminating traffic deaths

Subscribe now to get every issue of our print magazine as soon as it lands.

Could technology keep your brain going beyond death? Far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to make it happen, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores these ideas and how close they might be to reality.

Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion tomorrow.

Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST .

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO He’s discussed with confidants the possibility of returning. ( FT $) + Elon Musk has joined 165,000 signatories calling for his recall. ( Guardian ) + The Treasury Secretary wants them to hire an outsider. ( Axios ) + ​​Megaspeed says the alleged China spy left the company last year. ( BBC ) + Trump plans to name Nvidia an AI “national champion.” ( WSJ $) + Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 SpaceX has caught a rocket returning from orbit for the first time The feat brings fully reusable rockets closer to reality. ( Guardian ) + The feat shows what audacious engineering can achieve. ( Atlantic $) + Meanwhile, Ukraine says SpaceX is lying about Starshield speed restrictions. ( Reuters $)

3 The US and allies have agreed to guard AI supply chains from China Ten countries will collaborate to secure critical technologies. ( FT $) + Chinese AI stocks have plunged on export control fears. ( Information $) + Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 The US flight shutdown exposed weaknesses in air traffic technology Officials blamed the disruption on a faulty router installation. ( Reuters $) + It was a terrible week of outages. ( WP $)

5 The first in-body CRISPR treatment is set to reach patients next year The treatment could gain FDA approval as early as March. ( Nature ) + CRISPR has created female clones of male mice. ( MIT Technology Review )

6 Congress plans to make data centers pay billions more for power A proposed bill would shift grid costs onto tech companies. ( NYT $) + Utilities also want tech giants to pay more for power. ( Bloomberg $) + Is data center hatred all about electricity? ( MIT Technology Review )

7 Apple plans to launch its first smart glasses next year It’s betting on Siri to give the specs an edge. ( Verge )

8 Bill Gates has made billions from climate-polluting landfills His investment in a landfill operator is worth $29 billion. ( ProPublica )

9 ​​A new AI device turns everyday objects into needy virtual pets The tiny gadgets aim to encourage healthier everyday habits. ( Wired $)

10 Scientists made monkeys watch Minions to study their brains Their findings challenge traditional vision models. ( 404 Media )

Quote of the day

—Helen Toner, former OpenAI board member, tells The Verge that AI needs stronger governance than trusting tech executives to do the right thing.

One more thing

When Kenneth Wehr started managing the Greenlandic-language version of Wikipedia, he discovered that almost every article had been written by people who didn’t speak the language.

A growing number of them had been copy-pasted into Wikipedia from machine translators—and were riddled with elementary mistakes. This is beginning to cause a wicked problem.

AI systems, from Google Translate to ChatGPT, learn new languages by scraping text from Wikipedia. This could push the most vulnerable languages on Earth toward the precipice.

Read the full story on what happens when AI gets trained on junk pages .

—Jacob Judah

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ Adelaide Zoo is celebrating its first cassowary eggs in 34 years. + Photos fill the frame at the Epson Pano awards , which celebrate panoramic photography. + Indonesia has called an early halt to the world's largest deforestation project , saving up to 4 million acres. + After over a month on the loose in Yellowstone, a little dog called Luna has been reunited with her owners.

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.

Plus: A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble.

Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.
