scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is in its second and final week. To get an update on the state of negotiations among countries, we speak with longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He says rich, developed countries are still dragging their feet on a rapid transition away from fossil fuels while withholding the money that poorer, Global South countries need.

“Whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses which are totalling over a trillion right now, you need public finance,” says Rehman. “And the rich countries are saying, 'Our coffers are empty.' But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires.”

AMY GOODMAN : Yes, this is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. We’re broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit in Turkey.

ASAD REHMAN : We are in the midst of a crisis, of a crisis of crisis. We could see that with the killer floods, droughts and famines impacting people everywhere. Our ecosystems are collapsing. We’re about to breach the critical 1.5-degree guardrail with devastating consequences.

AMY GOODMAN : That was longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He was outside on Saturday, marching with thousands of people in the rain, demanding climate action, joining us now inside the COP .

We welcome you back to Democracy Now! , Asad. Why don’t we start off by talking about what has been accomplished here? We’re midway through. Democracy Now! will be broadcasting throughout this week. The end is supposed to be on Friday. There was a draft release, a release of a draft document, today by the head of the COP . It’s here in Turkey, but it is being — you can explain this — officiated over by Australia. What was said, and what wasn’t, and what are the key issues, like electrification?

ASAD REHMAN : Sure. Always a pleasure to be here, Amy.

And so, the cover note is a political instrument. It’s not a negotiated text. And it’s generally written by the presidency of the COPs. We have a bit of a unique situation in that we have both Turkey and Australia currently in charge of these climate negotiations. So, Australia says it’s in charge of the negotiations, and Turkey in charge of the COP itself. So, the cover note is — I mean, it’s an interesting thing, because we’ve seen these cover notes now appear often at COPs. Many of them make grand announcements and then disappear into the dust. You may remember, I think back in Glasgow, at COP26, there were announcements about phasing out inefficient fossil fuels. There was announcements about increasing the ambition of emission reductions by 2030. None of those things came to pass. So, you have to take these cover notes also with a pinch of salt.

Now, in the cover note itself, there are so many different pieces, often very, very contradictory. But cut through all of the jargon, and there are three key things that are at play there. The first is electrification. This is a call by the Turkish presidency themselves that by 2035, 35% of our energy needs are met are electricity. Now, on paper, it sounds great, but lift the hood, and there are some real issues at it. First of all, when they talk about energy, they’re talking about clean energy, which includes nuclear. Secondly, this is not about energy access, so it’s not about the close to 700-800 million people who currently don’t have access to electricity. Often what they’re talking about is electricity for the richest countries to power gas — energy-guzzling data centers, electric vehicles, etc. Secondly, there is no commitment about actually the finance that is needed or the technology. So, it’s going to sound really, really great, but will it deliver to those people? Probably not.

The second thing that’s in here is a lot about what is being called the overshoot. Look, the lack of action by developed countries to do their fair share has now taken us to the brink of breaching the critical 1.5-degree guardrail. We’ve seen the consequences all around the world, of course, devastating fires, floods, famines. But now what these rich countries are saying is, “Well, let’s go beyond the 1.5. And what we’ll do is we’ll bank on risky and unproven technologies to suck carbon out of the atmosphere,” which will, of course, be a green light for massive land grabs, for massive ocean grabs. And secondly, what we’ll do is open the door to even more dangerous geoengineering possibilities, as well.

And the third big thing in there is, of course, about finance. Now, rich countries haven’t been meeting their promises. If you remember all the way back to Copenhagen, Hillary Clinton promised rich countries $100 billion in climate finance. Less than a third of that was ever provided in real grants. And since then, just in one year alone, poorer developing countries, often trapped in debt, have paid 225 times more in debt repayments than they’ve got in climate finance. And now what’s being offered to them again is more debt-creating loans, not public finance. And this is really critical, because whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses, which are totaling over a trillion right now, you need public finance. And the rich countries are saying, “Our coffers are empty.” But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires, who, of course, are not paying their fair share of tax, or the corporations.

AMY GOODMAN : I want to go to the Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, who was just here at the COP31 last Thursday.

GRETA THUNBERG : We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights, and where basic necessities become luxury. And it is more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying; it is being killed. And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue. When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it becomes our duty, everyone’s duty, but especially the more privileged you are, the bigger your responsibility to stand up, to be the adult in the room and to fight for the rights of our human rights and for everyone’s human rights.

AMY GOODMAN : So, that was Greta Thunberg on Thursday. And, of course, the context of all of this, the backdrop is the war in Iran and the amount of money that is being spent on it, the terrible casualties as a result, and the — what it makes the world aware of: The price we pay for fossil fuels was the shutting down of the Strait of Hormuz. Then you have President Trump, President Xi of China and Putin about to meet in the first-ever trilateral summit on Thursday. Your thoughts of what should be accomplished here and what they should be dealing with there?

ASAD REHMAN : Look, I think we all recognize that we’re not just dealing with a climate crisis and breaching the 1.5. Our ecosystem, the very things that humanity needs to survive, let alone thrive, are collapsing around us. But we’re also facing a growing crisis of inequality, economic inequality. Millions, if not billions, of people are struggling, not just now in the Global South, but increasingly in the Global North, as well. And that’s given rise to a rise of authoritarianism, of far-right and fascist politics, who are weaponizing inequality against change, who are saying, “Raise the walls and fences, pour more money into militarization to protect us,” rather than actually fighting to ensure that everybody can live with dignity.

So, what these governments are proposing and are on the table, actually, is far away from what we actually need. What we really need is governments to be doubling down and saying, “Actually, we can make sure that people have adequate and affordable homes, that are warm during the winter and cool during the summer. We can make sure that people have the right to food, to good incomes, to good jobs. And we can make sure we do that not just for our citizens in the Global North, but citizens in the Global South.” Instead, what we’re having is world leaders who are turning their backs on multilateralism, who are turning their backs on humanity as a whole, and are saying, “Well, actually, there is no future but a future of brutality and of war and of conflict.”

AMY GOODMAN : What do you think of the United States not being here, the historically largest carbon and gas emitter? And then you have the current largest polluter, China, has one of the largest delegations there, though not the president, Xi.

ASAD REHMAN : Look, this place is important, because the U.N. climate space is one of the very few places you have where every single country is represented and where the voices of people who are most impacted can actually try and hold our governments to account, because, otherwise, this will be held in shadowy backrooms, the richest countries by themselves. So it’s important. And, of course, it’s not — it’s key that the United States is here, but the United States has been here and has done its best to disrupt and dismantle the climate negotiations.

The real question is, is: What about the other rich developed countries, the United Kingdom, the European Union and others? Are they stepping up and doing their fair share? Are they showing?

AMY GOODMAN : Are they?

ASAD REHMAN : Well, they’re not doing. I mean, I come from — I’m living in the United Kingdom. We’ve just greenlighted one fossil fuel expansion in Jackdaw. We have Rosebank, where the government is still hesitating. We’re about to expand airport expansions in Heathrow, and we’re giving a green light for more data centers. It’s sending the wrong signal to the rest of the world. It’s saying, “We are going to continue to pollute, but you don’t.” And what we need is finance and committed public finance. And what we’ve seen is these rich countries cutting their finance to the climate — to climate finance.

AMY GOODMAN : Well, we have to leave it there, but we are going to be here all week delving into these issues. Asad Rehman is the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

I want to really thank our team here in Turkey — some of us almost didn’t make it with the lockdown in the United States: Anjali Kamat, Nicole Salazar, Nermeen Shaikh, Tey-Marie Astudillo, Hany Massoud and Denis Moynihan. I also want to thank, in New York, Mike Burke and Deena Guzder and Messiah Rhodes and María Taracena, John Hamilton, Sara Nasser, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff, Robby Karran and Diego Ramos, as well as Laura Bustillos. I am Amy Goodman, here in Turkey for the U.N. summit.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

As delegates, industry lobbyists and civil society activists attend this year’s United Nations climate summit, known as COP31, we speak with international environmental lawyer Farhana Yamin about the state of global climate efforts. Yamin helped write the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement and has attended 28 of the last 31 U.N. climate summits. The Paris Agreement aimed to keep global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a threshold that climate scientists say the world will now overshoot.

“It’s a moment of great sadness, actually, for the world community that we weren’t able to start the phaseout, start the acceleration of the transition away from fossil fuels 10 years earlier,” says Yamin. “So, we’re about 10 years behind, but I hope that over time that we can accelerate.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

We’re broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit. That’s COP31 here in Antalya, Turkey. The U.N. summit comes 11 years after nations reached the landmark 2015 Paris Climate Agreement to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius — that’s 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit. But that limit is on track now to be surpassed.

On Friday, U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres addressed the summit. He urged nations to enact immediate and drastic reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

SECRETARY - GENERAL ANTÓNIO GUTERRES : An overshoot of 1.5 degrees is now inevitable. And our responsibility is to keep it as small as possible for as short time as possible and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees as quickly as we can. But that requires immediate and drastic emissions cuts, on the order of 6% every year over the next few years. But on the basis of current commitments of national determined contributions, the countries’ climate plans, we are heading for an overshoot as far as the eye can see, with temperatures about 2.5 degrees by the end of the century. And that is a recipe for catastrophe. Even a limited, temporary overshoot will intensify the devastating impacts we are already seeing. And that makes climate justice even more urgent.

AMY GOODMAN : That was U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres Friday.

We’re joined right now by Farhana Yamin, an international environmental lawyer who helped write the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. She’s attended 28 of the last 31 U.N. climate summits.

Welcome back to Democracy Now! It’s great to have you with us. You know, sometimes I think with the U.N. jargon and the letters or abbreviations of things most people in the world don’t know, it is — there are a hundred languages spoken here. That one is the hardest. So, first, I’d like you to talk about how you got involved, to the point where you were a key architect of the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, and what it means now that that 1.5 degrees — and what’s that all about? — is set to be surpassed.

FARHANA YAMIN : Yes. Thank you so much for having me, Amy.

I got involved because, actually, I stepped back from the negotiations and from my work in philanthropy, in climate philanthropy, in 2012, and I realized, actually, we were not phasing out greenhouse gases, which is what the key purpose and point of this process was. So I came up with this idea of phasing out greenhouse gases by 2050 to zero, which is the — which is the emissions target that is needed to be, at that time, in line with keeping temperatures to 1.5 degrees and well below two degrees. That was the emissions target. This is a temperature target. Most people, as you said, don’t really understand what the big difference is between 2 degrees, 1.5 degrees, let alone 3 degrees. This is temperature changes that we experience in the course of a day —

AMY GOODMAN : Right.

FARHANA YAMIN : — let alone a season. But globally, the whole of the Earth, its water, its oceans, its landmass, changing temperatures by that much means, you know, a calamity for the world’s ecosystems, for the oceans, for soils, for forest health. And that is what we’re seeing now. We’re seeing —

AMY GOODMAN : In fact, you were working with the Marshall Islands at the time.

FARHANA YAMIN : I was working with the Marshall Islands. And, actually, it was the minister of the Marshall Islands, Minister Tony deBrum, who pulled together this big coalition called the High Ambition Coalition in the run-up to the Paris Agreement, that struck a bargain amongst themselves. The ministers and the leaders of these countries said, “We will not fail,” as the Copenhagen conference — sorry to go back in time a little bit — which was COP15, had failed to adopt a successor treaty to the Kyoto Protocol.

AMY GOODMAN : That was the first climate summit that Democracy Now! attended, in Copenhagen.

FARHANA YAMIN : Yes, you go back that way. So, that summit failed, and then it took basically five years to get the Paris Agreement agreed, and another year to get it rapidly entered into force. And the small islands and the smaller nations played a key role, because, for them, it was life or death.

And really, the implications of now what we call the overshoot, which is basically we are hurtling past the threshold for keeping temperatures below 1.5, with almost inevitability, that is a moment of great grief, it’s a moment of great anger, it’s a moment of great sorrow, and it’s a moment of great anxiety, because the impacts associated with that for the most vulnerable in the world, let alone all of us. You know, I live in London. We still have wildfires in London, in England. You’ve had wildfires across the globe. Countries like Nepal are showing us what it now means for glaciers to melt and for those waters to burst unexpectedly and inundate huge areas of land, devastating loss of life. So, we’re seeing those impacts firsthand.

People are seeing the impacts also of rising fuel prices as a result of fossil fuel dependency. They’re seeing that on the cost of — on the cost of living, on their wage packets, on their transport and mobility bills. So, we’re seeing the dependency on fossil fuels.

And it’s a moment of great sadness, actually, for the world community that we weren’t able to start the phaseout, start the acceleration of the transition away from fossil fuels 10 years earlier. So we’re about 10 years behind. But I hope that over time that we can accelerate, and that’s what this COP is about.

AMY GOODMAN : How does the United States pulling out again from the Paris Climate Agreement, President Trump doing it twice, for his both terms in office, affect the negotiations here?

FARHANA YAMIN : It impacts us enormously, because many other countries have slowed down or followed suit. And it is not just the — it is now the third time in my professional lifetime that the U.S. has withdrawn from the climate treaties. The first time was obviously under George Bush. So, we’ve lost, you know, about 15 years as a result of just the uncertainty and the political weight that’s associated with climate denialism and having an anti-climate action stance. And I cannot say enough what that means in terms of the immense power — intellectual, financial, economic — that the U.S. has still today in the world. It acts as a brake. It acts as a hamper. And it is truly disruptive. They may not be here, but the dead weight of their nonparticipation is being felt.

AMY GOODMAN : So, can you explain this dispute around the release of the next report to be published by the U.N.-backed, Nobel Peace Prize-winning Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the IPCC ? Why are countries like Saudi Arabia, Russia and India pushing the report’s delayed publication — all three countries among the largest fossil fuel exporters or importers in the world?

FARHANA YAMIN : I think there are a number of reasons, but the main one is essentially to try and delink the science from really informing this process. Science has been a bedrock and has provided the impetus and the urgency and the basis for action. Legally, we’re required to act as a result of and in response to the best science. And I’m afraid, sadly, these tactics of trying to undermine the science or refuse to incorporate the science, or refuse to even note or acknowledge what the IPCC is doing, this particular time, it’s even more egregious. But these have been commonplace for the last 30 years.

And in fact, I was pointing out to some of my old dinosaur friends that at COP2, which was in 1996, we had just had publication of the second IPCC report, which was meant to inform the then-negotiations of the Kyoto Protocol, and the same group of countries, very similar group of countries, blocked the adoption of a decision at COP2. And actually, in that case, all of the ministers of the world were gathered and said, “No way. We are going to issue a ministerial declaration acknowledging the science.” And the blockers, as it were, were then noted in the COP report as a footnote to that. So, procedurally, I’m sure we will also find a way in which to acknowledge the science, give light and weight and evidence and visibility to climate science here.

AMY GOODMAN : Explain what the global stocktake is. Former Vice President Al Gore, vice president of the United States, was here and said, “Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the IPCC in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels.” What is this global stocktake?

FARHANA YAMIN : Yeah, in the Paris Agreement, we invented, basically, a five-year cycle of ratcheting up nationally determined commitments — essentially, the pledges and the targets that countries have themselves committed to — and collectively taking a stock of that, and then renewing our global commitment every five years. So, the assessment is called the global stocktake. It takes a couple of years. The science and the evidence of the implementation, all of that combined goes into it. It’s input into it, and out the other end should come more explicit guidance to parties, as well as these revised and more ambitious NDCs. That is what is meant to happen. NDCs are these five yearly targets that are meant to be a report.

AMY GOODMAN : ” NDC ” means?

FARHANA YAMIN : Nationally determined contributions, because they’re not internationally determined. We don’t have in the COP any right to tell a party individually what their target is, and they are not as legally binding in the way that the Kyoto Protocol commitments used to be. So these are a softer way of gaining international commitments to go forward. So, the global stocktake, the first one happened, and, in fact, it was very successful in giving a very clear signal to transition away from fossil fuel, to start that process and to ramp up ambition. And the second stocktake is now being readied for Ethiopia.

AMY GOODMAN : There are over —

FARHANA YAMIN : For the next — for COP32.

AMY GOODMAN : There are over 90,000 people here. And people right now can see people walking back and forth. Ninety thousand people people. I think it’s the largest COP yet. What are they all doing? And I don’t know if you know what percentage, because it’s grown every year, of fossil fuel lobbyists that are here and the enormous power that they exert.

FARHANA YAMIN : Yeah, I have — I have sort of mixed feelings about the sizes of the COPs, because sometimes it feels very overwhelming, and it’s very difficult to just navigate around. But in a sense, you can see that as a success of the climate regime. It is attracting more and more participants, including from developing countries, including from different constituencies — youth, women, Indigenous people. All of them have come in.

And sadly and unfortunately, the power and financial pockets of very powerful industries means that they can often send many more delegates. So, there is a disproportionate number of fossil fuel lobbyists here, as there were a few previous COPs. I think the numbers are something like, just alone — I read yesterday that there were over 600 delegates alone lobbying for carbon capture and storage, which essentially is one of the very contested solutions, a very expensive solution, a solution which means, once again, we will not be phasing out fossil fuels; we’ll be trying to continue with them.

AMY GOODMAN : What is the significance of this summit being held here in Turkey? President Erdoğan urged countries to make progress in the talks, but separately celebrated the discovery of two new oil fields with estimated potential of an enormous amount of fossil fuels.

FARHANA YAMIN : I think Turkey, like many other countries — Brazil last year, Australia, the U.K., where I am living — are, you know, I think, in a sort of very divided, confused state. On the one hand, they can see how much they’re benefiting, moving rapidly to green and clean sources of energy. Their populations, their citizens are voting with their feet and with their wallets in installing renewable energy, solar panels and so forth. Same with Australia. But at the same time, governments seem to be hedging their bets and expanding fossil fuels. And that is a tragedy. I hope that Turkey does not, in the end, go forward with that. But it is, in these very uncertain, volatile, chaotic war times, something that some countries are thinking, “I better also keep my options open.” And in fact, as we know — and all the economics are saying it — the shift to clean, renewable solar power, renewable wind power is much, much cheaper and doesn’t require a war, basically, to protect them.

AMY GOODMAN : And we’re going to talk more about war with our next guest, these times of war and the demands for accountability. Farhana Yamin is an international environmental lawyer who helped write the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement, has attended 28 of the last 31 U.N. climate summits.

Coming up, Asad Rehman of Friends of the Earth. He was out in the streets this weekend and now is inside the climate summit. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : A performance during the COP31 opening session here in Antalya, Turkey.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Democracy Now! is in Antalya, Turkey, where this year’s United Nations climate summit, COP31, is being held. For the second year in a row, the United States has not sent an official delegation to the international talks, in keeping with the Trump administration’s longstanding hostility to such efforts to address the climate crisis.

There are nearly 100,000 participants here at this year’s climate summit, including many civil society activists from Turkey and around the globe. Over the weekend, Democracy Now! was in the streets of Antalya to speak with some of the thousands of protesters who marched to demand urgent climate action, including many labor leaders.

“Trade unions care about a lot more than just protecting jobs. We have systemic demands,” said Lala Peñaranda, the Latin America coordinator for Trade Unions for Energy Democracy.

AMY GOODMAN : We are broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit, COP31, here in Antalya, Turkey. More than 190 countries are attending the summit, but for the second year in a row, the United States has not sent an official delegation. Shortly after returning to the White House, President Trump withdrew the U.S. from the landmark 2015 Paris Climate Agreement.

Here at COP31, climate activists have been demanding immediate action to confront the climate crisis. Earlier today, activists rallied against the plastics industry.

PROTESTERS : Less plastics! More life! Less plastics! More life! Less plastics! More life! Less plastics! More life! Less plastics! More life!

AMY GOODMAN : Over the weekend, Democracy Now! was in the streets of Antalya as thousands of protesters marched to demand urgent climate action. Democracy Now! ’s Anjali Kamat filed this report.

PROTESTER : We are children of this planet! We have a right on this planet!

ANJALI KAMAT : Over 10,000 people came out in the streets of Antalya, Turkey, this Saturday to participate in the People’s Climate March.

PROTESTERS : The people, united, will never be defeated!

ANJALI KAMAT : Despite a light rain, the mood was festive and defiant, with people from across Turkey and around the world demanding stronger climate action. From Indigenous rights to making polluters pay to ending the genocide in Gaza and the war in Iran, the protesters connected the dots.

PROTESTERS : Free, free Palestine! Free, free Palestine! Worker power! Worker power!

KIVANÇ ELIAÇIK: This is Kıvanç Eliaçık, labor activist. I’m with People’s Climate Summit. I’m based in Istanbul normally. Fossil fuels are killing the planet. Of course, there are a long list of demands, but from a trade union perspective, we are asking for a just transition, which we mean we want exit from fossil fuels, but we want job security, income security or pension rights. So we are asking for just transition. We want to keep the planet, but we want to keep the jobs, as well.

ANJALI KAMAT : Just as the COP opened last week, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced the discovery of two new oil fields in the southeast of the country. Kıvanç is one of the organizers of an alternative People’s Climate Summit that kicked off with Saturday’s march.

KIVANÇ ELIAÇIK: Turkey is co-hosting COP31 together with Australia. They are also destroying the nature to build new infrastructures to host this event. And while having the COP31 presidency, co-presidency here, Turkey has no plan for exit of fossil fuels. So, the meeting, the Turkish co-presidency focused on zero waste. It’s an important issue. Recycling, waste management is important issue. But we have no plans about fossil fuels. So we need a plan for fossil fuels.

PROTESTERS : Workers, united, will never be defeated!

ANJALI KAMAT : Labor groups made up a large portion of the march. Nearly 80 unions from over 40 countries met in Antalya last week to call for more public solutions to the climate crisis.

PROTESTERS : Worker power! Worker power! Worker power! Worker power!

LALA PEÑARANDA: My name is Lala Peñaranda. I’m the Latin America coordinator at Trade Unions for Energy Democracy. I’m based in Bogotá, Colombia. Trade unions care about a lot more than just protecting jobs. We have systemic demands. It’s really to reject the “privatize to decarbonize” agenda, to the fight for energy as a human right, not as a commodity.

ANJALI KAMAT : When you say “privatize to decarbonize,” what do you mean by that?

LALA PEÑARANDA: We saw a growing trend of both institutions, like the IMF and the World Bank, but also even some actors in the trade union movement, that were saying, “You know what? As long as we have a seat at the table, we’re fine. You can privatize energy, you can privatize public services, as long as we have a seat at the table and we have a job.” And we were saying, “No, no, the trade union tradition is to defend the working class — not the unions, not the union bureaucracy, the working class.” And that means that our public services, starting with energy, has to be public. It has to be in public hands, and it has to be for the people.

AKHATOR JOEL ODIGIE : Akhator Joel Odigie is my name, general secretary of the African Regional Organisation of the International Trade Union Confederation.

ANJALI KAMAT : And where are you coming from, sir?

AKHATOR JOEL ODIGIE : I am coming from Lomé, Togo. That’s where I am headquartered.

ANJALI KAMAT : And what is your main demand?

AKHATOR JOEL ODIGIE : Just transition for workers that is inclusive, that is financed. And more than ever before, the Belém plan of action, we need to begin implementation now. And we are not seeing that, unfortunately. The planet is heating up. We cannot continue to pretend that things are the same. They are not the same.

ANJALI KAMAT : And are people inside the COP31 meeting — are they addressing any of this?

AKHATOR JOEL ODIGIE : This is a challenge, we are saying. They are not listening as we would want. There is so much slowdown. To get to all of these, we need huge financing. Polluters must pay. Those that are polluting the climate should come forward with the resources.

SUNGHEE OH: OK, I’m SungHee Oh from South Korea, South Korean trade union.

ANJALI KAMAT : Are you feeling hopeful about anything coming out of this formal summit?

SUNGHEE OH: Not really, because, you know, the labor unions around the world, we have been demanding a just transition, you know, with guaranteed workers’ rights for many years. And they agreed to have a just transition mechanism in the COP30 — I mean, the COP governance, but they haven’t been able to include, you know, trade unions and workers in the negotiations. So, I don’t know. I’m not so sure. That’s why we gather here, and, you know, we try to put pressure on, you know, those government parties in the negotiation tables.

PROTESTERS : Polluters have to pay! Polluters have to pay! What do we want? Climate justice! What do we want? Climate justice!

ANJALI KAMAT : We also met a farmer from Pakistan who lost his harvest and livestock in the catastrophic floods of 2022 that displaced over 30 million people and inundated millions of acres of farmland.

ABDUL KHALIQUE LAGHARI : [translated] My name is Abdul Khalique Laghari. I’m from Dadu Province in Sindh, Pakistan.

ANJALI KAMAT : Laghari is part of a group of nearly 40 flood-affected farmers who are suing two of Germany’s most polluting companies for their emissions. They’re suing on the basis of a German court ruling last year that opened the door to companies being held liable for climate damages caused by their carbon emissions. Pakistan contributes less than 1% to global carbon emissions. Nasir Mansour from the National Trade Union Federation of Pakistan is supporting the lawsuit.

NASIR MANSOUR : We have made the polluters accountable. So, we are not only asking for a compensation, but we are all asking for the justice. So, it’s a symbolic kind of our venture. It will give a new boost and the hope to the other communities who suffer from the climatic displacement and the calamities.

ANJALI KAMAT : It wasn’t just groups from Turkey and the Global South at the march, but also activists from Europe still reeling from the heat waves this summer that killed over 50,000 people.

SORAYA FETTIH : My name is Soraya Fettih. I work for 350.org. I’m based in the southwest of France. Just last summer, I saw part of my region just burned to the ground because, yet once again, our politicians are doing almost nothing to fight the climate crisis that is happening. We lost people. We lost, like, our fields, some of our means of, like, livelihood. So, for me, coming here was a way to protest, fight for what’s needed.

ANJALI KAMAT : And, Soraya, are you going to be at the COP , or are you outside this whole week?

SORAYA FETTIH : I’m doing both. Like, I feel like we have to be everywhere and give it our all, because, again, like, the climate emergency, we can all feel it wherever we are right now. It used to be mostly the countries and the populations from the so-called Global South, those who did the least to, like, create this crisis, that would feel the most impact. But right now we are all feeling it, whether you are from the North or the South. And so, the urgency that we’re feeling, we need to translate it in proper action and hire the pressure, again, on our leaders and on our governments right now. They are just, like, not doing enough.

ANJALI KAMAT : As the march came to an end in Antalya’s Republic Square, the sun was out, and a group of Turkish activists unfurled rainbow flags and burst into song.

*PROTESTERS: [singing] O bella ciao, bella ciao, bella ciao, ciao, ciao…

ANJALI KAMAT : While climate justice was the focus of Saturday’s march, many of the participating Turkish groups raised concerns over domestic repression in other arenas. In September, Turkish authorities launched nationwide raids against the LGBTQ+ community, arresting over a hundred activists.

YAĞMUR ORHAN : We hide the flags on our backs, and then we open them. So we were able to use them today.

ANJALI KAMAT : This is Yağmur Orhan, a 21-year-old activist.

YAĞMUR ORHAN : We are starting a campaign called We Want Freedom. And we demand that our friends will be released immediately and stop this madness, honestly.

ANJALI KAMAT : Is there a sense of fear in the community, given the scale of the crackdown?

YAĞMUR ORHAN : It’s honestly a very scary environment. We feel that in our communities, in our homes, in our everyday lives, because we are being arrested, we are being accused of nonsense crimes, so that we can feel that very much. But we are sticking together. We are fighting against this together. So, we’re going to be OK. I’m sure about that.

ANJALI KAMAT : Do you feel like people are able to come out and say proudly that they are part of the LGBTQ community in Turkey?

YAĞMUR ORHAN : No, I don’t really think that. Trans people cannot transition because of this environment. People are scared of their families, the people, the government. So, not a very safe space right now.

ANJALI KAMAT : If people say, “How is this related to climate?” what would you say?

YAĞMUR ORHAN : We know today that the fascist government that is attacking the LGBTQ people today is the same one that attacks the nature, the animals, the people. So, we know that this is an intersectionality problem, so we are here today.

ANJALI KAMAT : As the gathering came to a close, we also ran into some veteran campaigners who have been advocating for climate justice for decades, both inside the COP and on the streets.

ASAD REHMAN : My name is Asad Rehman. I’m from Friends of the Earth in England, Wales, Northern Ireland. We are in the midst of a crisis, of a crisis of crisis. We could see that with the killer floods, droughts and famines impacting people everywhere. Our ecosystems are collapsing. The U.N. has warned we’re about to breach the critical 1.5-degree guardrail with devastating consequences on all of that happening, of course, on top of a global inequality crisis, where the rich and powerful are getting richer and richer, and more and more people are struggling to survive. So, we come to these climate talks with an urgent need for, one, governments to — especially the rich countries to do their fair share of action and to provide much-needed resources and finance, particularly for those on the frontlines, not just in the Global South now, but increasingly in the Global North, as well. Will rich countries provide real public finance? Now, let me tell you, just five oil companies in the last nine months have made profits five times the amount that the rich countries have handed over in public climate finance. There is abundant wealth, but it’s obviously in the hands of a very, very few people.

HARJEET SINGH : I’m Harjeet Singh. I’m with the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and Fill the Fund campaign. We want finance in the form of grants. We don’t want money that is going to further exacerbate the debt crisis. Developing countries are already struggling. And the reality is that developed countries only want to see how they can make money from this process and not to help communities who are facing the climate crisis right now. Unless and until finance is provided by developed countries, nothing is going to move. That’s the reality. Or, if we don’t see action on phasing out fossil fuels, we are going to see this crisis only intensifying, and that’s what we are seeing. Look at how we have actually breached the 1.5 degree Celsius target, and disasters are everywhere, not just in developing countries. Even the developed world is suffering now.

KUMI NAIDOO : My name is Kumi Naidoo. I’m from South Africa. I’m the president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative. Today, the fossil fuel industry holds a roughly morally equivalent position of what the slave-owning class did. They occupy — because, you know, the slave owners, when we were — people were saying, “We need a phaseout. It’s inhumane, and it’s a violation of all our religions,” and so on, they would say, “Oh, if we stop doing slavery, the whole world will fall apart. Impossible!” All those arguments that they gave, you will hear it now from the fossil fuel industry. “Everything will fall down,” and so on. And let’s hope that the fossil fuel industry gets a message that their days are numbered. And, you know, people must just remember one thing: Nobody anticipated the Berlin Wall would come down as fast as it did. Everybody thought it was going to be forever. And it happened. I believe that the fall of the fossil fuel industry will happen in the same way. And this moment needs, calls for massive, peaceful civil disobedience against the fossil fuel companies wherever they are, wherever they continue to operate. And I’m seeing it happening, and I think it’s going to grow in leaps and bounds in the months to come.

ANJALI KAMAT : For Democracy Now! , this is Anjali Kamat, with Hany Massoud and Nicole Salazar.

AMY GOODMAN : And thanks so much to Anjali, Hany and Nicole for that report from the streets of Antalya, Turkey, for the People’s Climate March on the Global Day of Climate Action this past Saturday.

Coming up, Farhana Yamin, a climate negotiator who’s been to nearly every COP — that’s climate summit — over the last 30 years. She helped negotiate the 1.5 degree Celsius limit in the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, that is now on track to be surpassed. What does this mean? We’ll get her reaction, and we’ll also speak to Asad Rehman from Friends of the Earth. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : Casey Camp-Horinek of the Ponca Nation of Oklahoma, here at the People’s Climate Summit taking place in Antalya on Sunday.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.title: The Intercept Sues U.S. Military Over Iran Casualty Tally and Blacklist of Journalists
scraped.description: Two lawsuits filed by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation push the military to comply with public information requests.
scraped.author: Jonah Valdez
scraped.h1: The Intercept Sues U.S. Military Over Iran Casualty Tally and Blacklist of Journalists
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Two lawsuits filed by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation push the military to comply with public information requests.

The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon in a pair of lawsuits demanding the release of documents related to the number of U.S. casualties in its war on Iran and the Department of Defense’s secretive blacklist of journalists.

One lawsuit , filed on Friday, responds to the department’s “repeated, unexplained changes” to its publicly available tracker showing U.S. service members killed or injured in the conflict with Iran — including a failure to acknowledge one soldier’s death for the six months after he died — that were documented by Intercept reporter Nick Turse. The shifting figures led one defense official to call the undercount a “ casualty cover-up .”

In August, Turse requested from the Pentagon, through the Freedom of Information Act, casualty-related records and briefing materials presented to Defense Secretary Hegseth and his chief of staff, directives and guidance on casualties, as well as communications related to casualties between Hegseth and his staff of advisers. A later request filed by The Intercept in September sought the financial costs of the Iran war since its start in February. In all cases, the government stopped responding to The Intercept and has failed to provide any documents.

“They need to come clean to the American people.”

A second lawsuit against Hegseth’s DoD, filed on Monday, follows a July conversation with The Intercept in which a spokesperson for U.S. Central Command admitted the military post keeps a blacklist of media members . While reporting on the shifting U.S. soldier casualty figures, the CENTCOM spokesperson, Richard Allee, threatened Turse that he would be “put on a list of people to disregard” for calling the command too often.

CENTCOM later denied the existence of such a list. But Turse spoke with an unnamed U.S. official who confirmed that “Hegseth’s office had a standing order not to engage with [Turse] and would deny it if challenged.” During the first Trump administration, Turse had been placed on a separate blacklist kept by U.S. Africa Command, also within the Pentagon, after he reported on the torture of prisoners at a remote military base in Cameroon used by the U.S. for drone surveillance.

Turse has since filed a public records request seeking a copy of any “lists of journalists that CENTCOM discriminates against or disregards.” The Freedom of the Press Foundation also filed a request for communications and guidance related to the blacklist, as well as any records related to the command’s response to Turse’s article on the matter, published in August . The government has yet to provide any such information to The Intercept or Freedom of the Press Foundation.

Most Read The Hegseth Vote Was Jeffries’s First Big Test. He Failed. Eoin Higgins OpenAI Fooled by Russian Pranksters Into Thinking They Were Speaking to Ukrainian Official Sam Biddle Trump Subpoenas Teachers Union for Info on Pro-Palestine Students C. Frances

“The military doesn’t get to decide which reporters it speaks to or ignores, especially when it’s engaged in legally questionable military actions and the human cost is at its highest. It’s not just the journalists who are harmed when the Pentagon behaves this way — the public and Congress are each denied critical information about what the military is doing in our name and with our taxes,” said Lauren Harper, Daniel Ellsberg chair on government secrecy, who filed FOIA requests for the blacklist on behalf of FPF. “If the Defense Department refuses to answer basic questions about how it engages with journalists, we’ll use the Freedom of Information Act to compel them in court.

The Intercept’s Turse called the Pentagon’s journalist blacklist “fundamentally un-American” and a way to avoid accounting for the real human toll of the ongoing war.

“Central Command wants to keep the sordid details of its wars — from civilian casualties in Iran and Yemen to U.S. military casualties across the Middle East — under wraps,” he said. “They need to come clean to the American people. We have to hold them accountable.”

Hegseth’s Department of Defense has long been hostile toward members of the media. In February 2025, days after Hegseth assumed office, the department forced out outlets such as NBC News, NPR, the New York Times, Politico, CNN, and the Washington Post from their Pentagon press desks. That October, Hegseth issued a new requirement in which journalists could only gain access to the Pentagon if they pledged to only report on information from government employees pre-approved by the Defense Department . This prompted most media outlets, except for the right-wing MAGA-friendly One America News Network, to surrender their press passes.

Trump has also targeted specific media outlets and individual journalists by barring them from the White House or Air Force One, though a federal court judge has since paused the bans, cautioning against possible violations of the First Amendment.

The Intercept and FPF’s lawsuits arrive days after Hegseth narrowly survived an impeachment attempt over his handling of the Iran war . The effort, led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and backed by Democrats, failed to garner enough votes to impeach Hegseth.

In addition to the war on Iran, incoming Democratic members of Congress, along with human rights groups, seek to hold Hegseth accountable for his bloody airstrike campaign on boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, in which the U.S. has killed more than 240 civilians, and his overseeing of the U.S. invasion of Venezuela .

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

I’M BEN MUESSIG, The Intercept’s editor-in-chief. It’s been a devastating year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

Jessica Washington

scraped.title: ICE Shot Pepper Spray Into a Car in a Traffic Stop, Then Broke a Detainee’s Collarbone
scraped.description: A new federal lawsuit accuses ICE and DHS of a batch of brutal warrantless arrests.
scraped.author: Jessica Washington
scraped.h1: ICE Shot Pepper Spray Into a Car in a Traffic Stop, Then Broke a Detainee’s Collarbone
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

A new federal lawsuit accuses ICE and DHS of a batch of brutal warrantless arrests.

Jose Rosito Roca Estrada and his friends were on their way to work in a van on June 27, when a car in front of them slammed on its brakes, forcing them to crash into it and ricochet backward on the busy highway.

Three more cars surrounded theirs, and an estimated 10 to 12 officers poured out. The agents screamed at the men to get out of the vehicle despite traffic whipping by, Roca Estrada and fellow passenger Elvis Manuel Mejia told The Intercept. The stalemate ended with the sound of shattering glass and an asphyxiating cloud of chemicals flooding the car.

According to a new federal lawsuit and photos from the scene shared with The Intercept, federal agents smashed the car’s back windows and “sprayed the occupants with pepper spray through the lowered side windows.”

Officers then dragged a scared and temporarily blinded Roca Estrada from the car. “I was afraid they might be robbing me,” 24-year-old Roca Estrada told The Intercept through a translator. “They did not identify themselves. I was worried they were kidnapping me because they were asking very personal questions.”

“They did not identify themselves. I was worried they were kidnapping me.”

The June attack is one of six stories described in a lawsuit brought by several groups — including the American Civil Liberties Union of Virginia, the Washington Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, the Legal Aid Justice Center, and multiple law firms — alleging widespread “unlawful and dangerous” warrantless arrests by immigration officials in Virginia.

On behalf of Roca Estrada and other plaintiffs, the groups are suing the Department of Homeland Security, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Acting Director of ICE David Venturella, and ICE D.C. Field Office Director Robert Guadian. They’re asking the court in the Eastern District of Virginia to force DHS to comply with congressional limits on warrantless immigration arrests and prohibit the agency from making immigration arrests without legally required individual assessments.

“They have a mandate from the Trump administration … to get creative and make arrests, however they see fit,” said Sophia Gregg, an immigrants’ rights attorney at the ACLU of Virginia. “The agents are ill-trained, and even when they do violate the law, there are no consequences.”

Roca Estrada said that the officers demanded to search his pockets, and when he declined, an agent threw him to the ground headfirst and dug his knees into his upper back. He remembered screaming as pain began to radiate through his collarbone. An X-ray reviewed by The Intercept would later confirm it was broken.

According to Roca Estrada and the lawsuit, officers began to punch and hit him in the back, eventually twisting his arm to place him in handcuffs and into the vehicle. Roca Estrada said that nurses who examined him after the alleged assault told him that blood had filled his lungs, and the lawsuit notes he was diagnosed with a broken clavicle and a lung injury. At no point, the lawsuit alleges, did officers ask the necessary questions to determine whether Roca Estrada was deportable or whether he was a flight risk.

Immigration officers are only supposed to make warrantless immigration arrests if they have determined “probable cause” to believe a person is unlawfully present likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. But in an effort to meet the Trump administration’s nationwide quota of 3,000 immigration arrests per day, the lawsuit alleges, the Department of Homeland Security has chosen to pursue an unlawful policy and practice of “arrest-first, investigate-later” — leaving a trail of traumatized victims who should have never been arrested in the first place.

In the first year of the Trump administration, immigration arrests drastically increased in Virginia. According to the lawsuit, in 2025, ICE made “970 arrests each month in Virginia and Washington, D.C. — nearly five times the average monthly arrest volume in 2024.”

Reached by The Intercept, a DHS spokesperson said that agency had “arrested Jose Rosito Roca Estrada, an illegal alien from Guatemala,” using Roca Estrada’s full name even though The Intercept had not provided it, but denied that its officers “fractured a detainee’s collarbone.” The spokesperson did not deny that officials had deployed chemical weapons, saying, “staff relied on their training to gain compliance.”

“Claims that agents did not properly identify themselves are FALSE. When our heroic law enforcement officers conduct operations, they clearly identify themselves as law enforcement,” wrote the spokesperson. “At NO time were any of the detainees thrown to the ground during the arrest. Allegations that our officers fractured a detainee’s collarbone during the arrest are FALSE.”

Most Read The Hegseth Vote Was Jeffries’s First Big Test. He Failed. Eoin Higgins OpenAI Fooled by Russian Pranksters Into Thinking They Were Speaking to Ukrainian Official Sam Biddle Trump Subpoenas Teachers Union for Info on Pro-Palestine Students C. Frances

Six weeks after Roca Estrada’s arrest, 18-year-old Britney Ramirez Corona was home caring for her 4-year-old sister in Norfolk, Virginia, when she found out ICE had detained her fiancé, his brother, and his brother-in-law.

It was another traffic stop, and Ramirez Corona, a U.S. citizen and recent high school graduate, had to go pick up their abandoned car. There, according to the lawsuit, an ICE officer demanded her identification, refused to let her get her wallet, and accused her of lying about who owned the vehicle. They handcuffed and pinned her, the lawsuit alleges — leaving her little sister to cry and wander into a busy road.

Eventually, ICE allowed another sister, 15, to come pick up the 4-year-old, then took Ramirez Corona into custody. She sat in “handcuffs, ankle shackles and a waist chain” for hours, according to the lawsuit, until her 15-year-old sister was able to bring her birth certificate — showing she was a natural-born U.S. citizen.

The lawsuit argues that Ramirez Corona’s arrest exemplifies an out-of-control trend of warrantless and often nonsensical arrests. Stephen Miller, then homeland security adviser and now the White House chief of staff, directed agents to “just go out there and arrest,” and the department seems to have complied.

“More than half of all the people ICE arrested in July 2026 did not have a criminal record,” the plaintiffs note. “And more than 500 people detained by ICE since January 2025 are U.S. citizens — another likely undercount — like Ms. Ramirez Corona.”

The same month that Roca Estrada says that federal agents temporarily blinded him, broke his collarbone, and beat him until his lungs filled with blood, Congress approved another $72 billion in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Immigrant advocacy groups warned ahead of the funding vote that additional money for ICE and President Donald Trump’s brutal immigration crackdown would mean more people would suffer a fate like Roca Estrada’s — or worse . The next month, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, both in their cars .

Physicians for Human Rights and the UC Berkeley Human Rights Center documented over 412 incidents of misuse of force by law enforcement agents at immigration protests from June 2025 to May 2026, including the use of chemical irritants like pepper balls and pepper spray — the same family of weapons Roca Estrada and Mejia suspect was set off in their car.

In ICE custody, 52 people have died during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, according to Human Rights Watch, while use-of-force by guards remains largely unknown.

“We have received many more reports of violent use of force against people,” said Jeff Migliozzi, the communications director for Freedom for Immigrants, which runs the National Immigration Detention Hotline, referencing hotline numbers from June and July. “The overwhelming forces of intimidation and fear and retaliation, the M.O. of ICE has not changed. But certainly, as more people are detained, there’s more incidents [of violence].”

The DHS spokesperson claimed that Roca Estrada and everyone arrested along with him were offered medical care but declined, adding that “one of the detainees indicated that he had a prior shoulder injury.”

Roca Estrada tells a very different story.

He says he spent the next month tossed between detention centers in Virginia and West Virginia. Because he was not given a sling, Roca Estrada fashioned one for his broken collarbone out of bedsheets. He said he largely went without medical care despite agonizing pain that prevented him from laying down at night.

Roca Estrada said it got so bad he nearly fainted, at which point he was taken to a hospital.

“After medical personnel offered to document his injuries and consult a forensic physician, officers abruptly removed him from the hospital and returned him to detention,” the lawsuit alleges. “For weeks thereafter, Defendants failed to provide the promised follow-up care.”

According to the lawsuit, none of this should have happened because Roca Estrada never should have been detained in the first place.

The suit alleges that immigration officers never asked the 24-year-old “about his immigration history, whether he possessed lawful status, where he worked, how long he had lived in Virginia, whom he lived with, whether he had family or community ties in the United States, or similar questions to assess whether he was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”

Other stories in the lawsuit follow a similar pattern. Catarina Rebeca Us Lopez, a 24-year-old woman from Guatemala, was detained in Centreville, Virginia, during a traffic stop around 6:00 a.m. with her husband. She alleges that masked officers blocked her car at a traffic light and forced her and her husband from the vehicle.

The officers falsely claimed that her husband had a deportation order, according to the lawsuit. But when her husband asked questions about the stop, Us Lopez alleges an agent pepper-sprayed him in the face and threatened to draw their weapons.

According to Us Lopez, officers did not “inquire about her immigration status, ask where she lived, inquire about her family, ask about her ties to the community, or otherwise conduct any individualized investigation concerning whether she was lawfully present in the United States or likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”

Instead, she claims that officers ignored her as she explained that she had work authorization and did not have a deportation order in place, and allegedly mocked her requests for answers and legal assistance.

For Roca Estrada, his physical injuries and trauma left him unable to work for a month. While he was detained, he also lost his apartment and had his personal belongings sent back to Guatemala without his consent, according to the lawsuit.

“The way that I was arrested … and the immense pain that I had to go through during this whole experience,” said Roca Estrada. “What happened to me was not just.”

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

scraped.title: The Year of the Pro-Palestine Super PAC
scraped.description: Pro-Palestine groups emerged to counter the pro-Israel lobby in the midterms this cycle — and won.
scraped.author: Akela Lacy
scraped.h1: The Year of the Pro-Palestine Super PAC
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Pro-Palestine groups emerged to counter the pro-Israel lobby this cycle — and won.

The recent midterm election cycle marked by historic levels of pro-Israel spending saw an emerging trend that aimed to counter their influence: a new crop of pro-Palestine PACs.

Led by American Priorities PAC, which formed in January as part of an effort by donors , including supporters of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who opposed U.S. military support for Israel, a cadre of pro-Palestine organizations spent more than $14.4 million on races this cycle. Almost all of their candidates won.

“In the midst of the genocide, we felt compelled to push every lever and engage in every way possible to push candidates and the [Democratic] party to catch up to its base,” said Margaret DeReus, who leads the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project and the Peace, Accountability, and Leadership political action committee, or PAL PAC . Both groups spent on pro-Palestine ads for the first time this cycle.

As DeReus and other leaders of the emergent pro-Palestine lobby told The Intercept, voters, especially Democratic ones, have become increasingly disillusioned with Israel and frustrated with politicians who support unchecked military aid to the country. “I don’t think there is an issue that I can think of where the party position, the mainstream party position, is so out of step with the base,” DeReus said.

The new pro-Palestine spending is a drop in the bucket compared to the more than $84 million the pro-Israel lobby poured into elections this cycle . AIPAC’s super PAC outspent pro-Palestine groups almost 6 to 1 — and that doesn’t include the more than $50 million AIPAC funneled directly to candidates. The pro-Palestine side may never match their opponents dollar for dollar.

“The point is, nobody has to outspend AIPAC,” said Beth Miller, political director at the advocacy group Jewish Voice for Peace Action. Her group doesn’t spend directly on elections and instead focuses on mobilizing anti-Zionist Jewish voters . “AIPAC is spending this much money because the message they are trying to force down voters’ throats is unpopular.”

“AIPAC is spending this much money because the message they are trying to force down voters’ throats is unpopular.”

The pro-Israel lobby long dominated the discourse on Israel policy before its flagship group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, started spending directly on elections for the first time in the 2022 cycle. But as AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups find their brand growing increasingly toxic amid public outcry over U.S. military support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, pro-Palestine money is shifting the terrain when it comes to election spending.

Simply put, Miller said, “Their message goes further because it’s popular.”

Most Read The Hegseth Vote Was Jeffries’s First Big Test. He Failed. Eoin Higgins OpenAI Fooled by Russian Pranksters Into Thinking They Were Speaking to Ukrainian Official Sam Biddle Trump Subpoenas Teachers Union for Info on Pro-Palestine Students C. Frances

Whether the spending is for or against the pro-Israel lobby, it’s rare to see political ads that directly address U.S. policy toward Israel. For one thing, the topic can be controversial — even if the controversy is manufactured.

When Rebellion PAC, a committee founded to back the 2020 congressional campaign of left-wing commentator Cenk Uygur, ran an ad supporting Abdul El-Sayed and connecting high grocery prices to U.S. support for Israel, the fallout threatened to upend the Michigan Senate race. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., called the ad antisemitic and took it as an opportunity to air her grievances with her former primary opponent, eventually switching her endorsement to Republican Mike Rogers. The PAC originally ran a version of the ad during Uygur’s short-lived 2024 presidential bid.

Voters didn’t seem to be swayed by the controversy, and El-Sayed beat Rogers by a comfortable 7 percentage points. “The drama comes from a handful of elected officials and an establishment that, at best, takes an outdated view of how Israel and AIPAC operate,” said Greg Krieg, spokesperson for American Priorities, which was not affiliated with the Rebellion PAC ad but did produce other ad spots that criticized the U.S. relationship with Israel.

“Not every ad we ran was about Israel, obviously, but the topic came up often because it united Democrats across the party’s ideological spectrum,” Krieg said. “This is not a controversial issue at a grassroots level.”

That new, vocally pro-Palestine PACs are backing successful candidates alongside veteran left organizations is a sign of health for a nascent effort, Miller said.

The midterms were “a test case of: Will this message resonate with voters? And the answer overwhelmingly was yes,” Miller said. “This is a sign of the increasing power and mobilization of the Palestinian rights movement in the political and electoral space.”

Groups like American Priorities and PAL PAC often endorsed the same candidates as progressive bench-builders like Justice Democrats and the Working Families Party. In some cases, the Palestine solidarity movement seemed to breathe a much-needed new life into the electoral left.

The pro-Israel lobby doled out bruising defeats last cycle, after making a promise to unleash its full arsenal to oust critics of Israel from Congress. AIPAC’s super PAC spent more than $25 million to unseat then-Reps. Cori Bush , D-Mo., and Jamaal Bowman , D-N.Y. — a quarter of the $100 million it spent on primaries in 2024 .

Reeling from those losses, progressive and Democratic strategists went back to the drawing board. Alone, they could never hope to have the same infrastructure or wield the same influence as a group like AIPAC. But together, they could more effectively pool their resources to tap into public opinion shifting further each year in their favor.

One of the new pro-Palestine groups, American Priorities, was born out of a desire to leverage that shifting public opinion against U.S. support for Israel into electoral wins. As the first truly pro-Palestine super PAC, the group spent $8.15 million backing 15 candidates this cycle, 13 of whom won. (The group also considered spending for Angie Nixon, a Florida democratic socialist who narrowly lost her bid for U.S. Senate, but ended up putting the money into another race.)

Twelve of the 20 candidates backed by PAL PAC won their races, including El-Sayed and Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, Adam Hamawy in New Jersey, Melat Kiros in Colorado, and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania.

The growing networks allowed groups like Justice Democrats to get involved in more races. It came back from its losses and had its most successful cycle yet, electing eight of the 15 candidates it endorsed, four of whom unseated Democratic incumbents. The group spent $5.5 million in total this cycle, including $4.6 million on ads across all its races. And it went much further: Last cycle, Justice Democrats spent a combined $3.3 million alone backing Bush and Bowman before they lost.

Together, IMEU Policy Project and PAL PAC spent $2.15 million on ads and bundling for candidates. “We ran on proud anti-genocide and pro-freedom platforms,” DeReus said. “We knew that this was a cycle where that platform could win, and we wanted to be a part of making that happen.”

Meanwhile, AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups saw diminishing returns on election spending this cycle, as they battled waning public opinion and increasingly concealed their spending in races.

“Their names often tell you very little about who’s behind them or what they’re actually trying to do — and their ads almost never mention Israel,” Krieg said. “Everybody is looking at the same polling. We have voters who agree with us, so we’re willing to say plainly what we stand for and put our names on it. When you’re pushing a position that voters don’t support, you’re naturally going to be a lot less transparent about what you’re doing.”

“When you’re pushing a position that voters don’t support, you’re naturally going to be a lot less transparent about what you’re doing.”

The general public had a greater knowledge of AIPAC’s brand and its role in maintaining a pro-Israel U.S. policy this time around, said Justice Democrats spokesperson Usamah Andrabi. This cycle also saw more candidates willing to translate public agitation against U.S. support for Israel into campaigns, he said, pointing to other efforts he said helped voters understand AIPAC’s role in elections from groups like TrackAIPAC .

“Voters’ awareness and opposition to Israel’s genocide and apartheid was raised so much higher due to grassroots movements and groups that organized against it,” Andrabi said. “We were able to — across every single one of our campaigns — talk about AIPAC as AIPAC, and talk about the genocide as something we wanted to end, and connect the dots for people.”

It’s a stark contrast to 2024, when Justice Democrats met with candidates whose top concerns were avoiding AIPAC’s wrath, Andrabi said. “Even then, in 2024, we were telling these campaigns, ‘Look, there’s no going under, around, behind, over AIPAC. The only way to defeat this lobby is to go right through them,” he said. “The political courage amongst a lot of Democratic candidates and a lot of people within the Democratic Party was just not there in 2024.”

As the 2028 presidential race begins to take shape , the same pro-Palestine groups are preparing to push candidates to meet voters where they are on Israel policy.

“Particularly with Abdul’s victory in Michigan, that win capped off a year that has really proved that Palestinian rights is an asset, not just in safe blue districts, but in the most critical of swing states,” DeReus said. Even President Donald Trump knows how much of a liability being pro-Israel has become, she added, pointing to his late-breaking claim on Election Day that the U.S. would end military support to Israel.

Potential Democratic contenders in 2028 would do well to take that lesson to heart, DeReus said, as groups like hers gear up to push candidates to support an arms embargo, sanction Israel, and recognize the genocide. She said the group hopes to see someone like Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., enter the race, but that it would also support Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., should she decide to run.

In DeReus’s view, “2024 was the last presidential election we will see where Palestinian rights were disregarded.”

This is not hyperbole.
