scraped.description: For over 40 years, one family has controlled (and reaped the spoils from) a 23,000-member California union. Rank-and-file workers are trying to change that — and say they are facing surveillance, intimidation, and interference from their own union’s staff.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

For over 40 years, one family has controlled (and reaped the spoils from) a 23,000-member California union. Rank-and-file workers are trying to change that — and say they are facing surveillance, intimidation, and interference from their own union’s staff.

UFCW Local 8 candidate Eric Marcuz outside a Save Mart. (Courtesy of Kelly McManus)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

E ric Marcuz is one of the most naturally gifted rank-and-file organizers I have ever met. Overflowing with passion for his union, love for his coworkers, and C4 Energy drinks, he has been spending what little time he has outside of working full time as a dairy clerk at a Safeway grocery store in Redding, California, driving for hours to visit grocery stores across the state and talk with his fellow union members.

Marcuz is running for president of United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 8–Golden State as part of the At What Cost slate, a group of seven rank-and-file grocery workers who are committed to giving their coworkers something that should be taken for granted: an opportunity to choose who leads their union. Standing in their way are staff supporters of Jacques Loveall, the local’s longtime president, whose family has maintained tight control over the union for more than four decades.

Loveall inherited the presidency from his father, Jack, in 2004, through an appointment by the union’s executive board. Neither father nor son ever faced a contested election for the presidency, and the union’s top officers and executive board have been filled through appointments rather than competitive elections. The Lovealls seem straight out of central casting for a Hollywood depiction of out-of-touch, self-serving business unionists, complete with exorbitant salaries, palatial offices, a private jet, and even a bronze bust of the family patriarch.

The At What Cost slate is fighting to introduce real democracy into their union. To do that, they must first collect hundreds of signatures from their fellow union members scattered across California. They have until November 17 to collect and deliver the required number of signatures. If they are successful, ballots will be mailed on November 21 and counted on December 7. The reformers have only the next few weeks during one of the grocery industry’s busiest times of year to campaign — if the union’s staff and leadership don’t stop them.

The UFCW is one of the largest private sector unions in North America, representing more than a million workers, primarily in grocery stores, retail, meatpacking, and food processing. These are some of the lowest-paid and most exploited workers in the labor movement, but also some of the most indispensable to daily life, as the COVID-19 pandemic made painfully clear. Nearly everyone comes face-to-face with a grocery worker every week. This gives grocery workers a strategically important position in an increasingly concentrated industry where powerful corporations squeeze workers through understaffing, speedup, and automation while consumers struggle with rising grocery bills.

Fights for democracy within megalocals — often the combination of multiple small union locals to create huge bodies that are difficult for rank-and-file workers to have real democratic say in, like UFCW Local 8 — have the potential to connect the fight for better wages and working conditions at companies like Albertsons, Kroger, Vons, Save Mart, and Safeway to the broader working-class struggle against runaway inequality. The stakes of this local election extend far beyond who will run the union. It raises the question of what kind of power tens of thousands of grocery workers could exercise if they were organized and mobilized to fight together.

Which is why, after donating to their campaign, I traveled to California to spend a few days observing Marcuz and other slate members as they crisscrossed the state gathering signatures, visiting nearly twenty grocery stores in multiple towns and speaking with dozens of unionized grocery workers. I heard firsthand how grocery workers are being crushed by the rising cost of living and stagnating wages, how excited many are at the possibility of new union leadership, and how terrified some of them are of the union’s current leaders and staff.

Dozens of workers described how union staff have been openly sharing their plans to harass and intimidate the At What Cost slate members as they try to gather signatures. Staff are also following behind At What Cost slate members and pressuring the workers they have spoken with into withdrawing their signatures to get them on the ballot, using a special form the staff have made specifically for this purpose.

One grocery worker, who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation, described how union staff were openly discussing efforts to prevent Marcuz from qualifying for the ballot. Staff explained that if Marcuz failed to collect the required 443 signatures, there would be no contested election and Jacques Loveall would remain president. Staff were out doing everything they could to keep him from reaching that threshold.

One produce clerk who has been a union member for over thirty years described Local 8’s well-known use of intimidation tactics to crush union democracy as “Jim Crow unionism.” He refused to sign Marcuz’s petition because he didn’t want “to end up in a ditch” for crossing staff.

The heavy-handed intimidation tactics I’ve seen here are clearly having the intended effect on some union members. But for others, watching their own union’s staff try to stop a fellow worker from running for office has backfired. Ryan Crahm, a longtime Save Mart employee, said he wasn’t going to get involved until he saw four union staff representatives swarm Marcuz in his store.

“It was straight up intimidation, and it made me pissed,” said Crahm. “I want to ask Jacques Loveall why he is so afraid to have someone run against him. And I want to know why it is that we never saw any staff reps before, but now that there might be an election, they’re in our stores all the time.”

D onning a baseball cap and a backpack filled with petitions, flyers, stickers, and homemade bandanas, the forty-three-year-old Marcuz is excited, urgent, and confident. Visiting store after store from 5 in the morning to 11 at night, he takes his time, listening, asking questions, and sharing his own experiences. His approach to petitioning resembles deep canvassing — a patient, open, and story-driven approach to sharing experiences while engaging with workers during a union drive or voters during an election campaign shown to be effective at winning hearts and changing minds — more than typical rapid-fire signature gathering. Few of his conversations run less than twenty minutes, and they typically cover a range of topics.

Workers repeatedly open up to Marcuz about their frustration with the union contract’s pay scale and how the basic building blocks of the good life — home ownership, a reliable vehicle, vacations — feel increasingly out of reach. California fast food workers have a $20 minimum wage, but under Local 8’s contract, it takes members working full time about five years to reach that hourly rate. Since many grocery workers struggle to get full-time hours, it takes many of them seven or eight years, even in the delis and in-store Starbucks franchises, to earn what they could be making on their first day working at a neighboring In-N-Out Burger.

Members also described unpredictable schedules, chronic understaffing, and the chaos caused by new artificial-intelligence-assisted inventory systems. Many were frustrated not only by the erosion of their contracts but also by how little say they had in negotiating them. There are no elected bargaining teams, and contracts are negotiated exclusively by the president and other appointed leaders and staff.

Members, including several stewards, repeatedly complained about union staff who are rarely in the stores, don’t return phone calls, can’t answer questions about the contract, and are seemingly never around when members need them. The local’s website doesn’t provide information on the twenty-plus appointed vice presidents who allegedly represent members, or which staff representatives service their stores and how to contact them. The local also refuses to provide members with digital copies of their contracts.

Remarkably, despite talking to dozens of union members, including more than a few who had worked in these stores for decades, I couldn’t find a single Local 8 member who had actually met Jacques Loveall. If the union was primarily known for anything, it is for its absence.

“My mind was blown by how little visibility we had into our contracts, union negotiations, and the leadership’s decision making,” said Marcuz. “I started driving down to the union meetings in Sacramento. They’re two and a half hours from my house and held once a quarter at 8 at night. I went to my first meeting, and it literally lasted five minutes. I was the only member there.”

Marcuz says he spoke up at a different meeting and asked whether, given the vast jurisdiction the local covers, quarterly meetings could rotate between different cities across the state to encourage more members to attend. He says the staff laughed him out of the room.

So Marcuz started a petition, collecting three hundred signatures from grocery workers in his area demanding that the meetings at least be live streamed over Zoom so members could listen in. This time, he says, staff angrily shouted him out of the room.

“Every time we tried to get involved, to make our union more responsive to the membership, we got smacked down. And once we start losing faith in our own union, we are on the road to no longer having one,” said Marcuz.

The At What Cost slate is proposing sweeping changes in how the union functions. They want elected bargaining teams, open negotiations that members can attend, local meetings that encourage member participation, a $20 minimum wage in grocery, and aggressive contract campaigns backed by leadership that isn’t afraid to strike over ambitious demands.

Marcuz and his small rebel army want to elect new officers, win better contracts, and fundamentally change who is exercising power inside their union, transforming members from mere spectators into active participants in the fight to better their working conditions and lives.

T he Loveall family has held tight control over UFCW Local 8–Golden State and its predecessor, UFCW Local 588, for more than four decades. Jack Loveall was first appointed president of the union in 1984 and ran it continuously until he retired in 2004, when his son Jacques was appointed by the union’s executive board to succeed him. At the time he retired, Jack Loveall was one of the highest-paid union officials in the country, making over $1 million a year in today’s money. The local owned a twin-engine business jet and had two pilots on staff to shuttle Loveall around the state. He oversaw the construction of a new union headquarters in Roseville, near his personal residence, which featured an 1,100-square-foot presidential office, the size of a modest house, complete with a sauna and marble wet bar.

The local also paid $28,000 a year to cover the cost of Loveall’s membership in an exclusive Roseville country club, an expense the union president justified to the press by stressing that it was a place to talk business with employers. During his final year in office, there were seven Loveall family members on staff, comprising a quarter of the union’s payroll.

Loveall built his empire through a series of mergers that expanded the union’s membership and assets while consolidating his control over its leadership. According to a 2004 investigation by the Contra Costa Times , critics accused Loveall of securing mergers by rewarding the officers of absorbed locals with lucrative positions in his administration.

When Local 498, a Sacramento meatcutters’ union with 1,600 members and $2.3 million in assets, merged into Local 588, its former president saw his annual pay jump from roughly $12,500 to $85,000, while its former treasurer’s pay increased from less than $11,000 to nearly $76,000. The mergers helped Loveall build an increasingly loyal staff and executive board, with well-paid positions that extended to the relatives of some officers.

But Loveall wasn’t always successful. Members of Local 1179 put a halt to a proposed merger with Local 588 by organizing an opposition campaign centered on Loveall’s pay and perks, arguing their dues would be better spent if their local remained independent rather than contributing to Loveall’s lavish lifestyle.

Responding to these criticisms, Loveall told the press , “Just because we run a union doesn’t mean we’re supposed to be paupers” and said that “my members don’t want me driving around in a stagecoach or working in some shithouse office.” The elder Loveall also bragged about how tightly he controlled the union membership, saying that members were “ready to do what I tell them to do.”

Jacques Loveall took over the top spot in 2004 but kept his father on the payroll earning more than $70,000 a year as a consultant, on top of his pension, until the elder Loveall died in 2020. Jacques is also chair of the Loveall Foundation for Children, a nonprofit founded in honor of his father and described on their website as being founded and run by “the staff, family and friends of UFCW 8–Golden State.” The union has financially supported the nonprofit for years, including $25,000 in 2025 alone, and at least one major collective bargaining agreement negotiated by Loveall obligates the employer to contribute three cents for every hour employees work directly to the Loveall Foundation.

The salary of the president is set by the union’s top officers and vice presidents, all of whom were appointed over time by other top officers and vice presidents as vacancies arose. At no point over the past four decades have any of the Local’s top officers or the twenty-plus vice presidents actually been elected by union’s membership.

Discussing this reality with other union members, Marcuz is blunt: “Our local hasn’t been acting like a union. It’s been run like a family business.”

T here have been past attempts by union members to challenge the Lovealls’ tight control over the union. But those who have tried have repeatedly encountered a familiar combination of intimidation, interference, and mergers that postponed or eliminated the possibility of a contested election.

Union activists in UFCW Local 1179 who were active in the effort to block the proposed merger with Local 588 reportedly experienced aggressive intimidation and surveillance from Loveall’s associates. According to an investigation by the Contra Costa Times , union staff began following reform activist Michael Ross-Smith, staking out his home and trailing him in union vehicles. In June 1994, three Local 588 business agents following Ross-Smith rear-ended his car in Walnut Creek, an incident documented in a police traffic collision report.

A union representative acknowledged to the press that staff had been following Ross-Smith but defended the practice as a legitimate effort to investigate Loveall’s political opponents.

In 1997, Raley’s grocery clerk Jack Nordby attempted to challenge Jack Loveall for the presidency. Nordby wanted to cut the excessive salaries of union officers and open contract negotiations to the membership. Following his announced run for office, Nordby alleges that union representatives followed him and his family, harassed him while he collected nomination signatures, and pressured workers into withdrawing their signatures from his petition. So many signatures were withdrawn that Nordby failed to qualify for the ballot.

Another reformer, Lorna Greenlee, described similar intimidation. Greenlee said two union representatives confronted her while she collected signatures, then berated her for hours. She and her daughter also reported seeing union representatives watching their home. Although Greenlee said she had nearly collected enough signatures to run against Loveall, she eventually withdrew out of fear.

The Lovealls have also benefited from mergers that postponed contested elections. In 2006, another reform slate, led by longtime meatcutter Doug Slaydon, was preparing to challenge Jacques Loveall. But before members could vote, Local 588 merged with Local 1288 to create UFCW Local 8–Golden State, postponing the election until 2008. Slaydon, who was fired from Safeway shortly after his attempted run for local union office, believed the merger was designed to prevent his challenge.

Nearly two decades later, the same maneuvers again threatened to derail the current election. In October, Local 8 members received an election notice announcing that ballots would be mailed in November. But buried in the notice was a provision stating that the election would be canceled if the local completed a merger with an organization called Staffing Agencies Federated Employees (SAFE).

None of the rank-and-file members of the At What Cost slate had ever heard of SAFE. The organization claimed to represent thousands of workers, but there was no evidence of where those workers were organized or what contracts SAFE had negotiated. What they did find were more connections to Loveall: a family member was listed as SAFE’s president on its initial federal filing just eight months before the election.

The At What Cost slate, working with the UFCW reform organization Essential Workers for Democracy, on which Marcuz serves on the organizing committee, challenged the proposed merger and called for a Department of Labor investigation. After a federal investigator began asking questions, Local 8 announced that the merger had been postponed indefinitely, five days after it was announced.

The election was back on. But that doesn’t mean the rank-and-file reformers would be allowed to campaign without interference.

O n November 2, Marcuz drove to the union’s headquarters in Roseville to pick up the nomination petitions that he and his slate needed to start collecting the hundreds of signatures required to qualify for the ballot. From there, he headed south toward Fresno to begin collecting signatures from grocery workers.

But shortly after leaving the union headquarters, where a bronze bust of Jack Loveall stands in the central hallway, Marcuz noticed a black pickup truck following him. When he stopped for gas, the truck stopped too. He recognized the driver as Jeff Berns, a senior Local 8 staff representative whose brother, Mark Berns, was appointed by Jaques Loveall to chair the election.

Multiple members of the Berns family have been on the local’s payroll going back decades. Mark Berns is currently the highest paid nonofficer staff member at the local, earning more than most of the vice presidents. He has repeatedly served as the local’s election chair, including in 2009, when the Department of Labor found that Local 8 had violated federal labor law by burying an election notice inside a union newsletter, mailed just a week after another issue with a nearly identical cover. The notice was so inconspicuous that members could easily have mistaken the second mailing for a duplicate and thrown it away without realizing an election was approaching.

Despite finding that the local had violated federal labor law, because investigators couldn’t identify any member who said they would have run for office against Loveall, the department concluded that the violation had not affected the election’s outcome and took no further action.

According to Marcuz, Jeff Berns told him that he intended to follow him throughout the day to make sure workers heard the Loveall team’s side of the election. And that’s exactly what he did. Berns followed Marcuz to a Save Mart in Fresno, where Marcuz and fellow slate member Mike Romero say three union representatives, including longtime Vice President John Micheletti, confronted them and interfered with their attempts to collect signatures. According to Marcuz, Berns threatened to invalidate every signature his slate collected.

This behavior continued as Marcuz left Fresno and traveled to meet Silas Saldivar, a twenty-six-year UFCW member and head clerk, at the Safeway where he worked in Modesto. Marcuz became so concerned for his safety that he called Saldivar, and they agreed to instead meet at Saldivar’s house.

I traveled with Marcuz to the Safeway in Modesto, where Saldivar recounted the story to me.

“I walked outside into my driveway to meet Eric and saw Jeff Berns pull up in front of my house in his truck. John Micheletti parked in front of my neighbor’s house and then got out of his car and started walking toward us. I looked at Eric and said, ‘Dude, is this guy serious right now?’ Those two guys sat outside and watched my house for over an hour,” said Saldivar. “I didn’t feel safe. I still don’t, honestly.”

While Saldivar was recounting this story to me, two union staff showed up at his Safeway. They kept their distance but made it clear that they were watching us. One pulled out his phone and began recording us.

Marcuz estimated that he had been followed for seven hours and roughly three hundred miles on November 2. The following morning, he filed a police report alleging stalking and harassment.

The intimidation hasn’t been limited to Marcuz and the other candidates. Less than a week later, Mike Denham, a Local 8 staff representative, showed up at the Perfect Union cannabis dispensary in Shasta Lake, California, where Marcuz had recently visited and received overwhelming support from members. Many workers were frustrated that they had never seen a copy of their union contract and couldn’t get one from the local. One supporter had asked Marcuz to leave a nomination petition so workers on other shifts could sign it, planning to return it to him later.

According to multiple workers who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from their union, Denham, the union staffer assigned to the dispensary, subsequently arrived and demanded that they either destroy the petition or turn it over to him so he could destroy it himself.

According to several members, Denham repeatedly insisted that Marcuz had acted “illegally” by leaving the petition with workers at the store. When workers refused to turn it over, Denham eventually left in frustration.

“It’s absolutely insane that our own union staff would come into our workplace to intimidate us to stop us from participating in our own union,” one worker told me.

Federal labor law guarantees the right of union members to participate in democratic elections. The conduct of Local 8’s leadership and staff could have legal consequences.

“The quantity and variety of the efforts by Loveall’s team are not only shocking, but likely unlawful, and could lead to the Department of Labor having to step in and rerun the election,” said Will Bloom, law professor at City University of New York and board member of the Association for Union Democracy.

A t a Vons grocery store in Fresno, multiple workers confessed to us that their union staff representative, Justin Putney, aggressively pressured them to sign the Loveall slate’s nomination petition. Workers told me Putney had forcefully instructed them to call him if Marcuz or anyone else from the At What Cost slate showed up so that he could come down and run them out of the store. It wasn’t long before that happened.

Members working in the Starbucks kiosk were signing Marcuz’s petition when Putney came running up. “There he is,” Putney announced. “I wish I could say it was nice to meet you, but it isn’t.”

Putney proceeded to lecture Marcuz about how “there is a right way and a wrong way to do things.” Putney, he said, had done things the right way. He had worked his way up through the union, starting as a steward before being appointed to a member advisory committee, then the executive board, and finally landing a position on staff.

Putney failed to mention that his father is also a longtime paid executive board member in the union — a point Marcuz raised and Putney didn’t dispute. According to Putney, Marcuz, by contrast, was doing it wrong. “You’re like someone who has been playing rec league soccer saying he wants to jump into the big leagues and play professional soccer.”

Marcuz responded that he believed democracy was the right way for members to decide who should lead their union.

“And I don’t think you should have the right to run for a job that you have no qualifications for,” Putney shot back.

Marcuz challenged Putney over the union’s bargaining record. “Our last contract was horrible,” Marcuz said. “It only provided a dollar raise for topped-out, high-seniority clerks. Nobody else got anything. We are barely able to survive on our wages. I can’t afford a house for my family. I can’t buy a truck. We can’t afford to shop in the stores where we work.”

“You can’t show me anywhere in the country where grocery workers have a better contract,” Putney insisted.

“Any contract that the membership fights for and wins together is better than one that is delivered from on high without our involvement,” Marcuz replied. “Members should be in the room when negotiating is happening. We should own the outcome.”

I introduced myself as a journalist following Marcuz’s campaign and asked Putney why he had rushed down to the store to confront him.

“He is a threat to the future of our members,” Putney told me. “It’s my job to protect the membership, and he represents a threat to that.”

I asked whether he thought it was appropriate for union staff to confront members who were exercising their democratic rights, and whether he had been instructing workers to alert him whenever Marcuz showed up so he could interfere with his campaigning.

“Yes,” Putney acknowledged.

Marcuz was incredulous. “How am I supposed to exercise my rights if everywhere I go I’m being accosted by people on the union’s payroll?” he asked. “I have a right to speak with members, and you’re showing up here just to stop that from happening.”

Putney maintained that he was simply encouraging workers to be cautious about what they signed. Marcuz wasn’t buying it.

“Discouraging people from participating in the democratic process of a union election is anti-union. This process should strengthen us as a union, because it should cause the incumbent union leadership to state and defend their platform. We should debate our visions and what we are fighting for, and the members should get to vote on the best ideas,” said Marcuz.

“But that is not what is happening. What’s happening is that I’m being followed, my conversations are being interrupted, and I’m being harassed by staff who have no honest interest in what I have to say and are only trying to stop others from hearing what I have to say. Let’s be honest. Your goal is to make sure that we don’t have a choice.”

Putney denied the accusation, but Marcuz continued.

“You tried to merge with a fake union that doesn’t really exist and that Jacques Loveall put his cousin in charge of. Staff followed me three hundred miles and sat in front of a member’s house for over an hour to try to intimidate me from participating. You have encouraged people in this store to report to you that I’m here so that you can come here and interfere with my campaigning,” he said. “None of these actions are to prove to the membership that your vision for our union is better. All of those actions are to prevent democracy in our union.”

As the exchange continued, a crowd of grocery workers were gathering to listen. Eventually, a distraught-looking manager approached Putney and asked to speak with him privately. Marcuz took that as his cue. We left the store so he could continue gathering signatures, hoping that he wouldn’t be followed.

L oveall and the executive board members supporting him are running together on the “Solidarity Works Team” slate. And their materials look deceptively similar to official communications from the union. “Solidarity Works” has been Local 8’s slogan for at least fifteen years, appearing regularly in union communications, especially those concerning contract negotiations. Loveall himself has described it “as the motto of UFCW 8–Golden State.”

A recent Solidarity Works Team mailer sent to every Local 8 union member’s personal address is virtually indistinguishable from an ordinary union communication. For one, the return address on the mailers is the union headquarters. For another, it features Loveall’s photograph and title as union president, invokes the local’s record of bargaining victories, and describes the Solidarity Works Team as a “network of member contacts” that lays “the groundwork for the solidarity, communication, and mobilization that will be needed when bargaining begins.”

A QR code on the mailer links to the Solidarity Works Team website, where members are encouraged to join the team by providing their contact information. What the mailer and website don’t mention is that the Solidarity Works Team is running for reelection. There is no information on any of the slate’s candidates other than Loveall, and the word “election” doesn’t appear anywhere on the mailer or the slate’s website.

The website is carefully crafted to lead members to believe they are signing up as part of the process of preparing for contract bargaining, not agreeing to receive information to vote in support of the current leadership in an election that isn’t mentioned anywhere.

While out visiting stores, multiple grocery workers told me that the union staff representatives had asked them to update their contact information to prepare for upcoming negotiations. The representatives handed workers their phones and had them fill out a sign-up page, only for the workers to later discover it was to receive messages from the Solidarity Works Team slate. Those members subsequently received text messages notifying them that “petition signing is under way” and warning, “Reminder: DO NOT sign anything for anyone you don’t know. Solidarity Works!”

The Loveall slate’s materials also issue stark warnings about “anti-union campaigns” and “attempts to weaken your bargaining power and possibly your benefits package.” In a video posted on the slate’s website, staff warn: “Be very careful with your signatures. Do not sign petitions. Do not sign cards. Do not trust the word of people who say they are with our union that you are not familiar with. Again, you should not be signing anything for anyone you do not know.”

Anyone who has organized a union will recognize these talking points. They’re the same warnings employers routinely deploy during union-busting campaigns: beware of outsiders, don’t trust anyone asking for your signature, don’t believe their promises, and don’t risk the wages and benefits you already have. Only this time, these warnings aren’t coming from an employer but from the union’s own leadership.

Jacques Lovall did not respond to an interview request for this story.

A t a Safeway in Lincoln, a suburb outside Sacramento, I meet Mary MacDonnell, who has worked in the grocery industry for over thirty years and supports the At What Cost slate. The night before we met, John Micheletti arrived at her store and began badgering her and others to sign the Solidarity Works Team slate’s petition. Micheletti loudly announced to a group of members gathered near her that “we are at war. The union is under attack. That is why I am here.”

MacDonnell has just finished her shift, and Marcuz and I are sitting on the bench outside the front entrance of the grocery store talking with her. She is emphatic that her union should be an organization of workers, run by workers, to fight for workers. That can’t happen if the union’s leadership is completely insulated from the membership and the staff and executive board are packed with relatives and appointed loyalists.

She says she was drawn to the At What Cost slate because they practiced what they preached. The slate is encouraging members to talk and listen to each other, to build relationships, to be courageous and more ambitious, and to see greater member involvement as a source of strength for the union, not a threat to be mocked or ham-fistedly suppressed.

As we are talking, one of the Loveall slate supporters from the night before arrives. He posts up with his back against the brick wall on the other side of the store’s entrance, conspicuously watching us.

“This has been hella intimidating,” MacDonnell sighs as she eyes the man. But then her resolve seems to harden. “I respect Eric, but at the end of the day, this is bigger than any particular candidate. I want a choice. And I’m just not going to allow them to take that away from us.”

Chris Brooks is a veteran labor organizer and strategist focused on building militant, member-led unions. He is a columnist at Jacobin .

scraped.body_text:

Anwar Shaikh, who died in October at 80, showed how capitalism really works: profit drives it, competition is a war, and crisis is the norm. Economist Clara Mattei argues that his work remains a guide to changing the world.

Economist Anwar Shaikh left behind students around the world and a vast digital archive of his work. (Institute for New Economic Thinking / YouTube)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

W riting about someone who has changed your life and to whom you owe so much is much more difficult than I would have thought. It is impossible to feel capable of delivering even a fraction of what it would take to fully honor the human and intellectual memory of Anwar Shaikh.

I met Anwar at a moment of great intellectual insecurity for myself that he helped me overcome. Now, in front of this blank page, that insecurity is back. At the same time, this state of mind allows me to fully reconnect with the memories of our first encounters and the development of a mentorship and friendship that has deeply shaped me as a scholar and as a person.

I t was 2015, and I was struggling to pursue the research for my economics PhD in Pisa, Italy. It had been a tough couple of years: after a five-year university degree in philosophy and history, the doctoral program had thrown me into hardcore economics courses. There were intense examinations in mathematics, econometrics, statistics, microeconomics, and game theory, which I had survived by studying nonstop and memorizing formulas that I would obsess over at night, half awake, half in my dreams. After so many examinations and so much peer pressure, it took me a while to find a subject I could feel passionate about.

Economics, as my course textbooks presented it, was a dry, abstract discipline, all about technique and not much about intellectual stimulation. I felt demotivated and especially out of place. Was I ever going to be fit for this?

I cared deeply about social justice and critique of the system — I read Karl Marx’s Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts and Karl Polanyi’s The Great Transformation — but none of it seemed to fit the current canon of scientificity. My supervisor, Giovanni Dosi, suggested I work on austerity, and I agreed, but I could not find an approach that was not so deeply economistic, focused only on debt and growth.

Finally, while desperately roaming the library, I found an article on Fascist economics in 1920s Italy. I realized its deep affinity with contemporary economic policies in Europe, especially Italy. That day, I had a moment of awakening and decided to embark on archival research to trace the genesis of these policies in the thought of the economists who were advising Benito Mussolini.

The research was challenging. I adhered to no specific methodological framework. To make sense of things, I realized I had to surpass the narrow limits of what history of economic thought, economic history, or economics meant for the profession.

In my scholarly journey, I had found supportive mentors — Nicola Giocoli, Alessandro Nuvolari, and George Peden, for example — but there was clearly not much space for me in Italian academia, especially within economics. I was not doing enough of what economics was supposed to look like, but to maintain my motivation, I could not conform.

This is when an email from Anwar changed my life forever. It read: “Dear Clara, I could not stop reading your paper once I started! It is excellent, and I hope you continue to pursue the parallels between the post-WWI rationale for austerity and the subsequent reincarnations in the 1980s and again now. Congratulations on a fine piece of work.” I remember gasping with happiness and a sense of recognition that I had never felt before. Really? A scholar like Anwar was taking my research seriously? And in an economics department?

In his role as chair of the Economics Department at the New School for Social Research, Anwar was responding to an exploratory email I had sent just a week earlier, inquiring about a visiting scholar position. I had only recently discovered the existence of a department where Marxian economics was part of the canon, where economics seemed to be about substance as well as technique. In that email, I had attached a chapter of my dissertation, but I had no expectation whatsoever that Anwar was going to open the file.

But he did, and from then on he would continue to make clear the importance of understanding the history of economic thought as integral to the analysis of capitalism itself. He wrote again inviting me both as a visiting scholar and to give a talk on my work to the department. That email exchange was a real turning point in my life’s journey.

When I arrived in New York City in September 2015, I went to Anwar’s office hours. His wisdom and generosity were traits that struck me immediately. He was not teaching that semester, but I would stop by his office to get his feedback on some ideas.

The week before my scheduled department talk, he told me: “You know, we are hiring, and you should apply.” The message was implicit: take this talk as an opportunity to showcase your work. At that point, I was exhilarated. The amount of adrenaline I felt leading up to that 4 p.m. Tuesday seminar was something I would never experience again.

Anwar fought hard for the department to hire me. I only learned this after I had begun working as an assistant professor of economics at the New School. He believed in me so strongly. I still have a hard time understanding why and have never felt worthy of such high esteem.

My dear colleague Ying Chen, whom the department hired at the same time as me, and I were both so lucky to have his support. We will miss those lunches, sharing different varieties of spicy Chinese food over conversations both fun and serious.

I n the summer of 2016, right before I moved to New York to start teaching, I helped organize a couple of stops for Anwar’s book launch in Italy. The stops were at the International University College of Turin and at my alma mater, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa. Anwar had just published his masterpiece , Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises .

There is one conversation with him I will remember forever: We were sitting at a café on the Po River, and he started telling me about the commitment and devotion it had taken him to produce his book. It had taken him over thirty years to completely reset the foundations of economics and the study of capitalism. He told me that escaping the traps of dominant economic theory was a sacrosanct mission to change the world, that deep study carried enormous transformational weight, and that it required sacrificing a lot of worldly distractions.

He emphasized that he had supported me so strongly because he had seen potential in my research and in my devotion to it. He believed I could make a critical contribution to the study of capitalism and the political dimensions of economics. The connection between so-called pure economics and fascism that I was unveiling was for him key to unsettling some accepted truths about our economic system.

It was then that I promised him I would persevere. And in times of demotivation, his words are always there to motivate me.

I spent another six years developing my book, The Capital Order . I always wondered whether the final result lived up to his expectations, but luckily, he did seem proud.

It was really thanks to Anwar’s influence and mentorship that I was able to give a sturdy theoretical foundation to the archival research, tracing its roots in the deep tendencies of our economic system. I also wanted the archival research to bolster the systemic analysis, especially of the deeply political forces that shape our economy. More generally, the book is the product of the intellectual milieu of the department Anwar introduced me to. The intellectual stimulation and methodological insights I received, including from colleagues like Duncan Foley, completely transformed it.

I remember the long conversations on the phone with Anwar during the COVID-19 lockdown, in which he meticulously commented on my interpretation of Ralph Hawtrey’s theory of inflation and explained how best to measure rates of exploitation and profit. His comments, often critical, were not easily digestible, and I would take them bit by bit and dissect them with Aditya Singh, my loyal research assistant, who was also Anwar’s student.

W hat Anwar has gifted us all is his formidable lens through which to interpret capitalism and challenge the mainstream. He offered a lucidity about the systemic tendencies of our economic system and a holistic approach that, as many, including Vivek Chibber , have already stated, bears comparison with that of Karl Marx himself.

In my years working at the New School, I attended two of Anwar’s graduate courses. I experienced firsthand how he was able to translate the titanic amount of knowledge in his book into effective pedagogical tools.

His story of the chicken pot pie, for example, embodies his capacity to convey the nature of capitalism in an intuitive and lasting way. Once Mary sold her chicken pot pie hobby to a business, it did not matter what was in the pies, which became full of hormone-treated chicken; what mattered was their price. With an image that stuck, Anwar explained the fundamental logic of value as being completely detached from use value, from those qualities that made the chicken pot pie so good.

Anwar delivered, like no one else, the antibodies against bourgeois economics, against those “theories” that only help hide rather than explain. In his book, as in his classes, students learned to wear different lenses through which to look at the economic world. They came to understand the slick capacity of the “perfectionist” and “imperfectionist” approaches to idealize markets, competition, and progress.

Shifting from one framework to another, examining their explanations of inflation, profits, and unemployment and their policy implications, Anwar was able to deliver a scathing critique of both neoclassical (perfectionist) and Keynesian (imperfectionist) economics. He tore down the edifice not just of neoclassical economics but also of its supposed Keynesian alternative with grace and precision. He unmasked how they shared much more than one would think, especially a common backbone of idealization and an urge to get back to perfection, which Keynesians thought state intervention could achieve.

As he put it in his brilliant interview with the Institute for New Economic Thinking: “The notion of imperfection is a dual of perfection; you can’t speak of imperfection unless you are implicitly paying allegiance to perfection, and I do not want to be trapped in that space.” He also recalled something I had felt deeply myself: “When I started as a graduate student, I was surprised to discover that the representation of the world was an idealized fictitious form that makes no sense to me, and that as an economist you had to accept that, then spend your time showing how the world is imperfect.”

That is why his blackboard did not have just these two possibilities: next to the perfectionist and the imperfectionist, there was a third column that had vastly more explanatory power. Anwar was not content with merely modifying the existing framework but spent thirty years rebuilding the foundations of economics from scratch. What he built was revelatory. And it had to start from real observation, from confronting the naked reality of capitalism.

Real economics, he liked to call it: an approach that vindicated and expanded, both theoretically and empirically, the most important intuitions of Adam Smith’s, David Ricardo’s, and especially Marx’s analysis, without calling it Marxist. In this, Anwar was adamant and would not accept compromises. He thought it important to get out of the niche, to avoid the self-sectarianism typical of heterodox economists.

As a matter of fact, he disliked the term “heterodox” for exactly that same reason: identifying yourself as an antithesis to the orthodoxy weakens the capacity of real economics to stand on its own feet and gain hegemony. As he wrote in the introduction to his book: “Its object of investigation is neither the perfect nor the imperfect but the real.”

A nwar’s whole economic edifice rested on one crucial intuition that, paradoxically, the perfectionist and imperfectionist paradigms had disregarded: profit drives all the system’s dynamics; it is the engine of the whole economic system.

The incessant quest for profits drives investment and economic growth. Profit shapes supply (firms produce with the goal of making a profit) and aggregate demand (purchases of inputs, plant, and equipment, and the hiring of workers and their capacity to consume). As he put it concisely in the slides he shared with me: “The profit motive always remains central, and its dominance creates the force field that shapes and channels microeconomic and macroeconomic outcomes. This is the proper meaning of the invisible hand.”

He reappropriated the meaning of Smith’s invisible hand not as a metaphysical myth of the eternal efficiency of the market but as the expression of those profit imperatives that operated through real competition. Through the lens of the profit motive, Anwar drew a few fundamental intuitions.

First, class struggle is at the heart of the system, and technological dynamism is one of its expressions. Modern economic analysis reduces capital to durable wealth and understands profit as a reward for abstinence and entrepreneurial search. Against this, Anwar reminded us that capital had nothing to do with the qualities of the commodity. Instead, it had everything to do with capitalism’s specific historical process — potentially infinite accumulation — and the class strugglethat grounds it.

Indeed, profit mirrors surplus labor, and as he says, the existence of surplus labor is a “social outcome.” He writes: “Surplus product only arises when the length of the working day exceeds the working time to reproduce the standard of living of the employed worker, that is, only when surplus labor is performed.” Technological progress is no proof of the fairy tale that capitalism exists to maximize consumer satisfaction with ever better commodities. To the contrary, firms invest in new technology to squeeze more surplus out of their workers and to cut costs below their rivals’. In real competition, firms that fail to do so don’t survive.

Second, the real rests on a conflictual structure, precisely the one that neoclassical economists seek to erase in favor of a harmonious scheme that persuades us to believe we live in the best of all possible worlds. Far from the “ballet” of perfect competition, it is a war of all against all.

The business literature showcased extremely well how the profit motive played out through real competition. In Anwar’s words, “Firms set prices; they try to survive; some win; some don’t; they use tools to attack each other. Roughly 70 percent of firms die within the first three years.”

As Chibber has pointedly discussed , this theory led Anwar to deconstruct traditional leftist understandings of the dysfunctions of capitalism. Capitalism’s violent outcomes do not stem from monopoly power “corrupting” competition; they arise precisely out of a system working as it should, driven solely by the quest for profit.

Third, crisis is the norm under capitalism, an expression of crucial recurrent patterns or “gravitational tendencies” that emerge out of the very dominance of the profit motive itself. As Anwar put it, “The history of market systems reveals recurrent patterns of booms and busts over centuries, emanating precisely from the developed world.” These include the great depressions of the 1840s, the Long Depression of 1873–1896, the Great Depression of the 1930s, the stagflation crises of the 1970s, and the great global crises of the 2010s. In this long-run perspective, excessive financialization was merely the trigger of the 2008 crash; its underlying cause was a crisis of profitability.

Anwar’s real economic framework can also explain other devastating features of our economic system, including the structural economic plunder of the Global South and permanent warfare as a stimulus to profitability that does not risk subordinating the profit motive to social goals. Such subordination is correctly seen as a threat to the capitalist order and labeled “socialistic.” My work on austerity’s structural role in managing capitalism — by repressing wages and preserving the social relations underpinning profitability — is charged by this theoretical insight. Indeed, it underscores how capitalist governments must find the “right” stimulus policies — those that do not challenge market dependence or the command of private investment.

T hese observations are important to avoid easy misunderstandings. Anwar was not a determinist. The patterns he discovered were important to guide systemic knowledge but did not eliminate agency.

Rather, Anwar developed a multidimensional structure of influence that is at once hierarchical and deeply historical. This is the significance of turbulent gravitation : a relatively small set of operative principles can explain a great variety of economic phenomena, without reducing the dynamics of capitalism to mechanical laws. There are observable patterns in the system — but humans can organize and change the system through political action.

This is the deeply historical and political approach that runs through Anwar’s analysis. He repudiated the bourgeois distinction between, on the one hand, “ahistorical laws” and, on the other, the “contingencies” of history. One must understand that classes, through their historical agency, create the very imperatives upon which they act, even as those imperatives bind them.

This is particularly important when it comes to the “gain-seeking behavior” that defines capitalism as a particular social form. The imperatives of profitability are not simply external laws bearing down on historical actors, nor are they merely the outcome of individual choices. Class relations and competition produce them historically, even as they confront those actors as real constraints that shape their actions. The beauty of Anwar’s economic analysis is that he could identify the underlying regularities of capitalism without abstracting them from the historical relations of class and agency through which actors continually reproduce them.

This also speaks to Anwar’s particular relationship to empirical data. He was emphatically empirical, but not a positivist. His argument was that classical assumptions are consistent with empirical reality.

He understood that data are never innocent. Data are not simply a collection of preexisting facts waiting for an observer. As he writes, “Theory intervenes not merely in the interpretation of events but in their very representation (and occasionally in their suppression, as we know only too well).”

His example of unemployment is particularly telling: the official definition counts someone as employed if they did any work at all for pay or profit. Such a definition masks a much bleaker picture of the realities of unemployment and underemployment as structural features of the system.

Anwar’s historical proclivity, expressed in his attention to social relations, is particularly clear in his passion for Michał Kalecki’s famous 1943 article, “Political Aspects of Full Employment,” which we discussed at length on many occasions. He thought this was one of the most important pieces of political economy ever written, as it clearly stressed one of the strongest Marxian intuitions: capital not only produces unemployment — it fundamentally depends on it.

Keynesian economics, with its utopian delirium of ignoring exploitation, had depoliticized the economy. It failed to realize that its goal — full employment — was technically possible, but that only a fascist dictatorship could achieve it without undermining capitalism. Indeed, only under fascism can you forgo the impersonal discipline of unemployment because political discipline is firmly in place.

I draw heavily on these conversations in my most recent book, Escape From Capitalism . Anwar reviewed it in detail and wrote a final blurb for it: “A book for the times. Mattei takes aim at the notion that the forces which regulate market and social outcomes are socially neutral. Mattei argues that we need to reject this framework, to ‘politicize our lives to participate in the transformation of the material and social reality around us’ at the local and global level.”

Anwar’s approach deeply inspired the book, and I try to bring it to life for a broader, nonacademic audience. I carry forward his conviction that economics is a social science and therefore a historical and political science.

I especially carry forward what I understand to be the fundamental Shaikhian spirit: it is only by explaining how capitalism really works that we can sharpen our tools to overcome it. Indeed, Anwar’s work has inspired generations of young people and won international acclaim.

A nwar was extremely supportive of my embarking on the journey to the University of Tulsa. He gave a brilliant opening lecture at the inaugural conference of the Center for Heterodox Economics there, which I had organized. He remained deeply supportive throughout the turbulent times at the university and when I began setting up the independent Forum for Real Economic Emancipation (FREE).

I helped organize a wonderful retirement celebration for Anwar, which produced a special issue on his work in The New School Economic Review . Afterward Anwar enjoyed his new home at the lake in Amherst, writing, fishing, cooking, and visiting friends like Robert Pollin.

We spoke on the phone often. Anwar had helped create the intellectual ethos of the New School for Social Research Economics Department and had opposed academic hierarchies all his life. He was appalled at the administration’s attacks , like firing tenured and untenured faculty members and blocking PhD admissions, which were effectively dismantling the department.

His recorded words at the retirement party ring true to all of us:

The important thing about democracy is that you have a voice. It does not mean you have to agree with me. You have to have a voice, and you constantly need to protect it, and you have to act on it. Look around you — no department anywhere has this kind of voice. So don’t give it up. No matter what they do. They are going to try to make you give it up. Don’t give it up. Go and strike if you have to. Close the place down.

I remember the shock of that phone call in which he told me he had cancer. I pretended it wasn’t real: his voice was so combative that it seemed impossible that anything could beat him. To the very end, as he heroically fought his devastating illness, he remained focused on his scholarship and on the possibility of delivering an abbreviated version of his masterpiece, updated with new empirical data.

Anwar’s archives at Bard College reveal letters that Joan Robinson and Nicholas Kaldor wrote to him in the 1970s, already recognizing the power of his work. Fortunately, Anwar leaves behind a considerable number of students, now spread across the world. A recent piece by Nikos Chatzarakis perfectly exemplifies their power to speak of his breakthroughs. As his former student Juan Santarcángelo, now a professor in Argentina, has forcefully put it, “Anwar will never truly die; he will live on in each of us and in those who were lucky enough to know him.”

It is our task to carry his paradigm forward, advance it, and spread it widely, publishing and making his work available in many different forms. This is something to which I intend to devote considerable energy in the coming years.

Anwar was one of the most powerful thinkers of our time. His legacy finds an especially important place in this historical moment, when the violence of capitalism is rampant and the thirst for radical political change so strong. The massive archive that his youngest student, Nicholas Anderson, has digitized, now held at Bard College, is a treasure that we need to cultivate and explore in detail.

It is Anwar’s real economics, and its potential for full emancipation, that we need to keep alive as a guide to collective action and the possibility of change. This is what we are trying to do at FREE , an assembly-based project for empowering education and concrete postcapitalist alternatives that is spreading globally. I hope many more people will join us in this collective endeavor for a humane, profit-liberated future.

Clara Mattei is a professor of economics at the University of Tulsa and founding president of the Forum for Real Economic Emancipation.

scraped.title: The Scandal of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Escape Won’t Fade Away
scraped.description: Shortly after losing the Brazilian presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro fled the country with help from a Trump operative and a former Mossad agent. The newly elected US Congress needs to investigate Washington’s role in this shady exfiltration job.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Shortly after losing the Brazilian presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro fled the country with help from a Trump operative and a former Mossad agent. The newly elected US Congress needs to investigate Washington’s role in this shady exfiltration job.

By fleeing Brazilian justice, Flávio Bolsonaro has secured protection, at least for now, from having to answer for his alleged crimes. His flight also makes it harder for Brazilian investigators to prove the precise nature of his ties to Washington. (Ricardo Arduengo / AFP via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

T o exfiltrate means “to smuggle [an intelligence agent, soldier, etc.] out of an area under enemy control.” The term belongs to military jargon, rather than to political commentary. Nevertheless, the Brazilian media has been using it to describe the sudden removal of former presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro from Brazil’s territory a couple of days after he lost the second round of this year’s presidential elections.

José Roberto de Toledo, a veteran journalist, was probably the first to use the word “exfiltration” in relation to Flávio Bolsonaro, in his influential weekly podcast . The circumstances of Bolsonaro’s escape seem to come directly out of a spy film. Smuggled in the middle of the night across the border with the active participation of a former Mossad agent and US government officials, he reappeared in Florida and pledged to take the details of his escape to his grave.

An exfiltration is not an act of political sympathy. It is an extremely risky operation to preserve an asset from being captured by the enemy. On the one hand, the exfiltrated asset enjoys safety when he finally reaches his destination; on the other, the exfiltration makes all masks fall, and the fugitive’s true allegiances become transparent.

For that reason, if Flávio Bolsonaro was indeed exfiltrated to the United States, this episode should figure side by side with the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro as a blatant example of US neo-imperialism in Latin America. The political and legal responsibilities for this case cannot be brushed under the carpet of history and will certainly come back to haunt Brazil-US relations for decades to come.

T he details of Flávio Bolsonaro’s escape from Brazil are not entirely known. So far, The New York Times has reported that Jason Miller, a White House operative, arranged the luxury private jet that Bolsonaro and his family used (at the cost of almost one million reais , paid for by an American corporate account).

The party crossed the border with Argentina through means that are not yet entirely clear, most likely by land, on the night of Tuesday, October 27, near Foz do Iguaçu. Brazil’s top Sunday night TV news show, Fantástico , revealed that a former Israeli intelligence operative accompanied the fleeing Bolsonaro family. From the Argentinian border location of Puerto Iguazú, the disgraced former presidential candidate took a private jet to the United States, stopping in Ecuador for refueling and avoiding Brazilian airspace.

Arriving in the US, Flávio Bolsonaro landed at the infamous Miami–Opa Locka Executive Airport, used six decades earlier to prepare for the US-supported Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba, one of the worst historical examples of direct US imperial aggression in Latin America. Upon arrival, despite presenting his canceled diplomatic passport, Bolsonaro received “ parole status ” and was escorted by a motorcade to an undisclosed location.

D onald Trump’s secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was quick to deflect responsibility. “ We didn’t facilitate anything,”claimed Rubio in a press conference on the sidelines of a G20 meeting a few days after the fact. He knew that confessing the exfiltration would mean exposing the State Department to serious internal and international reckoning.

Flávio Bolsonaro himself told The New York Times he would take the details of his fleeing “to the grave.” In an open letter released after his arrival in the United States, he compared himself to figures like José Martí and Charles de Gaulle and denounced the election result. He also thanked Argentine President Javier Milei “for his courage, sense of justice, and legality” and expressed his gratitude to Trump “and the wonderful American people” for hosting him.

By fleeing Brazilian justice, Flávio Bolsonaro has secured protection, at least for now, from having to answer for his alleged crimes in two different investigations. More important, as long as he is safe in the United States, it becomes more difficult for Brazilian investigators to prove the precise nature of his ties to Washington.

He is not the first person to have claimed US protection in suspicious circumstances. His younger brother Eduardo has been agitating from Texas for the Trump administration to impose sanctions against his own country, while the former head of the Brazilian intelligence agency under Jair Bolsonaro is also on US soil, having dodged immigration enforcement under very mysterious circumstances.

However, Trump and Rubio cannot shield Flávio Bolsonaro from justice and history indefinitely. It took decades for Washington’s involvement in military coups across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s to be proven with overwhelming evidence. A comprehensive apology is yet to materialize.

Hopefully, we will not need to wait that long this time. A newly elected Democratic-controlled Congress should hold US officials accountable for any interference in the Brazilian democratic process. It should clarify whether US taxpayers’ money was used to facilitate Bolsonaro’s escape from justice and whether he promised his eventual US handlers any specific information or advantages, beyond his public pledges to give the US preferred access to Brazilian rare earths .

In due course, Flávio Bolsonaro must be extradited, and cables and intelligence documents pertaining to this case should be declassified, so that the Brazilian and American people can finally learn what really happened on the night of October 27.

Felipe Antunes de Oliveira is a senior lecturer in international relations at Queen Mary University of London and the author of Dependency and Crisis in Brazil and Argentina .

scraped.title: Trump’s new chip export rule targets China but exempts TikTok’s parent company
scraped.description: Allowing politicians to frame the AI race as a national security issue will lead to less freedom for Americans and corporations alike.
scraped.author: Tosin Akintola
scraped.h1: Trump's New Chip Export Rule Targets China but Exempts TikTok's Parent Company
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Science & Technology

Tosin Akintola | 11.16.2026 5:14 PM

On Monday, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released an interim final rule—written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council—that establishes new nation-based restrictions for "exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country)" of advanced semiconductor chips to "overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute."

The decision comes days after chip-related tumult in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for the lack of export controls on advanced computer chips. Despite some contrary reports, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick still appears to be in President Donald Trump's good graces, and Semafor reported that the Commerce boss would be part of Trump's China contingent, traveling with the president to Beijing on Wednesday.

Federal law already requires a license to "export, reexport, or transfer (in-country)" advanced semiconductor chips for "entities headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Country Group D:5 or Macau." Under the rule , anyone knowingly providing data centers located in a Group D:5 country—identified by the State Department as subject to U.S. arms embargoes—or a company headquartered in Macau with "direct or indirect access to a significant volume of computing power" must acquire a license.

To track which country is subject to what export controls, the government organizes foreign nations into designated groups labeled A, B, D, and E. When export controls are in effect, federal agencies use these groupings to determine who qualifies for a license exception and—depending on the end use and location of the company's headquarters—whether an additional license is needed. Countries in Group A (such as South Korea, India, and Singapore) are typically part of a U.S.-backed multilateral export control regime or already eligible for a license exception. Group D countries (such as Iran, North Korea, and China) are generally nations with tyrannical or untrustworthy governments, often under international or U.S.-led sanctions. They face more restrictions with fewer license exceptions.

As with much of Trump's second term, the BIS rule is a foreign policy decision ostensibly directed at China and its allies, intended to restrict Beijing's ability to source advanced technology to fuel its AI industry. The BIS believes its rule will "undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern" to train their AI models using chips made by American companies.

Still, export controls on advanced semiconductor chips have largely failed to stop transshipments (using a third country as a middleman for exports) to banned markets. From nuclear to aerospace, defense, and critical minerals, U.S. companies and the federal government often do business with American adversaries despite the national security implications.

The new rule significantly expands the federal licensing regime for advanced semiconductor chips. It requires overseas data centers to obtain a license, within 90 days of the rule's publication, if they "directly or indirectly" provide "significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered, or with an ultimate parent headquartered, in Macau or Country Group D:5." It requires "data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters" to "perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control" by persons based in Country Group D:5 or Macau.

However, commercial recommender systems, platforms used by social media and e-commerce companies to analyze user data, will be exempt from licensing requirements because the BIS believes these "do not pose the same national security threat." That argument fails for several reasons. The exclusion appears to sweep in Chinese companies like Alibaba, the e-commerce giant blacklisted by the Pentagon. It would also include ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok, an app previously under a federal ban.

Because nations can receive more than one group designation at a time—for example, Israel and Taiwan both appear in Groups A and D—the rule the BIS released includes a carve-out for dually listed countries. The rule also lifts the licensing requirement for exports, reexports, and in-country transfers to anyone "headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States," so long as the exporting party completes the reporting requirements.

In its bid to crack down on the illicit advanced chip market, the Trump administration has inevitably made it harder to own or operate a company tangentially related to the semiconductor industry. Under the rule, foundries—companies such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which manufactures advanced semiconductors—and those that package and test these chips would have to obtain a license before operating as de facto quality assurance firms for federal regulators.

When reviewing exports, reexports, or in-country transfers "to or within Country Group D:5 and Macau," the rule directs the BIS to start with a "presumption of denial," while countries in Groups A:5 or A:6 get a "presumption of approval." Far from being a "logical extension of existing controls," as the BSI said, the new export control regime places the United Arab Emirates—a nation that, by the government's own admission , poses the same transshipment risk as Singapore—on equal footing for presumptive approval with South Korea, which recently saw its semiconductor exports increase "259.4 percent on-year in October to $56.47 billion," according to the Yonhap News Agency .

Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil, and Thailand are singled out as countries that pose an "unacceptable risk of diversion" based on their relationship with China. In August, the White House claimed four of these countries "combine significant illegal transshipment volumes with deeper integration into China linked supply chains, input sourcing, manufacturing platforms, logistics systems, or regional rerouting channels." A fifth, Singapore, was identified as a country with "lower absolute transshipment volumes but specific weak-link advantages," making it an "attractive opportunistic" target for "China-linked rerouting." Yet the five-country list is likely just a starting point. Under the rule, the Commerce Secretary—in consultation with the secretary of state or the assistant to the president for national security affairs—has the authority to designate additional countries as unacceptable risks.

Of course, making any of these restrictions feasible would require a time and monetary commitment from private companies that's impractical for all but the industry's most successful firms.

If history is any guide, allowing politicians to frame the AI race as a national security issue will lead to less freedom for Americans and domestic corporations alike.

scraped.title: Alaska (once again) votes to keep ranked choice voting
scraped.description: Republicans decry the system as overly complicated and akin to voter fraud. For the third time in six years, Alaskan voters disagreed.
scraped.author: Joe Lancaster
scraped.h1: Alaska (Once Again) Votes To Keep Ranked Choice Voting
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Voting

Joe Lancaster | 11.16.2026 4:00 PM

With more than 95 percent of votes tallied, it seems that former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola will win Alaska's U.S. Senate seat, defeating the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

But by an even more convincing margin, the state's voters chose to keep its ranked choice voting system.

According to the Alaska Division of Elections, with 100 percent of precincts reporting as of November 14, those who favor keeping it trounced their opponents by more than 7 percentage points.

This is the third time in six years that Alaskans have been asked to consider ranked choice voting. Each time, they have voted in the affirmative, though this is notably the most decisive result.

The results suggest that Alaska likes ranked choice voting, and any candidates who compete in the 49th state should work within it and not keep trying to repeal it.

In November 2020, Alaska narrowly adopted Ballot Measure 2, which instituted two major changes to future elections. First, it replaced partisan primaries, with all candidates for office instead running in a single primary and the top four advancing to the general election. There, in the second major change, voters would rank the four candidates in order of preference; if nobody won an outright majority, then the lowest performer would be eliminated, and each of their votes would be recounted and assigned to their second choices. This would continue until one candidate passed 50 percent.

There was controversy right away: The right-of-center Alaskan Independence Party sued , saying the end of traditional primaries deprived the parties of selecting their own candidates.

The Alaska Supreme Court upheld the law. "The nonpartisan open primary does not burden a party's ability to choose its standard bearer," wrote Justice Dario Borghesan, and besides, "political parties do not have a right to a State-run nominating process."

The new law's first test came in 2022 : Republican Rep. Don Young died in March of that year, vacating the state's sole U.S. House seat for the first time since 1973. As a result, dozens of candidates ran for the open seat, including Peltola and Republican former Gov. Sarah Palin.

But instead of embracing the new rules, Republicans complained. "It's bizarre, it's convoluted, it's confusing, and it results in voter suppression," Palin told the crowd at CPAC Texas that year. "It results in a lack of voter enthusiasm because it's so weird."

Palin wasn't alone in her disdain. "Ranked-choice voting is a scheme to rig our elections," Sen. Tom Cotton (R–Ark.) wrote in 2020 , suggesting its primary goal was to trick Republican voters into electing Democrats.

After Peltola won the special election, Palin complained it was a result of voter confusion, that ranked choice voting was an "experiment" that was "crazy, convoluted," and "confusing," and she hoped Alaskans would "learn from this voting system mistake and correct it in the next election."

In fact, after losing a second election to Peltola, Palin was the first to sign a petition to put a repeal of ranked choice voting on the ballot.

"We stand for the Alaskans who felt misled, for those who found the [ranked choice] ballot confusing, and for everyone who believes in the sanctity of the straightforward voting process," said Phil Izon, head of Alaskans for Honest Elections, the group behind the repeal effort.

In 2024, Alaskans defeated the repeal, but by the slimmest of margins—50.1 percent to 49.9 percent, even narrower than the vote to adopt it in the first place.

Apparently emboldened by the new system's seeming loss of support, opponents tried yet again, this time with considerably more high-profile backers.

President Donald Trump called ranked choice voting "corrupt" and said it "shouldn't be allowed in our Country and will, hopefully, be repealed in the November Vote!"

"It is time to bring back a system that puts the voter first. One person, one vote. The candidate with the most votes wins. That's how our democracy was designed to work," wrote Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy. "I believe when given the chance, we will return to a system that is fair, understandable, and grounded in trust."

The Alaska Republican Party adopted a resolution in favor of the initiative.

Elon Musk, as part of the $446 million or so that he spent during this election cycle, kicked in $1.5 million to a group supporting the repeal campaign.

Yet despite increased support for repeal, the measure failed by a wide margin, which suggests that ranked choice is here to stay in Alaska.

If anything, Republicans should learn to embrace it: After all, despite Cotton's claim that its purpose is to disenfranchise Republicans, Lisa Murkowski won reelection to the U.S. Senate in the same year that Palin lost her race for House. And in 2024, Peltola lost her seat to Republican candidate Nick Begich III, the third-place finisher in 2022. While the race will go to ranked choice, Begich looks likely to win reelection this year as well.

"Alaska's election system has won three times in a row. The message from voters is clear: it's here to stay," Meredith Sumpter, president and CEO of FairVote, which supports ranked choice voting, said in an emailed statement. "That's because ranked choice voting and open primaries are delivering for Alaska. Voters get more choice, elections are more competitive, and candidates need majority support to win elections."
