scraped.title: New PBS documentary explores the history of criminal justice in the U.S.
scraped.description: 'Crime and Punishment in America' tells the story of how America created the modern prison but failed to tame its justice system.
scraped.author: C.J. Ciaramella
scraped.h1: New PBS Documentary Explores the History of Criminal Justice in the U.S.
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Criminal Justice

C.J. Ciaramella | 11.16.2026 3:36 PM

A new four-episode PBS documentary series, Crime and Punishment in America , debuts tonight and offers a deeply researched and engaging history of the country's efforts to create a fair and humane justice system.

Written, directed, and produced by Lynn Novick and executive produced by Ken Burns, the documentary explores one of the most interesting but lesser-explored angles of our country's history. Like Reason 's recent cover story on the history of American prisons, the documentary recognizes that the question of what criminal punishment in a constitutional republic should look like has been, outside of the problem of race, perhaps the country's most consequential and enduring debate over the last 250 years.

America was in fact where the modern penitentiary was created in the early 19th century, in an effort to move away from the public punishments and frequent executions that the nascent American states had inherited from England's criminal code. In an interview with Reason , Novick says the fact that the penitentiary was a relatively recent invention was one of the most surprising things she learned during her research.

"I just couldn't really quite believe it, that this thing that seems so normal to us and has always been here—the prison, a place where you send people who have committed a crime for a period of time—that construct really didn't exist," Novick says.

The first generation of American prison reformers had noble intentions, but they also had an oversized confidence in their theories that resulted in macabre and fatal experiments with extreme solitary confinement. Novick says that one of her favorite quotes in the series comes from historian Rebecca McLennan, who says that the Founding Fathers had "a narcissistic self-regard that they could perform surgery on the souls of men."

The first wave of American prisons failed spectacularly, and the subsequent waves would continue failing in 40- to 50-year cycles, as the national mood swung back and forth between disgust over prison scandals and anxiety and outrage over crime.

The series features PBS' instantly recognizable documentary style of combining voluminous archival materials, A-list voice acting, immersive sound editing, and interviews with historians and firsthand sources to lead viewers through the historical arc of a big subject. The series features a who's-who of major figures in criminal justice over the past 50 years, from civil rights lawyer Bryan Stevenson to Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner to former California Gov. Jerry Brown, as well as former correctional officers and inmates.

One preview episode shared with Reason , "Episode IV: Getting Tough on Crime," begins with the infamous Attica prison riot in 1971 and moves through the passage of the Rockefeller drug laws and other harsh mandatory minimum sentences, the boom in prison construction during the 1980s, the creation of the victims' rights movement, through the tough-on-crime 1990s.

The documentary style is particularly effective in the case of more recent events, like the Attica riot and the retaking of the prison by state police, which left 30 incarcerated men and nine hostages dead. One of the Attica negotiators recalls in an interview with the filmmakers that, when the negotiating team was pulled out, many of the inmates, sensing that the standoff was only going to end one way, started handing him pieces of paper with phone numbers of loved ones to call if they died.

The biggest challenge for the series is that criminal justice intersects with so much of American history that there is too much material to conceivably cover. At times the documentary zips through sections that could be entire episodes, such as the failure of prohibition, the creation of Japanese internment camps during WWII, and the criminalization of abortion pre- Roe .

Still, Novick, who previously collaborated with Burns on The Vietnam War , Jazz , and Baseball , has a sure hand, and the depth of research and excellent interviews keep the material compelling, even for viewers familiar with many of the incidents the series covers. The story of how America created the modern prison system, maintained it despite its repeated failures, and exported it to the rest of the world is rarely told, though. For many viewers, Crime and Punishment in America will be an eye-opening look into some of the darker corners of American history.

scraped.title: Iran War Day 262: Iran Says No Nuclear Inspections Until War ‘Permanently Ended’
scraped.description: State of the Union: Houthi forces reportedly made gains in southern Yemen.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
Iran’s foreign ministry said Sunday inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) would not be allowed to visit its nuclear sites until the war with the United States and Israel was over. “We will not grant the IAEA access to the facilities until Iran's conditions are met and the war has permanently ended,” Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in an interview broadcast Sunday evening. The statement came days after the IAEA requested access to Iranian sites; inspectors from the nuclear watchdog went to the Bushehr nuclear power plant in September, but have not been allowed to visit other facilities since the war began.

In Yemen, the Houthis reportedly made territorial gains in the country’s south over the weekend, forcing pro-government forces from positions around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait. The Saudi-backed Southern Armed Forces said its fighters were redeploying to better defend the city of Aden, which serves as the de facto capital for Yemen’s internationally recognized government and appears increasingly under threat from the Houthis’ advance.

Oil prices continued to ease Monday, with Brent crude opening under $96 per barrel. AAA reports the average price of regular gasoline in the United States is $3.81 per gallon, and the average price of diesel is $6.00 per gallon.

Luke Nicastro is a senior editor at The American Conservative. Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

items.title: In Mexico, the CIA Is Playing a Dangerous Game
items.summary: Covert operations south of the border threaten to spiral out of control. The post In Mexico, the CIA Is Playing a Dangerous Game appeared first on The American Conservative. Latin America In Mexico, the CIA Is Playing a Dangerous Game Covert operations south of the border threaten to spiral out of control. (Cristopher Rogel Blanquet/Getty Images) Last week, the New York Times shed new light on America’s covert activities in Mexico, including the recent deaths of two CIA agents in the border s...

scraped.title: In Mexico, the CIA Is Playing a Dangerous Game
scraped.description: Covert operations south of the border threaten to spiral out of control.
scraped.author: Juan Rojas
scraped.body_text:
Covert operations south of the border threaten to spiral out of control.

Last week, the New York Times shed new light on America’s covert activities in Mexico, including the recent deaths of two CIA agents in the border state of Chihuahua. The Times ’ reporting shows how American intel officials built a relationship with a corrupt Mexican prosecutor, with the aim of establishing a base for counter-cartel operations. Because the Mexican government objects to U.S. spies operating in its territory, the CIA had to proceed with an extra degree of secrecy, working with state officials and other intermediaries to enable its presence south of the border.

The man at the center of the latest allegations is Guillermo Zuany Portillo, until May, Chihuahua’s anti-kidnapping prosecutor. In 2025, the State Department revoked Zuany’s U.S. visa over suspected cartel ties; four witnesses had previously accused the prosecutor of complicity in the 2022 murder of two police officers. Within months, however, Zuany’s visa was reinstated, as he took on the informal role of local pointman for the CIA.

Zuany, per the latest Times reporting, connected U.S. intel operatives with Chihuahua state police with the aim of developing a new special forces unit. Once embedded in the police force, CIA agents helped to plan enforcement operations and identify targets for raids. They routinely participated in these missions—even providing covering fire on at least one occasion—though they were careful to always conceal their identities by wearing Chihuahua state insignia.

In April, this unit conducted its largest operation: a raid on a methamphetamine lab in the remote Sierra Madre mountains, on the border with the narco-ridden state of Sinaloa. Four CIA officers participated; during their return back, the team’s convoy had to navigate winding roads through difficult terrain. One of the vehicles, carrying two CIA agents, encountered visibility issues, and plunged 300 feet into a ravine—killing all onboard.

The incident sparked a political firestorm between Mexico’s left-wing president, Claudia Sheinbaum, and Chihuahua’s conservative governor, Maru Campos. Sheinbaum has strongly resisted pressure from the Trump administration to allow U.S. security personnel to work in the country; moreover, Mexican law prohibits foreign agents from operating without express authorization from the federal government. And so far as can be ascertained, the roles of the deceased CIA agents were never cleared with Mexico City: one entered on a tourist visa , while the other came on a diplomatic passport.

Campos claims that she had no idea what the CIA was doing in her state, though Zuany stated otherwise in a text with the Times . In May, Campos also reportedly authorized a joint surveillance hub with five US agencies in Ciudad Juárez. While the governor has thus far avoided impeachment proceedings, her attorney general, César Jáuregui, has been arrested and charged with treason for the CIA breach. And after the latest story broke, federal and Chihuahua prosecutors issued warrants for Zuany’s arrest; Zuany has since fled to the U.S. where he now is reportedly under the protection of the American government.

There is, of course, reason to believe that Sheinbaum—who has deepened security cooperation with Washington in other areas—is more aware of CIA activities in her country than she has let on. A March car bombing of suspected cartel members outside Mexico City was later revealed by anonymous intelligence officials to have been the work of the Americans, who allegedly coordinated with Mexican authorities. There are two big questions worth asking here. First, which U.S. intel operations does Mexico City know about? And second, how far is the White House willing to go on this?

The record from Chihuahua suggests that the Trump administration is using a variety of tools to facilitate CIA throughout the country. To that end, the administration appears to be pursuing closer—and extralegal—ties with pliant opposition state governments.

Another is the revocation of visas and other potential punitive measures. Interestingly, visa revocations against elected officials have been deployed exclusively against politicians from Sheinbaum’s ruling Morena party, particularly those in areas along the U.S. border. Half of Mexico’s six border states are run by Morena, and half by opposition parties. Yet only Morena governors—Baja California’s Marina del Pilar, Sonora’s Alfonso Durazo, and Tamaulipas’ Américo Villarreal (although Villarreal has disputed the story)—have had their visas revoked, all over alleged cartel ties.

To be clear, none of the three Morena governors have been indicted, although the administration did take the unprecedented step of unsealing charges against the Morena governor of Sinaloa, Rubén Rocha Moya, earlier this year. And some opposition governors—Nuevo León’s Samuel García , for example, and Durango’s Estéban Villegas —are reportedly under investigation but can still travel freely to the U.S.

The pattern suggests that White House pressure on Mexican politicians is inversely related to the latter’s willingness to work with U.S. intelligence agencies for better or worse. Paradoxically, many of the CIA’s targets in Chihuahua often escaped, leading state officials to suspect that the now fugitive and U.S.-protected Zuany was tipping them off. Here, it’s worth asking whether the White House is ultimately more concerned with expanding agency access south of the border for its own sake.

Another possibility—not mutually exclusive with the theory outlined above—is that the Trump administration is most interested in weakening the governing party ahead of next year’s legislative and state elections (including in four border states). Polling suggests that Morena and its allies will once again dominate, though they may well lose their congressional supermajorities and some governorships.

Whatever the case, Trump is playing a dangerous game south of the border. If, as suspected, the CIA is acting unilaterally against traffickers throughout Mexico, the potential for further casualties and blowback is immense. Since the 1985 killing of DEA agent Enrique Camarena, Mexican cartels have avoided targeting U.S. citizens and especially officials for fear of overwhelming reprisals. This could change in the event of a broader U.S. intervention.

Many Republicans, including ostensible restrainers , believe it’s worthwhile to trade an open ended conflict with the IRGC for an open ended conflict with Mexican drug lords. This view is deeply mistaken. A military intervention in Mexico is quite likely to spiral out of control, bringing with it the potential for a new forever war—this time in our own neighborhood. Worsening disorder in Mexico would have grave economic consequences for America (it is, after all, our largest trading partner); perhaps most importantly, it could stoke a new migration crisis that undoes at a stroke the signature accomplishment of Trump’s second term.

Unglamorous as it may seem, Washington is better off leveraging the competent security partner it currently has in Mexico City. Fentanyl seizures south of the border have risen to record highs while seizures north of the border have plummeted to record lows; Mexico has also illegally extradited nearly 200 kingpins to the U.S. And contrary to her image as a progressive heroine, Sheinbaum has undertaken a surprisingly successful crackdown against the cartels in part thanks to a policy of mass incarceration.

Under Sheinbaum and Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch, monthly incarcerations have tripled relative to her Morena and opposition predecessors. If trends continue, Mexico’s prison population is set to rise to around 350,000 by the end of the president’s term, up from 220,000 in 2024. It is no coincidence that homicides have declined by roughly 50 percent since 2024. DEA Administrator Terry Cole has praised Harfuch for historic cooperation on security between both countries.

The Trump administration is currently reckoning with the disastrous costs of an aggressive military intervention conducted 7,000 miles away from the U.S. It would do well to avoid the risk of further adventurism on our very doorstep.

Juan David Rojas is a South Florida–based correspondent at The American Conservative . Before joining the magazine, he worked as both a private sector intelligence analyst and freelance journalist specializing in the Western Hemisphere. He is also a columnist at UnHerd.

items.summary: President Trump should follow through on his recently discovered nugget of self-knowledge. The post ‘No Deal’? Fine—Then Leave appeared first on The American Conservative. The Iran War ‘No Deal’? Fine—Then Leave President Trump should follow through on his recently discovered nugget of self-knowledge. Sometimes a little humility is a good thing. President Donald Trump wrote in a Thursday social media post that he was removing Vice President J.D. Vance from the Iran file because no deal with I...

scraped.title: ‘No Deal’? Fine—Then Leave
scraped.description: President Trump should follow through on his recently discovered nugget of self-knowledge.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
President Trump should follow through on his recently discovered nugget of self-knowledge.

Sometimes a little humility is a good thing. President Donald Trump wrote in a Thursday social media post that he was removing Vice President J.D. Vance from the Iran file because no deal with Iran is necessary. This announcement was taken as qualified good news in some quarters, including here at The American Conservative . My colleague Andrew Day has pointed out from early in the war that Trump does not seem to have what it takes to cut a deal with the Iranians, and that just walking away from a destructive and politically toxic war without a negotiated resolution is better than the so far regrettably thematic fluctuation between intense diplomacy and intense combat. Trump’s statement seemed like an intellectual step toward Andrew Day Thought, which is good.

The problem is that this fresh thought technology was not accompanied by any kind of indication that we’ll walk away. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” Trump wrote. That seems like a recommitment to the status quo—physical blockade and sanctions—but without the ornamental flourish of passing the occasional note to the Islamic Republic via the Qataris.

There is, of course, more than one way to skin the cat, and a sudden departure from the theater could be difficult to spin politically. (Although perhaps a big “Mission Accomplished” banner could do the trick.) Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute has suggested Trump may wind up favoring a “Swiss cheese solution,” whereby the U.S. quietly starts easing the blockade and removing assets from the neighborhood. But in fact the U.S. is still moving assets to the neighborhood, including a third aircraft carrier; the Treasury is issuing new sanctions against Iran; CENTCOM intends to expand the blockade to cover land routes under the auspices of something called “Task Force Iron Gate.” (I’m begging anyone who will listen: Can we cool it with the silly names?)

This all looks rather like the opposite of walking away. And without any negotiations ongoing at the moment, there are no possible goodies on the table to persuade Iran that discretion is the better part of valor, or, for that matter, any clear channel for rectifying chance misunderstandings that could lead to an unintentional escalation. Diplomacy is like Alcoholics Anonymous; as long as people keep coming back, it is to some degree working. Without diplomacy, well—it’s not exactly unfair to compare the parties involved to crazed dipsos on the loose and causing mayhem in the streets, is it?

The Trump administration has shown a consistent inability to pursue policies deliberately, consistently, and with strategic coherence on a timescale longer than about two weeks; this became clear no later than last April, when the White House launched its chaotic effort at trade rebalancing, a worthy goal that requires careful attention to detail and clarity about the actual intentions behind a given tariff. Indeed, the Iranians seem to think more and more that cutting a deal is impossible. (That’s what happens when you keep bombing people in the middle of negotiations.) For the White House, one strength of the economic war—fine, I’ll write it, “Operation Economic Outcast” (these names!)—is that it requires little strategic sophistication and can be tactically executed by some of the more competent members of the administration, like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. But, as I have written, the most optimistic outcome of the economic war is a new mess that we will have to clean up militarily. Short of the most optimistic outcome are a wide variety of unpleasant, uncontrolled escalation scenarios, particularly if the Iranians get desperate and decide that rolling the dice on more combat is a better bet than economic collapse. This is no way to run a railroad.

“No deal” is fine, if not optimal, but Trump needs to sh—ah, defecate or evacuate himself from the commode. Hanging around the Persian Gulf with heavy weaponry and no sort of engagement is just asking for something bad to happen. Otherwise, even unproductive negotiations seem like a safer bet. Let’s try to keep the drunks off the street.

Jude Russo is the managing editor of The American Conservative and a contributing editor of The New York Sun . He is a 2024–25 James Madison Fellow at Hillsdale College and was named one of the ISI Top 20 Under 30 for 2024.

scraped.title: Could it be satan? No, Huckabee, just the Americans you work for
scraped.description: The US ambassador demands fealty to Israel because of the bible and says the devil's work is behind opposition to the Iran war
scraped.h1: Could it be satan? No, Huckabee, just the Americans you work for
scraped.body_text:
The US ambassador demands fealty to Israel because of the bible and says the devil's work is behind opposition to the Iran war

“Satan has blinded the minds” of those against the Iran war, said U.S. Israel Ambassador Mike Huckabee in a late October interview . The devil “has captured their thinking,” he claimed. “I see it as spiritual darkness, spiritual blindness.”

“I know it sounds a little funny for an ambassador to be talking like this,” he said.

Yes, it does .

“Israel is not a political issue,” Huckabee also insisted (it’s not?) “It is a biblical issue. It's a moral issue.” He was referring to the importance of the Jewish state to many of Donald Trump’s American evangelical Christian supporters.

Huckabee said this right before the American midterm elections, in which the Iran war and U.S-Israel relations turned out to be significant issues helping to deliver big losses to Republicans.

Vice President JD Vance even lamented after the election that the war was in part the “the reason we lost is the war.”

But Huckabee rejected Vance’s conclusion. “I don’t agree with that because I don’t think that’s where voters are,” Huckabee said in an interview with Israel’s Channel 12 News. “In fact, if you look at the polls, the only group of people in America that really think that that’s an important issue are the Democrats on the far left.”

But that’s just not true. In fact, 74% of voters said the Iran war was a crucial or major factor in their vote according to exit polls . Gallup reported the week before the election that 77 % of registered voters considered the war “extremely” or “very important” to their vote.

Polling before the elections reflected an American public across the board — even Republicans — frustrated with the war and wanting an end to it.

Furthermore, because of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s role in convincing President Donald Trump to attack Iran, American opinion of Israel has plummeted , too. Exit polls indicate that some 50% of Americans think Washington supports the Israeli government “too much.”

That’s not just “the far left.”

But instead of engaging in self-reflection, Ambassador Huckabee is worried that American pastors aren’t having the right kind of influence over their flocks.

“Too many pastors in America are fearful that if they speak about Israel it might be divisive in their own church,” Huckabee said last week in Jerusalem to an international group of pastors, as reported by U.S.-based Jerusalem News Syndicate. “Well, if we are going to divide people, let’s at least divide them over something worth the division.”

“Go home and challenge something that is killing America and killing the faith in America and that is biblical illiteracy,” Huckabee told them. “Go home, be bold, be brave but most of all be biblical.”

What does this mean, exactly, “at least divide them over something worth the division”?

We know Huckabee is a Zionist because he called himself “an unapologetic one, because I believe the Bible,” in a Yeshiva University graduation address in May. There is nothing wrong with pastor-to-pastor advice. But there is something wrong with an American ambassador who is supposed to be representing the foreign policy of the United States, spending so much time on the taxpayer dime ostensibly advocating for fealty to another nation.

Huckabee doesn’t have the diplomatic post and all of the status, authority, residence, office and staff that comes with it to “be biblical.” That’s not his job.

“The Chief of Mission — with the title of Ambassador…and the Deputy Chief of Mission head the mission’s ‘country team’ of U.S. Government personnel,” reads the U.S. government embassy site on “The Role of an Ambassador.”

According to the job description, ambassadors’ responsibilities include, "speaking with one voice to others on U.S. policy – and ensuring mission staff do likewise – while providing to the President and Secretary of State expert guidance and frank counsel.”

Huckabee is supposed to report to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. What does Rubio think of his ambassador claiming that those American who opposed the Iran War have been “captured" or "blinded" by "satan”?

Moreover, does Huckabee think JD Vance has been blinded by Satan for repudiating the war? Is Pope Leo, the spiritual leader of 1.4 billion Catholics including 60 million Americans not “biblically literate” for condemning the U.S.-Israel war on Iran as unjust?

Such talk really does sound a little funny, ambassador, like the Church Lady on the 1980s-era “Saturday Night Live” asking “could it be… satan?” every time a guest said something she didn't like.

But the war is deadly serious and so should be the role of US ambassador anywhere around the world. Public officials are entitled to their own religious views and liberty. But there is something wrong if pastor-official Huckabee is conflating the interests of the U.S. with his personal biblical imperatives — that is the kind of theocratic thinking we are supposed to revile Iran for.

Perhaps it’s time to interpret Huckabee’s comments as more than silly one-offs and ask whether Trump should put a more serious person — one who puts American foreign policy interests before his own biblical ministrations— into the job.

items.summary: The Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is staring down the barrel of entering 2027 without a chair for the first time in its 51-year history. scraped.title: Squabble over leadership risks plunging the OSCE into crisis
scraped.description: With the unstoppable Europeans facing off against the immovable Turks, the obvious solution would be to drop objections to Georgia’s candidacy.
scraped.h1: Squabble over leadership risks plunging the OSCE into crisis
scraped.body_text:
With the unstoppable Europeans facing off against the immovable Turks, the obvious solution would be to drop objections to Georgia’s candidacy.

The Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is staring down the barrel of entering 2027 without a chair for the first time in its 51-year history.

The Europeans are wrestling Turkey to drop its veto over Cyprus’ bid, raising the stakes by loudly opposing the only other candidate, Georgia. Unable to win over Ankara, Europe should drop its objections to Tbilisi to avert a crisis.

With three weeks to go until the OSCE Ministerial Council in Lugano, Switzerland, on December 3, the organization remains deadlocked over who should lead it from 2027-28. The chairperson-in-office role rotates every two years and is normally voted on well in advance with agreement by consensus. EU member Cyprus was the first country to put its hat in the ring almost two years ago, in December 2024.

However, Cyprus’ bid has been vetoed by Turkey on the basis of the long-standing dispute over the division of the island in 1974 . There is a long history of enmity over the issue between NATO members Turkey and Greece, the latter of which has long backed Cyprus and opposed Turkey’s occupation of half of the island. Indeed, each country has vetoed the other across numerous areas of dialogue and cooperation. Just this past week, the Hellenic American Leadership Council (HALC) began lobbying the Trump Administration to veto Turkey’s candidate to become U.N. secretary general.

With this history in mind, it’s clear, at least to me, that the Turkish are never going to back down over Cyprus’ candidature for the OSCE chair role.

That leaves a second candidate, Georgia, which entered the race in January. However, in late September 2026, 14 European countries came out to block Tbilisi, without raising specific objections. This does not represent a veto. Instead, the EU has said that it will not consider other candidates apart from Cyprus, in an election that requires consensus.

Refusing to consider Georgia has resulted in the current stalemate. Europe is effectively taking the chairmanship to the wire, in a bid to force through Cyprus’ candidate. It’s not going to work.

This fight raises the real prospect of the OSCE entering 2027 without a chair, leaving it unable, for the first time, to agree on leadership, budgets or meaningful action on the core security priorities of its region, including on Ukraine.

The organization comprises 57 member states, including the United States, Russia , and most of Europe and Central Asia. A headless OSCE would cripple the only remaining body in Europe that exists to promote dialogue between countries in times of conflict. This at a time when European states have sidelined bilateral diplomacy with Russia because of the Ukraine war , such that the Europeans have been left out of last week’s Abu Dhabi peace talks .

With the unstoppable Europeans facing off against the immovable Turks, the obvious solution would be to drop objections to Georgia’s candidacy.

There are strong arguments in favor of Georgia. It straddles one of the hottest geopolitical crossroads in the world, with Russia to its north and Iran to its south. Turkey, while generally on good terms with Tbilisi, has a deeply troubled relationship with Armenia.

The fraught geopolitical tightrope that Georgia has had to tread on Russia is precisely why it would make a good chair of the OSCE. Indeed, Georgia assumed the chair of the OSCE’s Forum for Security Cooperation in April of this year — and with none of the attending drama.

The current government of Georgia has delivered an impressive track record of economic growth and reform that suggests it has the institutional credentials and credibility to lead. It remains a country committed to future membership in the EU despite the difficulties in the relationship, as the prime minister set out at the recent EU Enlargement Summit .

This last-minute European barrier to Georgia’s candidacy appears in part linked to the deterioration in Georgian-European relations since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. While the Georgian government has consistently and repeatedly backed Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity in official statements, it has found itself in the European crosshairs for not joining economic sanctions against Russia or getting involved with the war effort .

The reasons for this are pragmatic. Georgia suffered a brief yet devastating war against Russia in 2008 and the loss of a significant chunk of its territory in Abkhazia and South Ossetia. Having visited Georgia often over the past two years, it is clear to me that the loss of territory to Russia represents a deep scar that runs through Georgian society irrespective of which political party citizens support.

The idea that Georgia is a Russian ally because it refuses to expose itself to the risk of another damaging war is frankly ludicrous. Georgia still does not maintain diplomatic relations with Russia. Its careful positioning on the war has occasionally put it at odds with the government of Ukraine . And yet Ukraine is not opposing Georgia’s OSCE bid. Nor are the United States, Canada, Russia, Georgia’s immediate neighbours or the Central Asian participating states.

Georgia has faced criticism from Europe for clamping down on foreign-funded NGOs. Some Western commentators argue that U.S. and European lawmakers want to deliver a Maidan-style revolution in Georgia .

However, these disagreements are entirely incidental to the issue of Georgia’s candidacy to chair the OSCE. The organization was first founded in 1975 (initially as the CSCE) as part of the Helsinki Final Act to facilitate greater dialogue on security between western Europe, the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact. It has always been, purposefully, a big tent that even today can accommodate Russia and Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan, Turkey and Cyprus, Kosovo and Serbia, and so on.

It was perhaps inevitable at some point that a party to a frozen conflict within the group would one day step forward to assume the chairman role, prompting a veto from the other party. This is exactly what has happened with Cyprus’ candidature, which has become an immovable blockage with Europe and Turkey unwilling to give ground.

The EU is never going to win that fight, which leaves the OSCE deadlocked with mere weeks to run.

So, the Europeans are in the invidious position of not being able to force through their own candidate for the chairman role while blocking the only other credible candidate, Georgia, on procedural grounds. This is deeply unhelpful in circumstances where neither Ukraine nor Russia see objections to Georgia assuming the role.

If the OSCE enters a new year without a chair, the OSCE will have become a reflection of Europe’s divisions rather than a mechanism for managing them. It’s time for European nations to drop their objections to Georgia’s candidacy and avoid plunging the OSCE into 2027 in a state of crisis.

scraped.title: Trump's Africa envoy puts on a masterclass in bad diplomacy
scraped.description: Massad Boulos has taken a scattershot approach to affairs on the continent, flying far and wide while achieving little
scraped.h1: Trump's Africa envoy puts on a masterclass in bad diplomacy
scraped.body_text:
Massad Boulos has taken a scattershot approach to affairs on the continent, flying far and wide while achieving little

Since returning to the White House, President Donald Trump has increasingly relied on special envoys to deal with some of his most vexing foreign policy challenges.

While Trump slashed the use of special envoys in his first term, he has come around in his second term, in part because they allow him to bypass his career foreign service officers by compartmentalizing information from “deep state bureaucrats” who he has accused of spying on him and leaking his dealmaking to the press.

As in previous administrations, the current Trump administration has assembled a collection of envoys largely based on region and policy imperative. Regions like the Middle East , South and Central Asia, and the Arctic all have special envoys, as do specific countries like Syria, Belarus, Greenland , and Ukraine (currently vacant). Similarly high-profile or strategic policy objectives like hostage affairs and combating anti-Semitism also have designated special envoys.

But where the Trump Administration deviates from his predecessors is in Africa . There, he has mostly dispensed with the almost-30-year-old practice of appointing special envoys dedicated to chronically unstable areas like the Great Lakes, the Sahel, and the Horn of Africa; as well as country-specific envoys, as for Sudan or Libya.

Instead, the president relies not on a special envoy, but rather on a single senior adviser for Arab and African Affairs, Massad Boulos , whose greatest job qualification seems to be, not coincidentally, that he is the father-in-law to Trump’s youngest daughter, Tiffany.

Boulos’ appointment in April 2025 was not accompanied by the normal fanfare of previous envoys. In fact, the announcement itself was only two sentences long and did nothing to explain why he was appointed or what his role would be. No biography exists for Boulos anywhere on the State Department website; nor is he listed among the leadership of either the Africa Bureau or the Near Eastern Affairs Bureau — areas where Boulos appears to hold great sway in setting administration policy. The White House website similarly makes no mention of Boulos in any capacity.

And yet, despite the undefined nature of his role, Boulos has seen an almost exponential growth in his portfolio that has no parallel among Trump's other envoys. Nor is there any diplomatic or strategic logic to what countries earn his attention and when. At first glance, Boulos’ approach has seemed more in line with that of Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in promoting the president's peacemaking agenda, though, unlike Boulos, they feature quite prominently in the administration’s official communications, including the president’s Board of Peace website.

Boulos first entered the world of diplomacy in April 2025, when he was given the dual role of negotiating peace in the conflict between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda and promoting U.S. private-sector investment in the region. But quickly thereafter, he was seen at the president's side during the Oval Office meeting with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa the following month; and then again at an undefined White House “ mini-Summit “of leaders from West Africa that July, where the President also announced his intention to negotiate an end to Sudan’s deadly conflict .

Since then, Boulos has emerged as a sort of “ Forest Gump of diplomacy ,” arriving in Morocco to support Rabat’s claims on Western Sahara; in Libya to broker an “oil for unity” deal ; and then again on even more far flung issues, like Nigeria , Yemen , Lebanon , Algeria , where he has opined on topics stretching from the plight of Christians , to the Iran war, the Abraham Accords , and the war in Gaza.

To coordinate these massive diplomatic initiatives, he regularly appears in Brussels, Cairo, Abu Dhabi, and Ankara, to name just a few. But frequent flyer miles do not an effective envoy make. Indeed, many governments have privately expressed some bewilderment as to how and at what level Boulos should be received when he turns up in their country. Some don’t even know what he is there to discuss, since often the local U.S. embassy hasn’t arranged his meetings. Given that his title of “senior advisor” carries no diplomatic equivalent in the U.S. government or any other, it is rather his familial ties to the Trump clan that opens doors.

But even with the Trump calling card, it is questionable how much he has been able to achieve in his 18 months on the job. No doubt the mixed track record is in part due to his enormous portfolio, which would be too expansive for even a seasoned diplomat backed up by a team of career diplomats with experience on the disparate range of portfolios, let alone a “ small time truck salesman ” from Nigeria with no prior diplomatic experience.

It is odd, then, that Boulos is known to keep his own counsel, rarely traveling with more than one staffer and often not even including embassy staff in his meetings with host governments. It's no wonder that many of his diplomatic accomplishments can be described as one State Department colleague put it to me: “all sizzle and no steak.”

But such a scattershot approach to peacemaking and diplomacy can rarely deliver results that last, or get to the root causes of age-old conflicts. That is certainly the case in the peace deal he brokered between DR Congo and Rwanda, which to date has done little to actually pause fighting; or in Sudan where he has yet to unlock a ceasefire despite multiple rounds of U.S. sanctions; or in Libya, where his deal to create a unity government has been criticized as little more than a “pact that entrenches elite interests .”

What Boulos’ approach lacks, and what every envoy needs to be successful, is a strategic framework from which to operate — a roadmap that spells out what the administration's vision is; what it hopes to achieve; what resources it is prepared to make available; and what diplomatic team it has put in place to carry out this policy. None of these diplomatic building blocks appear to be in place for any of the peacemaking initiatives he has begun or any of the dizzying number of other diplomatic files he has opened. It’s hard to measure success when you cannot first define it.

Instead, Boulos has been deployed as a kind of diplomatic utility player, representing the administration at a U.S.-Africa business conference one day, peace talks the next day, and a minerals negotiation after that — sowing confusion all along the way, both within the State Department and among partner countries about what the U.S. approach truly is and who is in charge, since much of his portfolio would normally be handled by one of the State Department’s regional assistant secretaries.

Congress remains similarly in the dark. Typically, beyond helping to organize a “whole-of-government” response via an extensive interagency process, a special envoy would keep Congress, the media , and the wider policy community informed on the administration’s efforts. But with only a senior adviser title that comes with no Senate confirmation, Boulos has largely kept clear of Congress and the U.S. media. Here, too, absent that give-and-take over the administration’s policies, the bubble Boulos operates in has produced little more than an X feed chronicling his diplomatic adventures , but offering few details about the substance of his conversations.

As new Democratic congressional majorities arrive in Washington in January, they would do well to demand greater clarity from him about his role in setting administration policy, the strategy and resources he is employing, and the ultimate goals he is pursuing across such a vast and competing diplomatic landscape. Such clarity might help to achieve better outcomes in a region of the world where U.S. diplomacy still matters.

items.title: UK Apologizes To Women Convicted Of Baby Killing While Jailing Pro-Lifers For Prayer
items.summary: The United Kingdom further embraced death culture this week when its government pardoned 150 women who killed their children via abortion.

scraped.title: UK Apologizes To Women Convicted Of Baby Killing
scraped.description: The United Kingdom further embraced death culture this week when its government pardoned 150 women who killed their children via abortion.
scraped.author: Jordan Boyd
scraped.h1: UK Apologizes To Women Convicted Of Baby Killing While Jailing Pro-Lifers For Prayer
scraped.body_text:
The United Kingdom further embraced death culture this week when its government pardoned 150 women who killed their children via abortion.

The same country that notoriously arrests and fines people who silently pray outside of abortion facilities is extending pardons to 150 women who slaughtered their own babies. Removing convictions from women who were found guilty of killing their own children, which the United Kingdom government made a “priority” this year, is just one part of the country’s sweeping plans to decriminalize abortion.

Until August 2026, U.K. technically allowed elective abortions up to 24 weeks’ gestation, as long as two doctors agree continuing the pregnancy will harm the woman or her existing children’s mental or physical health. The Abortion Act 1967 also permitted the abortion of unborn babies who, while still in the womb, are deemed at high risk for “physical or mental abnormalities” or to be “seriously handicapped” if they are born.

This vague and sweeping provision already paved the way for hundreds of thousands of U.K. abortions each year . Under the country’s Crime and Policing Act of 2026, however, women from Wales to England are permitted to kill their unborn babies at any point for any reason without criminal consequences. The law was specifically designed to shield women who use back-alley and mail-order abortion methods to kill their babies from prosecution.

The move to sanction radical abortion for all is unsurprising given the U.K.’s dramatic embrace of death culture . Yet even the act of pardoning the small number of women who were prosecuted for killing their children isn’t enough for abortion-loving women and the activists who back them.

According to The Guardian , some of the U.K. abortion criminals are demanding their government issue a “formal apology” to them for the way they were treated.

“None of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison,” they told The Guardian.

Heidi Stewart, the chief executive of the U.K.’s top abortion business, the British Pregnancy Advisory Service, agreed that “for too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws.”

“While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice,” she claimed.

Contrary to the narrative touted by the U.K.’s pro-abortion regime, the prosecution of women who committed abortion crimes was rare and reserved mostly for the exceptionally violent and malicious. As The Federalist previously reported, most abortion-related prosecutions in the U.K. involved men “who have cruelly caused women to miscarry, often by brutal violence, as in the vicious cases of Kevin Wilson , Tony McLernon , and Carl Whant .” The handful of recent prosecutions aimed at U.K. women involved defendants who directly killed their babies late in pregnancy and in a remarkably cruel fashion.

One such example from 2015 involved the arrest and prosecution of a mother who suffocated her near full-term baby with mail-order poison and then lied to emergency responders that she was suffering a surprise “miscarriage.” The judge noted that the baby, approximately 32-34 weeks gestation, would have had a “very good chance of survival, but had no chance once you administered this drug.”

“He said the offence was so serious that immediate custody was required,” The Telegraph reported. He ultimately sentenced Natalie Towers to two and a half years in prison .

The Brits were never interested in throwing the hundreds of thousands of women who obtain abortions every year in prison. Even before it decriminalized abortion earlier in 2026, the U.K. was one of the most permissive abortion regimes in the world. Hundreds of thousands of women get taxpayer-funded abortions in England and Wales every year with the blessing and encouragement of the U.K. government .

The U.K.’s prosecution of a handful of women who executed their babies did little to deter the nation from becoming a haven for abortions. It was, however, a small acknowledgment that the innocent lives who were immorally butchered were human victims who deserved protection and posthumously deserve justice.

Now, that acknowledgment is officially gone. Even worse, it was replaced with an ideology that deems those who demand justice for the unborn to be the defendants — even if their pleas are only heard in Heaven.

More on the arrest of Isabel-Vaughan-Spruce, who has been charged with breaking a Public Space Protection Order (PSPO) for praying silently nearby an abortion facility in Kings Norton, Birmingham, on four occasions. pic.twitter.com/SOHFWzUX1U

While women like March for Life UK Co-Director Isabel Vaughan-Spruce fight repeated persecution from her government for “standing and silently praying inside a ‘buffer zone’” outside of a British abortion facility, U.K. women who are days or even hours from delivering a full-term baby can procure a DIY abortion of that child without punishment.

scraped.title: Alaska Votes To Keep Ranked-Choice Voting — Again
scraped.description: Alaska is projected to have defeated Measure 2, a ballot initiative seeking to repeal its top four ranked-choice voting system.
scraped.author: Shawn Fleetwood
scraped.h1: Flooded With Left-Wing Dark Money, Alaska Votes To Keep Ranked-Choice Voting — Again
scraped.body_text:
Ranked-choice voting’s ( RCV ) role in causing chaos in elections has led nearly 20 states to ban its use. Alaska voters, on the other hand, can’t seem to get enough of the controversial system.

Following weeks of tabulating votes from the 2026 midterms, the Last Frontier State is projected to have defeated Measure 2, a ballot initiative seeking to repeal its top four RCV system. According to preliminary figures , the measure is expected to fail by 7.2 points, with more than 95 percent of votes tabulated as of publication.

Under RCV, voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives more than 50 percent of first-choice votes in the first round of voting, the last-place finisher is eliminated, and his votes are reallocated to the voter’s second-choice candidate. This process continues until one candidate receives a majority of votes.

RCV was narrowly adopted in Alaska in 2020, thanks in part to backing from liberal Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s allies in the state. The system allowed Murkowski to survive a primary challenge in 2022.

Democrat and liberal Republicans’ use of RCV to defeat more conservative candidates drew nationwide attention to Alaska leading up to the Nov. 3 midterms. The New York Times dropped a bombshell report revealing how campaign aides for Democrat Senate candidate Mary Peltola and other party-aligned operatives found and recruited Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. (aka “Decoy Dan”) and other candidates to challenge incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in this year’s Senate race.

The goal, as it seems, was to find candidates with similar names to confuse voters and effectively siphon votes from Sen. Sullivan to help Peltola. While not officially called as of publication, Peltola appears poised to win the contested race.

Democrats have also won the state’s governor’s race, and an independent could potentially capture the at-large U.S. House seat due to RCV, according to unfinalized results .

[READ: The Senate Race In Alaska Is What A Rigged Election Looks Like ]

A measure to repeal RCV made Alaska’s 2024 ballot but was defeated by fewer than 700 votes after a wave of out-of-state dark money flooded in to defeat the measure. As The Federalist previously reported , the same forces also flooded the state this year to defeat Measure 2.

Unite America, the National Education Association, and the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) are among numerous left-wing organizations that collectively poured millions of dollars into the chief campaign opposing Measure 2. Those groups and many others who contributed to the effort are based in the Lower 48 and not Alaska.

items.title: Thomas Calls On SCOTUS To Assess Restrictions On Guns In ‘Sensitive Places’
items.summary: 'I harbor serious doubts that our nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions.'

scraped.title: Thomas: SCOTUS Should Assess Gun Control In 'Sensitive Places'
scraped.description: Justice Thomas is calling for the Supreme Court to examine the constitutionality of state restrictions on guns in "sensitive places."
scraped.author: Shawn Fleetwood
scraped.h1: Thomas Calls On SCOTUS To Assess Restrictions On Guns In ‘Sensitive Places’
scraped.body_text:
Justice Clarence Thomas is calling for the Supreme Court to examine the constitutionality of state restrictions on guns in “sensitive places.”

The justice’s remarks came in the high court’s Monday order list , in which the court declined to take up and hear arguments in Novotny v. Moore . The case deals with a challenge to Maryland’s prohibitions on gun owners carrying firearms in “sensitive places,” such as public demonstrations, mass transit facilities and vehicles, healthcare facilities, and more.

In his opinion respecting the denial of cert, Thomas said that he agrees with the court’s decision to reject the case because “each Maryland statute implicates a distinct historical tradition of firearm regulation,” and as such, “the breadth of petitioners’ challenge would complicate our review.” The justice added, however, that he is “skeptical” of the restrictions’ constitutionality and encouraged the high court to address the issue in future cases that come before them.

“In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case … we should consider the scope of States’ authority to ban firearms in ‘sensitive places,'” Thomas wrote. “The Second Amendment recognizes the people’s ‘inherent’ right to keep and bear firearms, a right that admits of only historically grounded exceptions. … Thus, when a State seeks to restrict the right to bear arms — including by limiting the places in which a law-abiding citizen may carry his firearm — the State must root its law in the Second Amendment’s ‘historical understanding’ by ‘demonstrat[ing] that the regulation is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.'”

The justice cited the court’s 2022 NYSRPA v. Bruen decision, in which the (6-3) majority affirmed Americans’ constitutional right to carry firearms outside the home for self-defense. The landmark decision created a two-step test that courts must use assessing gun restrictions possession. The majority said courts must first assess whether the regulated conduct is covered by the Second Amendment’s plain text, and if so, determine if that regulation is consistent with the nation’s “historical tradition of firearm regulation.”

Thomas acknowledged that the Supreme Court has previously recognized “a limited tradition of States’ regulating the right to carry firearms in certain ‘sensitive places.'” He underscored, however, that such a tradition “was narrow,” and that “expanding the category of ‘sensitive places’ … to all places of public congregation … would eviscerate the general right to publicly carry arms for self-defense.”

“Nevertheless, States have seized on the idea of ‘sensitive places’ to prohibit the peaceable carry of firearms in locations that bear little resemblance to legislatures, polling places, or courthouses,” Thomas wrote. “These restrictions stand on questionable historical ground. And, their cumulative effect is to prohibit firearms wherever people gather for eating, drinking, recreation, amusement, and free speech — an affront to the right of ‘law-abiding citizens’ to ‘carr[y] arms in public for’ their ‘ordinary self-defense.'”

The senior justice concluded his opinion expressing “serious doubts” about the legality of these restrictions under the country’s “historical tradition of firearm regulation.” “In an appropriate case,” he added, “this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry.”

Thomas’ remarks come weeks before the Supreme Court is set to hold oral arguments in Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins . A final decision in the consolidated cases will address the legality of bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles.

The deceased victim, 46-year-old James Stuart, was a manager at the building where Lambert owned a $1 million condo. The attack appears to have been targeted. Lambert, who killed himself at home shortly after the shooting, had spent over a year engaged in a costly and stressful legal dispute with his HOA and the building’s management company over what he alleged was a pervasive mold problem.

scraped.title: A Test Could Tell Me How I’ll Die. I Won’t Take It.
scraped.description: Would you want to know a future you cannot change?
scraped.author: River Page
scraped.body_text:
The porch swing creaked and my grandmother spat into her styrofoam cup. We called her Grynda, a portmanteau of Granny and her name—Linda—invented by my uncle’s first ex-wife. It was just the two of us out there, sitting with bellies full of Sunday supper. The spitting was relatively new, but endless, and the cup went everywhere she did, which wasn’t many places nowadays, and never anywhere alone. Between us were little couch pillows covered with pretty red chickens that she’d made herself not that many years ago. I remembered what she used to tell me about her mother—who everybody called Maw—and how Maw could wring a chicken’s neck with one fell swoop of her wrist for dinner.

Maw died when I was little, at the age of 87, sick with the same thing her daughter had, or at least something close. I never really knew her, and she never really knew me. According to the family, she spent her last few years in the past. She was convinced, for example, that I was her son Welton. When he was 2, his appendix had ruptured. His father, Maw’s husband, walked for miles into town to ask a rich man if he could borrow his car, but the man said no. By the time he got back home, Maw told him it was too late. Welton was retching green bile onto the floor. The family piled up in bed and laid with him until he died.

scraped.title: Why America can’t keep China down
scraped.author: Wolfgang Munchau
scraped.h1: Why America can't keep China down The great decoupling has only just begun
scraped.body_text:
“For me, l'affaire Huang obscures a far more troubling story.” (Vernon Yuen/Getty)

“For me, l'affaire Huang obscures a far more troubling story.” (Vernon Yuen/Getty)

Two things are increasingly clear. First, Jensen Huang was not forced to quit as chief executive of Nvidia because of an affair. Second, the honeytrap story is a diversion. The real question now is: a diversion from what? For me, l’affaire Huang obscures a far bigger, more troubling story, one encompassing the failure of a central component of US global strategy.

For years, Washington has relied on economic pressure — from dollar sanctions to tariffs — to keep its geopolitical rivals in line. Semiconductor bans too: the US long sought to keep China in the technological dark ages by restricting the sale and use of AI chips. Not only has this strategy now failed, it’s had the ironic consequence of pushing Beijing to develop its own home-grown alternatives.

The key player in the Huang saga is Megaspeed, the Singaporean firm for which Alice Huang (no relation) worked as a senior director. Megaspeed is a cloud-computing company that purchases advanced Nvidia computing equipment, before renting out capacity to clients that operate their AI systems. In other words: the classic cloud-business model.

In theory, US law restricted Chinese access to AI-infrastructure in third countries such as Singapore. But it’s downright naive to think that you can control both the dispersion of hardware, and the use of virtual capacities, when it’s so easy to hide your identity on the internet. After all, most modern computing power resides in what we figuratively call the cloud. I don’t want to push the metaphor too far, but the idea that any one country could control such a virtual world is absurd. And, as Bloomberg has noted, Nvidia didn’t even know where their physical chips were at any one time.

By Tom Ough

So, was Megaspeed instrumental in the smuggling of chips, or anyway helping Chinese companies gain access to cloud services US law should have prevented them from accessing? Probably — but it’s much worse even than that. Far more significant than the mere sale of a high-tech product is leaking the knowledge to produce it, let alone its more-advanced successor.

We know that Alice Huang was a corporate fixer. But the diffusion of knowledge across borders doesn’t really happen though people like her. Far more significant than Huang herself was the generation of Chinese students laboring away on PhDs in Western science and engineering departments. In mathematics, I recall an instance when an entire year group of graduate students was recruited from China. That’s unsurprising when British universities are critically reliant on Chinese students to remain solvent.

Since we ourselves educated an entire generation of Chinese scientists and engineers, why are we surprised that we fail to keep them down, especially when China itself now boasts some of the top universities on Earth? In the end, you can’t place an export ban on knowledge. Just look at the atom bomb, another technology invented in the US, but which was quickly acquired by both the Soviet Union and Red China.

It’s worth understanding how we got to this point with Nvidia. During the Bush presidency, US foreign policy was run by neoconservatives. Economic cudgels were there, but they played a subordinate role. Under Barack Obama, however, America became much more reliant on its financial arsenal. In a sense, this isn’t surprising. The dollar is the world’s dominant currency, meaning the US has control over any dollar transaction, even those conducted abroad. This made it possible for Washington to place secondary sanctions on countries — forcing foreign banks to comply with US policy or risk being cut off from the dollar, which for most would have been inconceivable.

There were technological arguments here too. As late as 2022, one could read that China was failing to produce chips as good as those in Taiwan or the Netherlands, both US allies. That ultimately led the Americans to think they could stifle Chinese technological leadership through lawfare alone. In 2018, Congress duly passed the Export Control Reform Act to strengthen the legal framework around high-tech products. A year later, the Department of Commerce placed Chinese giant Huawei on the list of companies that need a special license under Washington’s export-control regime. In 2020, again under the Trump administration, the US restricted Huawei’s access to chips manufactured abroad using US technology.

But the single biggest measure came in October 2022, this time under the Biden administration, which imposed a ban on the sale of high-performance semiconductors to China. That specifically included advanced AI chips: including those produced by Nvidia, with the ban widened to include the machines that build them.

That’s how US law became extraterritorial — the most important company that knows how to make these machines is ASML, based near Eindhoven. ASML is one of the greatest tech companies in the world right now, and which, together with its European supply chain of high-precision optical and mechanical engineering specialists, has carved out a profitable niche market. But dependent on the US for its own security through Nato, the Dutch government chose to yield to US pressure to make ASML follow Washington’s restrictions. Soon enough, the Biden administration went even further, restricting US citizens from working for any firm that could produce high-tech machines or even help with the distribution of sanctioned goods to China.

It’s a policy that continued with the second Trump administration. In April last year, shortly after the President announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs, his government imposed new licensing requirements to restrict the sale of an older generation of Nvidia chips, the H20. This was a dumbed-down processor designed specifically for the Chinese market, and which had previously not fallen under the restrictions. After China retaliated to US tariffs with tariffs of its own, as well as export controls, Trump undid the H20 ban, with an arrangement that the US would receive a 15% cut of any sale. At the start of 2026, Trump’s went further, authorizing a case-by-case licensing for the more powerful Nvidia H200 chip, albeit subject to certain restrictions.

In short, under Trump II, the direction of policy reversed. Yet it’s now clear that the US strategy of strangling China has failed. Quite aside from Nvidia, President Xi has asked Chinese firms to buy Huawei chips over those made by Nvidia or AMD, its US competitor. And why not? After all, Huawei has come a long way to catching up with its American rivals. They aren’t quite there yet, but, as with AI itself, the lag is now only a few months. With everything happening at Nvidia now, combined with other potential disturbances that could soon hit the AI industry, I wouldn’t be surprised to see China reach technological parity by 2030.

By Wolfgang Münchau

That’s the perverse effect of America’s various gambits — with the People’s Republic now poised to beat the US as its own game. And if that’s hubristic enough, the Americans have even less excuse given the lessons of other industries. Take cars, a sector German once dominated but which China has lately conquered. Ola Källenius, the chairman of Mercedes, lately expressed bewilderment about his company’s declining sales in China. But why? The fact is that, with better technological knowhow, the Chinese are buying their own cars, just as they’re making their own semiconductors.

There are broader lessons for the Europeans here too. Our economic sanctions against Russia are failing for the same reason that America’s chip policy foundered. Oceans are vast, borders porous, and the world of international commerce has so many backchannels that only a fool would think they could close every loophole. That’s especially true in Russia’s case: bordering 14 countries, and with over 20,000 kilometers of external land borders, strangling Putin’s regime by sanctions alone was never going to work.

As for the Americans, if their ill-conceived sanctions pushed China to sharpen its own chip sector, something similar is happening in finance. Both China and Russia have built payment systems based on the same blockchain technology behind cryptocurrencies. It’s early days, then, but the great decoupling from the dollar has begun. That matters far more than who, exactly, Jensen Huang had affairs with.

Wolfgang Münchau is the Director of Eurointelligence and an UnHerd columnist.
