scraped.body_text:
The case of Jane Doe at Cornell has galvanized the country in recent months. In October 2024, a sophomore at Cornell University now known as Jane Doe, went to a party at Chi Phi fraternity’s house. Doe accused seven Chi frat members of drugging her and raping her for hours on end. The District Attorney declined to prosecute the case when it was reported, citing her testimony for doing so. Cornell ran its own Title IX investigation, where it found she was sexually assaulted by two of the seven, resulting in expulsions for those two men; the other accused students were suspended. Jane Doe dropped out of Cornell. All the men deny the accusations, saying the sex acts were consensual or did not happen.

In September 2026, Doe filed a civil suit and the DA reopened the case. Governor Hochul appointed Attorney General Leticia James as special prosecutor to conduct a criminal investigation of the case. James has appointed Jacqueline Kelly to lead the investigation after lawyers of two of the accused filed petitions to disqualify James from the investigation after social media comments suggested bias in support of Jane Doe. Cornell hired a former U.S. Justice Department lawyer, Sally Yates, to conduct an independent review. A judge ruled last month that Jane Doe could remain anonymous to mitigate online harassment.

At the moment, the case is still ongoing, and no criminal charges have been announced. The case has caused a massive uproar on college campuses with over 60 campuses organizing walkouts and rallies under the banner “Stop Sexual Violence: From the Frat House to the White House,” in solidarity with Jane Doe demanding an end to sexual violence and more accountability from universities in ending rape culture on campuses.

This begs the question, what does it take to end rape culture in a society built on the objectification, sexualization and subordination of women within the framework of a deeply flawed justice system? An understanding of the origins of rape culture provides clarity on how to fight it while putting forth what we are fighting for: an end to women’s exploitation and for women’s liberation through the socialist transformation of society.

Many questions have come up as more and more facts surrounding the case come to light. Why didn’t Cornell investigate more? Why weren’t criminal charges raised? What support did Jane Doe receive? Why didn’t anyone ask more questions?

While we may never get answers to these questions, a very real pattern highlighted by Doe’s case is that women can’t get justice in a system that is designed to maintain the status quo.

The largest anti-sexual assault organization, RAINN (Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network) reports that 89% of victims of reported rape are women and girls and that nearly two in three U.S. women experience sexual harassment, with 60% of U.S. women being verbally sexually harassed at work or in public. The Center for Disease Control in 2026 further reports that nearly half of women experience some form of contact sexual violence in their lifetime.

You would think that a societal problem that’s so rampant and common would be handled as a social epidemic of sorts. Women, however, must deal with being shamed into silence due to victim blaming, fear of not being believed or fear of retaliation. If she does speak up to report the violence, the police and the courts find any possible excuse to avoid punishing the perpetrator. Every step is a battle to: report the violence, have it recorded as a crime, force an investigation, to force a prosecution, to force a trial and to win a conviction.

And say you get through each of these stages and the perpetrator is found guilty, the final sentencing may be unsatisfactory. The victim is attacked every step of the way with the media tearing her apart.

New York, where Jane Doe’s case is being investigated, has an additional hurdle. It is one of 19 states where there’s a “voluntary intoxication loophole ” in state law that makes it more difficult to prosecute cases when a sexual assault victim voluntarily consumed drugs or alcohol.

It makes sense that sexual assault and rape remain vastly underreported: only about one third of sexual assaults are reported to authorities. Those that do get reported require an intrusive exam to collect evidence for what are known as sexual assault kits. In order to provide valid evidence the exam needs to be conducted as soon as possible after the assault. Evidence in rape kits, once collected, notoriously goes untested. Failing to conduct DNA testing on evidence like blood, semen and skin retrieved from survivors’ bodies during SA exams means failing to use an effective techniques to identify perpetrators.

Efforts have been made over the last decade, such as the passage of the Sexual Assault Survivor’s Bill of Rights, which created an advisory group to recommend policies to decrease the rape kit testing backlog. Even with these positive steps forward, several states lack tracking systems for rape kits making it impossible to know how many have not been tested. In these unfavorable conditions, it’s no wonder sexual assault and rape go unreported the majority of the time.

The justice system is designed to maintain the status quo and send the message that sexual violence is excusable for some. This happened when during the Supreme Court nomination processs: several women accused Brett Kavanaugh of sexual assault, spurring actions across the country in the wake of the #MeToo movement. His confirmation as Supreme Court justice sent the message that the system will defend its “best” representatives – white men who defend racist policing, imperialist wars and uphold the patriarchy.

Earlier this year, Attorney General Pam Bondi’s complete mishandling of the Epstein files, from failing to redact the names to failing to bring justice to over 1,000 of Epstein’s victims, shows that nothing has really changed in how the capitalist justice system protects elite perpetrators

Another glaring example with parallels to the Doe case took place at Stanford in 2016, when a jury convicted Brock Turner of raping an unconscious woman. Prosecutors requested a six year sentence. Instead, Judge Aaron Persky sentenced Turner to six months. Six months. Judge Persky asserted: “A prison sentence would have a severe impact on him. I think he will not be a danger to others.”

There can be no justice in a justice system that refuses to see rape and sexual assault as crime, a system designed to fail women, particularly working class women.

Jane Doe went through all the institutions: a prosecutor’s office, a campus disciplinary panel and a civil court where she had to confront questions about her voluntary or involuntary drinking and her ability to consent over and over again in a biased system that protects power, money, the reputation of the elite and the future of young men who have bright futures in the ruling class. The justice system’s primary objective is to maintain the status quo, and as seen in the behavior of the Ithaca DA and Cornell, will only act when public pressure forces their hand.

Women all over the world, from advanced capitalist societies to developing societies, experience violence in a myriad of forms. From economic violence to domestic violence to sexual violence, the acts of violence are not random or isolated, but a symptom of women’s subordinate position in capitalist society. This subjugated position is not a coincidence or because it’s in the nature of men to oppress women. It has a concrete history that emerged with women’s status as property, a status that emerged with class society, a society where a tiny elite, driven by the quest for profit, own the means of production and a larger group of workers must sell their labor in order to survive.

In order to better understand this, let’s take a look back at anthropological studies of communal societies in human history where women were not relegated to a subordinate position. Frederick Engels, who studied early communal societies in The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State , argued women’s social position is a product of societal changes. Engels examined how people in these early societies got their food, shelter, how work was organized, who controls the results and how it shaped family forms, laws, institutions and ideas.

Human nature was not more humane, but the material conditions at the time, which required cooperation, was in turn reflected in the social relations. In communal societies, kinship was organized around the clan and descent was traced through the mother, creating matrilineal societies. Men and women often performed different work but everyone’s work was valued based on their contributions to the survival of the group. Tasks included hunting, gathering, food preparation, childrearing and caring for elders. The division of labor was created based on the ability to contribute to these tasks, not based on gender. Everything was owned by the communities as a whole; there were no social classes based on wealth or power.

A change occurred with the accumulation of wealth and private property, which led to the emergence of class society. The development of tools, agriculture and animal husbandry instead of hunting and gathering allowed for wealth to accumulate because for the first time more was produced than was needed to survive. This progress for humanity also led to the fracturing of society along lines of gender and class.

During the vast portion of human existence when people lived communally, the role of women, as gatherers and crucially as the people who fed and cared for babies and young children, was highly valued. Families traced lineage through the mother’s line. As new methods of agriculture and animal breeding created a surplus, men who had played a greater role in hunting sought to control the wealth and keep it for their sons.

As a result, over generations the matrilineal family was overturned; women became subordinate to men as their role at the center of communal life eroded. Men came to control wealth and resources, and monogamous marriage set the parameters for families. The marriage contract demanded loyalty from women as a way to maintain their position in society and pass along the accumulated wealth and private property to “legitimate” children only. At the same time, wealthy men were allowed to have multiple wives or mistresses. In later iterations of class society, the lord of the manor claimed the “droit de seigneur” or the “right” to have sex with a woman living on his property, on the night of her wedding; during chattel slavery in the U.S. men who “owned” enslaved people were notorious for raping enslaved women.

This historical development from social and public production to wealth accumulation and private production and ownership led to male-dominated families, the emergence of class society and what Engels describes as the “world historical defeat of the female sex.” Engels continues: “The man took command in the home also; the woman was degraded and reduced to servitude, she became the slave of his lust and a mere instrument for the production of children.” In essence, women became the property of men.

Understanding the origins of women’s oppression as rooted in class society better equips us to fight. This is not to say that class negates the importance of other forms of oppression. But, through this method of asking questions, we can look at the conditions that produced a reality and examine who it serves and what needs to be changed for it to end. This means change is possible through a fierce struggle; things do not have to stay this way. The social relations that maintain women in a subjugated position were created through the pressures of class society, which today is a deeply unequal capitalist system. To overthrow these social relations won’t be a gradual or automatic process, it will happen through militant struggle, when a revolutionary crisis arises. Patriarchy, like capitalism, has a beginning and it can also have an end.

The #MeToo movement of the late 2010s thwarted the culture of silence forced upon survivors of sexual violence generation after generation. Actresses in the entertainment business spoke out against sexual harassment in the industry amplifying a movent Tarana Burke began in 2006 to support young Black women who were victims of sexual violence. Millions spokr up, making public the shame they had been forced to carry privately, breaking the silence.

Some may argue that while some individuals faced consequences for sexual assault (for example, Harvey Weinstein, the man who made #MeToo viral, has received two prison sentences accumulating 31 years in prison after upwards of 80 women accused him of sexual assault), the movement did not create justice across the board for working class women nor did it stop sexual violence. Others may go further to argue that the #MeToo movement focused disproportionately on celebrities and rich women. Does this mean the #MeToo movement was not worthwhile? Of course not. It empowered women of all backgrounds, mainly working class women, to speak up and use their power to organize for collective solutions against rampant sexual violence.

In 2018, the union Fight for $15 and women’s committees of McDonald’s workers organized a one day strike of fast food workers at McDonald’s restaurants across the country to protest against workplace sexual harassment. They demanded enforcement of its zero-tolerance policy and mandatory training for managers and employees. Two years later, thousands of workers filed a $500 million class action lawsuit against workplace sexual harassment.

Unite Here, a union representing hotel workers, fought for years to provide workers with panic buttons to protect them from sexual assault and harassment. In 2018, the #MeToo movement provided an opportunity to pressure hotels in more localities to adopt the panic buttons including major hotel brands such as Marriott, Hilton and Hyatt.

The #MeToo movement also provided momentum for farmworkers in Florida through the Coalition of Immokalee Workers to enforce anti-harassment provisions in their Fair Food labor protection program. The program demands that all companies in the supply chain adhere to fair working conditions and due process for abuse complaints.

#MeToo created new spaces to organize against sexual harassment and violence and raised consciousness around the pervasiveness of sexual assault and violence. It shifted the terrain about how we collectively discuss sexual assault and violence and what justice looks like. However, the system that creates the conditions for violence against women remains the same. #MeToo teaches us that movements need to be broadened to include more sectors of society, like the McDonald’s workers did with #MeToo, that the struggles need to be connected to other fights for justice, and that we must fight in order to win.

“I am Jane Doe” exposes the hypocrisy of institutions like Cornell who were quick to expel student standing against the genocide in Palestine but took little action against students accused of rape. It also demonstrates that mass indignation and uproar were what forced Doe’s case to be reopened, not an act of benevolence from those in power. The student newspaper, the Cornell Daily Sun’s reporting, students taking action on campuses and countless people speaking up in solidarity with Jane Doe all created the pressure for Cornell, the DA and Hochul to act.

In this system, as unequal as it is, it is the duty of anyone fighting for a new society to fight for reforms and equality under the law. Rape culture is rooted in women’s historic status as property, subordinated to the man-dominated family. In order to change this culture, we need to change the conditions of women. This means fighting for important rights and fighting for a new society that removes the profit motive which keeps women in a subjugated and exploited position. And for women that means organizing for equal pay, the right to abortion and to reproductive freedom, to safe working conditions and to end sexism and sexual assault. Equality and justice are contradictory to a capitalist system. Our rights are rarely enforced and on the chopping block every 2-4 years, constantly threatened by legislatures and courts depending on who is in office and who they appoint.

History teaches us that nothing is permanent and that change is constant. But societal transformation won’t happen on its own. It takes organization and clarity about what we are fighting for , not just what we are fighting against . We are fighting against all forms of oppression and exploitation and fighting for a socialist future. And we are working to grow the movement with more and more people willing to struggle to end all injustices.

This is why it’s critical to fight for reforms and build independent organizations with their own demands and their own political program so their power cannot be co-opted. We are organizing to take power from the tiny elite of billionaires. Taking power means taking away the resources, profits and decision-making ability from this tiny elite and putting it in the hands of working people to use the resources and profits to meet the needs of the people and the planet. We need to attack the rotten core of capitalist inequality and bigotry in order to lay the basis for women’s liberation with a new system, a socialist system, rooted in the political and economic power of working people.

“I am Jane Doe” means solidarity: an injury to one is an injury to all, and the complete transformation of society is possible when the people move as one with a common goal and common vision.

items.title: From youth protests in Europe to international class struggle: IYSSE meeting in Türkiye discusses the perspective for the movement
items.summary: At an online meeting held by the IYSSE in Türkiye, speakers from France, Germany and Türkiye discussed how the youth protests sweeping Europe must be turned toward the international working class and the fight for socialism against war and austerity.

scraped.title: From youth protests in Europe to international class struggle: IYSSE meeting in Türkiye discusses the perspective for the movement
scraped.description: At an online meeting held by the IYSSE in Türkiye, speakers from France, Germany and Türkiye discussed how the youth protests sweeping Europe must be turned toward the international working class and the fight for socialism against war and austerity.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
On Tuesday, November 10, the International Youth and Students for Social Equality (IYSSE) in Türkiye held an online meeting titled “From the Youth Protests in Europe to the International Class Struggle: What Should Be the Perspective?” The meeting was attended by high school and university students and young workers. Alex Lantier, national secretary of the Parti de l’égalité socialiste (PES—Socialist Equality Party) in France, and Tamino Wilck of the IYSSE in Germany addressed the meeting by video.

Can Denizli, on behalf of the IYSSE , stressed that the meeting was itself an international event. The struggle of young people cannot be confined within national borders, he said. The source of the problems they face is the capitalist system, and youth must turn to the working class, the social force capable of building a world society based on human need. Denizli pointed to the explosion at the HABAŞ iron and steel plant in Aliağa, İzmir, the previous day, which, according to official figures at the time, had claimed the lives of 16 workers. He described the disaster as the result of safety measures being disregarded in the pursuit of profit.

Alex Lantier explained that France is passing through its deepest political crisis since the general strike of May 1968. The movement began on September 21 with the occupation of the Saint-Exupéry high school in Créteil, near Paris, and rapidly spread across the country. On October 17, high school students joined forces with the “yellow vests.” Even the Interior Ministry counted 550,000 demonstrators. The government has refused to make a single concession. Since September, more than 12,400 people, mostly minors, have been arrested. Dozens of young people have lost a hand or an eye because of police violence. On October 24, 70,000 police and soldiers were deployed.

Lantier traced the government’s intransigence to the bankruptcy of the French state. Public debt has reached €3.5 trillion, or around 120 percent of national income. Debt servicing alone this year amounts to €65 billion, more than either the education or the military budget. While the European powers are planning up to €800 billion in additional spending on rearmament, NATO is preparing a blockade of Kaliningrad.

The ruling class is pursuing a two-pronged strategy. Alongside repression, the trade union bureaucracies and Jean-Luc Mélenchon have been assigned the task of bringing the movement back under the control of the state. The bureaucracies held back the working class for six weeks and reduced national action to a single one-day strike on November 5.

Lantier pointed to the strike carried out on October 30 at 113 ports in 22 countries across five continents under the slogan “Dockworkers do not work for war.” This was a sign that the working class is beginning to enter the struggle against war. Action committees independent of the trade unions and the bourgeois parties, Lantier said, must unite through the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees (IWA-RFC) to prepare a Europe-wide general strike. Citing Trotsky’s Whither France? he stressed that a genuine general strike directly poses the question of power. The demands of young people and workers, he concluded, can be realized only through the expropriation of the financial oligarchy by the working class and the replacement of the European Union by the United Socialist States of Europe.

Tamino Wilck reported that the spark of the movement has leapt to Germany, where 120,000 young people took to the streets, 15,000 of them in Berlin. The protests directly link the struggle against cuts in education with opposition to war, compulsory military service and a rearmament drive unprecedented since Hitler. As one student in Berlin put it: “I don’t want to go to war. I know that the people fighting on the other side are not my enemies, that my real enemies are the ones giving the orders.”

Wilck said the answer cannot be to appeal to the government. The protests must become the starting point for the mobilization of the working class and a Europe-wide general strike. He recalled that on the very day of the protests, the Left Party (Die Linke) in Berlin decided to open coalition talks with the SPD and the Greens to continue social cuts and rearmament. Taking the movement forward, he stressed, means fighting against capitalism—that is, fighting for socialism.

In the second part of his remarks, Denizli addressed the significance of the international movement for young people in Türkiye. He said that the warning by Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahçeli, “Don’t try to emulate France!”, and Erdoğan’s declaration that “Türkiye is not a country to be surrendered to the street” were admissions of the fear gripping the ruling class.

Denizli noted that of the 24 million young people aged 15 to 34, 6.5 million are neither in education nor in employment. In the draft budget for 2027, the resources allocated to defense, internal security and interest payments exceed those for education, health care and social assistance. As an example of the international character of state repression, Denizli pointed to the case of the Ukrainian comrade Bogdan Syrotiuk.

On November 6, the Turkish Grand National Assembly approved the Mecca Agreement, which binds Türkiye to a military alliance with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that forms part of the US war against Iran. Denizli pointed out that the Republican People’s Party (CHP) also voted “yes,” and said that the “no” vote cast by the YENİ Party (NEW Party) should deceive no one. During the mass protests of March 2025, he recalled, the CHP leadership did everything in its power to prevent the movement from spreading to the workplaces.

Warning against the illusion that capitalism can be reformed, Denizli called for the building of independent rank-and-file committees in schools, workplaces and neighborhoods and for their unification at the international level through the IWA-RFC. He urged those in attendance to join the IYSSE and the Socialist Equality Party, stressing: “The choice before us is clear: socialism or capitalist barbarism.”

One of the contributions that followed focused on the case of Bogdan Syrotiuk. The speaker explained that the conviction handed down on August 10 was based not on a single act of espionage or sabotage, but on six articles published on the WSWS and on correspondence with its editors. The book The Case of Bogdan Syrotiuk , which brings together Bogdan’s writings and the documents of the case, was published by Mehring Books in September. The speaker called on participants to sign the petition at freebogdan.wsws.org .

Another participant spoke on the contemporary relevance of the 1917 October Revolution, whose 109th anniversary had been marked three days before the meeting. The speaker recalled that it was not diplomats, but the revolutionary movement of the working class, that brought the First World War to an end and stressed that what collapsed in 1991 was not socialism but Stalinism. Referring to the principles set out in “Socialism and the Fight Against War,” the statement issued by the International Committee of the Fourth International (ICFI) in 2016, the speaker explained that for young people in Türkiye this means fighting the war policies of the Turkish bourgeoisie, a member of the NATO alliance, and opposing the Mecca Agreement.

Another speaker addressed the correct approach to artificial intelligence and to Socialism AI, launched by the ICFI in December 2025. The ruling class, the speaker stressed, is using artificial intelligence for layoffs, surveillance, censorship and war. But the decisive question is not the technology itself, but which class wields it. Grounded in the Marxist classics and the WSWS archive of some 125,000 articles, Socialism AI is a tool for answering the questions of workers and young people based on the accumulated lessons of history.

Finally, an IYSSE member took the floor. Proceeding from Lenin’s dictum that “Without revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement,” the speaker presented the IYSSE’s program of theoretical education and invited those present to take part in it.

To set up an IYSSE chapter at your school and to take part in our online education program, contact us here .

items.title: Right-wing UK think tank revives “idleness” slur, demands Labour “finish the job” of cutting welfare
items.summary: The Centre for Social Justice report provides ideological cover for the Labour government’s assault on the welfare state, as ministers prepare vicious cuts to pay for increased military spending.

scraped.title: Right-wing UK think tank revives “idleness” slur, demands Labour “finish the job” of cutting welfare
scraped.description: The Centre for Social Justice report provides ideological cover for the Labour government’s assault on the welfare state, as ministers prepare vicious cuts to pay for increased military spending.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Britain’s Labour government is preparing a massive assault on the welfare state, targeting the disabled, the sick and the young. Its spearhead is a review of “Young People and Work”, due Tuesday, which proposes stripping under-25s of their sickness and disability benefits.

Milburn, a Blairite former Labour health secretary, trailed its main proposal in an interview with the Times . Under-25s would be barred from claiming the health element of Universal Credit or the Personal Independence Payment (PIP—the main disability benefit) and instead be placed on a new “youth allowance” paid at the standard Universal Credit rate.

Young people who fail to engage with the scheme would risk losing part of the allowance. Milburn declared, “A deal isn’t a deal unless there are potential consequences,” warning, “Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support.”

Backing Milburn, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his government is “ready to grasp the nettle.” Burnham came to office pledging he would not be “squeamish” about cutting welfare costs, on the understanding it was necessary to pay for a sharp rise in military spending.

In his October 28 budget speech, Chancellor John Healey reaffirmed the target of increased military spending to 3 percent by 2030 and 3.5 percent by 2035—overall to 5 percent including related infrastructure spending. “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” he reassured the House. Healey declared that Milburn’s review, and a parallel review of disability benefits by another Blairite, disability minister Sir Stephen Timms—due to report next month—would be critical to further welfare cuts.

The ideological ground for this offensive has been prepared by a sustained campaign in the right-wing media and think tanks, vilifying those unable to work, the sick, disabled, and youth not in education, employment or training (NEETs) claiming benefits.

Last month, the right-wing UK think tank Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) published State of Dependency , part one of its “Welfare 2030” inquiry, which aims to restructure the welfare system by the end of the decade. Its subtitle is “How a broken benefit system is holding Britain back.”

The report argues that the welfare state, founded after the Second World War, has led to “Broken Britain.” It says that blame for “two decades of stagnant growth” lies with the rising welfare bill, with £1.6 trillion spent on working-age benefits—“over £1.1 trillion more than its capital investment on transport, science and technology, and housing combined.”

Such talk of investment is a ruse for a more immediate aim: freeing up massive funds for rearmament. In March this year, the CSJ said in a statement that the “increase in welfare spending this year alone is equivalent to 15 advanced Royal Navy frigates, 220 fighter jets, or 250,000 soldiers’ salaries, more than three times the size of the regular British Army.”

The rise in welfare spending, “driven by soaring sickness and disability claims as well as increases to pensions and benefits, is adding fresh pressure to the public finances just as defence chiefs warn Britain must rearm in an increasingly dangerous world,” said its statement. The CSJ calculated that getting one million people into work would raise £18 billion a year—“enough to fund the entire increase needed to raise defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP”—and called for mental health benefits to be “tightened to more severe cases” and for certain benefits for under-22s to be scrapped.

The CSJ was founded by Sir Iain Duncan Smith, Conservative Party leader from 2001 to 2003. Its 2007 report, Breakthrough Britain , identified the causes of poverty as “educational failure; family breakdown; economic dependency and worklessness; addiction to drugs and alcohol; and severe personal debt.” Its antidote to the social problems produced by capitalism, outlined in its latest report, are that “Work matters”; “savings matter”; “Stable families matter” ( State of Dependency , 4.3 and 4.5).

The record of the report’s chair shows what this means in practice. Duncan Smith gained notoriety as Work and Pensions Secretary (2010-2016) in the five-year Conservative/Liberal Democrat coalition, which implemented savage austerity. He designed and implemented the hated Universal Credit (UC), which merged six benefits into one, subjecting claimants to brutal sanctions, delays and destitution.

The report holds up the government’s “age of austerity”, introduced following the global financial crash, as the model governments should emulate. Duncan Smith writes in the foreword about his government’s welfare cuts in 2010-2019, equal to “£28 billion” in today’s terms, asserting “It worked,” and “We must now find the courage to finish the job.”

The human cost of “the job” in that decade was harrowing . A study published in October 2022 found 334,327 excess deaths from 2012-2019 in England, Wales and Scotland, attributed to austerity. Trussell Trust food parcels rose from almost 26,000 annually in 2008/09 to over 1.33 million in 2017/18. According to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, the poorest 10 percent of households with children suffered a loss of income of approximately £4,000 a year during 2010-2019.

A study of 149 English local authorities ( Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health , 2016) found that for each extra 10,000 people reassessed under the Work Capability Assessment in 2010–13, there were six more suicides, 2,700 more self-reported mental health problems and 7,020 more antidepressant prescriptions. The UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities concluded in November that year: “the threshold of grave or systematic violations of the rights of persons with disabilities has been met”.

The same ideology runs through Chapter 5 of the CSJ’s State of Dependency. It’s “Broken Britain” second part has a section “Worklessness (Idleness)”, echoing the Beveridge report of 1942, which laid the foundations of the post-war welfare state. William Beveridge identified “Five Giants”: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness. Beveridge’s report departed from the Victorian notion that poverty was an individual moral failing, and idleness meant lack of opportunity to work, not laziness.

The CSJ purloins the language of the welfare state’s founding document to argue for its dismantling. Its tone harks back to the Victorian Poor laws with its distinction between the deserving and “undeserving” poor. Economic inactivity, it asserts, is “chronic in benefit Britain”, with undeserving claimants cast as “hidden unemployment.” A new concept is introduced: “medicalised worklessness.”

Welfare is presented as a barrier to fulfilling lives through work, with the idle workless stuck in the “benefit trap” while immigrants take jobs in construction, logistics, retail and hospitality. “Employers have gained unprecedented access to overseas labour”, while “taxpayers have absorbed the growing cost of domestic worklessness.”

In an entrenched low-wage economy, it is a myth that employment is a way out of poverty. Official figures show 13.4 million people in the UK were in relative poverty after housing costs in 2024/25, and around 68 percent (5.2 million) of working-age adults in poverty lived in households where at least one person was in work. The Joseph Rowntree Foundation’s cost of living tracker (summer 2026) found that 62 percent of low-income households—7.4 million families—had been unable to afford at least one essential item in the previous six months, the highest number since the survey began in 2021. The increase was fastest among households not receiving means-tested benefits.

The report is stuffed with statistics designed to alarm and divide, suggesting society’s wealth is wasted on work-shy scroungers. It notes that the Department for Work and Pensions pays out £309.5 billion annually, “more than the budgets for defence, education and policing combined”—while not addressing that State Pension spending, along with other pension-age benefits, accounts for 57 percent of the total welfare budget.

The CSJ complains that a claimant on UC health, housing support and the enhanced level of Personal Independence Payment—a benefit helping with extra costs of living with a mental or physical disability—can receive £27,400 annually, while 6.2 million full-time workers take home less. This only confirms that successive governments, in collaboration with the trade union bureaucracy, have presided over a low-wage economy.

The CSJ’s primary aim is to gut sickness benefits, PIP and the UC health component. “We reject the view that mental health conditions are inherently incompatible with employment”; the “low rate of unemployment obscures the rise of medicalised worklessness.” “Worklessness,” the report asserts, “appears not primarily as ‘unemployment’ … associated with cycles of boom and bust, but rather as ‘incapacity’.”

PIP, the main target, is a non-means-tested benefit and qualifying to receive it is a mammoth task. Those rejected can wait up to 12 months to appeal if they fail to qualify. Over two-thirds (67 percent) win at tribunal. Under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, moves to further restrict PIP were shelved in July 2025 due to backbench opposition prompted by fear of a huge social backlash.

The CSJ laments the costs of rising numbers of children diagnosed with ADHD and neurodevelopmental issues. “In 2025/26, the DWP spent over £5.3 billion on CDLA [Disability Living Allowance for Children], … Expenditure has almost doubled in real terms since 2019/20,” it writes. Disregarding the suffering and stress young people endured at the height of the COVID pandemic, and the overall lack of opportunities, it states, “NEET rates have shot up since 2021, now equating to over one in eight young people” as “A new generation is being drawn into dependency”.

The suggestion that youth are content with a life on benefits is belied by the mass Gen Z demonstrations sweeping Europe and internationally, demanding decent education, graduate jobs and a future free of climate despoliation, police oppression and war. The report’s own figures show that 76 percent of the 300,000 young people outside education and work who gave no reason for being “economically inactive” (the CSJ’s “other” NEETs) “were not claiming any benefits in 2025.”

Last month Burnham promised every young person a “high-quality technical pathway, work placements, apprenticeships and the skills and experience they need to secure a good job,” with “timely, high-quality mental health support”. This is offered in place of a university education that tuition fees and the rising cost of living are putting ever further out of reach, leaving it increasingly a route open only to the children of the wealthy.

For everyone else, the promise means schemes like Sainsbury’s “Modern Work Experience Programme”, promoted by Burnham, under which the supermarket chain would use 10,000 young people as unpaid labour. Behind the promise of pathways lies the threat in Milburn’s plan: under-25s stripped of health benefits and placed on a paltry, temporary “youth allowance”.

Politicians of all stripes and a frothing media are pushing for welfare spending to be redirected to the military. In a pre-Budget speech on October 20, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch complained that the extra spending needed to reach the pledged 3 percent of GDP on military spending by 2030 was “less than a third of the increase in welfare since Labour came to office.”

Endorsing the CSJ report, the Telegraph gave Duncan Smith an op-ed two days before publication. He wrote, “We can’t allow another generation to inherit a life of dependency”. The welfare system was “an economic opiate”, with “systemic bias in HM Treasury towards low-skilled migrant labour”. Relishing the opportunity to push its anti-immigrant agenda, the Tories’ house organ claimed that non-British nationals accounted for around four-fifths of the net rise in payroll jobs since 2014, citing Duncan Smith’s accusation that ministers have “repeatedly pulled the easy lever of immigration.”

The Times is running its own six-month “welfare inquiry” led by Fraser Nelson, a former editor of the right-wing Spectator , pushing for “radical action on pensions and welfare”. A Sunday Times editorial launching the campaign on October 11 declared that Burnham “must be the prime minister who finally stops kicking the can down the road. The time to act is now.” Nelson also endorsed the TaxPayers’ Alliance “Benefits Bill” postcode tool, designed to demonise those on benefits as the cost of living for millions worsens. The tabloid Sun lauded a “clever tool” uncovering “benefits hotspots.”

With Milburn due to report on Tuesday, Timms to follow next month and Healey having pledged welfare cuts next year, the assault on the sick, disabled and young is shifting from right-wing think tanks to government policy. This assault will generate enormous opposition among young people in Britain. Defeating the government’s brutal measures means building a working-class movement across Europe and internationally against war and the billionaire oligarchy, for socialism.

items.title: Democrats use Nvidia chief’s resignation to denounce Trump as insufficiently belligerent against China
items.summary: The Democratic Party has seized on the resignation of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, an associate of US President Donald Trump, to launch a broadside against the administration from the right, declaring that it is insufficiently belligerent against China.

scraped.title: Democrats use Nvidia chief’s resignation to denounce Trump as insufficiently belligerent against China
scraped.description: The Democratic Party has seized on the resignation of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, an associate of US President Donald Trump, to launch a broadside against the administration from the right, declaring that it is insufficiently belligerent against China.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
The Democratic Party has seized on the resignation of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, an associate of US President Donald Trump, to launch a broadside against the administration from the right, declaring that it is insufficiently belligerent against China and demanding an acceleration of economic decoupling between the two countries.

ABC, CBS, NBC, CNN and Fox together devoted about 40 minutes of their main Sunday talk shows to the Huang case, giving Democrats a platform to grandstand against the administration’s alleged ties to the “Chinese Communist Party.” All five programs together spent about six minutes on the war with Iran.

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland accused Trump on ABC’s This Week of “essentially siding with President Xi in the question of sending very high-end chips to China. That is crazy. That undermines our national security.” Van Hollen demanded that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick be fired over the Huang case.

Representative Jim Himes of Connecticut, the senior Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said on CBS’s Face the Nation that Nvidia had an incentive to sell its chips to China. Himes added: “It’s the government’s job, it is the commerce secretary’s job, and the president’s job to stop that from happening...”

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer told the Senate on November 10 that Trump “continues to show a troubling resistance to confront China on AI and to protect American national security.” Schumer demanded the passage of three bills “to cut off China’s access to advanced American technology before it’s too late.” Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and two other Democrats wrote to Lutnick on November 9. The letter said: “We call on the Department of Commerce to immediately halt exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to the People’s Republic of China...”

Huang, who presided over what was until last week the second most valuable company in the world, whose chips power the artificial intelligence boom, has been the leading public opponent of the policy of economic “decoupling” from China. Huang argued that American capitalism’s national security interests are best preserved by open competition with China, and that export barriers would have a net negative effect on American competitiveness. Huang said in Washington in October 2025: “A policy that causes America to lose half of the world’s AI developers is not beneficial in the long term, it hurts us more.”

Huang resigned as president and chief executive of Nvidia on November 12, the morning after a lengthy board meeting, following a sex scandal publicized in the New York Times and the New Yorker . The Times reported on October 29 that “American officials had concluded” that Huang’s lover, Alice Huang, a Chinese executive and no relation, was “a Chinese intelligence asset.” No agency has published evidence for the claim, and Himes, asked on Sunday how certain US intelligence was of the charge, answered, “I don’t think that we know.”

Huang flew with Trump on Air Force One to Beijing in May and sat at the head table at Trump’s state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September. In December 2025 Trump let Nvidia sell its H200 chips to China in return for 25 percent of the proceeds. Nvidia donated at least $20 million to Trump’s White House ballroom fund, the Times reported. Trump defended Huang at the White House on November 9, and the Times reported that Trump had urged Huang not to step down.

The Times published its first report on October 29, the Thursday before the midterm elections and three weeks before Trump’s next meeting with Xi. Trump is scheduled to meet Xi in Shenzhen on Thursday, for the third time this year. The Washington Post wrote on November 13: “Huang’s downfall, which has the potential to mark a dramatic shift in power, was ultimately set in motion by one of the capital’s most influential China hard-liners, national security adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.” The Post added that “the hawks are ready to seize on the moment to redirect the national agenda toward tougher policies on China.”

Emboldened by the Democrats’ aggressively anti-Chinese statements, the Republicans interviewed on the talk shows spouted open racism. Representative John Moolenaar of Michigan, the Republican chairman of the House China committee, said on Face the Nation that “every Chinese national can be pressured by the Chinese Communist Party to comply [with] whatever directives they have from the intelligence.” Moolenaar declared every Chinese national in the United States a potential agent of Beijing, and he thereby marked Chinese and Chinese-American scientists, students and workers as suspects in their laboratories, classrooms and workplaces.

The policy of economic “decoupling” from China was initiated by the first Trump administration and previewed by Vice President Mike Pence in a speech at the Hudson Institute in Washington on October 4, 2018. “At President Trump’s direction, we’re also implementing tariffs on $250 billion in Chinese goods, with the highest tariffs specifically targeting the advanced industries that Beijing is trying to capture and control,” Pence said.

The Commerce Department put the telecommunications company Huawei on its export blacklist in May 2019 and the chipmaker Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation in December 2020. Trump signed an order in November 2020 forbidding Americans to buy shares in companies that the government designated “Communist Chinese military companies.”

This course was continued under President Joe Biden, who kept every one of Trump’s tariffs on Chinese goods. Biden banned the export of advanced computer chips and chipmaking equipment to China in October 2022 and ordered limits on American investment in Chinese semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence in August 2023.

The 2026 midterm election expressed growing popular opposition to war and austerity. In the AP Voter Poll, which surveyed more than 100,000 voters, 64 percent called the attack on Iran the wrong decision, and about seven in 10 said the US economic system favored the wealthy.

Ahead of the election, a YouGov survey taken April 24 to 27 for the Institute for Global Affairs asked whether lawmakers should increase or decrease the military budget. Forty-seven percent said lawmakers should cut the military budget, and 10 percent said they should raise it.

The Democrats are determined to entirely defy the mandate given by the electorate and instead press for an even more aggressive foreign policy, centrally targeting Russia as well as China.

Representative Tom Suozzi of New York, a Democrat, is co-chairman of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus. Suozzi wrote in the Wall Street Journal on November 4: “Finally, we must scrutinize the administration’s decisions on spending, healthcare, energy and national security, especially the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and develop a clear plan to replenish munitions and ensure readiness.”

Meeks, Representative Adam Smith of Washington and Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island are the senior Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House and Senate armed services committees, respectively. The three said on November 11 of Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff: “They and Trump are working for Putin, not for the benefit of the people of the United States.” The three Democrats added, “Congress and the American people also understand that Putin responds only to strength.”

This is the policy the Democrats intend to pursue, accompanied by attacks on social spending. Smith, who is expected to chair the House Armed Services Committee, set the Democrats’ ceiling for the military budget on November 4 at $1 trillion. On November 9 Schumer and 20 other Senate Democrats joined the Republicans in voting to advance a permitting bill that slashes environmental regulations on major corporations and that Trump had called on the Senate to pass.

The Socialist Equality Party is organizing the working class in the fight for socialism: the reorganization of all of economic life to serve social needs, not private profit.

scraped.title: Mamdani's SRG Plan is a Classic Bait and Switch - Left Voice
scraped.description: Mamdani’s overhaul of the brutal police unit reflects a longstanding demand of New Yorkers, but the proposed changes merely give repression a new name.
scraped.author: James Dennis Hoff
scraped.body_text:
Mamdani’s overhaul of the brutal police unit reflects a longstanding demand of New Yorkers, but the proposed changes merely give repression a new name.

James Dennis Hoff

On Monday, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced highly anticipated plans to overhaul the structure of the New York Police Department’s repressive Strategic Response Group (SRG).

In a pre-recorded video with City Council Member Chi Ossé published on Monday morning Mamdani said, “New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat. We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation.”

The announcement follows months of increasing pressure from Mamdani supporters and the broader Left to get rid of the counter-terrorism and civil unrest unit, which has been used by three different mayors to crush protest and punish dissent in the city for more than a decade.

Unfortunately, despite the Mayor’s rhetoric his proposal is nothing but a classic bait and switch operation. The proposal gets rid of the SRG in name only, replacing it with a different repressive force, and will do nothing to protect protesters from further police repression. Like a used car salesman, the mayor has lured his supporters in with a shiny promise to get rid of the SRG, but instead sold them on a stripped down plan that merely obscures the coercive power of the police while doing nothing to protect the interests or increase the power of the working class.

Although originally presented in leaked reports to Politico and other news outlets last week as a proposal to “disband” the SRG, the mayor’s plan actually does nothing of the kind. The Strategic Response Group will not be abolished, as the mayor promised, but will instead be subsumed within the NYPD’s Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau. In its place the NYPD will create at least two new units specifically designed to control and suppress protest: a civilian Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD) and a new armed “Patrol Support Division (PSD)” to assist the CDDD with “crowd control.” Meanwhile, according to the New York Times , many of the SRG’s other tasks, including patrolling the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, will be performed by a police unit with yet another different name.

Despite all of the name changes and reshuffling, it’s clear that these new configurations are just a rebranded, perhaps slightly less lethal, but no less repressive version of the previous SRG. Armed police will still be deployed to deal with protests and the NYPD will still be allowed to use military grade weaponry, including dangerous long range audio devices (LRADs) capable of causing hearing loss and damage to disperse crowds. In an interview with ABC News on Monday alongside Mayor Mamdani, Tisch made this point very clearly: “nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions.” How the NYPD will determine the difference between a crowd and a demonstration remains to be seen.

These changes echo a longstanding demand of our movements, from Black Lives Matter to the movement for Palestine. The problem is that they will do little to alter the balance of power between the working class and the state. Regardless of whether the SRG exists or not, the longstanding tactic of using the NYPD to manage and limit disruptive protest in order to weaken the ability of working people and the broader masses to use their collective power remains the same. The fact that we now have a “democratic socialist” mayor overseeing such repression changes nothing.

Indeed, although Mamdani has said that decisions about the NYPD are ultimately up to him, not police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, the training, staffing, and deployment of this new unit will be entirely under the direction and control of the Commissioner. Tisch, who has regularly expressed her support for the SRG , also seems to have played a central role in crafting the proposal, and there is little reason to believe that the NYPD as a whole will be any less repressive than in the past.

The proposed changes reflect a deep-rooted hatred of the SRG, a racist, para-military like force, which has been used for years to stifle dissent and break up peaceful demonstrations. But they are also clearly a response to the widespread protests and criticisms of Mamdani that followed the shooting of Oscar Belgal by ICE agents in October.

This shows the importance of holding progressive leaders accountable, sticking to our demands, and prioritizing politics over pragmatism. However, they also reflect the limits of such pressure tactics. As the executive of the city that sits at the center of global capitalism, Mamdani’s ability to provide any concessions to the working class is almost entirely constrained by what capital and the state will allow, and as these proposals show, it ain’t much.

Ultimately, there can be no significant reform or abolition of the coercive powers of the state under capitalism. The power of the police can only be challenged through the mass organization of the working class as whole. As we saw after the huge Black Lives Matter uprisings of 2020, and the fightback against ICE in Minneapolis, people have the power to resist, to set the political agenda, and to win at least temporary concessions. But only if we remain organized and continue to build our power collectively. In the absence of a sustained and self-organized working class, with a clear independent political horizon, such gains can easily be undone.

New York City

Police Brutality

Zohran Mamdani

James Dennis Hoff is a writer, educator, labor activist, and member of Left Voice. He teaches at The City University of New York.

Twitter

The midterms exposed an important contradiction: millions want a break with the status quo, yet the elections strengthened the grip of the Democratic Party on U.S. politics. AOC 2028 makes DSA's choice immediate: mobilize behind the Democrats and negotiate a platform acceptable to them, or build an independent organization to resist the Right and fight for all of our demands?

Maryam Alaniz and James Dennis Hoff

Florida’s Attorney General issued a subpoena against DSA, accusing them of having connections to foreign governments. This is the latest attack in a growing campaign of repression against the entire Left.

Samuel Karlin

Eight people are dead after a Brooklyn building collapsed Wednesday. It’s another example of a system that treats housing as a commodity rather than a human right. We need safe, public housing under working-class control.

Emma Lee and Mike Pappas

Following an explosive political year, Minnesota Democrats dominated the midterm elections, but Minnesotans must remember that ICE was defeated by the people, not by the Democratic Party. We need a party that represents the working class and our struggles, not the capitalists.

Charlotte White

To recapture the spirit of the October 17 mobilizations across France, workers must be drawn into the fight, bureaucracies bypassed from below, and cross-industry assemblies built to organize a general strike.

Leon Bengochea

As tensions rise in the region, Trump, weakened by the midterms, has decided to postpone the launch of a new offensive. But the situation remains highly unstable, while the status quo — with neither war nor an agreement — is at risk of deteriorating.

Enzo Tresso

Spain’s first general strike in 14 years shut down car plants, ports, and highways. Electricity demand dropped almost 10 percent, and employers estimate more than 2 billion euros in lost output. Santiago Lupe goes through the data to show where the strike hit hardest, how it compares to the strikes in 2010 and 2012, and why linking labor demands to housing could open a new phase of struggle.

Santiago Lupe

A million signatures and a flood of angry calls show pressure building from below against Jeffries and Schumer — and against the idea that Democrats’ midterm sweep gave them a blank check.

Sou Mi

scraped.title: Medicaid Work Rules Don’t Apply to Native Americans. They Could Still Lose Coverage.
scraped.description: CHEROKEE, N.C. — Two months before the deadline to implement new Medicaid work requirements, states had yet to receive detailed guidance from federal health officials on how to exclude Native Americans from those rules, leading to a patchwork of eligibility checks that pose challenges for qualified enrollees trying to keep their health insurance. President Donald […]
scraped.author: Elyse Wild
scraped.h1: Medicaid Work Rules Don’t Apply to Native Americans. They Could Still Lose Coverage.
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

CHEROKEE, N.C. — Two months before the deadline to implement new Medicaid work requirements, states had yet to receive detailed guidance from federal health officials on how to exclude Native Americans from those rules, leading to a patchwork of eligibility checks that pose challenges for qualified enrollees trying to keep their health insurance.

President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act excluded Native Americans from having to meet the work requirements to keep their Medicaid eligibility. But the rules issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services didn’t provide a standardized system to help states identify Native Americans who should be excluded, leaving states to figure it out for themselves.

Native leaders fear the limited guidance will mean a repeat of the Medicaid “unwinding” in 2023 , when states resumed checking qualifications for eligibility after a covid-era pause. An estimated 850,000 Native Americans lost coverage by May 2024, often for paperwork reasons.

The latest carve-out for American Indians and Alaska Natives also left out some Indigenous people, such as Native Hawaiians .

“I’m nervous. I’m extremely nervous,” said James Burns, who oversees the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ Medicaid managed-care program in the Qualla Boundary, the tribe’s sovereign land in western North Carolina. “When you look at any state that’s rolled out Medicaid work requirements, the unintended consequences have been vast, and that’s what we don’t want to happen.”

CMS published its guidance on work requirements in June, instructing states to use data they already have before potentially asking Native enrollees for additional records. But the rule didn’t set a standard process for states to prove Native American status, allowing states to raise the threshold for proof higher than federal requirements.

The rule also didn’t require states to share data with tribes, coordinate with Native health providers, or advise on managed-care plans like the one Burns oversees. Managed-care programs contract with the state to provide Medicaid benefits and connect patients to providers when they need care.

In July, a tribal advisory group for CMS recommended that the agency require states to allow Native Americans to self-attest to their eligibility as the standard proof. The group also wanted CMS to require states to share their Medicaid eligibility data with tribal health programs to catch when tribal citizens are mistakenly kicked off Medicaid. The National Council of Urban Indian Health pushed for similar guidance .

Your contribution is appreciated.

Native leaders expect additional guidance to come, said A.C. Locklear, CEO of the National Indian Health Board , which advocates for federally recognized tribes. But Locklear said that if CMS waits until December to issue more specific guidance on the exemption, states will have already determined their own processes. CMS did not respond to KFF Health News’ questions about whether it planned to provide more guidance.

“There’s 30-plus states who are independently repurposing their administrative processes for this, and they really all happen in a vacuum,” Locklear said. “That’s why it’s really important for CMS to provide guidance.”

Falling Through the Cracks

KFF Health News asked 14 states how they would apply the exemption and found that they plan to ask tribal citizens to prove their status in different ways.

Arizona, Colorado, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, and Washington plan to let enrollees identify their tribal status on their Medicaid application forms. The Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System, the state’s Medicaid agency, will continue to allow tribal members to self-identify, then will confirm their status through the state’s data on services received through the Indian Health Service or tribally run health centers.

South Dakota linked its claims system to identify people served by IHS, according to the state Department of Social Services. Oklahoma relies on a data-sharing agreement with tribes dating to 2022, according to Cherokee Nation Health Services. North Carolina requires a tribal enrollment card, a tribal census record, or confirmation from the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ Tribal Option managed-care program.

“There’s still going to be folks that fall through the cracks,” said Locklear, a citizen of the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina.

In North Carolina, 3,400 Native Medicaid enrollees are verified as eligible for the exemption from the work requirement, health department spokesperson Summer Tonizzo said, and those enrollees will be automatically exempted. But the state doesn’t know how many more people might be eligible for an exemption through tribal citizenship.

And Native Americans who don’t live in states where their tribes are based may face challenges in affirming their status. About 87% of Native people live outside of what the U.S. Census Bureau calls tribal statistical areas, such as reservations, according to 2020 data.

A Navajo Nation citizen living in Connecticut, for example, may have a difficult time being identified by the state because it doesn’t have a close working relationship with the tribe based in the southwestern U.S., said Liz Malerba, director of policy and legislative affairs for the United South and Eastern Tribes. She’s a citizen of the Mohegan Tribe in Connecticut.

Most states didn’t say how many Native enrollees they had verified as exempt from the work requirement. Several said they don’t track tribal affiliation, noting that ethnicity questions that would show Native status on applications are optional. In a comment on CMS’ work requirements guidance, the National Council of Urban Indian Health warned CMS that “not all states collect data on their American Indian and Alaska Native residents.”

States, Tribes Prepare for Workload

The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ health system has spent five years building its managed-care program, which is the only tribal-run Medicaid managed-care program in the nation, said Gwynneth Wildcatt, a director with the Cherokee Indian Hospital Authority who sits on North Carolina’s Medicaid Beneficiary Advisory Council. All Medicaid enrollees in that tribe who need exemptions have them, thanks to that program, Wildcatt said.

A close connection with the state has made verifying its citizens for work requirement exemptions simple for the tribe, Wildcatt added, because its program is already integrated into the state Medicaid system. She’s a citizen of the tribe.

In Montana, Native people who self-declare their tribal status for the work requirements won’t be required to provide additional proof, said Jon Ebelt, a spokesperson for the state Department of Public Health and Human Services.

The state has one of the highest percentages of American Indian and Alaska Native residents in the nation and began work requirement checks in July. It’s one of four states, alongside Nebraska, Arkansas, and Georgia, that are doing those scans ahead of the Jan. 1 federal deadline. Iowa begins its program on Dec. 1.

But Native leaders said Montana officials hadn’t clearly communicated how Medicaid enrollees could prove their Native status when those checks began. The state saw one of the nation’s sharpest declines in enrollment during the Medicaid unwinding as people struggled to navigate a backlogged system . Most enrollees who lost coverage did so due to paperwork problems, which rippled through Native communities .

Jason Smith, a citizen of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes who leads the Montana Consortium for Urban Indian Health , said clinics serving Indigenous patients are still working to reenroll members who lost Medicaid during that time.

Smith said the state has done a good job addressing tribal priorities while implementing work requirements. But he’s still concerned about whether its system is ready to handle the workload of the new mandates. As of September , Montana still hadn’t hired the number of workers officials estimated are needed to handle the workload. And federal data shows Montanans can face long waits on the state’s helpline.

“Have they improved their communication and outreach?” Smith said. “Will people be there answering phones? It will take time to see.”

Have you tried to prove your eligibility for Medicaid under new rules that require people to show they are working, going to school, or participating in another qualifying activity? Click here to contact KFF Health News.

scraped.title: Chickasaw Scholar Traci Morris, Ph.D. and the Importance of Governing the Digital Realm
scraped.description: Overview: Traci Morris, a Chickasaw citizen and researcher at Arizona State University’s Sandra Day O’Connor College of Law, is advancing the concept of tribal digital sovereignty, helping Native nations assert self-determination and control over the technologies, digital infrastructure and data that affect their communities. Traci Morris said she loves to be at the cutting edge […]
scraped.author: Chickasaw Nation Media
scraped.h1: Chickasaw Scholar Traci Morris, Ph.D. and the Importance of Governing the Digital Realm
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Traci Morris, a Chickasaw citizen and researcher at Arizona State University’s Sandra Day O’Connor College of Law, is advancing the concept of tribal digital sovereignty, helping Native nations assert self-determination and control over the technologies, digital infrastructure and data that affect their communities.

Traci Morris said she loves to be at the cutting edge of emerging technologies while supporting First American tribes within that space. Her research and scholarship regarding tribal digital sovereignty links both loves together.

When most people think about sovereignty, they think about governance of land, people and institutions. However, now there is a new digital landscape that also needs governing. Morris, a Chickasaw citizen, works tirelessly through her publications and professional work at the Tribal Nations Policy Institute in the Sandra Day O’Connor College of Law at Arizona State University to ensure tribal nations can exercise their own self-determination over the existing and emerging digital world.

“I think we are going to be moving more from cybersecurity as an IT concern to sovereignty as a concern,” Morris said. “Any nation that can’t defend its systems can’t guarantee its services. So it’s more than just cybersecurity — it’s cyber sovereignty.”

Morris said ideas about digital sovereignty originated with the European Union (EU). When she was conducting research for a book about tribal broadband internet, Morris kept coming across the term “digital sovereignty” and something clicked for her.

“One day I went, ‘We’re tribes. We’re sovereign,’” Morris said. “I saw that they were talking about governance, and tribes have the ability to govern. I thought, ‘We can have tribal digital sovereignty.’”

Your contribution is appreciated.

Morris used the language the EU had been using to govern its own digital spaces and transformed it as a concept applicable to tribal nations. She said she had seen the EU create rigid structures and rules technology companies would have to adhere to. These rules go beyond the EU, often having a global effect. Morris noted, for instance, when people have to opt in on websites to allow tracking cookies, that rule came from strict EU guidelines.

“I invented the term as a way to talk overarchingly about exerting a sort of sovereign governance over digital spaces,” Morris said. “We can govern our spaces. We as sovereign nations can say what is on our land.” She said digital spaces are no different.

Morris started talking about tribal digital sovereignty at conferences and was encouraged by the response. She said many tribal and community leaders immediately understood the importance of what she was presenting.

The digital realm over which tribal nations have sovereignty includes all the technology that touches people’s lives. Morris said broadband internet and other related infrastructure lay the foundation for this digital landscape.

“It starts with whether or not internet works at your house,” Morris said. “Whether or not a student can do homework without having to drive to a parking lot for a signal. Whether or not an elder can use telehealth instead of driving two hours.”

According to Morris, broadband infrastructure is the most visible layer of the digital world, but deeper than that is data or information.

“There are two layers because we are a tribal nation,” Morris explained. “It’s the data that the tribe is protecting — whether it’s gaming data or data about our citizen enrollment — those are all proprietary and belong to our nation. But personally, it’s your enrollment records, your school data, your health records — those sorts of things. So tribal digital sovereignty is who decides what happens to that data.”

Beyond infrastructure and data is the ability of tribal nations to protect their own knowledge.

“Digital sovereignty also affects whether, and how, our knowledge stays with us,” Morris said. “So much of our information, our communities and our tribes have been taken from us, and digital and data sovereignty is how a nation sets its rules and takes care of it.”

Morris noted, in particular, the creation of Chickasaw TV for uploading videos about the Chickasaw Nation. Because the Chickasaw Nation has its own platform, it can govern how the information is seen, used and protected.

Chickasaw TV also allows the Chickasaw Nation to retain ownership and copyright protection over its content. For instance, Morris said if someone posts a ceremony on YouTube or Facebook, that knowledge is out there forever, and it cannot be pulled back. Having its own platforms allows the Chickasaw Nation to guard and protect tribal knowledge and heritage.

Morris hosted a conference last year on AI in Indian Country. Mari Hulbutta, director of data stewardship for the Chickasaw Nation, was on a panel and said, “Data is kin.”

“You could have heard a pin drop,” Morris said.

Morris said Hulbutta’s statement has stuck with her.

“Data is kin,” Morris stated. “How do we protect our kin? What do we do to take care of our kin? Why are we not doing that with our data?”

Morris said she is proud of how the Chickasaw Nation has approached this new digital realm as it protects the data and knowledge of its culture and citizens, while also providing critical infrastructure. However, Morris also looks toward the future, especially because technology changes come in months, not years.

“I definitely see it changing quick enough that right now, we are at a great point because everybody’s in the same boat,” Morris said. “Every community, the whole nation, everybody in the world is like, ‘What are we going to do? Are we going to regulate it? What does this look like?’”

Morris is the executive director of the Tribal Nations Policy Institute at the Sandra Day O’Connor College of Law at Arizona State University. With her position, as well as her specialized knowledge, Morris is able to help tribal nations across the country, making sure tribes have the information and the time to understand the new developments, which sometimes seem to manifest overnight.

“We, as individuals and as tribal nations, have the agency to make our own decisions and govern these spaces,” Morris said. “That’s such a powerful thing that people need to know.”
