scraped.title: Who Is Listening to Indian Country?
scraped.description: Overview: Tribal leaders say federal agencies are treating consultation as a formality, sidelining sovereign nations from decisions affecting their lands and funding. Opinion The Nov. 3 election brought historic victories for Native candidates, including the election of the first Native woman to the U.S. Senate. But as Congress meets for its lame-duck session, Tribal nations […]
scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Who Is Listening to Indian Country?
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Tribal leaders say federal agencies are treating consultation as a formality, sidelining sovereign nations from decisions affecting their lands and funding.

The Nov. 3 election brought historic victories for Native candidates, including the election of the first Native woman to the U.S. Senate. But as Congress meets for its lame-duck session, Tribal nations face a familiar question: Who in Washington is listening — and who is willing to change federal policy after hearing what Tribal leaders have to say?

Tribal consultation was designed to provide a mechanism for government-to-government dialogue on federal policies that affect their nations. President Bill Clinton strengthened federal tribal consultation policy through Executive Order 13175 , signed on Nov. 6, 2000.

The intention was never to make tribal consultation a performative exercise. It was never meant to be a box-checking function carried out by a bureaucrat. For Indian Country, tribal consultation is rooted in tribal sovereignty and the government-to-government relationship that comes with it.

Tohono O’odham Nation Chairman Verlon Jose recounted an incident that occurred on Aug. 25, 2026, when a caravan of construction workers attempted to enter the Tohono O’odham Nation but was turned away by tribal police. The workers were there to conduct pre-construction work for a proposed 62-mile border wall that President Donald Trump wants to build through the Tohono O’odham Nation’s reservation with Mexico — a project the tribal nation adamantly opposes.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Undeterred, the construction crew returned in the middle of the night, accompanied by Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) police and a Border Patrol tactical team

At 4:03 a.m., Chairman Jose received a call from a tribal citizen informing him that the caravan was already on tribal land and heading south. At 4:58 a.m., his email notification sounded. It was a message from a federal official informing him that a crew would be arriving to conduct pre-construction work.

“I forgot to let you know that we’re going to be coming out to the nation to do pre-construction work,” the email read.

“They were already here. He didn’t even know that,” Chairman Jose said in an interview with Native News Online . “They had the nerve to call that tribal consultation.”

An email announcing work underway is notification after the fact. It is not meaningful tribal consultation.

Last week, Tribal leaders called into question another so-called tribal consultation, this time conducted by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).

On Nov. 4, OMB Director Russell Vought, one of the primary architects of Project 2025 , issued a Dear Tribal Leaders letter announcing consultations for Nov. 9 in Washington, D.C., and Nov. 10 virtually. The notice gave Tribal Nations just two days to register and a few days to prepare for the consultation.

At issue were proposed revisions to Title 2 of the Code of Federal Regulations (2 CFR), known as the Uniform Guidance for Federal Financial Assistance.

These rules govern how agencies award federal funds and how recipients, including tribal governments, manage the money and account for its use.

The five-day notice, which included two weekend days, gave Tribal Nations little opportunity to properly review the proposal, consult with their tribal councils and legal advisers, determine its potential impact on their governments and prepare meaningful responses.

The National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) called the notice period unacceptable and said the process did not constitute meaningful tribal consultation.

NCAI Executive Director Larry Wright Jr. (Ponca) described what happened during the consultation sessions on Native News Online’s Post-Election Recap Livestream (Part 2) .

Wright said the Nov. 9 in-person session drew about 20 attendees but lasted only 22 minutes, with four people speaking. He called the treatment of elected tribal officials “shameful.”

“When you’re talking about true meaningful consultation you can’t do that in a three-minute soundbite,” he said.

The Nov. 10 virtual session drew more than 200 attendees and included 25 speakers over 90 minutes, Wright said. Federal officials cut off 20 speakers at the three-minute mark, sometimes speaking over them.

“It was pathetic,” Wright said.

Cherokee Nation Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr., another guest on the video consultation, also weighed in.

“The problem is the train’s been leaving the station on these rules and regs before tribes are brought in,” Hoskin said. “We can actually help the government be better and do better, but we’ve got to be in the room when they’re hashing out these plans.”

The federal government cannot respect sovereignty only when doing so is convenient. Consultation requires time for tribal governments to respond and a willingness by federal officials to change course.

The incoming 120th Congress offers an opportunity to insist on that standard. In the meantime, the question remains: Who’s listening to tribal nations in Washington?

Thayék gde nwéndëmen – we are all related.

Levi “Calm Before the Storm” Rickert (Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation) is the founder, publisher, and editor of Native News Online. Rickert was awarded the Best Column Award in the print/online category... More by Levi Rickert

scraped.title: InFocus: Is adopting permanent daylight saving time a mistake?
scraped.description: Many of us know how we feel when it's time to change our clocks. Some provinces and territories have put a stop to it. But is it a good idea?
scraped.author: Cierra Bettens
scraped.h1: InFocus: Is adopting permanent daylight saving time a mistake?
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

InFocus and the debate over changing the clock.

Many of us know how we feel when it’s time to change our clocks back in the fall and forward in the spring. Sleepy – maybe even a little disoriented.

Well, on Nov. 1, citizens in six provinces and territories didn’t experience any of that because their governments scrapped the dreaded seasonal time change.

Governments had two choices: stick with standard time or daylight saving time. Standard time gives you more sun in the morning – while daylight time gives you extended sun in the evening.

Most chose to extend daylight into the evening.

But will they regret their decision?

This week on InFocus, David Prerau, one of the world’s foremost experts on daylight saving time, explains why they might.

“What happened in the U.S. anyway is nobody was much against it until it actually occurred in January 1974,” Prerau, the author of Seize the Daylight, told host Cierra Bettens. “We had an incident in 1974 where there was an energy crisis, an unexpected energy crisis. And so they put in daylight saving time year-round for a two-year period, which they thought would cover the energy crisis. And most people thought it would be good until it happened.

“Everybody saw they had to get up in the pitch dark, go to work in the pitch dark, and most people thought the worst thing was that to send their kids to school in the dark, walking on dark city streets or waiting at the bus stop on dark country roads. And so it lost popularity very quickly in the US, and I think 1974 and even though it was only a two-year plan, they got rid of it after one year because it was so unpopular.”

Anishinaabe health scholar, Dr. Amy Shawanda, said if the government wants to adopt one particular time, she supports standard time. But she added, there are impacts of changing the clocks.

“It’s not natural to our circadian rhythms,” she said. “A lot of people will feel off when the clocks change because it’s not natural to our circadian rhythms. As Indigenous Peoples, we never had to change the clocks. We just lived on the land, and so it’s not natural to who we are.

“We should really move away from the daylight saving time and not adopt it at all, because it does really go against our own circadian rhythms. It goes against our biology.”

Cierra is the host and co-producer of the of the weekly APTN News InFocus podcast. She joined APTN in 2024 as a reporter-correspondent in Winnipeg after working in campus and city news. She’s currently completing her Master of Arts in Media Studies at Concordia University in Montréal. Cierra has mixed settler and Red River Métis roots and is a member of the Manitoba Métis Federation.

scraped.title: New Mexico judge finds state education reform plan deficient, additions due in 2027 - ICT
scraped.description: Education advocates say they are ‘hopeful’ for collaboration with the incoming Haaland administration.
scraped.author: Source New Mexico
scraped.h1: New Mexico judge finds state education reform plan deficient, additions due in 2027
scraped.body_text:
ICT

This story was originally published by Source New Mexico.

Matt Mondschein Source New Mexico

A New Mexico judge recently ruled that the state’s plan to address the landmark Yazzie/Martinez education equity lawsuit is deficient, and ordered the state education department to supplement the plan by March 2027.

In a Nov. 2 order , First Judicial District Judge Matthew Wilson found that the New Mexico Public Education Department’s remedial action plan, which addresses equitable education reform for at-risk students, is not comprehensive because it fails to address all previous judicial orders. Wilson also identified gaps in the action plan, including inadequate plans to address class sizes, textbook funding and summer school programs.

Wilson’s ruling came in response to objections filed earlier this year by several organizations, including the New Mexico Center on Law and Poverty and Transform Education NM, that requested the court order PED to rewrite the plan the department submitted last November .

Although Wilson agreed with plaintiffs that the plan is not comprehensive, the court did not grant the plaintiffs’ request that PED completely rewrite the plan to include stakeholder input. Instead, the court ordered PED to file a supplement by March 25, 2027. The additional materials must succinctly connect its remedial action to every constitutional violation in past court orders and provide ways to assess if remedial actions are successful.

Both PED and plaintiffs in the case found reasons to commend Wilson’s decision.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

In an emailed statement, PED spokesperson Janelle Taylor García said that the education department “welcomes” the order, “which upholds the department’s Action Plan and confirms that the state is on the right path to meet its obligations to New Mexico’s students.”

In regard to the required supplement to the plan, PED sees the order “as a valuable roadmap that provides greater clarity to the department in its work. The court said it is confident the PED can complete this supplement, and we share that confidence,” García said.

PED, she said, “remains fully committed to delivering an excellent education for every New Mexico student, especially those the original case was brought to serve. This ruling allows us to keep moving that work forward.”

Alisa Diehl, a New Mexico Center on Law and Poverty attorney representing the plaintiffs, told Source NM that Wilson’s order “confirms what we’ve been saying for a year now, which is that PED’s plan still doesn’t fully address what the courts require” and falls short in connecting its solutions with “actual steps that will lead to an education system that our children are entitled to.”

While the court agreed with plaintiffs that the PED plan is insufficient, it did not require the state to work with plaintiffs or stakeholders on its supplemental plan. “We remain concerned that another version that’s produced by the agency without the expertise and input necessary to develop many solutions isn’t going to produce the changes that we need,” Diehl said.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

The lawsuit has been a watershed moment in education in New Mexico. In 2018, a district court determined New Mexico had violated its constitutional duty to provide a sufficient education to its students, particularly Native American and low-income students, English language learners and students with disabilities.

In 2025, Wilson found that PED hadn’t complied with the 2018 court ruling and ordered the education department to file a remedial action plan to fulfill its constitutional obligation to provide education support for all students.

The latest ruling comes as Gov.-elect Deb Haaland prepares to take office next year, which education advocates say creates an opportunity for New Mexico to take a different approach and include further collaboration between stakeholders and PED.

“We have so much to offer the next administration in terms of scholarship, analysis and lived experience from the ground and classrooms,” Loretta Trujillo, executive director of Transform Education New Mexico, told Source NM. “So it would be really important for the next administration to really partner with us.”

The sentiment was echoed by Regis Pecos, co-founder of the Tribal Education Alliance, who said extending the timeline to March to supplement the plan “allows for the opportunity for more collaboration with new leadership at the PED under Gov.-Elect Haaland.”

Pecos said Haaland’s past comments , in which she called the plan inadequate and said she would bring the plaintiffs and tribes to the table, make him “hopeful” going forward.

“This has to be a collaborative effort,” Pecos said. “My optimism comes from Haaland’s comments while campaigning. That’s a fundamental change toward finally ensuring New Mexico fulfills its constitutional obligations.”

scraped.h1: Citing data center, tribal sovereignty fears, Nevadans push back against Trump-backed permit bill
scraped.body_text:
ICT

This story was originally published by Nevada Current.

Jeniffer Solis Nevada Current

A Trump-backed permitting revision bill is getting blowback from a growing coalition of Nevadans, who say its provisions will accelerate the buildout of new fossil fuel projects for data centers and cut tribes out of the regulatory process.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BBAAJA) is a wide-ranging package aimed at easing the construction of new energy infrastructure and mines by rolling back environmental, judicial, Tribal, and historic preservation protections.

If passed, the bill would weaken certain provisions in the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.

Nevada Democratic Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen were among 19 Democrats voting with the Republican majority Monday to advance the bill, arguing it would help hasten the approval of renewable energy projects, bring down utility costs and require data centers to pay for the grid upgrades they trigger.

But conservation groups warned the regulatory rollbacks would apply to all projects on public lands – everything from clean energy projects to fossil fuel pipelines built to fuel data centers.

Under the bill, federal land managers would be allowed to evaluate more projects on public lands using a less vigorous environmental analysis that requires a lower threshold for approval.

“This means that data centers and gas power plants would almost certainly be analyzed using” lower-level of analysis, said Patrick Donnelly, the Great Basin Director of the Center for Biological Diversity.

Once approved, projects would also be more difficult to stop. The bill would drastically reduce judicial review for projects on public lands, including limiting judges’ ability to halt construction on public lands for environmental violations, even if it would cause imminent and irreparable harm.

Provisions in the bill would prevent future administrations from revoking permits for projects that have already been approved. In practice, conservation groups say that could embolden the Trump administration to accelerate AI data center construction on public lands.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

“If Trump tries to ram through a bunch of data centers on public lands in the next 2 years, and we get a new Democratic administration for whom that is not a priority, they would be hamstrung and unable to change course. It would lock in public lands data center approvals forever,” Donelly said.

Nevada became the first state to get a data center approved on public land in July, but the project was ultimately rescinded following a lawsuit from the Center for Biological Diversity and Boulder City.

Donelly said, if passed, the environmental rollbacks in the permitting reform bill would “dramatically impact the permitting of Townsite Data Center” adjacent to Boulder City, “allowing the agencies to run roughshod over these laws while hobbling the enforcement mechanism that is meant to keep them honest.”

In a statement after her vote to advance the legislation, Cortez Masto criticized some of the bill’s provisions, saying she would not vote for final passage if changes to the National Historic Preservation Act — which protects historic properties and cultural resources — were not removed.

Native rights advocates in Nevada are adamantly opposed to that portion of the bill.

Beverly Harry, who is Diné and a Native community organizer in northern Nevada, said the Trump-backed bill should not have advanced after voters made their position clear during the midterms.

“We thought the American voice on how we should proceed now was clear. It just seems like what we’re seeing is our Democrat senators being disingenuous with how they view Nevadans and people within Indian country,” Harry said.

Under the bill, early consultation with Tribal Nations would be optional during the early stages of the permitting process, which would limit their ability to identify cultural resources and inform decision-makers of potential conflicts.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“There are already not enough opportunities or notice for tribes to give input or to educate themselves about what projects are up and coming and the infrastructure being put in place. It’s already weak,” said Lisa Grayshield, a member of the Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California and an associate professor at New Mexico State University.

The bill would also limit what projects need to go through the Tribal consultation process and what sites would qualify as culturally important.

Native organizers say the legislation would not only weaken government-to-government consultation and alter long-standing historic preservation reviews, it would allow the Secretary of the Interior to suspend funding and override the functions of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers if they miss new stricter response deadlines.

“These roles are very important to our tribe because they protect our stories, our songs, our cultural lands and burial sites, and our history for the next generation,” said Josh Dini, a member of the Walker River Paiute Tribe and founder of Prayer Horse Inc., a nonprofit created to protect Indigenous culture, land, and sovereignty. “If this bill goes through, I don’t know what’s going to happen. We won’t be able to stand up to protect our land, protect the people, and protect our sovereignty.”

Harry and several other Native organizers will hold a protest at the Bruce R. Thompson Courthouse and Federal Building in Reno on Friday to pressure Nevada’s senators to vote against legislation they say will weaken government-to-government consultation and alter long-standing historic preservation reviews.

“We could be exposed to larger amounts of pollutants at a faster rate because now everything is open for the gas, oil, and mining industries to just come in and do whatever they want. They still want everything that we have. They are still trying to steal everything that we have, and that is what this protest is about,” Harry said, adding that it’s dedicated to the late Mary and Carrie Dann, both Western Shoshone activists in Nevada.

Other Nevada officials have spoken out against the bill. Gov. elect and current state attorney general Arron Ford signed onto a letter warning that the permitting overhaul would weaken environmental protections and undermine state and Tribal Nation authority.

Changes to the Clean Water Act under the bill would “unreasonably curtail traditional state authority and lead to dirtier, more polluted waters in our states,” wrote more than a dozen attorneys general in the letter.

scraped.title: ‘Silent Warrior’: 100th anniversary celebration sidesteps Native contribution - ICT
scraped.description: Recognition still eludes Taffy Abel a century after he broke the color barrier in the National Hockey League
scraped.author: Charles Fox
scraped.h1: ‘Silent Warrior’: 100th anniversary celebration sidesteps Native contribution
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Charles Fox Special to ICT

Amid the excitement of the New York Rangers hockey team’s first-ever game in Madison Square Garden on Nov. 16, 1926, no one knew that Clarence “Taffy” Abel, the large defenseman from Michigan, was keeping a secret.

With the pageantry of an ice ballet troupe, the performance of the 126-piece West Point Cadet Orchestra, and the exhilaration of a 1-0 upset over the reigning champion Montreal Maroons, no one realized they had also witnessed Abel become the first Indigenous player to take to the ice in the National Hockey League.

The historic moment would not be revealed for another 13 years, yet now, 100 years later, Abel is still not fully recognized for breaking the NHL’s color barrier.

Few people knew that in 1926, however. Abel had been keeping his Ojibwe heritage hidden since his childhood, when his parents decided to racially pass as White to avoid having their two children taken to Native American boarding schools against their will.

The secret would be his ticket to success on the ice during a time when opportunities were limited for an Indigenous person. He became a member of the U.S. men’s hockey team in the 1924 Winter Olympics, carrying the U.S. flag through the streets of Chamonix, France, during the opening ceremonies, and helping bring home a silver medal.

It also allowed him to play hockey at the highest level in the National Hockey League, where he would appear in 333 games over his eight-year career and be part of two Stanley Cup-winning teams.

Today, Abel is recognized as the first Native American to participate in the Winter Olympics and is a member of the Hockey Hall of Fame, but he is known for his skills and not for breaking the NHL color barrier. Abel died in 1964 at age 64.

On Monday, Nov. 16, the New York Rangers will celebrate the 100th anniversary of the team’s first game in 1926. Abel was on the roster, but the barrier-breaking moment when he steps out onto the ice as an Indigenous player is not expected to be mentioned in the celebrations.

The NHL has stated the Rangers “will commemorate the anniversary of their first team without specific references to any players,” as the team plays the Montreal Canadiens. The game is part of the Original Six Series of nationally televised games on the TNT network celebrating the six teams that made up the NHL for 25 seasons between 1942 and 1967.

The NHL has likewise not recognized Abel as the first Indigenous player in the league, though he was inducted posthumously as a charter member into the Hockey Hall of Fame in 1973 for his bruising play on the ice.

“We are at the mercy of the record keeping of the time,” the league said in a recent statement to ICT. “There simply is no way that we can verify that no player of Indigenous heritage played in the NHL before Taffy Abel.”

Abel’s nephew, George Jones, begs to differ. As a member of the Society of International Hockey Researchers, Jones examined more than 150 players who preceded Abel in the NHL for evidence of Indigenous heritage, and found none.

He believes he has made the case that Abel was the first Indigenous player in the NHL.

“If he would have said at the time, ‘Hey, I’m Native American,’…They would have said, ‘Well, I don’t think we can do that at this time. Come back in 50 years,’” Jones told ICT about the uncle he often calls the Silent Warrior.

“I can tell you, he never would have gotten into the Winter Olympics as a Native American and he never, never, never, would have gotten into the NHL,” Jones said.

The NHL’s statement emailed to ICT, nonetheless, acknowledges Abel as a “pioneer.”

“On the 100 th anniversary of the franchise’s first game on Nov. 16, 1926, the National Hockey League salutes one of the original New York Rangers, Clarence ‘Taffy’ Abel,” according to the statement. “We celebrate his success and honor him as a pioneer, who, as a young man of Ojibwe heritage, surmounted the many hurdles faced by Native Americans of his day to forge a special place in hockey history.”

The New York Rangers did not respond to ICT’s requests for comments about the anniversary celebration, but the team’s website comes close to recognizing Abel’s accomplishments. A story that ran in 2023, “Red, White, and Blue,” highlighting American connections and influences on Ranger history, states that Abel is ”believed to be” the first Indigenous player in the NHL.

The issue of color barriers is complicated by the fact that each of the major sports leagues interpret their own racial barriers and how they handled race differently. Native American athletes have never been barred from Major League Baseball and the National Football League. In fact, the early NFL was dominated by Native Americans such as Jim Thorpe, who was also the league president of the American Football Professional Association, which was later renamed the NFL in 1920. And there was an entire team, the Oorang Indians in 1922-1923, that was composed entirely of Native players.

Professional basketball does not promote Wataru “Wat” Misaka, a Japanese-American, for the New York Knicks as the breaker of the color barrier even though he preceded the three credited barrier-breaking African-American players Chuck Cooper, Earl Lloyd, and Nat “Sweetwater” Clifton who would enter the league three seasons later.

A groundbreaking night

The New York Rangers hockey team was formed in 1926 by Madison Square Garden President George Lewis “Tex” Rickard after the New York Americans – the first hockey team in New York, formed in 1925 – proved to be an unexpectedly popular draw.

Nicknamed Tex’s Rangers by a New York Herald Tribune sports editor, the name soon stuck for the New York Rangers.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

According to the Rangers website, Abel was the first player the team signed to a contract, on Aug. 14, 1926, as well as the first American-born player for the team. The team took to the ice for its first game — with Abel in the mix — on Nov. 16, 1926.

The first game was quite an event, according to news reports at the time.

“There was enough fur, silk, and satin in the arena boxes alone to decorate the shop windows on Fifth Avenue,” wrote Brooklyn Daily Times writer James J. Wood regarding the crowd of over 13,000 in attendance at Madison Square Garden for the first game.

Before the game and in between periods, the Garden was “transformed into a veritable winter palace,” with an ice ballet company direct from a performance in Berlin, Germany, accompanied by a 30-piece orchestra, and a performance by the 126-piece West Point Cadet Orchestra.

After actress Lois Moran dropped the ceremonial puck, the game became a hard-fought defensive battle with the Rangers upsetting the champion Montreal Maroons 1-0. Player Bill Cook scored the first goal in Rangers history at the 18:37 mark of the second period, and Hal Winkler became the first goalie to earn a shutout in his NHL debut.

Abel would go on to play in all 44 games that season. His intimidating and physical play drew 78 penalty minutes. In one of the best debuts by a sports expansion team, the Rangers shocked the hockey world by winning the American Division. The following year they won the Stanley Cup.

Because of his size and “carcass rattling” style of play, Abel was nicknamed the “Michigan Mountain.”

Bryant McBride, who was the first Black executive in the NHL, grew up in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, and played for the Soo Indians, the junior hockey team Abel created in 1939.

“He was amazing, you know, he was an incredible player, well ahead of his time,” McBride said. “He was just monstrous. They said he was 6-foot-2, 220, but he played closer to 250 pounds. He was just a mountain of a guy for that time. His impact was real. It was very real, and he was a force to be reckoned with.”

Jones said Abel also had a softer side, particularly with him. Abel and his wife did not have any children.

“Taffy could head up the fear league,” Jones said. “A tough man, but, you know, he was always loving and caring for me. He had a special relationship with me, and I had a special one with him, too.”

Jones saw Abel’s concealing of his heritage as a way to force the public to give him a “blind audition” based on skill and free of racial prejudices and stereotypes.

“I think what is lost is the true, hardworking development of a person that started very young. It was determination. He was a fighter,” Jones said. “I mean, how many people can you think of from that era who were … not only an Olympian but a medalist and a flag bearer? There was never another Native American flag bearer.”

After helping the Chicago Blackhawks win a Stanley Cup in 1934, Abel retired following a contract dispute with the team. He was still considered one of the best defensemen in the league. The next Native American player would not enter the NHL until Henry Boucha, an Ojibwe from Minnesota in 1972, 46 years after Abel.

While there have been more than 100 First Nations Canadian players in the league, only eight Native Americans have skated in the NHL.

Promises kept

Abel’s parents began the practice of concealing their Indigenous identity in Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, in the early 1900s. The family was multi-racial, with Taffy’s father, John Abel, a White man originally from Fort Wayne, Indiana, and his mother, Charlotte Gurnoe Abel, from the Chippewa (Ojibwe) Sault Tribe.

The Abel family lived during a period when the U.S. government felt the best way to deal with the Native population was through methods such as boarding schools, stripping Native culture away from students and attempting to forcibly assimilate them into White society. It was a time of constant fear for Indigenous parents when a knock at the door could mean the arrival of government agents.

Abel took on the support of his family at age 20, when his father died. And in 1939, after the death of his mother, Charlotte, he created the Soo Indians, the junior hockey team, in his mother’s memory.

It was his first public acknowledgement of his Ojibwe lineage, which he had promised not to disclose while his mother was alive.

The secret had left him with a sense of void, and decades of depression, his nephew said.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Those feelings can be a form of survivor’s guilt, said Leora Tadgerson, a professor of Indigenous studies at Northern Michigan University and director of diversity, equity, and inclusion at the Episcopal Diocese of Northern Michigan. She is Anishinaabe, Finnish, and Saami.

“It’s mixed with a sense of imposter syndrome because they understand that they are Native, but they are not having to deal with all of the negative aspects that go along with racism in our country against Native people,” Tadgerson said. “And even back in the day, there have been stories about folks who just feel this deep, deep guilt for not enduring the same things that those folks went through when they went to boarding school.”

Inspiring new generations

The NHL has emphasized Willie O’Ree, the first Black player who entered the league on Jan. 18, 1958, when it comes to breaking the league’s racial barriers, despite Abel’s first appearance in the NHL preceding O’Ree’s by 31 years. In between there was Larry Kwong, a player of Asian descent, and seven Indigenous Canadians.

“I’ve known Willie, and he is a fine gentleman, and he should be recognized. But that doesn’t take away the fact that guys like Taffy Abel and Freddy Sasakamoose shouldn’t be treated in the same light,” said Ted Nolan, Ojibwe, a former NHL player and coach of the Buffalo Sabres and New York Islanders.

“That would hopefully inspire the next generation of players who are right on the fence of trying to hide their identity versus being proud of their identity,” he said.

Nolan grew up in Garden River First Nation near Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario. Though he suffered racial incidents as a player and coach, he was raised to be proud of his heritage, drawing inspiration from Indigenous NHL players such as Reggie Leach, Ojibwe, and Sasakamoose, Cree, as well as American Indian Movement leaders Dennis Banks and Russell Means.

Nolan, whose sons Jordan and Brandon also played in the NHL, feels the league has not made the same racial transformation as other major sports leagues. He stresses the importance of acknowledging the ground breakers who preceded him, like Abel and Sasakamoose, and telling their stories.

“It was very, very tough for those guys, and that’s why we need trailblazers to let kids know that racially profiling people in the past was detrimental,” he said. “It was very hurtful. But the truth always comes out.”

Nolan, who was awarded the Jack Adams Award as the NHL coach of the year in 1996, believes in coaching to the human spirit, making individuals proud of who they are and where they are going.

“When I played my first game in the National Hockey League, I laid tobacco for the people before me who had to fight so hard in order for me to be where I was at the time,” Nolan said.

“There’s not too much in our history books about our past. Stories change the projections of young people’s lives and who they are, and even how they treat people,” he said. “So, the more knowledge we can get out there and the more education we can get to people, the better ….

“Maybe [the negative past] hurts the league a little bit, but it could benefit the people a lot more than the [league’s] feelings getting hurt. Saving them is a lot more important.”

Not giving up

On Nov. 16, Jones will sit at his Florida home in front of his TV and watch the Rangers celebrate their centennial by playing the Canadiens. He had assumed this night — the 100 th anniversary of Abel first skating onto the ice — would be the culmination of his decades-long efforts to get his uncle the recognition he felt he deserved under the bright lights of the Garden. But it will not happen.

“Let me put it like this,” he told ICT. “I didn’t get any invitation to come up and sit at their box at Madison Square Garden. You think they would’ve done that, especially since Taffy was the first player they signed on August 14, 1926.”

It was an invitation that should not have been expected, given that he has long criticized the NHL, its Commissioner Gary Bettman, and the league’s board of governors with harsh, condemning language.

“I can imagine that there’s some written record out there that went through the NHL saying, ‘You don’t even breathe the name Taffy Abel right now,’” Jones recently reflected to ICT.

The 77-year-old Jones has had a tough year. On Jan. 1, he suffered a coronary event and was dead for approximately eight minutes. In September, he had two pulmonary embolisms caused by deep vein thrombosis in his right leg that put him in the hospital for five days.

Despite his health issues, Jones has continued his crusade “faithfully telling the Taffy Abel story.” He sees himself as the underdog, David taking on Goliath, battling the owners and leadership of the NHL.

He draws inspiration from the 1924 photo of Abel carrying the U.S. flag in the first WInter Olympics, an image he feels “is beyond iconic, it is sacred to me.” To the NHL leadership, he drops the gloves and says, “Bring it on.”

But time has become a fleeting commodity for Jones. What happens when the Rangers centennial celebration ends, the fans head out to the New York City streets, and the arena lights are turned off? Will the ground-breaking accomplishments of Clarence “Taffy” Abel also disappear into the darkness, becoming a century-old footnote? Will his legacy be remembered to inspire and educate, particularly young Native American and First Nation youths, or does the story of the Silent Warrior go silent?

In February, he campaigned for President Donald Trump to award Abel the Presidential Medal of Freedom, but heard nothing. He has no intention of giving up the push for his uncle to be recognized for contributions to society.

“Taffy was a warrior in every sense of the word,” Jones said, “fighting and sacrificing for inclusion and equality of Native American people in our country.”

scraped.title: How Olivia Dean holds the door open for the whimsy of girlhood
scraped.description: With multiple Grammy nominations for hits like “Man I Need,” Olivia Dean’s impact goes far beyond the accolades.
scraped.author: Haniyah P.
scraped.h1: How Olivia Dean holds the door open for the whimsy of girlhood
scraped.body_text:
With multiple Grammy nominations for hits like “Man I Need,” Olivia Dean’s impact goes far beyond the accolades.

Olivia Dean is a unifying force. Arguably, she’s a unifier of girlhood.

Whether you’ve been lucky enough to catch one of her live shows or you’ve simply been fed the clips on your For You page, there’s an undeniable force behind Dean’s music and her chart-topping album “The Art of Loving.” It’s in the way a crowd sings “Man I Need” back to her. It’s in the ways male listeners shamelessly belt the lyrics to her songs in the car. It’s in the comment sections, where strangers trade stories about the breakup, the move, the new friend, the version of themselves they’re finally making peace with. Dean didn’t just have a big year. She gave a lot of us language for the experiences many of us were navigating at a time when it felt like not only our personal lives, but the world, was falling apart.

Today, Dean received 6 nominations for her sophomore album in the categories of Record of the Year, Album of the Year, Song of the Year, Best Solo Performance, Best Pop Vocal Album, and Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance. It was an announcement that followed her being crowned Artist of the Year by Apple Music, weeks topping the music charts, and a four-night residency at Madison Square Garden in August. But the accolades and chart runs aren’t really why people love Dean.

“What sets Olivia apart is that she speaks from the heart, every time,” said Rachel Newman, Apple Music’s co-head in a press release celebrating her Artist of the Year appointment. “Her songs make you want to call a friend, dance in your kitchen, and tell someone you love them. She is open and genuine in everything she shares, and that connection is what turned a great year into a defining one.”

Under the ’70s glamour aesthetic marked by voluminous hair, the shimmering gowns, and the warm soul-pop that feels pulled from an elder’s record collection, is a young woman who has leaned fully into the messy, confusing reality of womanhood while still honoring the little girl who lives within her. That soulful yet carefree energy is what makes her standout, especially to women engaging with her music. So much of what’s marketed to young women asks them to pick a lane: be the hot girl or the healing girl, the hopeless romantic or the independent bad b— who can do bad all by herself. But throughout “The Art of Loving,” Dean shows the reality that many women are both. She wants the man but also wants her peace. She’s both tender about heartbreak and joyful about life. She’s both grown and giddy.

As one Threads user put it, “Olivia Dean is really for the girls in their healing era while simultaneously believing in love.” That word, simultaneously, does a lot of work. Dean makes room for the both/and that so many women are actually living.

Another fan wrote: “Yes, Olivia Dean is immensely talented, but the thing I love most, is that she just seems like a young woman having the time of her life. Happy, carefree, and unbothered. I want that for all young women.”

There’s something quietly radical about that wish, especially for Black women who are rarely given the grace to showcase their multifaceted nature anywhere beyond their professional lives. But the London-born daughter of a Jamaican-Guyanese mother shows it all on stage, allowing herself to cry, smile, and dance through the delight of it all. And it’s a powerful reclamation of joy that all women can relate to. At a time when systems are constantly trying to divide communities, if you search Olivia Dean on TikTok or Instagram, you’ll be flooded with videos of people from all walks of life singing, dancing, and crying to the same lyrics that unlock different memories and speak to the same human experience. As the title of her album suggests, Dean speaks to the fun, messy, sad, complicated layers of love.

For so many women and men from every background, her music has served as that reminder. The light yet soulful feeling that echoes through her sound is infectious. It lets you feel the full weight of her words while setting down your own stresses and worries for three and a half minutes. And for women, Dean is a reminder of the beauty and whimsy of girlhood that we all carry even as we navigate womanhood.

Growing into womanhood is messy. There are breakups and burnout, family expectations and bodies that change, and the constant pressure to have it all figured out. And while the internet likes to jokingly say “I’m just a girl,” the reality is that the dreams, pleasures and feelings of our younger selves stay with us. For some, that playful little girl is louder than others, but she’s there. And through her music, Dean manages to turn up the volume. Similar to how Chaka Khan affirmed that we are “every woman,” the “A Couple of Minutes” singer reminds us that we can be in our healing girl era, lover girl era, baddie era, boss babe era, and everything in between all at the same time.

scraped.title: Handwritten version of Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have A Dream' speech to be on display ahead of $10M auction
scraped.description: A handwritten copy of Martin Luther King's famous speech is set for auction next January and is currently on display in Atlanta.
scraped.author: Brandon Caldwell
scraped.h1: Handwritten version of Martin Luther King Jr.’s ‘I Have A Dream’ speech to be on display ahead of $10M auction
scraped.body_text:
The document was discovered in a drawer belonging to a key lieutenant in the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

Before the authentic, handwritten manuscript of Martin Luther King Jr.’s most famous speech gets sold to the highest bidder in January, the historical document can be viewed at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta through Sunday.

“It shows a genius at work, that these words didn’t just spill out perfectly,” Jill Savitt, president and CEO of the National CCHR, said. The speech is currently being housed in a wing dedicated to the Civil Rights Movement.

Written in blue ink, the handwritten version of the speech, King’s final draft of it, is set to fetch around $10 million at an auction next year benefiting the King Center and the Xernona Clayton Foundation. The handwritten document, considered a “treasure of American history,” is set to be auctioned by Christie’s on January 22, four days after the federal observance of Martin Luther King Jr. Day.

“It gives you chills to look at it,” Peter Klarnet, Christie’s manuscripts specialist, said. “Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr. King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time. It captures a moment that literally changed the course of our nation and makes it very real and very human. It’s an honor and privilege that Christie’s has an opportunity to present it to the world.”

A post shared by National Center for Civil and Human Rights (@civilandhumanrights)

According to Christie’s, the document was discovered inside a desk drawer belonging to Edward T. Clayton, who served as the head of public relations for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Clayton’s wife, Xernona, found the documents and preserved them.

“I’m just glad I looked in the drawer,” Xernona Clayton said.

Klarnet has stated Christie’s is trying to arrange additional showings of the speech before the auction takes place.

King’s most quoted speech is getting additional life beyond the auction. Netflix is set to release “The Baddest Speechwriter of All,” an extensive documentary that examines the life of Clarence B. Jones , King’s lawyer and speechwriter. Jones, who died earlier this year at the age of 95, helped shape the speech alongside King.

In his memoir, “Behind the Dream: The Making of the Speech That Transformed a Nation,” Jones revealed that the most stirring portion of the speech wasn’t written down, but instead was spurred by Mahalia Jackson shouting, “Tell ’em about the dream, Martin.”

“The Baddest Speechwriter of All,” which is co-directed by Ben Proudfoot and NBA star Stephen Curry, premieres on the streamer in December.

scraped.title: Mielle Organics founder Monique Rodriguez’s daughter Mia is carving out her own lane with a new role
scraped.description: At 21, Mia Rodriguez is bringing her own vision for Gen Z, community, and legacy to the beauty brand her mother founded.
scraped.author: Kay Wicker
scraped.h1: Mielle Organics founder Monique Rodriguez’s daughter Mia is carving out her own lane with a new role
scraped.body_text:
At 21, Mia Rodriguez is bringing her own vision for Gen Z, community, and legacy to the beauty brand her mother founded.

On a November evening that threatened to dip into the 40s, at after (h)ours at Manifest in Washington, DC, the chill stopped at the door. Once inside, you were warmed by an atmosphere curated and brought to life by Mia Rodriguez, Mielle Organics’ new next-gen Creative and Culture Advisor.

On Thursday, Nov. 12, the 21-year-old daughter of Mielle Organics founder and CEO Monique Rodriguez gathered several dozen guests at the Union Market speakeasy for the third installment of her D.I.M.E.S. Supper Club . This time, however, the evening came with the announcement that Mia was officially joining the beauty brand.

“It is a huge position, and it’s not about passing the torch or her following in my footsteps. She is carving out her own lane,” Monique, dressed in a red knit dress with gold accents, told the room.

“She is going to be responsible for a lot,” the proud mother continued as she stood beside her daughter, dressed in a gray-and-white graphic catsuit. “She is my legacy, and I know that she’s going to carry the torch very well.”

The role, slated to kick off in the new year, will be the start of a new chapter for the brand. A first of its kind, it builds directly on the momentum Mielle gained in reaching the next generation of consumers through initiatives like its Curl Collective and its outreach to historically Black colleges and universities. It is also an opportunity for Monique to see her legacy carried forward by her daughter, who is already carving out a path of her own.

Consumers can expect more outreach to Gen Z, the generation next in line to inherit the brand’s consumer base, as Mia rolls up her sleeves to crack the code on how best to reach them—although she has a few ideas. From social media engagement to more in-person experiences like her supper club, she hopes to bring a fresh perspective to Mielle.

Speaking with theGrio during the event, Mia said consumers can expect “to see a shift in catering towards my generation more, and just hearing our voices more, and just really interacting with us.

“The voice of Gen Z is social media,” she added.

With so much riding on the new role, she admitted she’s “nervous” about the responsibility. However, the former athlete is fully prepared to “do it scared.”

“I’m very driven. I’m very ambitious, and I have a lot of dreams that I want to accomplish,” she noted, adding, “So, yes, I’m gonna do it scared.”

Now, of course, she and her mom know how this looks. And while they’re even willing to embrace the label “nepo baby,” they both swear it’s more than that.

“I’m not gonna stray away from the fact that I am a nepo baby. I’m fully aware,” Mia admitted, before declaring, “I’m gonna embrace the fact that I’ve earned it.”

Her mother agrees. Mia, who is studying marketing at Hampton University, has already been building her own following, producing content, and creating opportunities for young women to connect through D.I.M.E.S. Supper Club.

“They were interested because of the work that she put in and the content that she’s been producing,” Monique explained. “She’s been growing her following on her own.”

Plus, the way Monique sees it, being her daughter might have gotten Mia in the door, but it won’t keep her in the room if she can’t deliver.

“Even if I open the door for her, she still has to do the work to keep that door open,” the founder continued. “Just because you are given access to these rooms means nothing if you don’t do anything with it.”

Monique, who founded Mielle in 2014 before its acquisition by Procter & Gamble in 2023, also sees this as a moment for her own legacy. This is another opportunity enabled by the progression and acquisition of her brand, and one lesson she hopes other Black entrepreneurs take away.

“What I really hope people understand is how legacy can still be passed down,” she said. “There’s still opportunity to continue your legacy and pass the torch to someone within your family.”

Legacy was a major and leading theme throughout Thursday’s supper club, where guests in their best cocktail attire sipped fruity cocktails, enjoyed a lavish buffet-style spread, and mingled as the music played. Members of the media rubbed shoulders with popular content creators, while photo opps and lively conversations gave the chic gathering a flow from start to finish.

Guests were encouraged to reflect on what other women had passed down to them and what they hoped to pass down themselves. Mia, who credits her parents with instilling her with her work ethic and drive, hopes this evening was the formal start of her own legacy. She maybe 21 and still in college, but the content creator was clear about how she hopes this role and her supper club live long after her.

“I’m not going to be 21 forever; I’m going to, you know, keep getting older. So I want this to be a position that will be extended beyond generations, and just to make that lasting impact,” she said.

“And to encourage others to be passionate about what they’re doing, and to embody that, and to stay true to that.”

items.title: Everything You Need to Know Ahead of ‘P-Valley’s’ Final Season
items.summary: It's almost time to head back down to The Pynk for 'P-Valley's' third and final season! But before we go, here's what you need to know!Read more...

scraped.title: Everything to Know Ahead of P-Valley’s Final Season
scraped.h1: Everything You Need to Know Ahead of ‘P-Valley’s’ Final Season
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

It’s almost time to head back down to The Pynk for ‘P-Valley’s’ third and final season! But before we go, here’s what you need to know!

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

Screenshot: YouTube

As bittersweet as it may be, “P-Valley” is on its way back to our small screens after a four-year hiatus for its third and final season. And trust us when we say, there’s plenty of unfinished business down at the Pynk!

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

But before you press play, we thought we’d give a little reminder and refresher of where things left off and what all you can expect from this new season—spoiler-free, of course!

So if you’re ready to head back down to Chucalissa next month, keep reading.

Most of your favorite Mississippi characters are coming back, don’t you worry! But if you want to get into specifics: Nicco Annan will return as Uncle Clifford; Brandee Evans will return as Mercedes; Shannon Thornton will return as Keyshawn; J. Alphonse Nicholson will return as Lil’ Murda; Gail Bean will return as Roulette; Morocco Omari will return as Big L; Thomas Q. Jones will return as Mane, and more.

There are also some fun cameos in the first episode that we can’t wait for viewers to see!

Related: Season 3 of ‘P-Valley’ Could Take a While

When we last left the Mississippi Delta, things were looking up for some of our favorite Pynk residents while others were dealing with some seriously messy circumstances.

Uncle Clifford managed to outmaneuver Autumn Night (played by Elarica Johnson) and save the club from being sold. But in doing so, she struck a deal with Corbin Kyle (Dan J. Johnson)—a top customer and the owner of coveted land that allowed The Pynk and the new casino development to coexist. However, there is a plus, as Clifford’s relationship with Lil’ Murda went to the next level thanks to their major PDA.

When it comes to Mercedes, she finally secured a future outside the club, purchased her own pole-fitness studio, and managed to get her daughter back home. As far as Keyshawn is concerned, her attempt to escape her abusive husband, Derrick (Jordan Cox), ended with her behind bars and her children still in his custody.

And just when you thought things couldn’t get any more complicated, Diamond (Tyler J. Lepley) was betrayed and subsequently kidnapped and tied up in a car trunk.

In the highly anticipated nine-episode third season, owner Uncle Clifford and her chosen family continue their efforts to survive, thrive, and carve out a future of their own in the Mississippi Delta.

When the newly opened Promised Land Casino floods Chucalissa with scrilla (a.k.a. money), our hometown heroes learn that more money does indeed bring more problems. At The Pynk, Clifford dreams of expanding her empire while Roulette breaks the club’s cardinal rule to build hers.

Meanwhile, as Lil’ Murda’s gang ties threaten to clip his wings, a caged Keyshawn fights to break free and take flight.

After a long-awaited return, “P-Valley” season three debuts on Friday, Dec. 4 with two new episodes. Subsequent new episodes will be available to stream weekly on Fridays only on the STARZ app and all STARZ streaming and on-demand platforms.

Now, let’s dive a little bit deeper into some of the main characters to keep your eyes on!

If you’ll remember, Uncle Clifford fought tooth and nail to keep The Pynk from falling into the hands of casino developers. But by the end of Season 2, she managed to strike a deal that allowed the club to stay open.

However, now that the Promised Land Casino is officially opening its doors, Clifford is looking to expand her empire and secure her place as one of Chucalissa’s bigtimers. But with new money comes new competition, and she’ll have plenty to navigate as she balances business, her relationship with Lil’ Murda and the ladies at The Pynk.

We should really call him BIG MURDA for the way he steps into this new season, and once you see the first few episodes, you’ll see why. When we find our favorite rapper in season three, he’s ready to take another shot at rap stardom. But thanks to his past gang affiliations, his plans appear to get complicated at every turn. Plus, his connection to Mane is also expected to create an interesting dynamic, as well as the response to him going public with Clifford.

There’s going to be a lot to unpack here, so stay tuned!

Now that Miss Mercedes has her daughter back and her own studio, you’d think things would be all good in the Chucalissa hood. But sadly, you’d be mistaken. When we find our girl in season three, she’s doing her best and trying her hardest to pursue something beyond the stage and “dream bigger dreams” than the ones provided at The Pynk. However, rough family dynamics and unfinished business will provide her with more muddy waters to wade through than she’d like.

If we’re honest, we’re still crying, shaking, and throwing up at how things transpired for Keyshawn last season. And knowing that we pick things right back up with her seemingly in jail, as shown above, is just too heartbreaking.

To jog your memory, after she tried to run away with her children, her abusive partner Derrick turned the situation against her, ultimately leading to her arrest and leaving her kids in his custody. And with no Diamond there to come to her rescue, she’s left trying to break free from her confinement and reclaim her life. Here’s hoping she finally gets the fresh start she’s been fighting for!

Miss Roulette, Miss Roulette, what can we say about your ambitions? Last season, she made quite the impression after joining The Pynk with her unapologetic attitude and desire to push boundaries wherever she went. Her relationship with the new girl, Whisper, also introduced an eyebrow-raising new dynamic to the club.

But now that season three has come around, we’ll see Roulette primed and ready to build an empire of her own, even if that means being at odds with Uncle Clifford at some point.

Heeeyyyyy Mane! While Thomas Q. Jones’ character is some top-tier eye candy, we’re not so sure how we’re gonna feel about him in this season. From what we know, it seems as if he’s gonna find himself in a few entanglements that will make viewers look at him twice. And while STARZ hasn’t revealed many specifics about his storyline and the conundrums he finds himself in, we already know whatever he has up his sleeve will make him one to watch.

Big L, the things you’ve seen and done for The Pynk! And we can only expect you to see and do a lot more in this third season. As Uncle Clifford’s longtime right-hand man, he’s helped keep things running while she handles the club’s many ups and downs.

Now that the casino is officially open, he’ll be back as part of the returning ensemble. And while we may not know exactly what he’ll have to take care of this season, we’re curious to see how he’ll help Clifford navigate this new and final chapter for The Pynk!

scraped.title: Katt Williams on Ending His Kevin Hart Beef & More Tea
scraped.h1: Katt Williams Explains Where He Stands With Kevin Hart Now, Drops More Tea in Ice Cube Interview
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

In a candid interview with Ice Cube and Mike Epps, Katt Williams explained how he ended his beef with Kevin Hart, his thoughts on Steve Harvey, and more.

By

Angela Wilson

Published

Katt Williams, Mike Epps, and Ice Cube (Screenshot: “Listen & Laugh” podcast, YouTube)

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

During a candid new sit-down with Ice Cube and Mike Epps, Katt Williams revealed the story behind how he and Kevin Hart finally called a truce, along with a fresh round of unfiltered takes that only he could deliver. From talking about his past 14 gun charges and rumors of him fighting after shows to his thoughts about Steve Harvey and Cedric the Entertainer, Williams held nothing back in yet another viral interview.

The Ohio native appeared on episode two of Ice Cube and Mike Epps’ podcast “Listen & Laugh” on Saturday, where he spoke about a variety of topics, including his long-standing beef with fellow comedian Kevin Hart and how he and Hart are now actually…friends!

During the interview (which has over three million views in two days), Epps referenced Williams’s surprise appearance as a guest roaster on Netflix’s “The Roast of Kevin Hart” in May, where he said Williams “told the truth” about Hart, who appeared unfazed by it all.

“Hey, this is my friend you’re talking about,” Williams interjected. “Sorry, Kev.” After a brief laugh, Epps noted that despite their rocky history, he was grateful Hart called him to be in a movie together after years of rumored beef. The conversation led to Williams explaining how he and Hart made amends.

“I didn’t like the guy,” Williams answered when asked how he felt when Hart called him to appear in a film together. “And I had reasons that I felt that way. […] I had reasons I didn’t like him, but when he contacted me, there was probably a list in my head of 15 things a motherf***er would have to say to get me to be off from on-sight, to we could be good. To his credit—or the credit of him and Netflix or whatever it was—he said everything I needed to hear him say. So he gave an apology that was worthy of being forgiven. There was no working involved in the conversation that we were having, but then, once that was behind us, now we can do whatever the work is that’s necessary.”

Katt Williams had to remind Mike Epps that he’s FRIENDS with Kevin Hart now after Mike started throwing RANDOM SHOTS at him and saying he DOESN’T LIKE HIM 😭💀 “This is my friend you talking about, easy… Sorry Kev” pic.twitter.com/3YgiKNa5bc

But that’s not all. Williams also dropped more bombshells in his interview, including his other comedy beefs.

In his viral interview with Shannon Sharpe in January 2024, Williams made it clear he is not a fan of Steve Harvey, claiming he plagiarized Mark Curry’s role as Mark Cooper in “Hangin’ with Mr. Cooper” on his series, “The Steve Harvey Show.”

RELATED: A Year Later, Was Katt Williams Right? Here Are All the Celebs He Dragged

When Epps asked whether Williams would be nice to Harvey if they ran into each other, Williams didn’t mince words. “Steve recently did an interview where he said he’s with the smoke. So, if I see Steve Harvey, I’m going straight for his knees.”

Mike Epps recalls a story Eddie Murphy told him about Katt Williams and Suge Knight showing up unannounced at his house early one morning, and Katt clears up the old rumor that he chased Tyler Perry with a broomstick: Mike Epps: “You know, Eddie Murphy told me a story. He said,…

Epps recalled a story Eddie Murphy told him about the time Suge Knight and Katt Williams popped up at Murphy’s house, adding that he wished he could have been a fly on the wall. “How did y’all get over there?” Epps asked.

“As a Jehovah’s Witness,” Williams replied through laughter. “I don’t know why Eddie Murphy told that story. He know exactly what—don’t let somebody tell you a story where [it’s like], ‘Oh, I just woke up and some scary individuals was there!’”

Immediately after, Epps brought up rumors that Williams once chased Tyler Perry with a broomstick. “Tyler Perry is six-foot-six. I ain’t chase [him],” Williams added.

On Club Shay Shay, Williams claimed he performed a joke in 1998 on BET’s “ComicView” that he says “The Original Kings of Comedy” star stole from him.

“I’m not gonna say nothing funny to Cedric,” Williams told Epps when asked how he would reply to a greeting. “I got 19 assault and batteries. I’m either gon’ go the opposite direction of Cedric when I see him, or I’ma be up on him before he know it.” Epps replied: “I believe you!”

Mike Epps and Ice Cube ask Katt Williams about his past 14 gun charges and rumors of him fighting after shows—prompting Mike Epps to reveal Katt once pulled a gun on him and chased him down the street: Mike Epps: “You put the guns in there?” Katt Williams: “Yup, the 14 gun…

Speaking of assaults and batteries, Williams also opened up about the criminal charges he detailed in his debut memoir, “Nine Lives, No Wives, and 69 Concubines.”

“The 14 gun charges in New York City, going to Rikers Island, yeah I was very transparent,” Williams said before Ice Cube recalled hearing how Williams had beat somebody up in an alleyway.

“Everything you’ve heard about this nigga he did it. Let’s get that out the way,” Epps said. “I have also been a victim of his before. He also pulled a gun on me before, chasing me down the street.” Williams clarified Epps wasn’t alone, claiming Faizon [Love] was also apart of the ordeal.

scraped.title: Here Are Some of the Highest Paid Women in Sports – The Root
scraped.h1: Here Are Some of the Highest Paid Women in Sports
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

From Trinity Rodman to Venus Williams, meet the women professional athletes making millions and proving that they deserve recognition both on and off the field.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

Jeeno Thitikul of Thailand (Photo by David Becker/Getty Images), Venus Williams (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images), Trinity Rodman (Photo by Soobum Im – FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

The money is talking, and these women athletes are making sure the world listens! From global superstars like Simone Biles to history-making talents like Trinity Rodman, female athletes are redefining what it means to win–on the field and in their bank accounts. We’re spotlighting some of the highest-paid women in sports and how they’re turning talent, visibility and opportunity into serious earning power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

But before we get into the numbers—according to Sportico and Forbes ‘ 2025 athlete earnings estimates—it’s worth recognizing what these women represent. Rodman’s groundbreaking new contract is particular proof that the game is changing. There’s still plenty of work to do when it comes to equity in sports, but these athletes are shattering ceilings, rewriting the rules and making room for the next generation. And for that, The Root is giving them their flowers.

With an estimated net worth of $2 to $4 million, Trinity Rodman signed a three-year deal worth more than $2 million annually, becoming the highest-paid player in the history of the National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL), according to Parade. A game-changer on and off the pitch, Rodman is making history on her own terms.

Madison Keys earned approximately $13.4 million in 2025, boosted by $4.4 million in prize money and $9 million in endorsements. Her Australian Open championship helped turn a career milestone into a major financial year.

RELATED : Coco Gauff and Arthur Fils Showcase Black Tennis Star Power at the Cincinnati Open

Coco Gauff is the highest-paid female professional athlete, with an estimated $31 million earned in 2025. While $8 million came from competition, another $23 million came from endorsements, proving her star power extends well beyond tennis.

Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus brought in approximately $30 million in 2025, splitting her earnings between $15 million in prize money and $15 million in endorsements. Her dominance on the court is paying off commercially, too.

“I train like I’ve never won, and I compete like I’ve never lost.” — Eileen Gu 🎙️: On Purpose with Jay Shetty pic.twitter.com/B56fXTmPin

Skier Eileen Gu earned approximately $23 million in 2025, with nearly all of it coming from endorsements. Partnerships with luxury and global brands have made the freestyle skiing champion a marketing powerhouse beyond winter sports.

Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark earned approximately $16.1 million last year, with roughly $16 million coming from endorsements. Despite limited playing time, her influence, sponsorship portfolio and basketball popularity continue to generate enormous business opportunities.

🚨🦁☢️ The winning putt for Nelly Korda #clutch @NellyLegion pic.twitter.com/lcyrRM0eSF

Golfer Nelly Korda brought home an estimated $13.8 million in 2025, including $11 million from endorsements and $2.8 million in golf winnings. Her partnerships prove her influence reaches far beyond the fairway.

There should be no surprise that the GOAT of gymnastics ended up on this list! Simone Biles earned an estimated $11 million in 2025, entirely through endorsements and commercial partnerships. Even without competing that year, the gymnastics legend continues to demonstrate the extraordinary financial power of an established global sports brand.

Elena Rybakina generated an estimated $12.6 million in 2025, collecting $8.6 million in prize money and another $4 million through endorsements. Her massive WTA Finals payday helped make it a particularly lucrative season.

Naomi Osaka is her ✨ pic.twitter.com/UTJzt8ohU1

Japanese-American tennis star Naomi Osaka earned approximately $12.5 million in 2025, with $10 million coming from endorsements. Her commercial appeal remains exceptional, demonstrating that her influence in fashion, culture and business extends beyond tournament results.

Amanda Anisimova earned approximately $10.8 million in 2025, including $7.3 million in prize money and $3.5 million in endorsements. Her breakthrough season and two Grand Slam final appearances significantly elevated her earning potential.

Poland’s Iga Świątek earned an estimated $23.1 million in 2025, including $10.1 million in prize money and $13 million through endorsements. Her championship consistency has made her one of tennis’s most valuable commercial stars.

The New York native is back in the semifinals 🔥 Jessica Pegula becomes the only woman on tour to win 50 matches in one season 👏 pic.twitter.com/pGhgaIfqva

Jessica Pegula collected an estimated $10.5 million in 2025, including $5.5 million in prize money and $5 million in endorsements. Her consistent performances and growing business interests make her a formidable force on and off the court.

Venus Williams earned approximately $10.2 million in 2025, with an estimated $10 million coming from endorsements. Even with limited tournament appearances, the tennis icon continues to turn decades of success into lasting commercial influence.

China’s Zheng Qinwen earned an estimated $20.6 million in 2025, including $19 million from endorsements. Her international appeal and commercial partnerships demonstrate just how valuable China’s rising tennis superstar has become.

Jeeno Thitikul earned approximately $10.1 million in 2025, including $7.6 million in golf winnings and $2.5 million in endorsements. Her record-breaking prize money and back-to-back CME Group Tour Championship victories fueled an impressive financial season.

scraped.title: Trump’s Kennedy Center Honors Faces Another Shake-Up as Ticketing Controversy Exposes Questions About a Deal Made Behind the Scenes
scraped.description: Trump's naming battle has escalated beyond the building's sign, with a federal judge blocking additional attempts to attach his name to Kennedy Center.
scraped.author: Rachel George
scraped.h1: Trump’s Kennedy Center Honors Faces Another Shake-Up as Ticketing Controversy Exposes Questions About a Deal Made Behind the Scenes
scraped.body_text:
Trump's naming battle has escalated beyond the building's sign, with a federal judge blocking additional attempts to attach his name to Kennedy Center.

The John F. Kennedy Center is moving away from its longtime nonprofit ticketing provider to another in a shady back-door move .

Amid President Donald Trump’s closure of the center on Sept. 15, the Kennedy Center Honors next month was forced to change locations.

The event will take place in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 7, 2026. For the first time in the event’s history, organizers will hold the ceremony off-site rather than at the Kennedy Center Opera House. The venue change follows the center’s planned closure for renovations.

That transition has impacted fans and delayed ticket sales.

Top-dollars donors and entertainers who want to attend must complete a submission form found on the Center’s site. There’s also an email listed for anyone looking to make “a contribution to receive advanced ticketing access.”

The ticketing change comes amid a federal lawsuit over Trump’s effort to add his name to the Kennedy Center.

A recent NPR investigation highlights potential conflicts of interest involving Richard Grenell, Live Nation, Ticketmaster, the Kennedy Center and the Justice Department.

While the center negotiated the Ticketmaster deal, then-president Richard Grenell was also receiving compensation as a board member of Live Nation, Ticketmaster’s parent company.

With 21 days left on the calender before the Kennedy Center Honors, current and former employees told NPR the delay stems from a planned move from Tessitura to Ticketmaster.

An NPR-obtained email shows artistic director Rick Canny claimed responsibility for shaping the Kennedy Center’s Ticketmaster deal. He also blamed unionized box office workers for delaying the switch. Then the center later laid off those employees in early October.

“Morning Edition” host A Martínez spoke with culture correspondent Anastasia Tsioulcas about the Kennedy Center’s decision to hand its ticketing operations to Ticketmaster.

When Martínez asked who pushed for the switch, Tsioulcas admitted, “That’s unclear.” But one name stood out.

She explained that Grenell served as Kennedy Center president while officials negotiated the new partnership with Ticketmaster.

The investigation also found that Grenell joined the board of Live Nation, Ticketmaster’s parent company, a few months after arriving at the Kennedy Center. He earned $260,205 in Live Nation board compensation in 2025 while leading the Kennedy Center through Ticketmaster negotiations.

Live Nation also identified Grenell as a representative in communications with government officials about its DOJ antitrust settlement. Earlier reports claimed he planned to recuse himself from potential conflicts involving the Kennedy Center. He has since left.

The partnership also raises concerns because Ticketmaster’s parent company, Live Nation, faces scrutiny over its market dominance, hidden fees and alleged unethical practices. A federal jury found the companies operated as a monopoly and harmed ticket buyers in a trial this past April. Once online viewers got word about antother change that goes against tradition, the reception was not pretty.

“Just a week after the biggest change election in a generation, where monopoly power was routed at the ballot box, Trump’s Kennedy Center pulls this,” wrote one person.

Another said, “Ric Grenell needs to resign from Live Nation’s board of directors. Did he actually recuse himself? What role did he play in the DOJ settlement discussions? Congress needs to investigate. Every fan buying tickets through Live Nation and Ticketmaster should demand Ric Grenell’s resignation from Live Nation’s board.”

The Kennedy Center’s latest changes have left its annual celebration facing a very different reality.

For nearly five decades, the Kennedy Center Honors brought entertainment’s biggest names together inside the institution’s historic Opera House.

Now, the December ceremony will take place at an arena while organizers navigate delayed ticket sales and a controversial new ticketing arrangement.

The Ticketmaster partnership has also raised questions about potential conflicts of interest involving Grenell and Live Nation.

Meanwhile, Trump’s fight to put his name on the Kennedy Center continues despite multiple court defeats.

The combination of a forced venue change, a leadership shake-up and an increasingly contentious business arrangement has put the institution under a different kind of spotlight.

For an event built around celebrating some of America’s most influential entertainers, the biggest spectacle surrounding this year’s ceremony may have nothing to do with the honorees.

NEW: Ric Grenell took $260,000 from Ticketmaster’s parent company while running the Kennedy Center. The Kennedy Center was negotiating a switch to Ticketmaster at the same time. https://t.co/X8m3Oc3ZT8
