scraped.title: How Nelson Mandela’s Party Lost Its Grip on South Africa
scraped.description: South Africa’s ruling ANC suffered its worst local election defeat as opposition parties gained ground, coalition talks intensified and questions mounted over President Cyril Ramaphosa’s leadership.
scraped.author: Jaidyn Bridgeforth
scraped.h1: How Nelson Mandela’s Party Lost Its Grip on South Africa
scraped.body_text:
South Africa’s ruling ANC suffered its worst local election defeat as opposition parties gained ground, coalition talks intensified and questions mounted over President Cyril Ramaphosa’s leadership.

South African political parties were bargaining Friday over who would govern Johannesburg and Tshwane, the municipality that includes Pretoria, after voters handed the African National Congress its worst result in local elections.

The Democratic Alliance finished ahead of the ANC in both municipalities, but neither party secured a council majority, according to The Associated Press . That gives smaller parties considerable influence over coalition negotiations that will determine who governs two of the country’s most important urban centers.

The ANC, once led by Nelson Mandela, remains South Africa’s largest party. Its share of the national municipal-election vote fell nearly 15 percentage points in five years, to 30.76%. The Democratic Alliance received 24.64%, while the uMkhonto weSizwe Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, finished third with 9.76%. ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula called the result “catastrophic.”

Former President Thabo Mbeki, who succeeded Mandela, questioned whether the ANC’s leadership should take responsibility for the party’s electoral defeat. Speaking on the “African Renaissance Podcast” last week, Mbeki said Ramaphosa would be right to step down, as ANC leaders deny reports that he had offered to resign are true.

He suggested that other senior party leaders should also consider taking responsibility. However, Ramaphosa and Mbalula denied the reports. ANC leaders met Thursday to discuss potential coalition partners, and the Associated Press said the party planned to reveal the results of those talks Saturday.

For many voters, the election came down to what happens when they turn on the tap or need the city to pick up the trash. Years of unreliable water supplies, electricity outages, and deteriorating roads have worn down confidence in local government.

Corruption scandals have further eroded public trust, while widespread unemployment and poverty continue to disproportionately affect Black South Africans. Political analyst Ralph Mathekga told Al Jazeera that the election results reflected growing frustration over failing public services and corruption.

That anger carries particular weight given the ANC’s historical significance in the fight against apartheid. In April 1994 , Nelson Mandela cast his first vote at Ohlange High School in Inanda, near Durban. He chose the school because it was founded by John Langalibalele Dube, the ANC’s first president, whose grave was located nearby.

The election was South Africa’s first in which citizens of all races could vote. The ANC won nearly 63% of the vote, and Mandela became the country’s first Black president.

Apartheid enforced white minority rule through laws that institutionalized racial segregation and systematically disadvantaged the Black majority. Its economic legacy remains evident today, with Black South Africans continuing to bear a disproportionate share of the country’s poverty and unemployment.

The ANC had already lost its parliamentary majority in 2024, the first time since 1994. It won about 40% of the national vote and formed a government of national unity that included the Democratic Alliance.

The ANC also faced a challenge from within its own ranks. Zuma broke with the party, was expelled, and went on to lead a rival political movement, the uMkhonto weSizwe Party, commonly known as MK.

In this month’s municipal elections, MK finished first in eThekwini, the municipality that includes Durban, securing 38% of the vote. The result gave Zuma’s party a significant role in negotiations over who will govern the city.

The immediate deadline is Nov. 26, when municipal councils are expected to hold their first meetings and elect their political leaders, according to South Africa’s Business Day. The coalition agreements reached before then will help determine who secures the mayor’s office. Residents will ultimately judge the incoming governments by whether they can keep water flowing, maintain roads, and deliver the basic services voters have demanded.

scraped.title: 'You’re So Pathetic!': Trump Explodes at Reporter Over FAA Ground Stop, Throws In Racist Jab, Then Walks Straight Into an Admission He Didn’t Catch
scraped.description: President Donald Trump sent a message to Americans dealing with a nationwide aviation shutdown that disrupted more than 10,000 flights, saying he wasn’t
scraped.author: ArLuther Lee
scraped.h1: ‘You’re So Pathetic!’: Trump Explodes at Reporter Over FAA Ground Stop, Throws In Racist Jab, Then Walks Straight Into an Admission He Didn’t Catch
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump sent a message to Americans dealing with a nationwide aviation shutdown that disrupted more than 10,000 flights, saying he wasn’t taking responsibility.

But when a reporter asked whether the president had been too busy overseeing White House construction projects while the nation’s air travel system was falling apart, Trump had plenty to say — just not about the questions surrounding his administration’s priorities.

Instead, he attacked the journalist, calling her “pathetic” and questioning her “talent.”

Monday’s exchange outside the White House followed Trump’s remarks on the FAA’s unprecedented nationwide ground stop. Friday afternoon’s shutdown lasted over four hours and stranded passengers nationwide.

Trump accepted no responsibility and did not explain his prolonged silence. He defended his construction projects, blamed past administrations for aviation system problems and insisted he had no reason to intervene.

The confrontation began as Trump prepared to board Marine One for a trip to Asia. Reporters questioned him face-to-face for the first time about Friday’s shutdown, prompting his first public remarks on the crisis.

When a reporter asked him to respond to critics who said he focused too much on Washington construction projects while the nation’s airline systems crumbled, Trump immediately defended the White House renovations.

“The White House is flawless. Listen to me, I know you don’t see dirt, but if you take a look at the White House,” Trump told the Black reporter. “You never notice broken windows, obviously, from where you come. I don’t know. But we had 18 broken windows, the exterior plaster was falling off the wall, and it was an embarrassment.”

Trump then applauded himself for the work he had completed before insulting the reporter, NBC News White House correspondent Yamiche Alcindor.

“Take a look at the helipad. Listen to me! You’re so pathetic. You don’t have talent.”

Trump continued defending the work, arguing that maintaining the White House was his responsibility as president and dismissing the renovations as inexpensive.

“I have a responsibility to make sure the symbol of our country is in decent shape, and it takes me 10 minutes a day, very little time,” he said, according to Raw Story. “I don’t do it. You don’t see me on a scaffold.”

When Scott pressed him about why he was requesting additional money for the projects, Trump attacked her again.

“This doesn’t cost money. This is peanuts. This is called talent. Talent,” Trump said. “You don’t have talent. You know? You don’t know what a… You don’t know what a broken column is.”

“And losers like you come out, and they say, ‘Why are you focused on the White House?’ Because the White House is a symbol of our country,” Trump concluded.

The exchange came as Trump’s administration was asking Congress for tens of billions of dollars to overhaul the country’s aging air traffic control infrastructure. The administration initially requested $30.1 billion on Friday before increasing that figure to $50 billion later that night.

Trump suggested Monday that the disruption could have one positive outcome: persuading lawmakers to approve the additional funding.

“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” he wrote on Truth Social on Sunday. “It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old — RIDICULOUS!”

But when asked about his own responsibility for the shutdown, Trump offered little indication that he believed he should answer for the failure.

“I was in the White House during the ground stop. I didn’t think there was any reason for me to do anything,” he said.

Asked directly what responsibility he accepted for the shutdown, Trump replied : “I don’t take any responsibility.”

He praised Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and other officials for handling the situation. Everyone remained safe, and no one suffered injuries, he said.

The president’s response followed days of criticism over his absence during the crisis. During Friday’s flight groundings, Trump remained behind the scenes as Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin addressed reporters. Trump posted about unrelated topics, including reviving American entertainment, without publicly addressing the aviation emergency.

Mullin defended the president’s decision to let Cabinet officials handle the public response, saying Trump puts leaders in place and allows them to lead.

Trump eventually blamed the Biden administration for the system’s condition, a position Duffy also embraced. On Sunday, Duffy told CNN he accepted responsibility for what previous administrations had handed down.

The outage began Friday afternoon when the FAA ordered the first nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks. More than 10,000 flights were grounded or delayed after communications problems disrupted the system. Officials later pointed to a routine router replacement as a possible trigger, although the precise cause remained under investigation.

Trump’s decision to defend his construction priorities while demanding billions for aviation upgrades also drew criticism from some of his own political allies. Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene questioned why he had devoted so much attention to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation while saying almost nothing about the aviation emergency.

“Trump constantly railed about fixing the reflection pool so much that he used the last day before massively losing the midterms to give a speech in front of the reflection pool bragging about he fixed the reflection pool,” she wrote, according to The New York Times.

She added that while Americans were worried about a possible attack during the aviation disruption, “President Trump doesn’t even issue so much as a Truth Social post.”

Online critics also criticized the president’s response, accusing him of prioritizing personal construction projects over problems affecting ordinary Americans.

One critic said : “A million people stranded and all Trump can talk about are his vanity projects. He really is awful! To the reporter’s question, Trump thinks it should have been fixed by other Presidents – he was one of those “other” Presidents for four years.”

Another questioned his apparent disconnect from the crisis, writing : “He’s on another planet. It’s obvious the people around him aren’t leveling with him. He’s digging a deeper and deeper hole. Embarrassing.”

Others accused Trump of treating public money as his personal spending account, writing : “@realDonaldTrump doesn’t give a damn about America. He’s treating the Treasury like his personal ATM and the taxpayers like his sugar daddy. Buying himself diapers & buildings while Americans get the bill. Y’all elected a convicted felon, then handed him the national credit card.”

Q: What do you say to critics who say you were too focused on DC construction projects while our airline systems were crumbling? TRUMP: The White House is flawless. Listen to me. It takes me 10 minutes a day. Take a look at the helipad. Listen to me! You're so pathetic. You… pic.twitter.com/4AUWni51oS

scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Pataxó Indigenous people protest the arrest of a female vice-chief in Brazil’s Bahia
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Pataxó Indigenous people occupied the entrance to the Civil Police station in the city of Eunápolis, in the far south of Brazil’s Bahia state on Nov 12. It was a peaceful protest against the arrest of two Pataxó leaders in the Barra Velha Indigenous Territory. Erilsa Braz dos Santos, known as Uruba Pataxó, vice-chief of Barra Velha Mother Village, and communicator Karen Pataxó were arrested on Nov. 11 on suspicion of drug trafficking in the region. The Pataxó deny the accusations.

Karen was released, but Uruba remained in custody and was transferred to a prison in the city of Teixeira de Freitas on Nov. 12, sparking outrage and mobilization among Indigenous people on social media. “This is a political accusation, because she is a leader who defends her people and her territory,” a protester said in a video published on Instagram by the Media and Art Research Center (Nupomar) and Barra Velha Village during the Eunápolis demonstration.

Uruba and Karen were detained during Operation Barra Velha , carried out by the Civil and Military Police in Bahia’s Porto Seguro municipality. According to Indigenous leader Dário Pataxó, the imprisonment is intended to silence those who speak out against drug trafficking in the territory. “We know that their intention is to stop the movement. Uruba is one of those on the frontline. They’ve already stopped [Cacique] Suruí, who was president of the Barra Velha Council of Chiefs and is facing proceedings under house arrest . And now they want to stop Uruba,” Dario told Mongabay by phone.

Uruba is a teacher, regional coordinator of the United Movement of Indigenous Peoples and Organizations of Bahia (Mupoiba), and secretary of the territory’s Council of Chiefs. In a statement, Mupoiba pointed to an “ orchestrated engine driven by forces serving predatory large landholdings and rural militias” to persecute land defenders while armed attacks against Indigenous communities are investigated slowly. The organization compared the tactic to the escalation against the Terena and Guarani-Kaiowá peoples in Mato Grosso do Sul state. On Nov. 10, Chief Dione Alcântara Terena, a regional coordinator for Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs, was arrested in Campo Grande on allegations of participating in an organized scheme to invade rural properties in the region.

The Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil (APIB) recorded 40 reports of political violence against 30 Indigenous people in 15 states during the 2026 elections, including seven killings and 11 death threats. The Indigenous Federation of the Pataxó and Tupinambá Nations of Southernmost Bahia (Finpat) said land disputes, which fuels conflicts in the area, fall under the jurisdiction of the Federal Court .

The Indigenous Missionary Council (Cimi) is monitoring Uruba’s imprisonment alongside the Public Defender’s Office in Bahia. They said no drugs or weapons were seized during the operation. The defense is preparing a habeas corpus petition.

scraped.title: Environmental groups challenge Mexico’s rollback of protections for world's smallest porpoise
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Environmental groups challenge Mexico’s rollback of protections for world’s smallest porpoise
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

MEXICO CITY — Environmental groups are fighting against relaxed fishing regulations in the Gulf of California, where the last of the vaquita, the world’s smallest porpoise, is close to extinction.

In October 2026, changes to the regulations dramatically reduced the area where fishing is prohibited in vaquita habitat. In response, several environmental groups have asked a court to halt the changes, arguing that they threaten the last approximately 10 vaquitas ( Phocoena sinus ) remaining in the world.

“The court can stop this rollback before more of the habitat is exposed to deadly nets,” said Aleira Lara Galicia, executive director of Greenpeace Mexico, one of the groups that filed the Nov. 6 injunction request . The Center for Biological Diversity and the Conservation of Marine Mammals of Mexico were also listed as petitioners.

The vaquita averages around 1.5 meters (5 feet) long and weighs up to 54 kilograms (120 pounds). It’s endemic to the Gulf of California, also called the Sea of Cortez, where illegal fishing has decimated vaquita populations over the last three decades.

The decline is primarily the result of bycatch in gillnets, which hang down vertically in the water and can drown a vaquita when it gets entangled.

Many gillnets are illegally set for totoaba ( Totoaba macdonaldi ), an endangered fish with a swim bladder that sells for thousands of dollars on the black market, primarily in Asia.

To protect the vaquita and other marine life, the gulf has a series of layered and overlapping protected areas. A 225-kilometers squared (approximately 87-miles squared) “zero-tolerance area” (ZTA) prohibits all navigation and fishing. The largest protected area is an 11,000-km2 (4,247-mi2) “gillnet prohibition zone.” However, the new regulations reduce the size of that gillnet-free zone by nearly 86%, to 1,562 km2 (603 mi2). The new regulations also establish a transit route through the ZTA, allowing boats to get from one side to the other instead of going around the critical habitat.

The injunction petitioners said the new transit route fragments the vaquita habitat. They also said enforcement should extend to the entire area where vaquita have been documented. In 2025 and 2026, vaquita were seen outside of the ZTA, the groups note. They also called for fishing communities to receive support to transition away from gillnets.

“There is no need to wait for another case of bycatch before taking interim measures to preserve the conditions essential to the vaquita’s survival,” they told the court.

The Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources said in an October statement that it’s committed to vaquita conservation and will continue to coordinate with other government agencies.

“The government of Mexico reaffirms its commitment to working with communities, scientific institutions, civil organizations and international bodies to jointly advance the protection of the vaquita and the well-being of the populations of the Upper Gulf of California,” the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection said in a statement .

scraped.title: The power of the paddy: Japan looks to rice fields to help mitigate flooding
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: nandithachandraprakash
scraped.h1: The power of the paddy: Japan looks to rice fields to help mitigate flooding
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

OSAKI, Japan — Osaki, an agricultural community in northeast Japan, has struggled with flooding in recent years. The area was inundated in 2015 , 2019 and 2022 , when heavy rains breached river embankments.

In response, Osaki farmers and local government have installed more than 5,000 small, earthen dams in the rice paddies that surround the community, according to city officials. They say they hope the dams will mitigate flooding by keeping more water contained to the fields.

Speaking to Mongabay, Osaki city officials attribute the uptick in floods, in part, to climate change. It’s a pattern seen across Japan, where climate change-fueled heavy rainfall events have increased in frequency and intensity, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.

In response, officials are rethinking their approach to flood control, with increased focus on “green infrastructure” solutions in rice paddies and other agricultural areas.

Japan’s agricultural sector is in decline: The average age of a farmer was nearly 70 in 2026 and the country’s rural population is on a steady downward trend . Agricultural land near cities has been converted into suburbs and industrial zones; these low-lying urban areas can be particularly vulnerable to flooding.

With declining agricultural land in mind, researchers have been assessing the flood mitigation potential of not only current agricultural land but also abandoned fields. They say that these assessments highlight the importance of understanding site-specific conditions and developing local countermeasures against flooding.

“We need to look at the value of the remaining farmland from various perspectives, re-recognize it, and work to conserve it,” Yota Imai, an associate professor at Tokushima University who studies the flood mitigation function of agricultural land in Japan, told Mongabay during a video call.

Rice paddies — constructed with raised ridges to store water as part of the cultivation process — can help mitigate flooding in two main ways: by temporarily trapping water and by absorbing it into the soil.

“Of course, there is a limit to their capacity,” Takeshi Osawa, an assistant professor at Tokyo Metropolitan University who has studied green infrastructure and disaster mitigation, told Mongabay via video call. “But this temporary storage can slightly delay the inflow of water into irrigation canals and rivers, helping avoid peak flows that could result in flooding.”

While the soil of dry fields can also retain water, dry-field crops such as soybeans are more likely to sustain damage from heavy rains compared with rice plants, Osawa adds.

Many of Japan’s rice-producing regions have been gradually developed over hundreds, if not thousands , of years, with farming communities utilizing the low-lying topography of floodplains while endeavoring to control the flow of water.

The Osaki plain, with mountains to its west and rivers flowing through it, is one such region. Although fertile, the area is susceptible to not only floods but also droughts and cold summers, making skillful water management essential for generations of farmers.

Although the Osaki community has managed water resources through hardscape solutions, such as artificial river embankments, for roughly 300 years, farmers and city officials started utilizing the paddies themselves for flood control around the 1960s, according to city officials.

“The community has utilized rice paddies as floodwater retention areas by temporarily diverting river water into them, to mitigate flood damage to settlements,” said Masahiro Ito, a member of Osaki City’s River Basin Flood Management Division, during an interview with Mongabay. “This helps prevent river embankments from being breached.”

As of 2025, Japan contained roughly 4.2 million hectares (10.4 millions acres) of agricultural land, including roughly 2.3 million hectares (5.7 million acres) of rice paddies, according to government data. Total agricultural land has decreased by roughly 30% since the early 1960s.

Agricultural abandonment is an ongoing issue particularly affecting hilly regions with less favorable farming conditions and is due, in part, to aging farmers and labor shortages, according to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries.

Abandoned agricultural land in rural areas is often left as-is, according to Imai. Meanwhile, land near cities may be developed for housing, commercial facilities, or, in recent years, solar farms. Such land use changes “will generally cause the land’s flood mitigation function to decline,” he said.

However, abandoned agricultural land left as is may not necessarily lose all flood mitigation potential.

“Looking at common trends across a broad range, my current view is that as long as farmland [isn’t subject to land use change] — regardless of whether it is partially abandoned or not — it will likely provide a certain degree of disaster mitigation,” Tokyo Metropolitan University’s Osawa said.

With heavy rain events expected to increase in frequency in Japan due to climate change, researchers warn that “gray infrastructure” like large, concrete river dams and levees may not be enough to prevent flooding.

“It’s generally acknowledged that we need to utilize rice paddies for flood mitigation more than ever before,” Tokushima University’s Imai said, noting that effectiveness may vary depending on factors such as location and rainfall patterns.

In recent years, both the national government and various municipalities have incorporated a watershed-level approach to flood prevention.

Shiga Prefecture, located in central Japan, has been a pioneer in incorporating rice paddies into local flood mitigation plans, according to Osawa. The prefectural government, which also positions its disaster mitigation measures as a climate change adaptation strategy, established a flood management office in 2006 and uses a “site safety level” system to assess and prepare for flood risks by location.

Paddy dams are used to boost paddy fields’ flood mitigation potential. The dams, installed in paddy drainage holes, have a smaller-than-usual opening to slow the flow of water. Niigata Prefecture on the west coast of Honshu Island is Japan’s premier rice-producing region and has been a leader in paddy dam implementation for over 20 years .

In Osaki, city officials have worked with agricultural groups and the prefectural government to implement paddy dams since 2021. The officials say they have installed dams across roughly 20% of Osaki’s paddy land so far, an area equivalent to about 1,700 hectares (4,200 acres).

“That speaks to how bad the flooding can be!” Katsuyoshi Takahashi, a member of the city’s Rural Areas Development Division, told Mongabay in an interview.

As artificial wetland habitats, Japan’s paddy fields also support biodiversity — provided agricultural chemicals aren’t used to excess. Research shows that in addition to ecosystem services, Japan’s rice paddies provide habitat for an estimated 5,000 species .

Although there isn’t a direct correlation between biodiversity conservation and flood prevention, the two benefits can overlap, according to Imai.

“Maintaining contiguous farmland and rice paddies without developing them is, of course, beneficial for flood retention, and since wildlife — especially birds — require extensive habitats for conservation, this can create a win-win scenario,” he said.

Abandoned paddy fields can potentially open new doors to conservation.

In a chapter of the 2022 research anthology Green Infrastructure and Climate Change Adaptation , Imai and co-authors assessed a conservation project in Toyooka City, Hyōgo Prefecture, where abandoned paddy fields were restored as wetlands with the goal of providing habitat for the Oriental white stork ( Ciconia boyciana ), an endangered bird once extinct in Japan .

They found that the abandoned fields’ water storage capacity was improved through wetland restoration. Citizens and city officials removed vegetation and rebuilt levees to help water accumulate and create an environment where the storks’ prey could flourish, Imai told Mongabay. However, he cautioned against drawing broad conclusions about flood mitigation based on this single example.

Osaki City, too, is keen to preserve its paddy fields, wetlands and traditional farmsteads as wildlife habitats. The area contains two registered Ramsar Sites , wetlands of international importance — the Kabukuri-numa wetland and surrounding rice paddies, as well as the Kejo-numa reservoir — that provide habitat for migratory geese and other wildlife, and help to mitigate flooding.

In 2017, the Osaki area was also recognized as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System (GIAHS), a framework run by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). The city aims to use the designation to raise farmers’ income and draw people to the area, said Motoyuki Miyake, a member of Osaki’s GIAHS secretariat.

“Maintaining paddy fields is crucial for the conservation of biodiversity, and it’s important to ensure farmers can make a living from them through various initiatives,” Miyake said in an interview with Mongabay.

Installing paddy dams, in addition to boosting flood control, likewise “demonstrates a commitment to maintaining these areas as paddy environments for the foreseeable future, with the cooperation of farmers,” he added.

Banner image: The sharp-tailed sandpipers ( Calidris acuminata ) rest on a berm in a rice paddy in Mie Prefecture, Japan. Image by Alpsdake via Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 4.0 ).

items.title: Under Trump, black lung disease is surging among Appalachia’s coal miners
items.summary: The administration’s attempt to revive the declining industry is leaving workers — and the planet — behind.

scraped.title: Under Trump, black lung disease is surging among Appalachia’s coal miners » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: The administration’s attempt to revive the declining industry is leaving workers — and the planet — behind.
scraped.author: Kim Kelly
scraped.h1: Under Trump, black lung disease is surging among Appalachia’s coal miners
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

On President Donald Trump’s watch, a quiet epidemic has been left unchecked to prey upon Appalachia’s workforce. Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, the incurable progressive pulmonary disease better known as black lung, now affects 32% of longtime underground miners in Central Appalachia, which includes Kentucky, Virginia, and West Virginia.

That’s just one alarming statistic cited in a new report from Reimagine Appalachia, a coalition of organizations working to improve the lives of workers in Appalachia.

During Trump’s second term, his administration has taken an active role in weakening federal environmental regulations, handing over more land to mine operators, and privileging coal production over more renewable energy projects, while gutting a Biden-era rule meant to protect coal miners from black lung.

We can't do this work without you. We've set an ambitious goal of raising $60,000 by the end of the year. Will you donate to support climate journalism today?

“The Trump administration has put substantive energy and funding toward expanding the coal industry without taking complementary actions to expand protections for the miners on whom the coal industry depends,” the report authors wrote.

A pet project of President Trump in his second term has been boosting what he calls “beautiful, clean coal.” The administration has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into new coal facilities, and Trump has bragged that “the United States is opening up new mines at the fastest pace since the 1950s.”

Demand for coal has continued to decline, but its extraction helps fuel climate change. As recently as 2024 , coal was responsible for almost half of all carbon dioxide emissions from U.S. electricity generation, while providing only 15% of its power. Both underground and surface coal mining operations release climate-warming methane into the atmosphere.

Meanwhile, black lung cases have increased more than 60% since 2018, to the highest rates since 1978.

For decades, coal dust presented the greatest danger to miners’ respiratory health; mine operators did little to prevent its spread, and generations of workers fell victim to the demon of the coalfields. After the passage of the 1969 Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act , which introduced a federal coal dust exposure limit as well as robust safety standards and engineering controls, the rate of black lung cases dropped by 90%.

In 1974, the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommended a stricter limit for the respirable crystalline silica that causes black lung disease. The Institute stated that miners should not be exposed to more than 50 micrograms per cubic meter during any 10-hour shift of a 40-hour work week, noting that compliance ​“should prevent adverse effects of crystalline silica.”

But the current limit, which was implemented in the 1970s, is still twice that – and that’s assuming mine operators comply. The permissible silica exposure threshold for coal miners remains double that of every other industry, including construction.

In the 1990s, black lung rates began to climb again. Advances in mining machinery had allowed coal companies to speed up production and compel their workers to cut through more and more tons of silica-laden quartz in pursuit of ever-thinner coal seams. Workers who were exposed to large quantities of that silica in its respirable form began to get sick after less time underground, and those who were diagnosed rapidly progressed to the most severe form of the disease. What was once thought of as an “old man’s disease” is now felling workers in their 30s and 40s.

“In the coal industry, all the easy coal is mostly gone,” said Thomas Edwards, a former coal miner with black lung disease from Big Stone Gap, Virginia. “Now they’re going in, and they’re getting the smaller seams of coal, and they have to cut the rocks just to get the coal. So they’re being exposed to a lot more dust and silica than they were years ago, and now, at a younger age, they’re becoming more disabled.”

None of this is a secret, or even a surprise. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health has been chronicling the uptick in black lung cases, and journalists have been sounding the alarm on its resurgence since the 2010s. The risks of silica exposure have been well known and documented since the 1970s, and miners have been calling for a federal silica standard ever since. Powerful mining industry interests oppose efforts to further regulate their operations, though, and multiple presidential administrations have come and gone without concretely addressing the problem.

Without strict oversight, some mine operators have found ways to dodge their federal dust sampling obligations. As journalist Chris Hamby has reported , the system the Mine Safety and Health Administration used to monitor miners’ exposure to dust allows employers ample room to get creative – and the consequences of getting caught have been minor. Federal underfunding and chronic understaffing left the Mine Safety and Health Administration less able to effectively penalize offenders. The decline of unions in the region left workers without a safeguard, and those who worried about their working conditions hesitated to speak out for fear of retaliation. It was a recipe for disaster — and it didn’t take long for the bodies to start piling up.

“There are more patients who have silica-induced lung disease now than in the past,” said Dr. Drew Harris, assistant dean of continuous education at the University of Virginia School of Medicine and the medical director at Stone Mountain Health Services. “This is a problem that is settled. We know the science behind it; we know what’s causing this disease; we just now need to act on it. There is no reason why coal miners should be allowed to be exposed to more silica dust than every other industry.”

During the Biden administration, coal miners, public health advocates, and their allies came tantalizingly close to securing a new federal silica standard. In 2024, the Mine Safety and Health Administration issued a final rule entitled “Lowering Miners’ Exposure to Respirable Crystalline Silica and Improving Respiratory Protection,” which would have halved the permissible level of silica exposure for coal miners. Mine operators were given April 14, 2025, to come into full compliance, which they protested as still too soon. Meanwhile, miners criticized the rule as too permissive – there is no “safe” level of silica exposure – but applauded it as a step in the right direction after many years of inactivity.

“People in Congress are from an area totally the opposite of where we’re from,” Edwards said. “If you wanted a living wage, you worked for a coal company or around a coal company. Now I’ve got black lung, and I’m paying that price.”

The miners’ victory was short-lived. By 2025, Trump was back in the White House, and his administration quickly moved to bury the rule. The Trump-controlled Mine Safety and Health Administration used various maneuvers to postpone and ultimately quash enforcement; many months later, the original rule has been gutted, and its proposed replacement renegotiated with industry interests in mind.

The United Mine Workers union condemned the changes. “This proposal creates a massive enforcement gap while boasting about cutting nearly $25 million from monitoring and nearly $4 million from medical surveillance,” the union said. “[The Mine Safety and Health Administration] has forgotten that its only responsibility is to protect miners’ health and safety.”

In the meantime, hundreds more miners have been exposed to toxic levels of silica. More have been diagnosed with black lung; more have needed lung transplants or oxygen tanks. More have died.

The rollback of the silica exposure rule comes on top of other Trump-era threats to coal miner health. In April 2025, Elon Musk’s DOGE team and the Robert F. Kennedy Jr.-led Department of Health and Human Services announced a raft of deep cuts to the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, laying off two-thirds of its highly specialized workforce, including 400 mine safety inspectors, and shutting down several regional offices as well as its Coal Workers’ Health Surveillance Program, which screens miners for lung disease and monitors health outcomes. (A judge has since ordered the administration to restore the cut programs and bring some National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health employees back to work.)

“We are watching a complete breakdown in the federal safety net meant to keep coal miners alive. When federal regulators fall asleep at the wheel, coal operators step in and put production goals ahead of human safety,” United Mine Workers of America international president Brian Sanson said in a statement.

scraped.title: Cincinnati prepares for climate migrants » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: The Ohio municipality became the first U.S. city to release a climate migration readiness plan.
scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: Cincinnati prepares for climate migrants
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

As seas rise and wildfires and hurricanes grow more intense, some people are asking where they could move to reduce their vulnerability.

Cincinnati is one of several northern inland cities promoting itself as a potential destination. This year, it became the first U.S. city to release a climate migration readiness plan .

Tim Robustelli is with the Future of Land and Housing program at New America, a think tank. He says an influx of new residents could bring many benefits.

Robustelli: “Economic development, entrepreneurship, and of course, with more economic activity with larger populations, that’s a larger tax base.”

But he says as Cincinnati and other cities plan to attract and support new residents, they also need to protect current residents from being left behind or pushed out.

For example, cities can provide rental assistance and create policies that protect tenants from eviction if property values rise.

Robustelli: “Other tools like property tax breaks … can sort of help offset some of the increased costs you see with redevelopment and gentrification.”

And he says grants and low-interest loans can help people pay for critical home repairs so they can stay in their homes long-term.

So cities can welcome new residents and support those who have lived there for generations.

scraped.h1: Could a data center’s waste heat warm a North Carolina town?
scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

16 November 2026

In the Carolinas, Ohio, Texas, and many other states, Democrats routed incumbent Republicans in this month’s elections at least in part because voters fear an onslaught of AI data centers — the massive computer warehouses that threaten to suck up water supplies, increase climate and air pollution, and drive up energy costs.

Voters didn’t just take their anger out on politicians. In red and blue areas alike, they also approved dozens of ballot measures pausing or restricting data centers, adding to the over 450 moratoriums already in place across the country .

The backlash has left state and local leaders grappling with how to put guardrails on the facilities and ensure they benefit nearby communities.

A forthcoming deal between a data center and Enfield, North Carolina — an overwhelmingly poor, majority Black town of 2 , 000 — could offer a groundbreaking example of what such development might look like.

For years, Enfield leaders and their allies have been working toward a clean energy vision that includes a solar farm to supply residents with power, a new substation to help distribute those renewable electrons, and a thermal energy network — a shallow form of geothermal that could replace inefficient water heating, space heating, and cooling. But they’ve faced a dearth of funding and fierce policy headwinds under President Donald Trump.

Then, this summer, Halifax County, where Enfield sits, announced it was selling property to Wyoming-based Quiet Data Centers , a land development firm, for a 100 , 000 square-foot facility. The industrial site is 2 miles outside the town but needs to tap into its wastewater systems.

For Enfield Mayor Mondale Robinson, that presented a bargaining opportunity. Now, he and top officials from Quiet are negotiating a community benefits agreement, a legally binding document that ties developers to certain benchmarks. Among other commitments, Robinson wants the company to fund the entire $ 16 . 2 million clean energy plan.

What’s more, he wants the data center to join the thermal energy network, which could provide a surge of excess heat to meet the whole town’s needs. If the plans come to fruition, it would be the first time in the U.S. that a data center has connected to such a system.

Brendan Morris, Quiet’s chief development officer, confirmed to Canary Media that the discussions were ongoing and that all of Enfield’s aims were on the table. ​ “ I think things are possible,” he said. ​ “ We’re new to this community and new to the county. We look around and see how a new business and a new data center coming into the area can make a positive impact.”

Robinson, a self-proclaimed progressive, acknowledges that the midterms were a rebuke of the tech sector’s buildout. ​ “ Everybody should be against dirty data centers,” he said. But he believes the not-in-my-backyard approach has too often stuck communities like Enfield with polluting projects rejected by wealthier areas. That’s why he wants a data center that’s built sustainably and with community input. ​ “ There’s nothing progressive about saying we are against something, without saying what we are for,” he added.

A year ago, Lancaster, Pennsylvania, became the first local government in the country to sign a community benefits agreement with a data center project, according to researchers at the World Resources Institute. The agreements have long been used for other types of developments, from manufacturing plants to solar farms, said Danielle Riedl, research associate at the nonprofit.

“ But now, of course, the conversation — seemingly everywhere — is focused on data center development,” she said. Still, the agreements are no silver bullets. ​ “ You really want to see CBAs as one tool, together with zoning policies, development agreements, and other accountability mechanisms.”

In Halifax County, Quiet has pledged to mitigate some common data center complaints. At a public meeting this summer, the company said the 88 -megawatt facility will plug into the Dominion Energy grid on its own dime and pay for all the electricity it needs, according to the local news outlet RRSpin . It will run backup generators for no more than 30 minutes a month, on average, unless there is an outage.

But the company also has to alleviate the immense heat generated by racks of computers inside the facility. And while Quiet has pledged to use closed-loop cooling — a less-water-intensive process than sending waste heat to cooling towers, where water then evaporates — the technology is expensive and noisy.

That’s where the thermal energy network comes in. The system is essentially a network of ground-source heat pumps. They’re analogous to air-source heat pumps, but move heat between the buildings and the earth rather than the outside air, thanks to a water-based solution that flows through a system of buried pipes.

Some data centers in Europe are already plugged into such systems as a way to release excess heat. The same technology could be used in Enfield, providing cooling without the noise and at less cost, said Eric Bosworth, a pioneer on utility-run thermal energy networks who runs his own consultancy called Thermal Energy Insights. ​ “ It gives a layer of resiliency, and it’s going to save them money on cooling, too,” Bosworth said, referring to Quiet. ​ “ Every [unit] of heat that they send to the network is going to be cheaper than putting it up through their chillers.”

The nonprofit Enfield Energy Futures won a seed grant earlier this year to design the thermal energy network. But receiving funding from Quiet for the geothermal project — and the entire clean energy plan — would be game-changing.

A transparent, robust community benefits agreement with Quiet, said William Munn, Enfield Energy Futures executive director, would be ​ “ an incredible opportunity to take some of this unfettered wealth and set Enfield on course to take care of itself, make decisions for itself, and to be able to grow and sustain itself for the long term.”

The data center’s participation in the thermal energy network would be a boon in wintertime, when residents face extreme utility bills of $ 500 a month or more. During the region’s sweltering summers, Quiet’s excess heat could prove more challenging to handle.

“ There’s no free lunch in physics,” Bosworth said. Solutions could include disconnecting the data center from the network or installing a technology called absorption chillers. ​ “ You’re essentially using a chemical reagent to produce cooling from waste heat. So, you could put in one of those systems and continue to harvest heat through the summer months, and benefit the network with cooling.”

As part of the seed grant, Brian McAdoo, associate professor at Duke University’s Nicholas School of the Environment, and his students have already been testing heat levels and soil properties to fine-tune specs for the network. Now, his team is also reworking the system plan for the potential addition of the data center.

“ One possible way of getting rid of heat from a data center would be through groundwater,” McAdoo said. ​ “ Since we have so much water in the coastal plain sediments, if you put heat in one place, it can take that heat and move it.”

McAdoo will weigh all the options with Morris and the rest of the Quiet team. ​ “ We’re going to look at the plumbing. We’re going to look at the mechanical. We’re going to look at the heat that’s being produced,” Morris said. ​ “ Every climate is different. North Carolina is different than North Dakota, which is different than Helsinki. That’ll give us the parameters to go back to Enfield.”

The research and design work is time-consuming, part of why a final community benefits agreement, if it materializes, is likely still weeks, or even months, away.

“ Rushing to get something on the books that is incomplete does a disservice to what the data center may be able to offer our community, but it also does a disservice to our residents,” Mayor Robinson said. ​ “ I don’t think any of us are living up to our full potential by signing agreements before things are completely understood.”

16 November 2026

More than 25 , 000 homes across New England will be keeping warm this winter with new energy-efficient, low-emission systems paid for, in part, by federal funds. The households are participants in a five-state effort to boost cold-climate heat pump adoption that launched one year ago this month.

While that is well short of the ultimate goal of 580 , 000 heat pumps installed in four years, the growth of the program — the New England Heat Pump Accelerator — in its first months has supporters feeling confident about its chances for success.

“ We’re very, very optimistic about this goal,” said Ellen Pfeiffer, a fellow with Energy Solutions, a clean energy consultancy that is helping implement the programming, during a webinar last week reviewing the program’s first year. ​ “ We see vastly more participation just with these added incentives.”

The accelerator — a joint endeavor between Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island — is backed by $ 450 million from the federal Climate Pollution Reduction Grants program, which was created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. It was, and remains, a rare example of a major Biden-era initiative making headway despite the Trump administration’s relentless efforts to eliminate federal clean energy and environmental funding.

New England is particularly well poised to take advantage of heat pumps because of its current reliance on fossil fuels. More than half the single-family homes in Connecticut, Maine, and New Hampshire use heating oil, as do large portions of those in Massachusetts and Rhode Island. Propane and natural gas are also in wide use.

Switching to a heat pump yields substantial monthly bill savings for most oil customers and a significant portion of propane and natural gas users. It also cuts climate-warming pollution: The only emissions associated with heat pumps are those produced by generating the electricity needed to operate the systems.

“ It’s the closest thing we have to a magic trick in the energy industry,” said Andy Frank, deputy commissioner of energy and technology policy at the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.

The accelerator program is slated to last four years, but it aims to leave behind a permanently transformed market in which accessible prices, readily available equipment, and a well-trained workforce make heat pumps the default choice for home heating well into the future. The long-term goal is for heat pumps to make up 90 % of heating system sales in the region by 2040 .

“ We are shifting what is bought and sold in the market,” said Dylan Voorhees, senior consultant at nonprofit clean energy advisory Vermont Energy Investment Corp., an implementation partner.

The centerpiece of the effort is the midstream incentive. Distributors — the plumbing and equipment supply companies that sell to contractors — receive an incentive payment for selling cold-climate heat pumps and heat pump water heaters. They get to keep a small sum, and the rest is passed on to the buyer as a discount: $ 300 incentive for heat-pump water heaters and $ 650 for space-heating heat pumps in four states. Maine has chosen to concentrate its program exclusively on heat-pump water heaters, using the accelerator money to fund its existing incentives.

The money helps make heat pumps more financially appealing to consumers and gives distributors a reason to keep the equipment in stock for quick and easy purchases. So far, nearly 90 % of the region’s distributors are signed up to participate in the program.

“ Working together allows us to send the market one consistent signal instead of five different ones,” said Tara Donadio, senior manager of policy and programs for Northeast Energy Efficiency Partnerships, another implementation partner.

Though the accelerator incentives are relatively modest, they can be stacked with other state rebates — $ 900 for a water heater in Connecticut, for example, or an average of $ 5 , 800 for a heat pump in Massachusetts — providing an additional financial nudge.

The accelerator is also funding state- and community-level pilot programs that address barriers to heat pump adoption. Massachusetts, for example, plans to create a lending program for window heat pumps, which will allow homeowners who need new heating systems to warm their homes while researching the best option, rather than just replacing their old natural gas or oil-burning equipment. New Hampshire will offer below-market-rate loans for consumers swapping fossil-fuel systems with cold-climate heat pumps.

A third arm of the program focuses on developing a well-trained workforce by upskilling existing contractors, supporting small businesses, and nurturing a pipeline of new workers to meet the expected surge in demand. The initiative ran three in-person classes this year and released nine online training videos, with more offerings planned for 2027 .

As the accelerator enters its second year, the team is focused on getting those state and community pilots off the ground, as well as assessing what aspects of the program have gone well and what can be improved. The coalition is confident in its progress so far and that its successes will only multiply going forward.

“ We’re off to a fabulous start,” Voorhees said.

scraped.title: Ezra Klein is Wrong about the Permitting Bill
scraped.description: The devil’s in the legal and technical details.
scraped.author: Abigail Dillen
scraped.h1: Ezra Klein is Wrong about the Permitting Bill
scraped.body_text:
Congress is considering BAAJA, a permitting package that could fast-track fossil fuel projects and weaken bedrock environmental laws. Our Analysis

Congress is considering BAAJA, a permitting package that could fast-track fossil fuel projects and weaken bedrock environmental laws.

Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Our Stories

The devil’s in the legal and technical details.

By Abigail Dillen / Policy and Legislation Team

Ezra Klein is urging Congress to roll the dice on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) even though he admits in his latest column that he is “unnerved” by the differing impacts of this bill by Hill staffers and conscious that “legislation at this scale rarely plays out exactly as its architects expect.” As he recognizes, much of the 400+ page bill is “dedicated to technical changes to other laws.” Nevertheless, he remains sure that the bill will engender better politics and a nation that can deliver all the goods we need.

Earthjustice has analyzed BAAJA , including the recent manager’s amendment , and we have detailed the ways it would change the federal energy and environmental laws that we work with every day. While we very strongly support BAAJA’s package for transmission and grid reforms, the overall deal gives President Trump more power, weakens environmental protections, undermines Tribal sovereignty, and diminishes access to the courts. Very serious changes to bedrock laws and judicial review demand equally serious consideration and debate. But there has been none here — no debates, no committee hearings, no legislative reports. Legislators cannot simply assume that a major overhaul of federal law will make our lives better, not worse.

While the title of Klein’s piece tries to try to sell BAAJA as an affordability bill, there is no modeling to suggest that it will deliver relief that people will feel any time soon, if ever. Commonly- cited modeling by the well-respected Rhodium Group projects annual savings of only $50-78 on household electricity bills in 2040. BAAJA does include important provisions that may compel data centers to cover the costs they impose on the electric grid, but that depends on the development of a new policy at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and subsequent implementation by states.

Regarding clean energy deployment, Rhodium projects a wide range of outcomes, from deployment of as little as 17 GW to as much as 249 GW over the current baseline. The high end assumes “continued meaningful cost declines for clean technologies with more expensive fossil fuel prices.” However, BAAJA does nothing to address the perfect storm of tariffs, high interest rates, and lost tax credits that are eroding the competitive cost advantage that renewables should enjoy relative to methane gas. Meanwhile, methane gas prices remain relatively low. For now, we appear to be living in the Rhodium scenario that assumes “much less reduction in the cost of clean resources paired with very low prices for fossil fuels.” That scenario yields only modest incremental gains in clean energy deployment and 0% reductions in greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. Even in the mid to low emissions scenarios, Rhodium projects cumulative emissions reductions of 3% and 4% respectively by 2040. These projections are all consistent with an ongoing gas rush that BAAJA would speed up.

In short, it is unconvincing to promote BAAJA, standing alone, as an affordability bill or a climate bill. Maybe that is why Klein leans into the intertwined arguments that BAAJA would deliver (1) a victory for a better functioning democracy and (2) an all-around solution for red tape.

Regarding democracy, he states that “[t]he bill represents Democrats and Republicans deciding that the fight over what gets built should play out in elections and markets rather than in the bowels of administrative agencies and courts.” To start, it’s wrong to imply that this bill is the product of any sort of considered bipartisan agreement. Again, there has never been a single hearing on BAAJA, and the Democratic Senators who negotiated the bill did so without involving their colleagues. With the exception of Senator Whitehouse, every single Democrat on the Environment and Public Works (EPW) committee voted no on moving the bill to a vote. Its passage would represent a rush job, not a deliberate agreement about the best path forward.

Based on our litigation experience, it’s also wrong to suggest that BAAJA would move the fight for our future out of the courts and into the realm of electoral accountability. Given ambiguous and even inscrutable drafting, BAAJA would drive more not less litigation. For most parties, BAAJA would make it harder to secure meaningful relief. But for the most powerful companies, it would invite litigation to secure new, extraordinary remedies. Regardless of elections, BAAJA would constrain new presidential administrations from shifting policy and responding to new and evolving circumstances.

On the red tape front, Klein points to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) as the problem, and the Sunzia transmission line as the evergreen example of permitting dysfunction. Absolutely, the Sunzia project took way too long to permit, but it was proposed in 2006 and is an extreme example from a different time. Klein never acknowledges that Congress has passed a litany of changes to NEPA in recent years. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 created, among other things, a federal permitting council and a permitting fast track for large projects — for better or worse. Congress also made very significant changes to NEPA in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, including more NEPA exemptions and specific timelines for action. On top of all that, the Supreme Court limited the scope of NEPA review dramatically just last year in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, Colorado .

BAAJA would not solve a live problem, but it would create a new one by eliminating any enforceable obligation to undertake the most basic environmental review and public disclosure of impacts. Further, dispensing with upfront public engagement under NEPA and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) would foreclose an important opportunity to surface problems and solutions at an early stage of project development. Eliminating enforceable obligations to take these simple steps at the outset would make the federal government less transparent and accountable at a time when people very much want it to be more of both. In the Trump administration, NEPA has been a critical tool for subjecting extremely harmful federal actions to judicial scrutiny. For example, Earthjustice, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), and many state attorneys general (AGs) have relied on NEPA to prevent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from converting warehouses into massive, inhumane detention centers.

At a time when meritorious lawsuits are often the only check on the Trump administration’s abuse of power, BAAJA would give it more license and immunity for illegal actions. Klein never grapples with the fundamental threat that this presents in a Trump administration helmed by Stephen Miller.

Members of Congress must be real about the ways that BAAJA would accelerate the Trump agenda over the next two years. As the President has promised, his administration would super-charge “Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before” while the war on wind and solar would continue. Now that the Supreme Court has given the president the power to hire and fire commissioners of once-independent agencies at will, he can force the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to follow through on its recent promises to “ unleash natural gas ” without a commensurate push for clean energy.

More broadly, President Trump would cash in on new powers to provide “project certainty” for developers of all kinds. The administration would lock in federal authorizations for polluting projects, most likely in communities that are routinely targeted for pollution. It would move fast to confer private rights to drill, mine, log, construct data centers, and otherwise exploit public lands. Klein himself recognizes the concern that “Trump would issue all manner of illegal permits to drill on public lands that will then be protected by the bill’s provisions in the future.” But while he concedes that this would be a “huge problem,” he brushes it off, stating that “the bill’s architects don’t think it’s true.” But the views of the bill’s architects don’t matter. It’s the courts that will interpret BAAJA’s ambiguous provisions. And in the end, it will be the Supreme Court that gets the final word, driven by a conservative supermajority that has been actively hostile to climate protection, energy transition, and social justice.

Then there are the glaring problems that Klein entirely fails to address. BAAJA systematically undermines Tribal sovereignty and the ability of all communities to uplift and preserve history and culture — this as the Trump administration is taking unprecedented steps to erase history and demolish cultural heritage. Speaking at a rally representing 1,200 Tribal nations and organizations, Martin Luther King III put it this way : “For 60 years, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act has given communities a voice when federal projects may affect historic places. It asks federal agencies to identify what matters, consider the effects of their plans, and consult with those whose heritage may be at stake. It does not say that we cannot build. It says that before we build, we must listen.”

As state Attorneys General are warning , Tribal and state governments, including newly elected governors, would lose much of their power to protect waters and wetlands under BAAJA. This is especially troubling given the Supreme Court’s decision in Sackett v. EPA , which curtailed federal protection of wetlands very dramatically. The bill would also allow states to take over Endangered Species Act permitting, a move that would jeopardize the survival of imperiled species while complicating the federal permitting process immensely.

Klein elides all of these concerns and urges passage of BAAJA on grounds that the “single most important climate policy going forward is for Democrats to win elections so that they have the power to set climate policy in the future.” Agreed. But why would this bill be popular with voters who turned out in record numbers to reject Trump?

Maybe Klein is assuming that voters won’t notice or remember that Democrats passed this bill in the immediate aftermath of a historic wave election. That would be a mistake and a betrayal. Eviscerating laws that protect our health, our communities, and the environment will hurt people in profound ways that they will notice. Abandoning federal trust obligations and government-to-government relations will create rifts that will not be forgotten. And we can be sure that President Trump will brag incessantly (and accurately) that this deal codifies a suite of regulatory changes that he has proposed as part of his “America First Agenda.”

Building everything, from clean energy infrastructure to gas pipelines and dirty data centers, is not a prescription for sustaining the momentum of a transformative election. An overwhelming number of people have experienced what happens when the most powerful companies in the world can build whatever they want as fast as they want without transparency or guardrails. They want it to stop, and their analysis is sharp. It is not going unnoticed that BAAJA’s package for pipelines is precisely crafted to speed up gas delivery to power more and bigger data centers complexes .

Support for Democrats is at best fragile. Rather than passing a bill that will do predictable and enduring damage, Democrats should negotiate a better deal that reforms the law without dismantling it. Transmission reforms have bipartisan appeal: gas-fired power plants will benefit from expanded transmission capacity as much or more than clean energy generators. Speed-to-power is still an imperative from the perspective of AI hyperscalers. These structural incentives will remain in the next Congress and can drive the votes needed for a bipartisan deal. Democrats can and must pursue legislation that protects people and their well-being while incentivizing the infrastructure that will genuinely serve all of us.

Policy and Legislation Team

Established in 1989, Earthjustice's Policy & Legislation team works with champions in Congress to craft legislation that supports and extends our legal gains.

We’ve received your feedback — thank you!

“Take a deep breath — but not too deep if you live near a coal ash dumpsite.”

Stay informed on how we hold accountable those who break our environmental laws.

To donate by check, phone, or other method, see our More Ways to Give page.

Daily news & progressive opinion—funded by the people, not the corporations—delivered straight to your inbox.

A project of Common Dreams

Phoebe Trotter, Food & Water Watch, ptrotter@fwwatch.org Judith Nemes, Environmental Law & Policy Center, jnemes@elpc.org Josh Blatt, Union of Concerned Scientists, jblatt@ucs.org Mark Drajem, NRDC, mdrajem@nrdc.org Alex Formuzis, EWG, alex@ewg.org Don Carr, Alliance for the Great Lakes , dcarr@greatlakes.org Lisa Bralts, Prairie Rivers Network, lbralts@prairierivers.org

Today, a coalition of public health and environmental organizations filed a petition calling on the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to lower the federal safety threshold for nitrates in drinking water to 1mg/L. The current threshold of 10mg/L was first adopted in 1975 and EPA has never updated it since. Public health research in the intervening 51 years clearly shows that nitrate-contaminated drinking water at levels far below the current standard is associated with increased risk of cancer, birth defects, and more.

Today, at 11 a.m. ET, petition authors Food & Water Watch , Environmental Law & Policy Center, Union of Concerned Scientists , NRDC , Environmental Working Group , Alliance for the Great Lakes and Prairie Rivers Network will host an online press briefing on the full petition details.

Unchecked factory farm and chemical fertilizer pollution are the nation’s primary sources of waterway nitrate contamination. Today roughly 1 in 3 Americans — nearly 120 million people — are exposed to dangerous nitrate levels in their tap water. The petition filing comes as Trump’s EPA has apparently abandoned a re-assessment of nitrate’s toxicity and eliminated the offices responsible for conducting such assessments, scuttling years of work done under prior administrations.

Tarah Heinzen, Legal Director at Food & Water Watch, said : “Nitrates are poisoning America and Trump’s EPA is asleep at the wheel. Unfettered industrial agriculture pollution is pumping these toxic chemicals into the water we drink, and hardly anything is being done about it. The science is clear: Current regulations are not protecting our health. EPA must lower the safe drinking water limit for nitrates and start holding the polluters responsible accountable.”

Under the Safe Drinking Water Act, EPA has a responsibility to update safety thresholds as public health research evolves. Today’s petition outlines the research establishing nitrate health risks, presents a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis, and provides a roadmap for EPA to address this problem at the source and at the tap.

Tens of millions of people from California to Delaware are exposed to particularly high nitrate levels because of pollution from industrial agriculture. For example, 46% of Iowans are exposed to nitrate levels over 1mg/L. With more factory farms and chemical fertilizer use than any other state, Iowa has the nation’s highest surface water nitrate contamination and fastest rising cancer rates. This summer, more than 600,000 Des Moines area residents faced a second consecutive year of water restrictions, while nitrate removal systems ran a record 193 days.

Dr. Stacy Woods, Research Director at Union of Concerned Scientists, said : “The U.S. is facing a quiet public health crisis. Since EPA set the nitrate drinking water standard decades ago, scientific research has revealed links between lower levels of nitrate and cancer, adverse birth outcomes, and other serious health effects. The need for action is urgent, because nitrate levels linked to increased health risks have been reported in water systems serving tens of millions of people across the country.”

Nancy Stoner, Senior Attorney at the Environmental Law & Policy Center, said : “EPA is using a report from 1962 to set the nitrate drinking water standard – 64 year-old information. It completely fails to consider the cancer risk associated with drinking nitrate-contaminated water. It is way past time for EPA to set a new standard to protect public health.”

Anne Schechinger, Senior Director, Agriculture & Climate Research at the Environmental Working Group said: “The science on the threats of nitrate exposure has advanced, but our public health protective standards have not. We now know that even low-level exposure can have serious health consequences, yet federal policy continues to rely on an outdated threshold that fails to protect millions of people. The EPA must urgently update the drinking water standard for nitrate.”

Angela Blatt, Senior Agriculture Policy Manager at the Alliance for the Great Lakes, said: "Communities across the Great Lakes region are already paying the price for nitrate contamination, whether through costly drinking water treatment or higher nitrate levels in the water coming from their taps. Lowering the federal nitrate standard to 1 mg/L is an important step toward protecting public health, but treatment alone cannot be the answer. We also have to address the problem at its source by preventing excess fertilizer and manure from contaminating our water. Pollution that starts upstream creates real costs downstream, and stronger action is needed to stop shifting those costs onto communities and drinking water systems."

J.P. Rose, Director of Soil Health at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council), said: “For decades EPA has given industrial agriculture a free pass to pollute, and now one in three Americans is drinking water with dangerous levels of nitrates. Tackling agricultural pollution at the source and improving treatment will help ensure all Americans have access to safe drinking water.”

Robert Hirschfeld, Director of Water Policy at Prairie Rivers Network said: “Illinois, like much of the Corn Belt, has a nitrate problem driven largely by fertilizer runoff from farm fields. Research increasingly links nitrate to colorectal cancer and other health risks at levels far below today’s legal limit. That limit is based on decades-old science and gives Illinois families a false sense of security about our tap water. We need a nitrate limit that reflects the best available science.”

Demand for stricter nitrate regulation is growing. Earlier this year, 83 groups called on EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Health & Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . to take emergency action to protect drinking water from industrial agriculture’s nitrate pollution. Advocates and communities in five states - Iowa, Minnesota, Wisconsin , Oregon and Washington - also have filed petitions for EPA emergency action to protect private well users from this same contamination.

scraped.body_text:
To donate by check, phone, or other method, see our More Ways to Give page.

Daily news & progressive opinion—funded by the people, not the corporations—delivered straight to your inbox.

A project of Common Dreams

Nicole Rodel, Oil Change International - nicole@oilchange.org

Romain Ioualalen, Global Policy Lead at Oil Change International , said:

“The draft text makes the right diagnosis, but the medicine it offers could have deadly side effects. Our dependence on fossil fuels has created an unprecedented economic, social, and environmental crisis. Addressing the shortfalls in climate finance and scaling up renewable energy to displace fossil fuels offers a way out. But, you cannot diagnose fossil fuels as the sickness and let fossil fuels be part of the cure.

“A 35% electrification target is only a win if it doesn't lock in decades of more fossil fuel dependence. This COP needs to send an unequivocal signal that electrification must be powered by renewables, not more fossil gas masquerading as clean energy, or massively scaled up CCS and carbon dioxide removal. Governments need to commit to what the just energy transition actually requires. That means an immediate end to fossil fuel expansion, massively scaling up renewable energy, and delivering the public finance needed to make a fast and fair transition possible. The text emphasises the need for Global North countries to meet with public climate finance obligations, but risks being a futile commitment without true accountability measures. As climate costs escalate and climate finance is slashed, rich governments have to deliver the trillions in public money. They can mobilize trillions by ending fossil fuel subsidies, taxing big polluters, and changing unfair financial rules.

“We must not forget that the cover decision is only one piece of the puzzle in Antalya. We need to see real progress on the just transition mechanism and the Climate Finance Work Programme to give countries the building blocks to accelerate climate action.”

Oil Change International is a research, communications, and advocacy organization focused on exposing the true costs of fossil fuels and facilitating the ongoing transition to clean energy.

scraped.title: Reports Say Trump Lied About Ending Aid to Israel, Funding Will Be Maintained
scraped.description: Israeli outlets report that officials are, in fact, working to renew the funding for another five or 10 years.
scraped.author: Sharon Zhang
scraped.h1: Reports Say Trump Lied About Ending Aid to Israel, Funding Will Be Maintained
scraped.body_text:
Israeli outlets report that officials are, in fact, working to renew the funding for another five or 10 years.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump’s claim on Election Day earlier this month that the U.S. was ending its annual funding to Israel at the end of 2026 was a lie, Israeli outlets have revealed, catching Trump in a last-ditch effort to boost Republicans that was seemingly nothing more than a PR stunt.

According to reporting by Israeli outlets Times of Israel and Ynet , several Israeli and U.S. officials say that there is no such deal in place between the countries. In fact, the current agreement being hashed out is for the U.S. and Israel to enter another memorandum of understanding (MOU) when the current one ends to continue sending Israel aid.

Details have yet to be worked out, but the general outline consists of a 5- or 10-year deal to phase out the U.S.’s annual $3.8 billion in annual aid sent to Israel. One version of this, according to Ynet , is for the U.S. to maintain current funding levels — with $3.3 billion of that funding allocated under the Foreign Military Financing program — for five years, after which it would be cut off.

The goal of striking a new deal, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has openly acknowledged , is for the U.S. to wind down such financial support of Israel while further integrating the U.S. and Israel’s military sectors, with some measures to do so currently slated for passage by Congress . This would allow the countries to maintain a more secretive technology- and intelligence-sharing relationship with less public oversight.

The current MOU would continue to be funded through its end date in 2028, the reports said. Both Israeli and U.S. officials were taken aback by Trump’s announcement on November 3, reports have found, and Israeli Finance Ministry officials told members of Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, on Monday that they were not informed of the announcement nor do they know when the funding will be cut off.

Ynet and Times of Israel are right-wing outlets that often support ultranationalist movements in Israel. However, the reports add credence to suspicions that Trump was bluffing when he made his announcement. At the time, Trump openly said that he was making the announcement in order to stave off attacks from the left about Republicans’ fervor for supporting Israel, as polls portended his party’s major losses in the midterm elections.

Experts and advocates for Palestinian rights had cast doubt on the announcement. U.S. taxpayers could still be on the hook for $10 billion in outstanding military orders from Israel in coming years if Trump ends the MOU early, according to a State Department letter sent to Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) and reported by The Wall Street Journal on November 4. This is because the MOU is structured so that Israel orders U.S. weapons and equipment in advance, and is later provided the money by the U.S. to pay for it.

“It’s not plausible there will be a total cut-off starting January 1,” said Josh Paul , a former State Department official working on foreign arms procurement, to The Intercept shortly after Trump’s initial announcement. “My guess is that he was speaking off the cuff with the next 10-year memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Israel in mind, but did so in a way that is at best inaccurate or imprecise.”
