Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. scraped.title: Environmental Groups Warn Nitrate Pollution Is “Urgent Threat to Public Health”
scraped.description: A petition sent to the EPA calls for tighter restrictions on a contaminant increasingly associated with many cancers.
scraped.author: Carey Gillam
scraped.h1: Environmental Groups Warn Nitrate Pollution Is “Urgent Threat to Public Health”
scraped.body_text:
A petition sent to the EPA calls for tighter restrictions on a contaminant increasingly associated with many cancers.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

This story was originally published by The New Lede .

Sixteen environmental and public health groups filed a legal petition with U.S. regulators on Monday seeking new restrictions on nitrate contamination — a type of water pollution the groups say is driving a “public health crisis across the country.”

The petition calls for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to slash the Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) for nitrate in drinking water to 1 milligram per liter (mg/L), down from the current federal standard that allows for up to 10 mg/L. The groups are calling for the Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG) to be set at 0 mg/L, which essentially would acknowledge that no amount of nitrate is considered safe for human health over lifetime exposure.

Such moves are warranted because scientific research shows that current levels of contamination pose “an urgent threat to public health,” including increasing the risk for certain cancers, the petition states.

The petitioners cite analysis showing that surface water levels of nitrate across the nation are increasing while nitrate monitoring is decreasing.

“One of the things we have sought to do here is to do the EPA’s job for it,” said Tyler Lobdell, an attorney with Food & Water Watch, one of the groups leading the petition effort. “One hundred and twenty million on people being serviced by public water systems are told the water is perfectly safe when the science says it is not.”

The petitioners include the Environmental Working Group, the Center for Biological Diversity, the Center for Food Safety, Food & Water Watch, Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council, among others.

The petition blames not only the EPA but also federal, state, and local lawmakers and other public officials for failing to address nitrate pollution, which is linked to cancers and other health problems.

The groups cite excessive application of synthetic fertilizers, the “over-application” of animal waste from concentrated animal feeding operation (CAFO) onto farm fields, inadequately treated sewage and industrial discharges, and failed septic systems as culprits for the nitrate-laden water.

The legal petition for rule making requires a response by the EPA and could set in motion further legal actions, Lobdell noted.

When asked about the petition, the EPA said it would review it and said it is “committed to ensuring all Americans have access to clean drinking water.” However, the agency noted it completed its most recent review of drinking water regulations, including the regulations for nitrate, in July 2024, evaluating available studies and applicable data. And based on that information, there was no need for a revision of the MCL, the agency said. The agency said it will consider new studies for its next review.

The current standard of 10 mg/L for drinking water was initially set in the 1970s and finalized in 1991 at a level that was set to avoid causing methemoglobinemia, also known as blue baby syndrome. All public water systems are required to monitor for nitrate contamination to determine compliance with that MCL.

But research on nitrate health impacts has grown over the past 35 years and there is now a large and growing body of evidence that consuming even low levels of nitrate-contaminated water is associated with colon and rectal cancers, and ovarian cancer, bladder and kidney cancers, as well as other adverse health impacts such as neural tube defects and low birth weights in babies.

The petitioners said they identified 3,205 community water systems serving roughly 119.7 million people that recorded at least one nitrate sample at or above 1 mg/L between 2021 and 2023.

The petition comes as many U.S. states, including key farming states, wrestle with concerns about nitrates. Iowa, in particular, has drawn national scrutiny for its high levels of nitrate in prominent waterways and climbing rates of cancer.

Scientists point to farm operations as largely to blame for nitrate contamination, both because of the runoff of fertilizer applied to fields of corn and other crops, and the runoff of liquified manure generated by large livestock operations that is also often spread on farm fields. The runoff carries nitrates and phosphorus into surface and groundwaters, and ultimately into drinking water.

Iowa tops the list of U.S. states with the highest mean levels of nitrate in surface waters from January 2015 through August 2026, according to the petition, which cites analysis of water quality data from multiple national, state, and local monitoring systems. Iowa is followed by Minnesota, Delaware, Illinois, Indiana and Kansas.

People who get their drinking water from wells are at particular risk as nitrate is commonly found in groundwater.

“For decades EPA has given industrial agriculture a free pass to pollute, and now one in three Americans is drinking water with dangerous levels of nitrates, JP Rose, director of soil health at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in a statement. “Tackling agricultural pollution at the source and improving treatment will help ensure all Americans have access to safe drinking water.”

One of the primary drivers of agricultural nitrate pollution is overapplication of fertilizer; synthetic nitrogen fertilizer is the largest nitrogen source in 41% of U.S. watersheds, the petition states.

Along with lowering the allowed levels of nitrate in drinking water, the EPA should take new steps to address the source of the nitrate pollution by implementing greater controls at the source point, the petition states. The petitioners point to cover cropping, wetlands protection and restoration, riparian buffers or field border strips, and crop diversification as practices that can help reduce nitrate pollution.

The petitioners noted that stricter regulations on nitrate pollution would also benefit ecosystems and fish and wildlife. Dozens of species listed under the Endangered Species Act are at risk due to the water pollution the petition notes.

The Iowa Environment Council (IEC), which has been pushing for stronger controls on nitrate contamination in that state, supports the call for strengthening the MCL, said IEC general counsel Michael Schmidt. But he noted a lowered MCL would not affect private wells, many of which exceed the 10 mg/L limit that applies to public water supplies. The state should take steps to help protect private well users in the near-term without waiting for EPA to act, he said.

Lowering the MCL for nitrate in drinking water could prove very costly for water utilities if the sources of the contamination are not significantly restricted. The current cost of nitrate treatment is “a substantial financial burden on water utilities,” according to recent research. Utilities spent up to 9% of their overall operating budgets just on nitrate treatment, according to a 2018 study by the Northeast-Midwest Institute.

The Association of Metropolitan Water Agencies did not respond to a request for comment on the petition. Neither did the the American Water Works Association.

The groups petitioning the EPA argue that their analysis demonstrates that an MCL of 1 mg/L is both “technically achievable and economically justified.”

They also say that the human health benefits of a lower MCL more than justify the costs of compliance. They say their analysis shows a nitrate MCL of 1 mg/L would “conservatively result in approximately $364.1 billion in present-value health benefits, compared with approximately $94.5 billion in compliance costs, yielding approximately $269.7 billion in net benefits over the 50-year analysis period.”

Nancy Stoner of the Environmental Law and Policy Center said in a press conference that the federal government should provide financial support to utilities to help them comply with a lowered standard.

“Americans should not suffer the adverse health outcomes resulting from drinking nitrate contaminated water because funds are not available to ensure safe drinking water, nor should communities be burdened with the full costs of reducing nitrate contamination driven by underregulated industrial agriculture,” the petition states.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $28,000 in the next 72 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

Carey Gillam is a journalist and author of Whitewash: The Story of a Weed Killer, Cancer and the Corruption of Science . She’s also a researcher for U.S. Right to Know , a nonprofit food industry research group.

scraped.title: COP31 Draft Shows Rich Nations May Offer Debt-Creating Loans for Climate Finance
scraped.description: Asad Rehman says Global South countries need public finance to adapt to the impacts of climate change.
scraped.author: Amy Goodman
scraped.h1: COP31 Draft Shows Rich Nations May Offer Debt-Creating Loans for Climate Finance
scraped.body_text:
Asad Rehman says Global South countries need public finance to adapt to the impacts of climate change.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation .

The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is in its second and final week. To get an update on the state of negotiations among countries, we speak with longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He says rich, developed countries are still dragging their feet on a rapid transition away from fossil fuels while withholding the money that poorer, Global South countries need.

“Whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses which are totalling over a trillion right now, you need public finance,” says Rehman. “And the rich countries are saying, ‘Our coffers are empty.’ But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Yes, this is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. We’re broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit in Turkey.

ASAD REHMAN: We are in the midst of a crisis, of a crisis of crisis. We could see that with the killer floods, droughts and famines impacting people everywhere. Our ecosystems are collapsing. We’re about to breach the critical 1.5-degree guardrail with devastating consequences.

AMY GOODMAN: That was longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He was outside on Saturday, marching with thousands of people in the rain, demanding climate action, joining us now inside the COP.

We welcome you back to Democracy Now! , Asad. Why don’t we start off by talking about what has been accomplished here? We’re midway through. Democracy Now! will be broadcasting throughout this week. The end is supposed to be on Friday. There was a draft release, a release of a draft document, today by the head of the COP. It’s here in Turkey, but it is being — you can explain this — officiated over by Australia. What was said, and what wasn’t, and what are the key issues, like electrification?

ASAD REHMAN: Sure. Always a pleasure to be here, Amy.

And so, the cover note is a political instrument. It’s not a negotiated text. And it’s generally written by the presidency of the COPs. We have a bit of a unique situation in that we have both Turkey and Australia currently in charge of these climate negotiations. So, Australia says it’s in charge of the negotiations, and Turkey in charge of the COP itself. So, the cover note is — I mean, it’s an interesting thing, because we’ve seen these cover notes now appear often at COPs. Many of them make grand announcements and then disappear into the dust. You may remember, I think back in Glasgow, at COP26, there were announcements about phasing out inefficient fossil fuels. There was announcements about increasing the ambition of emission reductions by 2030. None of those things came to pass. So, you have to take these cover notes also with a pinch of salt.

Now, in the cover note itself, there are so many different pieces, often very, very contradictory. But cut through all of the jargon, and there are three key things that are at play there. The first is electrification. This is a call by the Turkish presidency themselves that by 2035, 35% of our energy needs are met are electricity. Now, on paper, it sounds great, but lift the hood, and there are some real issues at it. First of all, when they talk about energy, they’re talking about clean energy, which includes nuclear. Secondly, this is not about energy access, so it’s not about the close to 700-800 million people who currently don’t have access to electricity. Often what they’re talking about is electricity for the richest countries to power gas — energy-guzzling data centers, electric vehicles, etc. Secondly, there is no commitment about actually the finance that is needed or the technology. So, it’s going to sound really, really great, but will it deliver to those people? Probably not.

The second thing that’s in here is a lot about what is being called the overshoot. Look, the lack of action by developed countries to do their fair share has now taken us to the brink of breaching the critical 1.5-degree guardrail. We’ve seen the consequences all around the world, of course, devastating fires, floods, famines. But now what these rich countries are saying is, “Well, let’s go beyond the 1.5. And what we’ll do is we’ll bank on risky and unproven technologies to suck carbon out of the atmosphere,” which will, of course, be a green light for massive land grabs, for massive ocean grabs. And secondly, what we’ll do is open the door to even more dangerous geoengineering possibilities, as well.

And the third big thing in there is, of course, about finance. Now, rich countries haven’t been meeting their promises. If you remember all the way back to Copenhagen, Hillary Clinton promised rich countries $100 billion in climate finance. Less than a third of that was ever provided in real grants. And since then, just in one year alone, poorer developing countries, often trapped in debt, have paid 225 times more in debt repayments than they’ve got in climate finance. And now what’s being offered to them again is more debt-creating loans, not public finance. And this is really critical, because whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses, which are totaling over a trillion right now, you need public finance. And the rich countries are saying, “Our coffers are empty.” But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires, who, of course, are not paying their fair share of tax, or the corporations.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to go to the Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, who was just here at the COP31 last Thursday.

GRETA THUNBERG: We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights, and where basic necessities become luxury. And it is more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying; it is being killed. And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue. When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it becomes our duty, everyone’s duty, but especially the more privileged you are, the bigger your responsibility to stand up, to be the adult in the room and to fight for the rights of our human rights and for everyone’s human rights.

AMY GOODMAN: So, that was Greta Thunberg on Thursday. And, of course, the context of all of this, the backdrop is the war in Iran and the amount of money that is being spent on it, the terrible casualties as a result, and the — what it makes the world aware of: The price we pay for fossil fuels was the shutting down of the Strait of Hormuz. Then you have President Trump, President Xi of China and Putin about to meet in the first-ever trilateral summit on Thursday. Your thoughts of what should be accomplished here and what they should be dealing with there?

ASAD REHMAN: Look, I think we all recognize that we’re not just dealing with a climate crisis and breaching the 1.5. Our ecosystem, the very things that humanity needs to survive, let alone thrive, are collapsing around us. But we’re also facing a growing crisis of inequality, economic inequality. Millions, if not billions, of people are struggling, not just now in the Global South, but increasingly in the Global North, as well. And that’s given rise to a rise of authoritarianism, of far-right and fascist politics, who are weaponizing inequality against change, who are saying, “Raise the walls and fences, pour more money into militarization to protect us,” rather than actually fighting to ensure that everybody can live with dignity.

So, what these governments are proposing and are on the table, actually, is far away from what we actually need. What we really need is governments to be doubling down and saying, “Actually, we can make sure that people have adequate and affordable homes, that are warm during the winter and cool during the summer. We can make sure that people have the right to food, to good incomes, to good jobs. And we can make sure we do that not just for our citizens in the Global North, but citizens in the Global South.” Instead, what we’re having is world leaders who are turning their backs on multilateralism, who are turning their backs on humanity as a whole, and are saying, “Well, actually, there is no future but a future of brutality and of war and of conflict.”

AMY GOODMAN: What do you think of the United States not being here, the historically largest carbon and gas emitter? And then you have the current largest polluter, China, has one of the largest delegations there, though not the president, Xi.

ASAD REHMAN: Look, this place is important, because the U.N. climate space is one of the very few places you have where every single country is represented and where the voices of people who are most impacted can actually try and hold our governments to account, because, otherwise, this will be held in shadowy backrooms, the richest countries by themselves. So it’s important. And, of course, it’s not — it’s key that the United States is here, but the United States has been here and has done its best to disrupt and dismantle the climate negotiations.

The real question is, is: What about the other rich developed countries, the United Kingdom, the European Union and others? Are they stepping up and doing their fair share? Are they showing?

AMY GOODMAN: Are they?

ASAD REHMAN: Well, they’re not doing. I mean, I come from — I’m living in the United Kingdom. We’ve just greenlighted one fossil fuel expansion in Jackdaw. We have Rosebank, where the government is still hesitating. We’re about to expand airport expansions in Heathrow, and we’re giving a green light for more data centers. It’s sending the wrong signal to the rest of the world. It’s saying, “We are going to continue to pollute, but you don’t.” And what we need is finance and committed public finance. And what we’ve seen is these rich countries cutting their finance to the climate — to climate finance.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, we have to leave it there, but we are going to be here all week delving into these issues. Asad Rehman is the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

I want to really thank our team here in Turkey — some of us almost didn’t make it with the lockdown in the United States: Anjali Kamat, Nicole Salazar, Nermeen Shaikh, Tey-Marie Astudillo, Hany Massoud and Denis Moynihan. I also want to thank, in New York, Mike Burke and Deena Guzder and Messiah Rhodes and María Taracena, John Hamilton, Sara Nasser, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff, Robby Karran and Diego Ramos, as well as Laura Bustillos. I am Amy Goodman, here in Turkey for the U.N. summit.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $28,000 in the next 72 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

scraped.title: Battered by the midterms, abortion foes turn the screws on the GOP
scraped.description: They want the Senate to stall Trump’s FDA pick unless mail-order mifepristone ends now.
scraped.author: Nina Martin
scraped.h1: Battered by the Midterms, Abortion Foes Turn the Screws on the GOP
scraped.body_text:
Mother Jones illustration; Shawn Thew-Pool/CNP/Zuma ;Soumyabrata Roy/AP

After a midterm election that proved to be catastrophic for their movement, anti-abortion leaders are intensifying their pressure on the Trump administration and the lame-duck Republican Congress to crack down on abortion pills—even if the election results demonstrate just how unpopular such an action would be.

“It’s impossible to sugarcoat it,” Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of the leading anti-abortion organization Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, wrote in a scathing Election Day memo . “Tonight’s results are a disaster for the unborn, for their mothers, and for the country as a whole.” She blamed Republican consultants who—in “begging for an election without abortion as a major voting issue”—turned off conservative voters. “Republican turnout was the major problem in this election,” Dannenfelser wrote, “and it was a major problem among the pro-life base.”

The group is urging Republican senators to delay the confirmation of Dr. Heidi Overton as FDA commissioner if the Trump administration does not commit to “immediate” suspension of Biden-era rules that allow the abortion drug mifepristone to be prescribed via telehealth and dispensed through the mail. A committee vote on Overton’s nomination is set for this week.

In addition, SBA wants Republicans to force the FDA to commit to “reforms” in its ongoing safety review of mifepristone—a study the administration launched last year, but which the agency has delayed into 2027. The group’s senior vice president of legal strategy, Erik Baptist, said the study now underwa y has “serious flaws.”

Under normal circumstances, the anti-abortion organization would be expected to push hard for Overton to be confirmed while Republicans still control the Senate, given her anti-abortion history . In a 2023 brief for the ultra-right America First Policy Institute, Overton—who currently serves as a White House domestic policy adviser— wrote that mifepristone, one of two drugs in the standard abortion-pill regimen, is “dangerous to women.”

But after the midterms debacle, abortion opponents aren’t in a trusting mood. “Confirmation is not a coronation,” Baptist said in a statement on the SBA website.

As STAT has reported, Overton’s confirmation has also run into problems over her role in crafting the Trump administration’s vaccine policies, with outgoing Louisiana Republican Bill Cassidy, who heads the Senate HELP committee overseeing her nomination, calling it “almost disqualifying.” In a post on X last week, Cassidy said he hasn’t decided yet whether to vote for Overton, citing “the lack of trust that exists due to broken promises and irresponsible decisions from other officials within the Administration.”

Cassidy is also an anti-abortion stalwart who launched an investigation last spring into abortion-pill manufacturers and urged the FDA to take action against pill suppliers. Assuming all Democrats vote against her, a single GOP defection would be enough to sink Overton’s nomination, STAT reported.

SBA’s demands reflect deep fury among social conservatives at the failure of the Trump administration to take meaningful action over the past two years to cut off the flow of abortion pills—and a rising panic at the enormous new powers that pro-choice Democrats will soon wield at all levels of government.

SBA’s demands reflect deep fury among social conservatives at the failure of Trump officials to take meaningful action over the past two years to cut off the flow of abortion pills.

After Donald Trump won reelection in 2024, anti-abortion hardliners began pressing his administration to clamp down on mifepristone and enforce the 19th-century Comstock Act , a federal criminal obscenity statute that, if revived, would amount to a national abortion ban.

But Trump has blamed his past election setbacks on the abortion issue. This cycle, White House officials reportedly told the Justice Department to delay taking any major action that might provoke a political backlash, while also assuring abortion opponents that after the midterms, “the gloves will be off.”

Instead, it was Democratic voters who took the gloves off. Thanks to the blue tsunami, newly empowered Democratic governors and lawmakers are poised to repeal abortion restrictions, codify new protections, and enshrine reproductive freedom in state constitutions. In Texas , which has enacted some of the most radical anti-abortion laws in the country over the past decade, a stunning statewide Democratic sweep has already led to major policy shifts. The day after winning his race, incoming Texas attorney general Nathan Johnson announced he would stop suing out-of-state abortion-pill providers and drop out of lawsuits against Planned Parenthood and the FDA.

Abortion opponents have long understood the existential threat to their movement posed by mifepristone, which the FDA approved in 2000. But they have been unprepared for the way these pills have transformed abortion access since the end of Roe v. Wade four years ago. Thanks in part to the Biden administration’s rules that eliminated the requirement for in-person dispensing, around 15,000 patients are accessing the medication every month, even in states with near-total abortion bans. Pills now account for almost two-thirds of abortions in the US.

Red states have filed a series of lawsuits challenging the FDA’s regulation of mifepristone. Despite more than a hundred studies around the globe showing that the drug is safe, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and then-FDA commissioner Marty Makary announced a new safety review last fall. But among abortion opponents, the new study was considered to be merely a delaying tactic to get past the midterms. In a court filing in October, the FDA said it didn’t expect to complete the review until next March. That timeline—as well as the agency’s description of how it is conducting the study—have further alarmed SBA and its allies.

“ It is a tragedy that the Biden-era mail-order abortion drug regime remains in effect,” SBA’s Baptist said, “because the Trump administration has thus far chosen to defend and enforce it.”

Meanwhile, anti-abortion leaders have renewed their pleas to the Trump administration to enforce the Comstock Act. “President Trump can take action right now to stop the flood of illegal abortion pills,” Texas Right to Life posted on its site. Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated before the election that he was receptive to the idea.

But any such move would result in “serious blowback” for Trump and his political allies, Drexel University legal scholar David Cohen told me last week. “The anti-abortion movement [claims] the Republicans failed on abortion because they weren’t extreme enough,” he said, “but everyone knows that’s just nonsense.”

Since the Dobbs decision in 2022, voters have weighed in on 22 abortion ballot measures around the country, including three in Virginia , Missouri , and Nevada this fall, with the pro-choice side winning 60 percent of total votes. “It’s pretty compelling evidence that the American people want abortion rights,” Cohen said. “And I think Donald Trump has understood that for the past two years, which is why he hasn’t done some of these extreme things.”

scraped.title: Inside the fight to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia
scraped.description: Silicon Valley allies are reportedly building a “war room” to return the disgraced Nvidia founder to power.
scraped.author: Alex Nguyen
scraped.h1: Inside the Fight to Bring Jensen Huang Back to Nvidia
scraped.body_text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shoots T-shirts into the crowd at the company's global artificial intelligence conference on March 18, 2025. Andrej Sokolow/picture-alliance/dpa/AP

Jensen Huang’s followers are attempting to rally support for the ex-Nvidia boss’ return after he resigned last week over multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving Alice Huang, a woman whom US intelligence identified as a possible spy for the Chinese government.

The online campaign “ Bring Jensen Back ” has nearly 180,000 signatures as of Monday morning, telling members of Nvidia’s board to reinstate the former CEO while “an independent investigation establishes the facts” and until they can “provide compelling evidence that his removal is in Nvidia’s best interests.”

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the letter adds. “Thank you, Jensen. We stand with you.”

A New York-based law firm hired by Nvidia’s board has reportedly already begun an investigation into whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence or compromised company or national security secrets. The FBI has been investigating the tech billionaire’s affair with Alice Huang for at least a year . The US government is also scrutinizing Nvidia and its former CEO to determine how much they knew about companies that bought their chips, rented out remote access, or smuggled them to others banned by the US government.

The “Bring Jensen Back” campaign lists SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk and YouTube co-founder Steve Chen as signatories, along with current and former Nvidia employees—whom the campaign calls “Nvidians” —shareholders, and supporters. President Trump, who has repeatedly defended his friend following reports of the personal scandals, told reporters Monday that he “ would not mind ” if Jensen Huang were reinstated as CEO, saying he thinks Huang had “learned a big lesson.”

Over 20% of NVIDIANs have signed the letter! 💚 But we need more voices! NVIDIANs, please take a moment to read and sign the letter, and help spread the word! #standwithJensen #bringjensenback https://t.co/yQcJEkUtXO pic.twitter.com/kUFyk3hIJN

According to the Financial Times , Huang is discussing a potential return with allies. One supporter said they were assembling a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his comeback and would try to win support from the Trump administration.

While those pushing to reinstate Huang likely have a range of motivations, the company’s future does not seem to be a top priority. As Nvidia’s stock continues to plummet , the support seems to stem from the idea that we owe appreciation specifically to the former CEO.

“For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building NVIDIA. He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed,” the online campaign states in its letter . “This company is the work of his life. That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now.”

According to Fortune , Nvidia’s interim CEO, billionaire Colette Kress, has been at the company for over ten years and played a key role in managing Nvidia’s shift in focus from chipmaking for video game hardware to powering the AI industry as CFO.

But Kress’ qualifications were never really the point. The campaign isn’t asking whether Nvidia needs Huang. It’s insisting that Huang deserves Nvidia, technology that is, as my colleague Inae Oh wrote last week, “primarily led by men, designed by men, and is far more likely to be used by men.” In Silicon Valley, a federal counterintelligence investigation is apparently just a bump on the road back to the corner office.

scraped.title: Jim Jordan and the plot against America
scraped.description: The soon-to-be minority leader was once called a “political terrorist”—by a member of his own party.
scraped.author: David Corn
scraped.h1: Jim Jordan and the Plot Against America
scraped.body_text:
Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) on Capitol Hill on Tuesday. Jacquelyn Martin/AP

A version of the below article first appeared in David Corn’s newsletter, Our Land . The newsletter comes out twice a week (most of the time) and provides behind-the-scenes stories and articles about politics, media, and culture. Subscribing costs just $5 a month—but you can sign up for a free 30-day trial .

Jim Jordan is everything —or just about everything—that’s wrong with Washington.

The combative House Republican from Ohio was credibly accused of having been aware of the rampant sexual assault of college wrestlers at Ohio State University when he was an assistant coach and doing nothing to halt it. He has been a prominent useful idiot for Russian leader Vladimir Putin, denying for years that Moscow meddled in the 2016 election to help Donald Trump. He was a chief election denier in 2020 and schemed with Trump to overturn the results. In 2023, a review of his (until then) nearly 17 years in Congress found that he had not been the primary sponsor of any legislation that became law. He’s in politics to fight, not to serve.

The lesson House Republicans have drawn from the shellacking: Give the American public more of what it soundly rejected.

Yet this week, House Republicans, after receiving a historic thumping from an electorate obviously fed up with Trump and his party, chose Jordan, one of the Trumpiest and most pugilistic members of Congress, to be their leader once they are relegated to minority status in January. With Trump and MAGA in steep decline, the surviving House Republicans opted to move ahead with an acerbic extremist who’s been a top lieutenant in the Trump cult. In 2021, former House Speaker John Boehner, a fellow Republican and Ohioan, referred to Jordan as a “political terrorist” and said, “I just never saw a guy who spent more time tearing things apart—never building anything, never putting anything together.”

The lesson House Republicans have drawn from the shellacking: Give the American public more of what it soundly rejected.

Jordan’s perfidy has been well documented. The 2025 HBO documentary Surviving Ohio State featured former Ohio State wrestlers who said Jordan had known of the sexual abuse of student athletes and took no steps to protect them. (Richard Strauss, a physician for the university’s athletic department, sexually abused at least 177 male students between 1979 and 1997.) “To say that [Jordan] knew nothing, that nothing ever happened, it’s a flat-out lie,” former Ohio State wrestler Dan Ritchie maintained in the film. (Jordan has denied he was aware of the abuse.)

His Russian denialism is thoroughly covered in my new book, How Russia Won: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and the Fight for America . Aping Trump, he ceaselessly pronounced the Trump–Russia investigation a “hoax.” He falsely claimed that Hillary Clinton’s campaign had orchestrated the FBI’s Russia investigation as a Deep State conspiracy against Trump. By covering for Trump, he covered for Putin. He was so fierce in this disinformation campaign that Trump awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom for supposedly unmasking the “Russia hoax” and taking on “Deep State corruption.” Jordan was also a prominent proponent of the bogus charge—which was likely Russian disinformation—that Joe Biden had accepted a $5 million bribe from a Ukrainian energy company.

After the 2020 election, many House Republicans endorsed Trump’s Big Lie that the election had been stolen from him. Jordan went further and actively conspired with Trump.

Most distressing is that this fellow—who by being selected the next GOP House leader is now positioned to be House speaker should the Republicans win back the chamber—was part of Trump’s plot in 2020 to destroy the republic. In the weeks after the 2020 election, many House Republicans endorsed Trump’s Big Lie that the election had been stolen from him. Jordan went further and actively conspired with Trump.

In 2023, when Jordan unsuccessfully sought the House speakership, Mother Jones reporter Dan Friedman and I detailed his 2020 machinations. Here’s a condensed version.

Following the election, Jordan spoke at a “Stop the Steal” rally in front of the Pennsylvania State Capitol. He publicly spread election conspiracy theories, such as bogus claims that Dominion Voting Systems and Smartmatic had rigged the vote against Trump. He called for a congressional investigation and demanded a special counsel be appointed. He endorsed state legislatures canceling vote tallies and selecting their own presidential electors. He demanded that Congress not certify Biden’s victory in the ceremony scheduled for January 6, 2021.

And behind the scenes, he plotted with Trump. According to the final report of the House select committee on January 6: “Representative Jordan was a significant player in President Trump’s efforts. He participated in numerous post-election meetings in which senior White House officials, Rudolph Giuliani, and others, discussed strategies for challenging the election, chief among them claims that the election had been tainted by fraud.”

Jordan was “involved in discussions with White House officials about Vice President [Mike] Pence’s role on January 6th,” the report noted—conversations that focused on whether Pence could block the certification of Biden’s win. Jordan was one of 10 Republican members of Congress who attended a White House meeting on December 21, 2020, in which the topic was how to pressure Pence to undo the election.

Six days later, Trump held a phone call with Acting Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen and Acting Deputy Attorney General Richard Donoghue. Trump pushed the pair to publicly declare that this had been an “illegal” election. He cited three Republican politicians supporting this claim: Rep. Scott Perry of Pennsylvania; Doug Mastriano, a Pennsylvania state senator; and Jordan, whom he praised as a “fighter.”

When Rosen told Trump that the Justice Department couldn’t “snap its fingers and change the outcome of the election,” Trump responded: “I don’t expect you to do that. Just say the election was corrupt and leave the rest to me and the Republican congressmen.” Trump did not explain what he meant or what the GOP House members—presumably including Jordan—intended to do if the Justice Department falsely declared the election fraudulent. Rosen and Donoghue refused to issue such a statement.

Jordan knew a lot about Trump’s attempt to sabotage the constitutional order and the runup to the January 6 riot. But he refused to share any of this with the public.

A week after that, on January 2, 2021, Jordan led a conference call in which he, Trump, and other House members discussed strategies for delaying the January 6 certification of the vote. “During that call,” according to the January 6 committee, “the group also discussed issuing social media posts encouraging President Trump’s supporters to ‘march to the Capitol’ on the 6th. An hour and a half later, President Trump and Representative Jordan spoke by phone for 18 minutes.” It is not publicly known what the two discussed.

Three days later, Jordan texted White House chief of staff Mark Meadows to pass along advice that Pence should “call out all the electoral votes that he believes are unconstitutional as no electoral votes at all.”

On January 6—a day of violent chaos and insurrection—Jordan spoke with Trump by phone at least twice. That day, Jordan also received five calls from Giuliani, and the two connected at least twice in the evening, as Giuliani was attempting to encourage members of Congress to continue objecting to Biden’s electoral votes.

Jordan knew a lot about Trump’s attempt to sabotage the constitutional order and the runup to the January 6 riot. But he refused to share any of this with the public. When the January 6 committee subpoenaed him and several other Republican members of Congress to obtain information related to its investigation, Jordan and the others refused to cooperate. Jordan has never fully explained his role in Trump’s machinations, let alone apologized.

Like Trump, Jordan got away with his part in their attempted betrayal of the United States.

In the days after the January 6 riot, Jordan tried to claim that he was never an election denier. But at the time, we showed that was a lie:

. @Jim_Jordan claims he never said the election was stolen. That's not what the video shows. Let's roll the tape, shall we? pic.twitter.com/wOLI9l3TQW

Jordan was a co-conspirator in Trump’s effort to overthrow American democracy. His elevation to top Republican in the House is a reminder of the threat Trump and the GOP still pose to democracy.

The House Republicans choosing Jordan as their leader is akin to Trump naming Stephen Miller his White House chief of staff. This choice is not about governance. This is about political warfare. But after the electorate’s dramatic rejection of the Trumpist politics of hatred, bigotry, disinformation, and division, it looks as though House GOP members are still fighting the last war—one that they decisively lost but will keep pursuing no matter the potential damage to the nation or their own party. For such a destructive and perhaps suicidal crusade, Jordan is the right man to lead it.
